en: Preface to the *Biographies of Lay Practitioners* (Jushi zhuan). The Master Zhiguizi, manifesting in the form of a layman (*upāsaka*) to preach the Dharma, has composed the *Biographies of Lay Practitioners* and requests that I write a preface for it. The preface says:
Master Zhiguizi studied Buddhism, turned his heart toward the Pure Land, and made the vow of certain rebirth there. Upon thorough investigation...
The cause for rebirth in the Pure Land lies in a single thought of purity; that single thought of purity constitutes the very cause for rebirth.
How much more so, then, when such thoughts succeed one another without interruption—could there be anyone who does not attain rebirth or behold Amitābha?

Zhi Guizi cultivated the Pure Land with uninterrupted continuity of thought; his study of the Buddha-dharma may indeed be called profound. Looking up to the former practitioners, he was truly peerless.

Far-reaching! It expresses how the myriad dharmas all return to the same source. To save oneself and to save others, and through saving others to save oneself—the intent behind the composition of this book may indeed be called earnest.
If one knows the Way, such a person can manifest in the body of a layman (*jushi*) to preach the Dharma.
Therefore, I joyfully preface this work to inform those in the world who read the *Biographies of Laymen* (*Jushi Zhuan*). Written by his fellow student, Wang Jin.
In the *Biographies of Lay Buddhists* (*Jushi zhuan*),

the general principles for recording figures within the Buddhist community are specifically focused on those who were officials or laypeople (*baiyi*). Thus, there exist the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of the Dharma) by Master Sengyou,

the *Guang hongming ji* (Extended Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of the Dharma) by Vinaya Master Daoxuan, the *Fofa jintang* (Buddhism as a Golden Fortress) by Xinta, and the *Jintang* (Golden Fortress) by Yao Mengchang.
Record of Collected Essays. Xia Shufang’s *Faxi Zhi* (Record of Dharma Joy) takes the śramaṇas as its primary focus while also incorporating external protectors.

As for works that record events and accounts from various sources, there are Zhi Pan’s *Fozu Tongji*, Nianchang’s *Fozu Tongzai*, as well as the *Chuan deng lu*, *Xu chuan deng lu*, *Wudeng Huiyuan*, *Donglin Zhuan*, and *Wangsheng Zhuan*. The matters and statements recorded in these various texts intersect with one another.
There are variations in detail and brevity; some works suffer from prolixity, while others suffer from oversimplification.

As for the *Fen Deng Lu* by the layman Zhu Shien, the *Xian Jue Zong Cheng* by Guo Ningzhi, and the *Chan Deng Lu* by the layman Li Shicai, all of which are based on the *Wu Deng Hui Yuan*, they merely extol the vehicle of the patriarchal school (*zong cheng*) but remain incomplete regarding the various gates of samādhi. Now, ten passages have been excerpted from these various texts.
Fifth, regarding the separate examination of historical records, the collected works of various scholars, the catalogs of various sutras, and the miscellaneous treatises of the hundred schools:
these exceed all other books combined. I have edited and compiled them into more than fifty biographies, detailing the causes and conditions for their entry into the Way.

Regarding the signs and stages of attaining the Way, those with aspiration may each follow their own capacity—whether through the Chan school, the doctrinal teachings, or Pure Land—to cultivate their realization and aspirations.
Provided they possess both teacher and disciple, there were few records prior to the Tang dynasty, such that one could easily peruse them all.
Since the Song dynasty, the texts have become vast and extensive; it is difficult to exhaustively investigate everything that has been heard or seen by the ears and eyes.
I further hope that broad-minded and elegant gentlemen will favor me with their precious collections, assisting me in my deficiencies.
Writings that protect the Dharma must flow forth with sovereign ease from the ocean of the radiance of Prajñā; only then are they worthy of esteem.
Regarding the contents of this book, those that do not pertain to the true essence of the life of wisdom have been excluded in their entirety.

For instance, while Wang Jianqi’s “Stele for Toudousi” and Wang Jian’s “Record of Śākyamuni’s Attainment of Enlightenment” are indeed elegant and extensive, their literary style overshadows the substance.

As for their substance, what does it have to do with the Way? Liu Zihou’s *Epitaph for the Various Śramaṇas* was praised and admired by Su Shi; yet, his attempt to harmonize Confucianism and Buddhism in that single epitaph for Caoqi has no connection whatsoever to the essential purport of the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*. This is all the more true of the writings of Wang Mojie and Bo Mengde. As for the prose of the scholar-officials of the Yuan and Ming dynasties— [The text continues: ...their style is like that of a man who, having lost his way in a vast wilderness, suddenly encounters a great city. He enters it and finds within it all manner of treasures and rare goods, yet he does not know how to distinguish them.

He merely gathers them up and carries them away, unaware that they are all counterfeit and worthless. Thus, while their words may appear elegant and refined, they lack the true spirit of the ancients. They are like those who, though possessing the outward form of a vessel, are empty within; or like those who, though wearing fine robes, have no virtue to sustain them. Their compositions are often verbose and redundant, lacking the clarity and precision of the masters of old. They prioritize rhetorical flourish over substance, and thus fail to transmit the authentic teachings of the sages. To claim that such works represent the pinnacle of literary achievement is to mistake the husk for the grain and to lose sight of the fundamental purpose of writing. It is a pity that later generations have come to value these superficialities so highly, thereby obscuring the true path of the Way. Therefore, one must be discerning and critical when evaluating such texts, lest one be led astray by mere appearances. Only by returning to the core principles of the ancients can one truly grasp the essence of the literature. Otherwise, one remains mired in the trivialities of the world, unable to transcend the limitations of conventional scholarship. This is why the wise of antiquity sought the Way through literature, rather than seeking literature for its own sake. To understand this distinction is to begin to comprehend the true nature of the arts. Thus ends this brief critique. May readers take heed.
Regarding these characters, many of them draw from both Confucianism and Buddhism; yet they must necessarily correspond in both practice and understanding before they are worthy of being adopted.
Otherwise, they will merely result in frivolous discourse—how could they be worth counting?
Those who have falsely claimed affiliation with the Chan school are numerous; figures such as Xia Song, Lü Huìqīng, and Zhāng Dūn are hardly worth mentioning.
As for the two masters Bái and Sū, although they possessed other merits within the Buddhist tradition, they had no connection whatsoever to the Chan school.
Among the recorded *jīyuán* (critical encounters) found in various books, there is nothing worthy of being adopted. Others, such as Hán Tuìzhī, Lǐ Xízhī, and Zhōu Màoshū—

The various masters, such as Ouyang Yongshu, dedicated their lifelong vows entirely to the protection of Confucianism. Their occasional expressions of sympathetic joy regarding a single principle or circumstance were insufficient to enhance the prestige of the Buddhist gate;
it would have been inappropriate for them to engage in forced associations and artificial syncretism to embellish their own school, which would have resulted in error and delusion.
Such a deviation from the principles of the teachings is no small matter; therefore, in the process of selecting and evaluating this work, I have been quite...
Preserving the subtle intent, I dare not compromise with mere shadows and echoes, lest I misrepresent the ancients, misrepresent my own mind,

or misrepresent the principles of the teachings. As for Páng Jùshì regarding the *zōng* (essence), Lǐ Chángzhě regarding the *jiào* (teachings), and Liú Yímin regarding the Pure Land— [these are the hundred...]
They were the masters of their age. That each of these three high officials (sanguo) had his own specialized transmission was out of respect for their teachers.

As for others who established their own specialized transmissions, they were for the most part far beyond their peers and difficult to match; though they did not all take these three high officials as their sole standard, they nonetheless came close to them.

The foundation for ascending the stages (*bhūmi*) and realizing the fruits of the path lies in the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*). These five precepts are, in their entirety, the five constant virtues (*wu-chang*). Without practicing the five constant virtues, how can there be the five precepts?

The various ministers of the Southern and Northern Dynasties failed to understand the principles of loyalty and filial piety; they spoke recklessly of *prajñā* (wisdom), trafficking in the teachings of the Tathāgata.
As for those such as Wei Shou and Yao Xuan, who rashly claimed to be among the enlightened; and Shen Yue and Jiang Tong, who unworthily defiled the ranks of the precept-holders.
In this chapter, those who slander the Dharma through their physical actions—such as Cui Hao and Fu Yi—are found guilty of a crime even more severe than this.
The ocean of purity does not admit corpses; to cut them away and cast them out is surely not an act of excessive severity.

As for those such as Wang Mojie, Liu Zhitou, Guo Gongfu, and Zhang Tianjue, who were initially deluded but later returned to the truth, their offenses may be excused. To follow the principle of "honoring the good according to their merit" is also a worthy aspiration.

Regarding the purport of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, and concerning those who have spoken of the Three Teachings since antiquity, is there anyone more excellent than Dazhu? Someone asked about the similarities and differences among the Three Teachings, to which he replied:

"For those of great capacity, they are identical when applied; for those of limited faculties, they appear different when clung to. In essence, they all arise as functional manifestations from the single nature."
The distinctions in capacity and insight result in three types [of practitioners]. Whether one is deluded or awakened depends on the person, not on the similarities or differences between teachings.

Those who have realized this principle were Li Boji of the Song dynasty and Zhao Dazhou of the Ming dynasty. During the Northern and Southern dynasties, Buddhists and Daoists contended with one another;

during the Tang and Song periods, Confucians and Buddhists vied for supremacy. This was entirely because they did not know that within the true and eternal nature, there is fundamentally no such thing as sameness.

This is different. To seek out branches and pluck leaves, how could there ever be an end? As for the arguments of Zhou Yanlun, Ming Xiulie, Zhang Tianjue, Li Chunfu, and several others—while it cannot be said they were without merit in disentangling entanglements and blunting sharp points, when their actual substance is examined, they are mostly characterized by divergence and convergence.
When a lion bites a man, the Han-dog merely chases after clods of earth. The wise look at the finger and know where it points; the ignorant, however, [cling to the finger itself].
To mistake the finger for the moon—how could the world ever hope to exhaustively discuss the Three Teachings with Dazhu?
Among those included in the biographies, there are those whose life stories cannot be detailed in full, such as the various eminent scholars of the literary establishment.

It is not that their deeds were unrelated to the Buddha-dharma; rather, their accounts are not recorded here because they have already been set forth and documented in the official dynastic histories. This is not the intended scope of this work.
There are those whose life stories cannot be treated with brevity, such as the masters Zong Rulin, Zhao Dazhou, Zhou Jingwen, and Xiong Yushan.
Their engagement with the world was the very spirit of their study of the Buddha-dharma.
That all their worldly affairs and social interactions were entirely in accord with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*)—is this not so? Is this not so?
This work began in the summer of the Gengyin year and was finalized in the autumn of the Yiwei year.

Throughout this interval, in discerning the subtle differences between the Zhi and Mien rivers [of ink], and in deliberating what to omit and what to retain, the assistance of Mr. Wang Dashi of Wu County was most significant. Mr.
Luo Taishan of Ruijin traveled back and forth to Suzhou, where we constantly engaged in mutual refinement and settled matters of inclusion and exclusion. Finally, when the book was completed, Wuyi...
Prince Yuan looked over the text and recited it once through; filled with praise and joy, he donated gold for its carving.
May all who see or hear it rejoice, resolve to attain Bodhicitta, and realize the fruit of perfection. Thus, the labor of seven years spent in compilation shall not have been in vain.
In the boundless ocean of blue lotuses and fragrant light, may we all, through a single thought of sincere devotion, ascend together to the other shore. Not so.
Also composed with joy.
Verses for the *Jushi zhuan* (Biographies of Laymen) by the disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts, Peng Jiqing. Narrated.
I have heard that the response-bodies of Avalokiteśvara number thirty-two;
The spiritual friends of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra likewise number fifty-three.
Appearing in the forms of bhikṣus and laymen, And in various realms of gods and humans— Like clouds in the sky, Taking no fixed shape as they follow the wind, Or like waves upon the ocean.
From the sun, five colors appear; That which the eyes of sentient beings perceive Is always ablaze with conceptual discrimination.
How could they know the wondrously luminous mind? Being non-dual, how can there be two? Recall that since beginningless time, In a single thought-moment you have failed to realize [yourself].
Amidst birth and death within the six realms, Thought after thought, you enter the cycle of saṃsāra.
The habituation of greedy defilement has long been deep; true color has become obscured and dim. Drawn by the power of ignorance, one falls into a cluster of inverted evils.
Having encountered this birth through causes and conditions, one hears the unsurpassed Dharma and, with a profound heart, sheds tears of compassion.
Kneeling long before the Buddha, one vows to exhaust this retributive body.
May the suffering of saṃsāra be forever stilled; with a single thought of Amitābha, one shall ultimately attain the Buddha-way.
With reverent devotion, uphold the pure precepts and repent for all past transgressions.
Contemplate the Dharma-realm body as illusory and inconceivable—how much more so when encountering this land of Zhendan, the source from which the Mahāyāna emerged.
A lotus blooming amidst fire appears from time to time as a rare marvel; How excellent is the worthy one of Donglin, who employs skillful means to open the gateway of expediency!
There are also Pang and Li, who uphold the two wheels of teaching and practice;

In the transmission of the lamp, there have always been those who follow in his footsteps, inexhaustible like space. Though we now dwell in this age of the Dharma’s decline, [the light continues to shine].
Fortunately, the penal codes have not yet been extinguished; I have gathered these ancient texts into this collection.
Like a light that shines even when the night is dark, like the sun, the moon, and the myriad stars revolving through the four worlds, may this work illuminate them all.
May the one and the many mutually encompass one another, and may all enter the field of Bodhi. By this merit, I dedicate it to all sentient beings.
Those of the present and those of the future, Who share this same affinity and gather together, May each read the books I have composed And give rise to the unsurpassed mind. Namo Buddhāya!

Regarding the eastward transmission of the Buddha-dharma: it began with Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.

In the third year of Yongping, the Emperor dreamed of a divine being sixteen feet tall, with a halo of light around his neck, flying before the palace hall. The following day, he inquired widely among his ministers as to what kind of deity this was.
Fu Yi stepped forward and said: "According to the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Records of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou), in the fourth month of the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao’s reign..."
On the eighth day at dawn, a great wind arose and the palaces and the dwellings of the people shook.

That night, light of five colors appeared, its radiance piercing through the Taiwei constellation and pervading the four quarters, manifesting in shades of blue and red. The King asked the Grand Astrologer Suyou, "What omen is this?
He replied, "A Great Sage has descended to birth in the West; a thousand years hence, his voice and teachings shall spread abroad."
In this land, the King had an inscription carved in stone and buried it before a celestial shrine in the southern suburb.
Calculating by the years, it has now been one thousand and ten years. Is this perhaps what Your Majesty dreamed?
The Emperor agreed that it was so, and dispatched eighteen men, including Langzhong Cai Yin and Doctors Cai Jing and Wang Zun, to travel westward in search of the Way. They reached Da Yue...

In the kingdom of Shìguó, he encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhú Fǎlán, who were carrying a cotton-padded image of the Buddha commissioned by King Udayana, along with the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*, as they traveled eastward.
They subsequently accompanied him to Luoyang, where the Emperor established a monastery outside the Yong Gate;

from this, the teaching of the Image [of the Buddha] flourished. Thereafter, while there were many princes, dukes, and nobles who offered prayers and sought blessings, those who truly understood it were rare indeed.
As for that Way, scholars and officials judge it by the texts of the Five Classics and dismiss it as a heterodox art.
There was one named Mou Rong of Cangwu who composed the *Lihuo Lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) to explain it. He asked: "Why do you correctly call him 'Buddha'? What does 'Buddha' mean?"
Mouzi said: "The Buddha is the primal ancestor of the Way and its Virtue, the progenitor of the divine and the numinous. 'Buddha' signifies awakening. He manifests through mysterious transformations;
he divides his body and disperses his form; he can be circular or square, small or vast, hidden or manifest."

Treading upon fire, one is not burned; walking upon blades, one is not wounded; dwelling in filth, one is not defiled; encountering calamity, one suffers no misfortune. When wishing to travel, one flies; when sitting, one radiates light. Therefore, he is called a Buddha (*buddha*). Question: Why is it called the Way (*dào*)? What is the nature of the Way? Mouzi replied: "Way" means guidance. It guides people toward non-action (*wuwei*). If one is pulled forward, there is nothing ahead; if one is led back, there is nothing behind. It is like water flowing downward; it is like the wind blowing across the plains. It is like the sun and moon illuminating the four quarters. It is like the earth supporting all things. "The hands and feet [are used for service]. Now, the śramaṇas shave their heads. How can this contravene the words of the Sage? It does not accord with the way of a filial son. Mouzi replied:

"In the past, a man of Qi was crossing the Yangtze River by boat when his father fell into the water. His son rolled up his sleeves and seized his father by the hair, overturning him until the water flowed from his mouth, and his father’s life was restored.

Now, seizing one's father by the hair and overturning him is the greatest possible act of unfiliality. Yet, if one did not do so, the father would have died; because the son acted thus, the father survived. Therefore, the sages established the rites based on the principle of 'following the circumstances' (zhìqíng)."
However, in order to preserve his father’s body, he stood with folded hands and practiced the constant duty of a filial son. When his father’s life was cut short by water, Confucius said:
"One may be able to follow the Way, but one cannot yet be expected to exercise discretion. This refers to what is appropriate according to the timing of circumstances.

Furthermore, when Taibo cut off his hair and tattooed his body, he conformed to the customs of the Wu and Yue; thus, he departed from the principle that the body, hair, and skin are received from one's parents. Yet Confucius—
Your son praised this, saying it may be called the ultimate virtue. Viewed from this perspective, if one possesses great virtue, they are not constrained by minor matters.
A śramaṇa abandons family wealth and forsakes wife and children; they do not listen to sounds nor gaze upon forms. This is the height of yielding. How could this contravene the words of the Sage?
How could it fail to accord with filial piety? Question: The Buddha said that when a person dies, they shall be reborn. I do not believe this.
Regarding these words, Mouzi said: "The body is like the roots and leaves of the five grains; the soul and spirit are the seeds and fruit of the five grains.

Roots and leaves must inevitably wither and die, but how could the seeds and fruit ever come to an end? A questioner asked: "The Way of the Buddha reveres non-action (*wuwei*), delights in giving, and maintains the precepts with constant vigilance.
Yet now, śramaṇas indulge in wine and spirits, some even keep wives and children, and they take goods at low prices to sell them for profit."
"Venerable sir, you exclusively practice deception and fraud; can this be called 'non-action' (wuwei)? Mouzi replied:

"A skilled wheelwright can provide others with axes, chisels, and marking lines, but he cannot make them skillful. A sage can transmit the Way to others, but he cannot make them tread upon and practice it.
Gaoyao could punish those who steal, but he could not make the greedy become like Yi Yin and Shu Qi. Such is the nature of the five punishments."
One can execute those who are lawless, but one cannot cause an evil person to become a Zeng or a Min.
Yao could not transform Dan Zhu; the Duke of Zhou could not instruct Guan and Cai. Was it that the teachings of Tang were not manifest, or that the Way of Zhou was incomplete?
Yet, there was simply nothing that could be done with such evil persons. A questioner asked: "The words of your discourse are abundant and its style is brilliant; this is truly your eloquence."
Mouzi said: "This is not a matter of disputation; it is simply that because my learning is broad, I am not deluded.

He was asked: "Is there a method for having broad learning? Mouzi replied: "It comes from the Buddhist scriptures. Before I understood the Buddhist scriptures, my delusions were even greater than yours.

Although I had recited the Five Classics, they served only as mere ornamentation and did not produce any real fruit. Once I had beheld the teachings of the Buddhist scriptures and examined [the works of] Laozi..."
The essential point for you is this: maintain the nature of tranquility and detachment; observe the practice of non-action (*wuwei*).

When looking back upon worldly affairs, it is like standing at the edge of a celestial well to peer into a valley, or ascending Mount Song or Mount Dai to behold a mere mound. A questioner asked: "In the past, when I was in the capital, I entered the Eastern Pavilion and roamed the Imperial Academy.
There I observed the standards of the eminent scholars and listened to the discourses of the Confucian community. Yet I have never heard—"
To cultivate the Buddha-way is what is noble; to diminish one’s own appearance is what is supreme. Why, then, do you indulge in this [the pursuit of fame]?
Mōuzi replied: Lǎozǐ said, "Fame is a harm to the person; profit is a stain upon conduct.
To rush toward narrow openings and strive to conform to the age—this is the practice of inferior scholars and that which mediocre scholars abandon. How much more so for the Ultimate Way!"
Vast and boundless! This is the conduct of the supreme sages. It is as profound as heaven and as deep as the ocean;
it is not for those who peer through a wall or those who are merely clever calculators to fathom.

Seeing that the world was in turmoil at the end of the Han dynasty, he repeatedly declined appointments from the provincial authorities.

When the Governor again entrusted him with a mission, he did not set out due to the mourning for his mother. Subsequently, he sighed and said: "Laozi severed the pursuit of sagehood and abandoned wisdom to cultivate the self..."
He preserved his authenticity; the myriad things could not disturb his will, and the whole world could not alter his joy. Thus he was worthy of esteem.

Thereupon, he applied himself keenly to the Buddha-dharma while simultaneously studying the five thousand words of Laozi. He roamed freely according to his own will and never served in office throughout his life (from the *Fozu tongzai* and the *Hongming ji*).
An Wuan was a native of the country of Anxi. His character was upright and pure; he was an upāsaka who strictly observed the precepts and was widely versed in the various scriptures.

At the end of the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, he traveled to Luoyang for official service and held the rank of Commandant of Cavalry. He frequently engaged in discussions on the principles of the Way with śramaṇas.
At that time, the monk Fotiao was translating the *Fajing jing* (Sūtra of the Dharma-Mirror); An Wuan orally translated the Sanskrit text, while Fotiao committed it to writing.
[The Emperor] received [him], and both the words and the intent were successful; this is recorded in later generations (from the *Chū-sanzō-ki-shū*).
Zhi Gongming, whose courtesy name was Qian and also known as Yue, was a native of the Great Yuezhi.

His grandfather, Fadu, led several hundred people from his nation to submit to Chinese rule during the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty and was appointed General of the Household for Good Conduct (*Shu-shan Zhong-lang-jiang*). Gongming was seven years old at the time.
While playing on a bamboo horse at a neighbor’s house, he was bitten in the shin by a dog. The neighbor wished to kill the dog and take its liver to apply to the wound.
Gongming said, "Heaven created this dog to guard and bark for people. Had I not come here, it would never have bitten me.
The fault lies with me; it does not concern the dog. Even if killing it would have cured the injury, it should not have been done, let alone when it provides no benefit."
Consequently, they incurred great sin. Thereupon, several dozen households in the village were moved by his words and ceased killing living beings altogether.

At the age of ten he studied secular writing; at thirteen, he studied Sanskrit (Brahmi) script. He mastered the languages of six kingdoms, read widely through the scriptures, and comprehensively mastered the arts and crafts.
He once received instruction from Zhi Liang, who in turn had been instructed by Zhi Chen. During the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling, [these works] were newly translated.
Most of the Buddhist scriptures were translated by Zhi Qian; during his time, he was acclaimed as one whose broad knowledge surpassed anyone else, with none exceeding the "Three Zhis.

Toward the end of Emperor Xian’s reign, encountering the chaos of banditry, Zhi Gongming and several dozen of his fellow villagers fled their homeland to seek refuge in Wu. On the day they first set out, they possessed only a single blanket.

A guest followed them who was suffering greatly from the bitter cold for lack of a blanket; Gongming called him over and lay down with him. By midnight, [the guest]— (Note: The source text ends abruptly at this point.)
A guest snatched the blanket and departed. The next morning, his companions asked where the blanket was; he explained the circumstances to them. They all said, "Why did you not tell us?
He replied, "If I had told you, you would surely have punished me for the crime of robbery. How could it be right to kill a person over a single blanket?
Those who heard this marveled at him in admiration. Upon arriving in Wu, Sun Quan, the ruler of Wu, heard of his extensive learning.

Xue Youcai was summoned for an audience. The Emperor questioned him on the profound and obscure meanings within the scriptures; Gongming responded to these challenges with such clarity that there were no doubts left unresolved.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and appointed him as a *boshi* (Court Scholar), charging him with instructing the Crown Prince.

He frequently translated twenty-seven scriptures, including the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, the *Dharmapada*, the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses*, and the *Nidāna*; his phrasing and meaning were elegant and magnificent.
This was transmitted to the world. Later, when the Crown Prince ascended the throne, [Zhi Dun] retired to Mount Qionglong and no longer engaged in worldly affairs.
He followed the monk Zhu Falan to further refine his observance of the five precepts. All those he associated with were exclusively śramaṇas.
At the age of sixty, he passed away in the mountains (from the *Collection of Records of the Tripitaka*).
Zhu Shulan was originally a native of India. His grandfather, Lou-tuo, was fond of learning and possessed high moral integrity. At that time, the king was unrighteous;
a certain general, having incurred the king’s wrath and fearing execution, sought to recruit Lou-tuo to join him in rebellion.
Lou-tuo refused him, whereupon the general killed Lou-tuo to incite the uprising. Lou-tuo’s son, Dharmasila, was previously residing in another country when he heard [the news].
Luan immediately fled to Jin with two of his wife’s brothers who had become śramaṇas, settling in Henan. There he fathered Shulan.

From a young age, Shulan followed his two uncles to receive instruction in the scriptures and the Dharma; upon hearing them once, he immediately attained realization. He became proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit languages as well as writing.
However, by nature he was flighty and impulsive, fond of hunting. Once, while encountering a tiger, he fell from his horse and broke his right arm. His mother frequently rebuked him.
She maintained her prohibitions and never altered them. After some time, she adopted a vegetarian diet and then ceased [her practice]. Shortly thereafter, she died suddenly.
Three days later, she revived and said that she had entered a vermilion gate where the halls were made of gold and silver. She saw a man who identified himself as her grandfather.
He said to Shu Lan, "I have cultivated goodness for many years and have now received this retribution. You are a sinner; how could you have come here? He then commanded the guards—

Shulan said, "I have been a disciple of the Buddha for generations and have always made offerings to two śramaṇas. What crime do I have that I am being punished? The ox-head man replied, "This..."

He soon regained consciousness and, thereupon, changed his ways to cultivate compassion, dedicating himself solely to the sutras and the Dharma. This was in the first year of the Yuankang era of the Jin dynasty.

He translated more than one hundred thousand words of the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (Fàngguāng jīng) and a different version of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Shortly thereafter, he encountered the death of his mother.
Upon completing her funeral rites, he was caught in the chaos caused by Shi Le. He fled to Jingzhou, where later, without apparent illness, he suddenly informed his acquaintances, "I am about to die.
A few days later, he passed away. (From the *Chū sānzàng jìjí*).

Zhu Changshu was also a native of India who migrated to the Wu region at the beginning of the Jin dynasty. He served the Dharma with the utmost sincerity and was particularly devoted to the recitation of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.
Once, when a neighboring house caught fire and Changshu’s own home lay downwind, he commanded his family not to move, but to focus their minds single-mindedly on Avalokiteśvara.
In a short while, the fire suddenly extinguished itself. There were some youths who... [intentionally omitted].
They marveled at this. One night, they secretly bound torches together and threw them onto his house; yet all four throws were extinguished.
They were greatly astonished and regarded him as a deity, each hurrying back to their own homes. The following morning, they went together to Changshu, prostrating themselves to offer thanks.

They recounted the events of the previous day. Changshu said, "I possess no supernatural powers; it was solely through the power of recollecting Avalokiteśvara. You gentlemen should simply cleanse your hearts and believe."
Do not fear yourself. Thereupon, throughout the local community, everyone came to know the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct).

Que Gongze was a native of Zhao. During the reign of Emperor Wu of Jin, he resided in Luoyang. He lived in a state of profound tranquility and detachment, reciting the *Zhengfahua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) daily.
After he passed away, his friends held a memorial assembly at Baima Temple. By evening, they began the recitation.

Sun Xinggong, whose name was Chuo, was a native of Zhongdu in Taiyuan. Having moved to Kuaiji, he early on admired the practice of profound stillness and purity.

This is the wondrous delight beyond the mundane world; it is the primordial illumination within the realm of existence. Now, as for the Buddha, he is one who embodies the Way (*dharma*). As for the Way, it is that which guides all things.
Responding to stimuli and flowing in accordance with conditions, it acts through non-action (*wuwei*) yet there is nothing it does not do.

Because it is non-active, it is empty, tranquil, and spontaneous; because there is nothing it does not do, it spiritually transforms the myriad things. The natures of these myriad things—whether high or low—are [all encompassed therein].

"Do the sages possess a mind intent on killing? He replied, "No. The questioner said, "If one truly knows they have no such mind toward killing, then it is surely the hearts of the common people that are being killed.
As times shifted and eras changed, the world grew increasingly coarse or refined. Before the era of knotted cords, all was in a state of harmonious tranquility (*táohé*).

By the time of the reigns of Yao and Shun, rites and laws first arose; reaching down to the Three Dynasties, the net of punishments became as dense as tiger-skin patterns, and the axes and hatchets [were brought forth]."

Despite such severity, they still do not desist; it reaches the point where ruler and minister destroy one another and father and son harm each other, their mutual devouring exceeding even that of jackals and tigers.
The Sage knew that human nature is so firmly rooted in killing that it could not be extinguished in a single day;
therefore, he gradually suppressed it to seek the Middle Way. It was like a viper biting one's foot—one cuts off the foot to save the body—or an abscess forming on the flesh.
To decide between them is to save one's life; to lose one for the sake of preserving ten is a weighing of what is light and what is heavy.

By taking this as a standard and seeking further, it is sufficient to awaken one to their ultimate convergence. Someone may object: "The teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius were suited to their times, whereas the Buddha wishes to discard them all at once."

By what means, then, can violence be punished, wickedness be halted, and the multitude of living beings be governed? The answer is: Zhou Gong and Confucius are the Buddha; the Buddha is Zhou Gong and Confucius. "Buddha" means awakening (*buddha*).
The meaning of awakening is the realization of all things. Adapting to the world and establishing norms for things is likewise according to the times.
The teachings of Zhou and Confucius remedy extreme decay, while Buddhist teaching clarifies the fundamental source. Together they form the beginning and the end; their ultimate aim is not different.
Thus, in the eras of Yao and Shun, the two sovereigns were paragons of lofty yielding; in the times of Tang and Wu, the two rulers brandished their halberds amidst the hardships of war.
Between profound silence and fierce wrath, their outward traces may be as distant as Hu and Yue; yet, as for that which gives rise to these traces, how could it ever have any boundary?
Therefore, those who seek by way of opposition always encounter duality, whereas those who proceed by way of conformity find unity everywhere.

Someone may object: "The teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius take filial piety as their primary principle; among the three thousand offenses, none is greater than failing to produce an heir. Yet the Way of the śramaṇas involves abandoning and severing ties with one’s progenitor;

it neglects the service of providing physical care while alive and ultimately cuts off the ancestral offerings of blood and grain. Nothing could more severely oppose reason or wound human sentiment than this. And...
[The Emperor] said: "To propagate the Way and honor benevolence so as to extensively save all living beings—without the skin, where would the hair have its attachment?

He replied: "Father and son are of one body; their destiny is shared. When the father prospers, the son is honored; when the son is honored, the father is dignified. Therefore, filial piety is what is most precious.
Its value lies in being able to establish oneself and practice the Way to bring eternal glory to one’s parents. If one were to crawl about in one’s bosom, eating three meals a day..."

Though one may sacrifice to them, one cannot cause the myriad things to honor oneself, nor can one rely upon the entire world for support; yet by using these offerings to nourish one's parents, the resulting honor is immediate and proximate.
In ancient times, the Buddha was a crown prince who abandoned his kingdom to study the Way. He spread branches to form a canopy and tied grass to serve as a mat.
Sitting upright for six years, he perfected the Way and was titled "Buddha. Thereupon, he wandered beyond the three realms, freely transforming beings within the infinite reaches of existence.
He brought the great multitude of the depraved back to the correct path; among the various māras and followers of heterodox ways, there were none who did not submit and obey.

At that time, heaven was clear and earth was moist, and all things flourished. Crawling creatures were nurtured by the numinous essence, and those that were withered and parched were transformed from decay into splendor.
Returning his illumination to his own kingdom, he widely spread the sound of the Dharma; his father-king attained awakening and likewise ascended to the site of enlightenment.
To honor one’s parents through this—what filial piety could be greater than this? Yet worldly people do not examine its origins, nor have they entered its marketplace;
they offer blind words and reckless theories, suddenly launching attacks and challenges. With the light of a firefly or a candle, they doubt the brilliance of the three luminaries;

with a drop from a crack in the grass, they marvel at the capacity of the deep ocean. This may be called being familiar with great beings while insulting the mandate of Heaven. Thus it is said: ...having already [done so].

He inherited his father’s rank as Marquis of Changle. During the reign of Emperor Ai, he served as an Attendant Censor (Sanqichangshi) concurrently holding the post of Director of the Bureau of Historiography (Zuozhelong).
When Huan Wen intended to relocate the capital to Luoyang, public sentiment was filled with doubt and fear; Xinggong submitted a memorial vehemently opposing the plan.
Although Huan Wen was greatly incensed, he ultimately could not refute him. He was subsequently appointed Chief Justice (Tingwei) and died at the age of fifty-eight (*Book of Jin*, *Hongming ji*).
Xie Qingxu, whose courtesy name was Fu, was a native of Shanyin, Kuaiji. By nature he was serene and possessed few desires; he lived in seclusion on Mount Taiping for over ten years.

He placed profound faith in the Great Dharma, maintained a lifelong fast, and devoted himself to the service of the Buddha. He tirelessly invited others to join him in this work of transformation and edification.

He personally annotated the *Anban Shouyi Jing* (Sūtra on Mindfulness of Breathing), providing a preface which states: "As for the 'mind' (*manas*), it is the foundation from which all sufferings sprout. It continues: "To turn one's back..."
The fundamental source of correctness has become wild, deluded, dissolute, and unrestrained beyond measure. In the space of a finger-snap, it revolves nine hundred and sixty times;
in one day and one night, there are thirteen billion thoughts. What a single body has sown spreads like creeping vines throughout kalpas.

All those within the three realms who follow inverted views have been lost since childhood in the deep current and cannot turn back by themselves. Thus, the Perfectly Awakened One, out of compassionate pity, opens the way to the Correct.
The path of wisdom gradually blocks the subtle stirrings of anger and desire, opening the essential way of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing).

By merging birth and cessation into profound stillness, one extends the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) to nourish tranquility. Establishing the ten insights (*daśaprajñā*), one enters the subtle; tethering the runaway feet of the nine spirits.
To prevent the torrential flood of the seven consciousnesses is what is meant by "guarding the mind" (*shouyi*). If one were to subdue coarse defilements and sweep away the fetters of outflows,

closing off forms and sounds from sight and hearing, blocking worldly thoughts through meditative stillness, and riding upon the auspiciousness of tranquil detachment to receive the noble blessings of the heavens—
yet if one’s correct resolve is ruined by frivolous pleasures and past habits are submerged in social indulgence, then the field of merit...

Through arrogant attachment, one wastes away day by day; as the roots of poison arise in succession, transgressions follow one after another. Thus, one revolves through the five destinies for billions of kalpas, difficult to extricate oneself from.

Ensnared in the net of desire, one suffers as if in a most grievous and deep prison. This is due to a lack of wisdom and a delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), failing to contemplate that it is the gateway to the Way that makes this so.
Even regarding those who ride upon wisdom to enter *dhyāna*, there are three classes: some fear suffering and take pleasure in the extinction of form.
Those who dwell in *nirvāṇa*, whose resolve lies solely in self-deliverance and who do not strive for the benefit of others, are of the Vehicle of Non-attachment (*anupādāna-yāna*).

Or, those who look up in aspiration toward the wondrous marks (*lakṣaṇa*) yet still maintain a state of "sending away" [phenomena] and lack [great compassion], and who do not establish great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) but have exhausted the bonds of conditions, are termed *pratyekabuddhas*.

As for the Bodhisattva, they profoundly penetrate that which is originally existent and elucidate the non-existence of causes and conditions. Those who penetrate the original [nature] find that existence is itself empty; those who elucidate non-existence [find that] through causes...

Conditions are eternally quiescent. Because they are inherently empty, one does not emerge from existence to enter non-existence; because they are eternally quiescent, one does not exhaust conditions to return to emptiness.

If one sets the mind upon the essential point and attains awakening to the principle through contact with existence, then one need not rely on the external to quiet the internal, nor depend on dhyāna to produce wisdom.
Therefore it is said that an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva does not follow the four dhyānas. If defilements and dust obscure the mind...
As for the fact that wisdom does not remain permanently established, one must temporarily rely on *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) to still its wandering thoughts.
This is like a farmer clearing the land or polishing a mirror. Thus, weeding and tilling do not constitute the land itself, yet when the land is cleared, the seeds flourish;

polishing and scraping do not constitute the mirror itself, yet when the mirror is polished, it reflects with clarity. Furthermore, he once personally transcribed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and placed it in the capital.
He went down to Baima Monastery. The monastery had been engulfed by a neighboring fire, such that its furnishings and other scriptures were all reduced to ashes;
yet the text of this scripture alone remained intact, with only the edges of the paper slightly scorched. He subsequently returned to the Nanshan area of Ruoye because his mother was elderly.

Xi Qin, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, submitted a memorial recommending him for office, but he did not rise to accept the invitation as a Doctor of State. At that time, the moon eclipsed the constellation Shaowei, and the diviners...

He chose a recluse to represent him. People said it should have been Dai Kui. Shortly thereafter, Qingxu passed away. Kui, courtesy name Andao, was a native of Qiao Commandery. He also possessed noble conduct;
during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu, he was repeatedly summoned but did not comply. He was skilled in literary composition as well as the arts and crafts.
Desiring to create a statue of Amitābha Buddha, he concentrated his thoughts for three years before the carving was finally completed. He then welcomed it to Shanyin.

At Lingbao Monastery, Xi Chao saw [the monk] and performed a prostration. He took some incense in his hand, which suddenly rose in smoke, reaching as far as the eye could see toward the heights of the clouds.

The multitude all marveled at this divine marvel. His son, Yongyong (Yong), was able to carry on his father’s legacy. (From the *Collection of Records from the Tripiṭaka*, the *Book of Jin*, the *Records of Mysterious Auspiciousness*, and the *Pearl Forest of the Dharma Garden*).
The Master Zhinüi said: "During the era of Mouzi, the Buddha-dharma had not yet flourished widely. Yet Mouzi was deeply devoted to its Way; was he not a man who went forth alone?
Furthermore, figures such as An Shigao, Zhi Qian, and Zhu Falan—who propagated the Dharma, upheld the precepts, guided the faithful, and transformed the doubtful—were also truly rare individuals.
Toward the beginning of the Eastern Jin, the influence of the teachings gradually spread. Wang Dao, Yu..."
Zhu Falang, Zhou Yi, Xie Kun, Huan Yi, and their peers all once associated with the Indian monk Śrīmitra. Xie An resided on Mount Dongshan and subdued his mind through the teachings of Zhi Dun.
When Zhi Dun was summoned by imperial decree to lecture on the sutras within the palace, he encountered the lost texts of the *Zong* (Essentials).

Those who clung to the literal letter of the scriptures disparaged him. Upon hearing this, Xie An sighed and said: "This is like Jiu Fangyin’s appraisal of horses; it captures the essence while disregarding the superficial details."

Huang selected those who possessed divine spirit and noble steed-like vigor. As for Wang Xizhi, Wang Tanzhi, Wang Xun and Wang Min, Xu Xun, and Xi Zuochi—each of them maintained close contact with the monastic community.
For the most part, they were men of renown whose words endured, each manifesting a profound and far-reaching character.

During the Xiankang era, when Yu Bing assisted in the administration of government, he submitted a memorial proposing that śramaṇas should perform full ritual obeisance to the sovereign. This was referred to the Bureau of Rites for deliberation; He Chong and others [responded as follows].
He maintained that it was improper to destroy its original foundation. He submitted his memorial three times, and the opposing deliberations were consequently shelved.

Sengchong was a man of profound faith in the Buddha-dharma; the expenses he incurred for feeding monks and constructing temples were beyond measure. Once, Ruan Yu said to him, "Your aspirations are as vast as the universe, and your courage surpasses that of all antiquity.
Sengchong asked why he said this. Ruan Yu replied, "I have sought to govern a commandery of several thousand households and have not yet succeeded; you—"
"Is it not also great to become a Buddha? This was likely said in jest. Hui-chong’s younger brother, Hui-zhun, held himself in high esteem and possessed few desires;

he wore his sash loosely at his cottage gate and recited Buddhist sutras daily. Although many other scholar-officials were devoted to the faith, there are few accounts of their practices or standards of cultivation that have been heard of, and thus they cannot be recorded here.
It was only upon reaching the transition between the Jin and Song dynasties that the flourishing era of Donglin began. [End of fragment]
Since that time, spiritual transformations and divine manifestations have continued to arise in succession. I have recorded the biographies and discourses of the various worthies from Mouzi onwards;
although they have not yet reached the profound depths [of ultimate truth], their intent is already far-reaching. It is like the flow of the Min River, which begins as a mere trickle.
"Could it be that this is not essential?
Wang Dashen said: 'It is an indispensable text within the tradition. Although the recorded events and words are simple, they are nonetheless close to reality.
Throughout the transmission of the thousands of scriptures and myriad classics, is there anything that lies outside the purport of these Forty-two Chapters?'"

Throughout the emergence and disappearance of thousands of sages and myriad worthies, has there ever been one outside of this guidance through the transformation of non-action? "Buddha" means awakening;
he has brought it to its ultimate fulfillment. This concludes the second volume of the *Biographies of Laymen*.
The Biography of Liu Yimin:
Liu Yimin, whose given name was Chengzhi and courtesy name Zhongsu, was a native of Pengcheng. He was a descendant of Liu Yuan, the Prince of Chu of the Han dynasty.

Orphaned at a young age, he served his mother with filial piety. He was well-versed in the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi and did not conform to the customs of the worldly age. Initially, he served as a military aide (*canjun*) to the regional governor.

Wang Mi, Minister of Education of the Jin; Huan Yuan, Chancellor; Xie Kun, Palace Attendant; and Liu Yu, Grand Marshal, successively recommended him for office. Each time, he declined resolutely. At that time, Dharma Master Huiyuan was residing at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu, practicing the *nienfo sanmei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi). Yao Yimin went to rely upon him. Master Huiyuan said, "Your official emolument is lofty and grand; why do you not accept it? Yimin replied: [He then recited the verse: "The Way is vast and boundless, yet I have already entered its gate; the world is narrow and cramped, yet I have already left its dust. Master Huiyuan said, "Excellent! You truly possess the spirit of a man of the Way. He then gave him the name "Yimin" (Left the Dust). Yimin later composed the *Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection) in ten fascicles. He also authored the *Shamen Bujielun* (Treatise on the Monk’s Non-Breaking of Precepts) in two fascicles, the *Xiaozi Jiepin* (Chapter on the Lesser Precepts) in one fascicle, and the *Fajie Shu* (Commentary on the Dharma Realm) in one fascicle. He also compiled the *Zhu Weimojie Jing* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) in three fascicles, the *Lushan Ji* (Record of Mount Lu) in ten fascicles, and the *Jingzhong Ji* (Record of the Meditation Hall) in one fascicle. All of these works were widely circulated. In the second year of the Yongchu era (420), he passed away at the age of sixty-eight. He was buried at the foot of Mount Lu. His disciples erected a stupa for him at the temple. Emperor Wen of Song bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Great Master of the Great Vehicle. His remains were enshrined in a stone chamber within the temple grounds. Later, during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, the monk Huiguan moved the stupa to the western side of the temple. It remains there to this day. "Since your arrival, have you not had the intention to focus on the Pure Land? Thus, he fashioned images of the Three Sages of the West, established a vegetarian fast, and founded a society.
The assembly numbered one hundred and twenty-three people. The surviving subjects engraved this oath upon stone, the words of which say:
'Now that the principle of conditioned transformation is clear, the signs of coming and going are manifest. Since the numerical laws of response and resonance correspond, then goodness..."
The retribution for evil is inevitable. By contemplating how those who merely crossed arms [in friendship] have silently sunk into oblivion, one realizes that the timing of impermanence is pressing;
by examining how the three types of retribution urge one another on, one knows that it is difficult to extricate oneself from perilous destinies.

This is why our fellow practitioners of virtue are vigilant at night and diligent by day, looking upward in thought toward a means of salvation. For the spirit may be reached through resonance, but it cannot be sought through outward traces.

If one must feel the presence of a reality, then the path to the unseen realm is but a few paces away; yet if one seeks it without a guiding master, how vast and boundless will it be—where is the ford?

Now, fortunately, through a response that required no prior deliberation, the collective hearts have been moved toward the western region. Upon reading these verses, faith was opened and sincere emotion was stirred from within.

Thus, the spiritual resonance reached me even in my dreams; my joy exceeds that of a child’s arrival. Thereupon, the patterns of the clouds manifest their brilliance, and the shadows are perfectly harmonized.

This was created by the Divine; its success arose from the harmony of principle, not from human exertion. This is truly a case where Heaven has revealed its sincerity, and where the profound workings of destiny have gathered together.
Yet, their achievements vary and their merits are not uniform; though morning prayers are identical, the destinations to which they return at evening are far apart.
Regarding the bonds of my teachers and friends, this is truly lamentable. Therefore, with deep sighs, we have issued this summons, straightening our robes before the Dharma...

In the hall and other places, he bestowed his single-minded devotion; harboring a profound resolve in his secluded retreat, he vowed that all people together would travel to these transcendent realms.

Thus, with a start that surpassed the ordinary, he was the first to ascend to the divine sphere. He did not seek solitary excellence upon the cloud-capped peaks, nor did he forget the preservation of others in the deep valleys.

Thereafter, he wondrously beheld the celestial countenance, and his mind was opened to pure illumination. Through awakening, his consciousness transformed the mind; through transformation, his physical form was renewed. Relying upon the lotus...
Amidst the flowing waters, I sheltered beneath jade branches to compose these verses; my cloud-like robes drifted to the eight extremities of the world as I spent my years amidst fragrant breezes.
Facing the three paths of suffering, I offered my distant farewell; looking up at the celestial palaces, I took my long leave.
Continuing the path of the multitude of spirits, I set the Great Awakening as my goal. Is this pursuit of the Way not truly magnificent? The Remnant People crossed the stream north of Xilin.
He established a separate meditation hall where he refined his study of fundamental principles while concurrently observing the prohibitive precepts.
He once sent a letter to Guanzhong to engage in scholarly debate on the meaning of the scriptures with Master Kumārajīva and Sengzhao. He composed the "Verses on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation.

After residing there for half a year, while in a state of meditative concentration, he saw the Buddha’s light illuminating the ground, which all turned the color of gold. Fifteen years later, while in the midst of reciting the Buddha's name, he beheld Amitābha.
The Buddha’s jade-white light shone forth as he lowered his hand to comfort and receive him.
The survivor said, "How may I obtain for myself the Tathāgata to rub the crown of my head and cover me with his robe? Suddenly, the Buddha rubbed his head and drew out his *kāṣāya* to clothe him.

On another day, he again dreamed of entering a pool of the seven treasures, where he saw lotuses of blue and white; the water was deep and clear, and there was a person whose head was marked by a circle.
A *svastika* appeared upon his chest, and he pointed to the water in the pond, saying, "This is water of eight virtues; you may drink from it.

When Yimin drank the water, it was sweet and delicious. Upon waking, a wondrous fragrance issued from the pores of his skin. He then said to those around him, "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have arrived.
He invited monks to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* nearly several hundred times, while Yimin burned incense before the images.
Prostrating twice, he offered this prayer: "By means of the bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni, I know that there is Amitābha Buddha.
This incense shall first be offered to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, next to Amitābha Buddha, and thereafter to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
It is by virtue of the merit of this sutra that I have been able to be born in the Pure Land. By this merit, may I [be joined] with all sentient beings..."
He was born together with the Pure Land; thus he was distinct from the multitude. Lying upon his bed, facing west with palms joined, he passed away in a state of serene stillness.

He had previously instructed his son, Yong, to construct a tomb directly within the monastery grounds and not to use a coffin or outer casket. This occurred in the sixth year of the Yixi era, at the age of fifty-nine.

The lay followers of Yicheng and the monks of the society who had passed away beforehand were all present at his side;

they bowed before Master Huiyuan and said, "Master, you conceived the aspiration for enlightenment long ago; why have you come so late? Thereupon, he extended his life for seven more days and then passed away.
