Biographies of Eminent Laymen, Volume Three, Two: The Biographies of Zhang Wangzong and Zhou Lei.
Zhang Laimin, styled Ye, was a native of Xunyang. By nature he was filial and fraternal; he ceded all his fields and residences to his younger brother, sharing both their joys and sorrows.

He shared [his merit] with his nine clans. Although repeatedly summoned by the provincial and regional administrations, he did not respond. When the imperial court commanded him to accept the post of Attendant-at-Large (Sanqishi), he likewise declined.
He entered Mount Lu to join the White Lotus Society and was known as a disciple of Master Huiyuan.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, he took leave of his family, entered his room, sat upright, and passed away at the age of sixty-nine (*Donglin Zhuan*).
Zhang Xiushi, whose given name was Quan, was a descendant of the Ye clan. He possessed a lofty and detached temperament, cherished antiquity, and delighted in the Way.

He labored in the fields with a hoe and never ceased carrying his scriptures even while working. When summoned as an Attendant Censor of the Household, he did not rise to the call. Yu Yue, pitying his poverty, recommended him for the post of Magistrate of Xunyang, but he likewise did not accept.
Subsequently, he entered Mount Lu to rely upon Master Huiyuan, where he investigated and mastered the profound depths of the Buddhist sutras.

He attained awakening and entered [the path]. In the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty, he faced west, recited the name of the Buddha, and passed away without illness at the age of sixty-five (*Donglin zhuan*).
Wang Qiao was a native of Langya; he served as the Grand Governor of Linhe and later joined the White Lotus Society under Master Huiyuan.

Together with Liu Yimin and other worthies, he composed poems on the *Nianfo Sanmei* (Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection). Of these, Qiao’s poem alone has been transmitted to the world. The poem says: "The wondrous function resides herein:
traversing existence and surveying non-existence. The spirit proceeds from obscurity to penetration; consciousness, through illumination, refines the coarse.

Accumulating the minute leads naturally forward; the foundation of merit is fundamentally empty. One dissolves those three contemplations and forgets this remaining hair’s breadth. The second [verse] says: "Silent and still, how..."

Beginning: Treading upon the primordial source, he penetrates the subtle and profound; in a state of melting unity, he forgets his destination. Thus he expands the spiritual radiance, and his mind roams the distant realm.

He does not need to tread upon the mechanisms of the world, employing them with emptiness and meeting them with rarity. Its third part says: His divine countenance is as naturally solidified as the sky, a perfect reflection amidst the morning clouds.

Transforming along with all beings to reach universal harmony, they join this multitude with the Buddha. Their responses are not limited by fixed methods, for those who receive them distinguish themselves according to their own capacity.

Serene and profound as a mirror, they cast off the turmoil of worldly dust. The fourth [section] says: Alas, throughout my life, I have long lacked wisdom and insight. Entrusting myself to one of lofty and profound virtue, I hope to rely on the power of the unseen;
I contemplate turning even a hair’s breadth of merit toward that unfathomable depth. This most sublime aspiration focuses the mind upon the Western Realm, reaching far beyond.
The Duke composed a preface for it, saying: "Now, what is meant by 'samādhi'? It refers to the state of single-minded contemplation and tranquil reflection.
When contemplation is single-minded, the will becomes unified and undivided. When reflection is tranquil, the vital energy (*qi*) becomes empty and the spirit becomes lucid.

When the vital energy is empty, wisdom awakens to its illumination; when the spirit is lucid, there is no obscurity that it does not penetrate. These two are the primal symbols of spontaneity, which, when unified, bring forth their function."

Furthermore, while the names of various samādhis are exceedingly numerous, none is more sublime in merit or easier to advance toward than the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata is the Honored One who exhausts the source and reaches the ultimate stillness; his spiritual essence merges with transformation, responding without being limited by any particular form.

Therefore, those who enter this concentration become oblivious and forget all cognition, such that they take the object of focus itself as the mirror. When this mirror is bright, internal illumination reflects one another, and the myriad phenomena—
It arises therein. Though it is beyond the reach of the ears and eyes, hearing and seeing proceed from it. Thus, the numinous marks are profoundly unified, lucid, and spontaneous;
the primal resonance strikes the heart, and obstructed emotions melt into clarity. If it were not for the ultimate subtlety of the world, who could participate in this?
Therefore, the worthies who uphold the Dharma all contemplate the accord of a single principle, moved by the realization that every moment of time is fleeting.
I am weary and fearful that my provisions for the future have not yet been accumulated. Therefore, I cleanse my mind in the Dharma Hall and straighten my robes to face the pure direction.
At midnight I forget to sleep, and at dawn I rise with diligent effort. I hope that through the merit of steadfast application, I may fulfill the aspiration of the Three Vehicles.

May I look upward to assist those who leap forward like the pulling up of the *mao* grass, and look downward to lead the weak and advancing by holding their reins from behind. Thus, when I survey these various compositions of brushstrokes, how could it be otherwise?
Is it merely a matter of literary composition? (From the *Hongming ji* and *Lushan ji*; Qiao Zhi—some editions read Qi Zhi, which may be his style name.
Zong Shaowen, whose fame was brilliant, was a native of Nanyang. He was exceptionally skilled in the lute and calligraphy, and refined in theoretical discourse.

Although Yin Zhongkan, Huan Yuan, and Liu Yu all summoned him to serve as their secretaries (*zhubushi*), he did not accept. He subsequently entered Mount Lu to attend upon Master Huiyuan, where he built a dwelling to reside.
He resided at the White Lotus Society. Subsequently, his elder brother Zang became the Governor of Nanping and pressured him to return with him to Jiangling.
There, he lived in seclusion, detached from the world, and cultivated crops to provide for his family. Prince Yijì of Hengyang visited him personally;

Shaowen, wearing a horned cap and cloth robes, was ushered into the audience but did not bow. The Prince asked, "Is it appropriate to appoint a man such as you to a high salary? He replied: [text continues]
He said: "Official emolument is like autumn grass; it withers as soon as the season passes. When the Song dynasty received the abdication of the throne, he declined three summons.

He had a refined love for mountains and waters; he traveled west to the regions of Jing and Wu and climbed south to Mount Heng. Returning to Jiangling due to illness, he sighed, saying: "Old age and sickness have arrived together; I shall not be able to ascend famous mountains again.
I shall only clarify my mind to contemplate the Way, traveling through them while lying down. All the places he visited were depicted in paintings.
He inscribed this on a wall and said to others, "When I play the *qin* and move its melodies, I wish to cause all the mountains to resound.

He also composed the "Treatise on the Immortality of the Spirit" (*Shen bumie lun*), a brief excerpt of which states: "The spirits of the myriad beings, though their ultimate nature is equal, migrate and flow according to conditions, forming coarse or subtle consciousnesses.
Now, Shun was born to Gu; the spirit of Shun must certainly not have been produced by Gu. Thus, [the spirit] is Shang..."
Furthermore, this spirit is not something produced by Shun. Prior to its birth and growth, it already possessed both coarseness and subtlety.
Since its fundamental nature was established before life began, one knows that it is not extinguished after death. That which is called "spirit" describes that which wondrously permeates all things.
If it were created by depending on form and perished following the destruction of form, then form would be its fundamental basis.

What is so marvelous about these words? Truly, one who can clarify the fundamental nature that is neither born nor extinguished, and who adheres to the learning of daily diminution—diminishing it again and again until reaching non-action (*wuwei*)—will find that in non-action there is no longer anything corresponding to birth. Where there is no birth, there is no body;
yet where there is no body, there is spirit. This is what is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Now, the Yellow Emperor, Yu Shun, Duke Ji, and Confucius are those whom the world...

These are those whom one looks up to with faith. Observe their letting the reins go to ascend to heaven, the dragon’s submergence and the phoenix’s soaring, the turning back of the wind to raise the grain, and the abstention from grains while strumming the lute and singing.
All of these arise because they take the exhaustion of the spirit as their essence; thus, the responses of their divine efficacy are extraordinary and beyond fixed measure.
Now, the various portents of good and ill fortune described in the *Hongfan* all originate from the mind.

Even such phenomena as a white rainbow piercing the sun, Venus entering the asterism Mao, the growth of millet in a cold valley, or the collapsing of city walls and the falling of frost—all these arise from human sentiments and manifest far away as celestial events;
they are truly like form and shadow to one another. For there can be no form without a shadow, and no sound without an echo; likewise, there can be no sentiment without its outward manifestation.

There is no lack of retribution. How could it be limited merely to such phenomena as the sun being pierced or frost falling? There is nothing that does not respond in accordance with circumstances and adapt to specific conditions;

no object can conceal its form. Yet, whether these effects are manifested within the person or disseminated through events, they are interwoven and complex, manifest and obscure, vast and boundless—who can perceive their ultimate limits?
The myriad transformations fill the world, and the multitude of forms meets the eye; all are the result of the subtle resonance of the spirit throughout ten thousand generations.
Thus it has been gathered. Therefore, the Buddhist scriptures state: "All phenomena arise from the mind," and further: "The mind is the root of all dharmas;

the mind creates heaven, and the mind creates hell. This is the meaning of these passages. Consequently, one who purifies the mind and cleanses the emotions will surely be reborn in a realm of exquisite beauty;
whereas one whose emotions are turbid and whose conduct is defiled will surely remain forever stagnant within the three miserable realms. Indeed...
The sacred, perfectly illuminating consciousness that is free from thought and contrivance arises because the mind is severed from objects and remains as spirit alone;
thus, the fundamental state of empty clarity abides eternally from beginning to end and cannot wither.

Now, by realizing emptiness and stilling the mind, the functions of the mind cease and emotional consciousness subsides, whereby spiritual intelligence becomes complete. Yanzi knew this to be so; therefore, he dwelt amidst existence.
If there were nothing, then one would treat reality as if it were empty; one would not see any transgression and thus would not retaliate.

Now, observing that Yanzi was frequently "empty-handed," we know that what seems to exist is in fact non-existent. Furthermore, things hidden in a valley or a boat undergo change faster than a flash of lightning.

The future has not yet arrived, the past has already perished, and the present does not abide. In the span of a single instant, there is not a single hair’s breadth upon which one can rely. Thus, [it is clear that all is empty].
What could one possibly cling to and consider as truly existent? How extreme is the obscuration of the spirit by the pretense of existence! Suppose there were a bright mirror here:

if filth and impurities gather upon it, when they are slight, its reflection remains clear; when they accumulate, its reflection becomes faint; and when they grow thick, though it reflects, it does so dimly.
The spiritual principle of man is analogous to this. The pretense of existence burdens the spirit, resulting in varying degrees of refinement or coarseness.
This is consciousness. Consciousness is attached to the spirit; therefore, although death occurs, it does not perish.

By gradually progressing toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one will surely reach the point where practice culminates in exhaustion, thereby exhausting the fundamental spirit. This is what is called *nirvāṇa*.

Now, the reason why the Ultimate Way has not been manifest since antiquity is that people cling to their lives. Yet suffering arises from life; the deluded do not understand this. Furthermore, time is without [beginning].
When still, it is so; when in motion, it is inexhaustible. The countless and boundless kalpas that have passed in the past are all traversed in a single instant, reaching even unto this very moment.
Now, by accumulating these instants, one reaches a hundred years; yet how much time has truly passed, for rarely does one even reach half of that span?
Indeed, those things that charm the body as if it were morning dew generally lack any enduring or far-reaching reality. Why, then, do you indulge in such foulness?
To rot within the span of a few moments, while allowing the long-enduring spirit to suffer injustice—how could one fail to distance oneself from such a remote and distant style?
He passed away in the twentieth year of the Yuanjia era at the age of sixty-nine (from the *Songshu*, "Biography of Donglin," and the *Hongming ji*).
Zhou Daozu, whose given name was Xuzhi, was a native of Yanmen. After his father passed away, he crossed the Yangtze River and settled in Yuzhang.

At the age of twelve, he went to Fan Ning to receive instruction; he mastered the Five Classics and the Five Wai-chuan. He cultivated his will in secluded retirement, specializing in the study of the *Laozi* and the *I Ching*.

Later, he joined the White Lotus Society on Mount Lu, believing that while the physical body could not be discarded, all remaining worldly attachments should be severed; consequently, he remained celibate for the rest of his life.
His wife wore plain clothes and ate simple vegetarian food. When the imperial court summoned him to serve as a *Taixue* (National University) *Boshi* (Doctor), he did not accept.

When Liu Yu launched his northern campaign, the Heir Apparent was stationed at Pengcheng and invited [Huiyuan] to stay at Andong Temple. He was invited to lecture on the *Book of Rites*. After more than a month, he returned to the mountains.

When Liu Yu returned to his headquarters, he again dispatched an envoy to welcome him. Upon the establishment of the Song dynasty through the abdication of the throne, a lecture hall was established for him outside the eastern gate, where he gathered students to teach.
Regarding the instruction in the Rites Classics, someone asked: "You are a retired scholar (chushi) by body, yet you frequently attend the royal court; why is this? He replied:

"For one whose mind races toward the imperial gates, the rivers and lakes are but shackles. For one who has forgotten both [the mundane and the transcendental], even the marketplace and the court are but mountain caves."

He was then titled Master Tongyin. Not long after, he retired from his post on the pretext of illness at Mount Zhongshan. He passed away in the first year of the Jingping era (423 CE) at the age of sixty-seven (*Songshu*).
Lei Zhonglun, whose courtesy name was Mingzong, was a native of Nanchang. In his youth, he entered Mount Lu to serve under Master Huiyuan, where he applied himself with devotion to learning.
He did not involve himself in worldly affairs, but was profoundly versed in the study of the *Mao Shih* and the Three Rituals (*San Li*).

When his home province appointed him as an official (*congshi*), and the court summoned him as a Retired Gentleman of the Attendants (*yuanwai sanqi shilang*), he declined both positions. At over fifty years of age, he wrote a letter to his sons and nephews to explain his principles, saying:
"The length of one's life is entirely predetermined by destiny; beyond this fixed allotment, nothing can be achieved through human intelligence or effort."
Seek it. You should simply follow what you have received and not cause harm. Since my youth, I have been afflicted by chronic illness; by nature, I am fond of seclusion.
Thus, even in my childhood, I harbored the intention to travel afar. Upon reaching the age of twenty, I eventually took up residence at Mount Lu.
There I served Master Shi, at which time our teachers and friends were dedicated to training others and propagating the Way. I looked outward with admiration for them.
My fellow scholars harbored within them a sense of yearning and inspiration. Thereupon, we purified our spirits through divine clarity and delighted our minds with the ancient classics.
We exerted our wills and applied ourselves with diligence, continuing from night until day. Now, there was a love for mountains and rivers, and sighs over meeting and parting;

these were truly sufficient to penetrate principle and assist one’s nature, establishing a career of tireless effort. In this joy, we forgot our worries and did not realize that the morning sun had grown late as we wandered. From this point on...

For over twenty years, I have lived amidst the winds of the Way. Now that my profound mentors have passed away and my virtuous friends have withered and vanished, I was further beset by calamities and rebellious acts against Heaven, through which I tasted every bitterness of sorrow.
My former sincere aspirations were suddenly exhausted in a single day; my mental faculties are desolate and scattered, and my emotions have decayed.

Therefore, I have come to join you all in returning to till the fields at the foot of the ridges, dwelling in the mountains and drinking from the valleys. Human affairs have long been severed, and the days and months [pass on].
I have remained here without dwelling elsewhere for ten years suddenly. The sun is nearing the Mount Yanzi, and how much further is there on the path ahead?
Now that senility has not yet arrived and my decline is not yet sudden, it is still possible to rouse my will toward what I aspire to and let my mind rest upon what I entrust myself to.
To lodge my sincerity in the bridge to future lives and to concentrate my vital energy in the cultivation of my final years—my aspirations lie entirely within this. From now on...
He departed for the west; from then on, he did not concern himself with any domestic affairs, great or small.

In the fifteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he was summoned to the capital, where he established a lecture hall at Mount Jilong to gather disciples and teach them. He was appointed as a Secretariat Drafter (Jishi Zhong), but he did not accept the post. Shortly thereafter, he returned to Mount Lu.
In the twenty-fifth year, he was again summoned to the capital, where a residence was built for him below the western cliffs of Mount Zhong, called the "Hermitage for Summoning the Recluse.
He was commissioned to lecture on the *Śrāddha-sūtra* (the Scripture on Mourning Rites) for the Crown Prince and various princes. He passed away that same year at the age of sixty-three (*Song shu*).
Zhi Guizi said: "Among the one hundred and twenty-three members of the White Lotus Society, only seven lay practitioners (jushi) can be recorded.
One such as Kang Le, whose talent was so keen, sought to join the society, yet Master Huiyuan refused him. Truly, one must be cautious about whom one associates with!
Beyond these seven individuals, their lingering influence and surviving writings cannot be found; I, too, am unable to recover them."
And thus he praised him. The Biographies of Laymen (Jushi zhuan), Volume IV:
The Biographies of Dong, He, Wei, Chen, and Liu of Anyang.
An-yang Juqu Hou Jing-sheng was a native of Lin-cheng County in T’ien-shui. He was the younger cousin of Mo-shun, the King of Ho-hsi.
By nature he was open-minded and possessed a powerful memory. Having received the five precepts in his youth, he applied himself with keen intent to the inner scriptures (Buddhist teachings).
In his early years, he once traveled to the kingdom of Yü-tien, where he visited the Kuo-mo-ti Great Monastery and encountered the Indian Dharma Master Buddhasena, from whom he sought instruction.
He inquired about the meaning of the Way and received the *Śrāmaṇera-śikṣāpada-sūtra* (Secret Sūtra on the Essentials of Dhyāna for Healing Illness).

Subsequently, he returned east to Gaochang, where he obtained one scroll each of the *Avalokiteśvara-dhyāna-sūtra* and the *Maitreya-dhyāna-sūtra*. Upon returning to Hexi, he immediately translated the *Dhyāna-yao*.
After several years, when Emperor Tao of the Wei dynasty conquered Hexi, An-yang fled to the Song. Huizhi maintained humble intentions and did not involve himself in worldly affairs;
he frequently stayed at pagodas and monasteries. He was the first to produce the *Avalokiteśvara-dhyāna-sūtra* and the *Maitreya-dhyāna-sūtra*.

Meng Yi, the Governor of Dan-yang, saw them and praised them, requesting an audience with him and providing generous offerings. This continued until the second year of the Xiaojian era, when the bhikṣu...
When the nun Huijun heard his recitation of the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, she requested permission to transcribe it; he subsequently produced it in five fascicles.
In that same year, at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong, he further brought out one fascicle of the *Buddhamātṛ-nirvāṇa-sūtra*. An Yang resided in seclusion, having severed ties with wife and children.

He took no pleasure in fame or profit, but lived at ease among his fellow practitioners, expounding and transmitting the scriptures. For this reason, both the monastic and lay communities paid him their respects.
Toward the end of the Daming era, he fell ill and passed away (as recorded in the *Collection of Records of the Tripiṭaka*).

Dong Ji was a native of Yuqian. His family had served the Dharma for three generations, and Ji himself was particularly diligent in his practice. He constantly observed the precepts and recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Whenever the people of the village where he lived fell ill, they would invite Ji to recite the sutra, and they would invariably recover.

A fellow county resident named He Huang also served the Dharma; he died from poisoning and invited Ji to attend the funeral rites. The river waters were suddenly swollen, making it impossible to cross. Ji prayed silently.
While crossing the Daishi River carrying his sutras in a cloth bag while naked, the bag and sutras were suddenly swept away by the current as he reached the bank.
He was deeply grieved and remorseful, and went to the house of Huang to confess and reproach himself. In the blink of an eye, he saw the sutra bag upon a high seat;
upon opening it to inspect, they had never been moistened. Thereupon, the people of the district all simultaneously embraced the Dharma. [This occurred at] the western side of Ji’s house.
To the north there was a mountain, lofty and perilous, where many malevolent spirits and demons abounded, causing harm to the local inhabitants.

Ji wished to subdue them, so he cleared four or five *mu* of the mountain land, constructed a small hut, and set up a high seat. He recited the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* for over a hundred days, and the harm to the people finally ceased.
Later, several men came to visit him and said, "We have heard that your virtuous conduct is pure and austere; therefore, we have come to observe you."
He further requested one thing, thinking it would be granted: "This mountain has belonged to my family for generations, and now you have come to dwell here.

Fearing that we might encroach upon one another, I wish to establish a new boundary, using the felled trees as the demarcation. Ji knew he was a mountain spirit and said, "I covet this tranquility to recite the scriptures;
I do not interfere with you. I pray that you will grant me your protection. The spirit consented and departed.
After one night had passed, outside the four boundaries of the land cleared by Ji, all the trees were withered and dead as if scorched by fire (*Mingxiang ji*). He Tan-yuan was a native of Lujiang;
he was the son of Wan-shou, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief of the Song dynasty. From his youth, he had honored the Dharma and maintained its precepts.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Precepts: at the age of eighteen, while observing the mourning period for his father, he became so emaciated with grief that he fell ill.
Consequently, he turned his heart toward the Pure Land and invited several monks to his home to repent for his past karma. As time passed, his devotion grew ever more earnest.

One night, after the recitation of the sutras was finished and the other monks had fallen asleep, Tan-yuan suddenly began to chant and recite by himself. The monks, finding this strange, questioned him; he replied, "I see the Buddha’s body, golden in color, its light..."

He was over ten *zhang* tall and approached from the west, flanked by banners and flowers that filled the void of space. The Buddha, with a radiant and smiling countenance, commanded Tan-yuan to depart quickly.
Tan-yuan had always been frail and weak, yet at this moment his spirit became bold and resolute; he then took fragrant flowers and scattered them into the air.
At the fifth watch, he suddenly passed away. A fragrant scent lingered within the residence for several days before it finally dissipated (*Mingxiang ji*).
Wei Shizi was a native of Liangjun. He was born during the Song dynasty and was a devoted and diligent follower of the Buddha.
He led his children and grandchildren in cultivating the practices for the Western Pure Land, though his wife alone did not believe. His daughter fell ill and died, only to revive after seven days.

She immediately ascended a high seat and recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, then descended to address her father, saying: "I have departed and gone to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Both I and my father—"
In the ponds of each of her elder brothers, there were large lotus flowers; they were destined to be born within them, yet their mother alone had none.
Unable to bear this sorrow, she returned home to inform them of the matter. Having finished speaking, she passed away. From that time on, the mother also began to uphold the Dharma (*Mingxiang ji*).
Military Aide Chen Zhen was a native of Huāróng in Jīngzhōu and the elder brother of the Tiantái Meditation Master Zhìzhě.
While serving the Liáng dynasty as Military Aide to the Household Troops of Prince Pǔ'ān, he reached the age of forty when he encountered the immortal Zhāng Guǒ, who said to him:
"I have observed your physiognomy; your allotted lifespan has already ended, and you will die within one month. Frightened by this, the Military Aide reported it to the Wise One (Zhìzhě).

The Wise One bestowed upon him the *Tóngméng zhǐguān* (Basic Stopping and Contemplation for Beginners) and instructed him in the practice of the Vaipulya Repentance Method (*Fāngděng chàn fǎ*). First, he was to be equipped with ten dharmas:
first, clear faith in cause and effect; second, the arising of profound dread; third, the deep cultivation of shame and remorse; fourth, the seeking of the extinction of transgressions.
The method: namely, one should practice in accordance with the Dharma as clarified in the Mahāyāna sūtras regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Fifth, confessing past transgressions; sixth, severing the continuous mind; seventh, giving rise to the mind that protects the Dharma; eighth, making great vows to deliver all sentient beings;
ninth, constantly recollecting the Buddhas of the ten directions; tenth, contemplating that the nature of sin is non-existent.
Born [into this state], one adorns the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) with these ten dharmas.

Wearing clean garments, burning incense, and scattering flowers, one practices according to the Dharma before the Triple Gem for seven days, twenty-one days, one month, three months, or even for a year, repenting with single-minded devotion.
Thus, grave offenses are extinguished and meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) manifests. The military official, following these instructions, practiced day and night without ceasing.
Chai died before a full year had passed, and his son saw him again. Greatly astonished, the son asked, "What medicine did you take to reach this state?

Chai replied, "I merely practiced the method of repentance; I never took any medicine. The son placed his hands over his forehead and said, "How marvelous! The power of the Way transcends death and surpasses birth.
Later, while in a state of meditative concentration, Chai ascended to the celestial palace and beheld a golden hall with a plaque inscribed: "The Palace of Chen Zhenzhi."

"In fifteen years, I shall be born here. When the time arrived, he visited all his relatives and acquaintances to bid them farewell, sat upright, and passed away (*Fozu tongji*, "Small Stop-and-Contemplation").

Liu Qianzhi was a eunuch during the reign of Emperor Xiaowen of the Wei dynasty. During the Taihe era, feeling distressed that he was a mere remnant of the penal system, he submitted a petition requesting to enter the mountains to cultivate the Way.
He brought with him a copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and recited it day and night, abstaining from grain and subsisting only on water.

After twenty-one days, his beard and mustache suddenly grew back, and he regained the physical appearance of a man. His spiritual mind became enlightened, and he attained a profound understanding of the esoteric meaning of the teachings. Thereupon...
Exhausting his essence, he composed the *Huayan jing lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) in six hundred fascicles and presented them to Emperor Xiaowen.

The Emperor’s reverence and faith increased manifold, and consequently, the teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* flourished at that time. (*From the Dàtáng nèidiǎn lù [Record of Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang]: Huayan jing shu chāo [Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra].

Regarding the Shu Chāo, it states that Tánqián was a person of the Northern Qi dynasty and that he conceived his resolve after hearing of the third prince who burned his body as an offering to Mañjuśrī. However, upon examination, the Northern Qi did not have the "Tàihé" era name; furthermore, while all the princes of the Wei and Qi dynasties are listed in the histories, none record an incident of self-immolation. Therefore, based on the *Nèidiǎn lù*, this account has been excised).
Yancong was a native of Quanzhou. During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he resided in Yangzhou, where he constructed a vihāra and transcribed the Lotus Sūtra.
Both monastics and laypeople held him in such high esteem that they constantly sent money to provide for his needs. Later, someone borrowed ten thousand coins from him for the cost of the scriptures;
having no other choice, Cong gave them to him. On the way back, the borrower’s boat capsized midway, and the money was lost. On that very day, Cong entered his storehouse.
He saw ten thousand coins as if they had just emerged from water and marveled at this. Shortly thereafter, a man reported that his boat had capsized;
it was then realized that the money in the treasury was precisely what he had borrowed. A merchant went to Xiangting Lake to sacrifice to a deity;
at night, he dreamed that the deity said, "You all have given these offerings to Yan Fahua for the purpose of copying scriptures. Other such responses [to his piety] were likewise numerous.
It was extremely numerous. Gong eventually completed his transcription of the scriptures. Toward the end of the Daye era, his descendants still transmitted his craft;

bandits made a pact not to enter his village, and the villagers relied upon him for their protection. At the same time, in Xinfan of Yizhou, there was a man named Xun who lived about thirty li west of the county seat in a place called Wangli Village.
He was skilled at calligraphy, yet he held himself in such high esteem that he refused to write for others.
Although people insulted and beat him, he paid them no heed. One day, taking up his brush, he went to a village ahead and wrote the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in the air in all four directions.
After several days, having finished, he said, "Let the devas read this well. At first, the people did not perceive anything extraordinary about it.
Later, there was a great thunderstorm; a young cowherd stood in the midst of the area where the writing had been—about a zhang in diameter—and the rain could not reach him.
The ground became damp. Thereafter, whenever it rained, the cowherds would invariably take shelter there.
