The differences arise from expediency; thus, while the teachings of Confucius and Śākyamuni differ, their underlying Way accords. The understanding is identical because of its subtlety; thus, while the Sanskrit and Chinese languages are separated, their transformative influence is communicated.
It is simply that because the responses [of sentient beings] vary in refinement or coarseness, the teachings are divided into the secular and the monastic.

Furthermore, because the lands are situated to the east or west, the nations are delimited as internal or external. Yet, in encompassing divine transformation and forging all living beings, there is no difference. Nevertheless, although the Ultimate Way is one...

At a crossroads, confusion arises; the ninety-six heterodox schools all claim to possess the Way. If one merely listens to their names, it is impossible to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox;

yet when one examines their teachings, the true and the false naturally separate. To laugh at the refined with the crude, or to slander the true with the false, is like a blind man facing Li Zhu and claiming, "I am the one who sees clearly.
Subsequently, an imperial edict was issued for the śramaṇa Huizhen to verify the scriptures at Dinglin Monastery. His merit...

Biqi requested to leave the household life. He first burned his hair and beard as a self-vow, and the imperial decree granted his request. He subsequently changed his attire at the monastery and took the name Huidi.
He passed away before a full year had elapsed (from the *Book of Liang*).

Fu Yishi, whose courtesy name was Zai, was a native of Lingzhou in Beidi. He was fond of learning and skilled at composing literature. During the mourning period for his mother, he grieved so profoundly that he became emaciated to the point of being skeletal;

thus, his fellow scholars praised him. Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty, having heard of his reputation, summoned him to serve as a scholar for the compilation of histories and appointed him as the Secretary of the Sanguo Commandery.
Yishi was a devout believer in the Buddha-dharma and studied the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sādhana* under Dharma Master Huilang of Xinghuang Temple.

[The author] states: Having thoroughly mastered all their studies, there was at that time the Dharma Master Taixinsong, who composed the *Wuzheng lun* (Treatise on Non-contention) to disparage Huilang.
[Huilang] accordingly composed the *Mingdao lun* (Treatise on Clarifying the Way) to resolve those difficulties. Its summary says:

The *Wuzheng lun* states, "Recently, there have been proponents of the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*) who have successively slandered various masters and rejected the various schools of learning. While discussing the Middle Way, they harbor biased attachments; their speech forgets [the truth]."
They harbor [their views] while competing for individual victory; they study the *Abhidharmakośa* only to become further adversaries.

Once enmity and rivalry have been established, great strife arises. With such a mind, one accumulates karmic offenses. If these offenses do not cease, will the mass of suffering within birth and death not increase all the more?
The answer is: The rise of the Three Treatises has long since occurred. Nāgārjuna originated their source, eliminating the heterodoxies of internal studies.

Regarding partiality: Deva expounded its essential tenets to sweep away the heterodox attachments of the non-Buddhists, desiring that the Great Transformation flow without obstruction and that the primal wind be propagated without decline.
His words are vast, his intent far-reaching, his Way broad, and his influence deep.
This is truly the soaring flight of dragons and elephants, the powerful movement of the Kun and Peng; how could Jian Cheng, with his clipped wings, ever hope to rival them?
Alas! In recent times, the world has become shallow and decadent, and there are no more men of vast learning. People merely practice the minor arts to transform the minds of the ignorant;

as these habits gradually infect the customs, they have consequently lost their way on the true path. They compete only with one another in speculative interpretation, each following their own arbitrary constructions. While the branches and leaves proliferate in vain, the fundamental source is daily obscured.
One teacher’s explanation differs from another’s; they alter the ancient tenets and each establishes new doctrines. Among fellow students—

From within these, one selects what seems awakened and distinguishes it again; thus, through successive layers of mixing and compounding, they become doubly numerous. To employ them all together, the mind lacks a definitive standard;
to select and act upon them, which could be deemed correct? Is this not like wounding the apertures of the primordial chaos or damaging the sprouts of a magnificent tree?
Though others may say "it is not a horse" and one’s house may hold a numinous serpent, such views are like a cup that never fits its contents or a cake drawn upon the ground.
The learning of Mount She was not like this. Adhering to a single honored principle, it was free from the folly of arbitrary alteration;

it expounded meaning based on the texts while blocking off the tendency toward subjective conjecture. His words were not premeditated, and his principles were not contrived in advance. He responded only upon perceiving conditions and moved only after seeing the opponent.
Thus, at times he encompassed all things without end, and at times he dissolved into nothingness. In all such exchanges, he was ever responsive.
Examine this thoroughly according to reason: what jealousy or deceit has led you to offend the various masters? Furthermore, as for what these masters have taught—is it subject to refutation or not?
If it is subject to refutation, then its being refuted is only natural. If it is not subject to refutation, then your refutation fails to reach it.

Why then do you, O Dharma Master, alone conceal and protect it, refusing to allow it to be refuted? Moreover, the teachings comprise both the Great and Small Vehicles, all fully contained within the sacred scriptures.
The texts of the Mahāyāna explicitly refute the "lesser paths. Now that the Great Dharma is being propagated, how could one not speak of the intent of the Mahāyāna? The *Vigrahavyāvartanī* states:

"The Way of Non-contention (araṇa) is common to both the internal [Buddhist] and external [non-Buddhist] traditions. That which you require as a point of contention is merely using the derivative to rescue the fundamental;
it is to lose the fundamental while laboring over the derivative. Why is this so? If one relies on external scriptures and searches through their books...

Prior to the time of Qie, reaching back to the era of Chun, people were simple and honest in their hearts and practiced the teaching of non-speaking. At such a time, what dispute could there have been?
We thus know for certain that the absence of dispute from the very beginning is the true nature of things. The response says: One must not hold exclusively to either "dispute" or "non-dispute.
Furthermore, how can one distinguish between the fundamental and the derivative? Since there has never been dispute from the outset, how can you be certain it is not so?
Furthermore, as for disputing about "now," what proof is there that it is not the original? For one who stands behind and looks toward the front, it is the "front";
for one who stands in front and looks toward the back, it is the "back. The matters of front and back are just like "this" and "that": when one calls this "that," it becomes "that."
To call this "that" and that "this"—wherein do these names reside? By means of this, all things may be known.

From beginning to end, from prior to subsequent, regarding right and wrong, good and evil—can these not be constantly maintained? How can one, relying on their own cleverness, neglect the eyes and ears of others?
Indeed, like bubbles arising and perishing, or a fire-brand whirling in a circle, one enters the pit of confinement and suffers the bonds of restraint. Life...
Sorrow and fear give rise to afflictions; what is their fault? It is because they arise from various views that are not in accord with the Way.
Those who are in accord are not so: they neither act nor do they refrain from acting. Good and evil cannot coexist within them, yet they have never been separate from good and evil.
Birth and death cannot reach them, yet they remain eternally within birth and death. Thus, they attain eternal liberation.
I let things be as they are. When the bright moon is in the sky, all waters reflect it; when the pure wind is in the forest, all the pipes of nature resound.
How could I be opposed to things? Yet I do not enter the stench of putrid fish nor take pleasure in rotten rats—how could I be the same as things?
Who can know me? Let us walk this path together, vast and magnificent. How could there be any more seeing of contention as wrong and non-contention as right?

If one truly desires to examine what is authentic and what is false, and to observe gain and loss, there is nothing better than relying on the words of the sages and worthies, and scrutinizing the principles of action and withdrawal.
By investigating from beginning to end and comprehensively verifying both the internal and external, one shall ensure that empty rhetoric has no place and that deceptive ways naturally vanish.

I request to wait for a later occasion to observe their subtlety. [He served as] Successive Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Sub-Secretary of the Heir Apparent, and Palace Attendant. [Posthumous title: Lord.

Upon the accession to the throne, he was appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shuji Kan) and General of the Right Guard (Uei Shōgun), concurrently serving as a Chamberlain for the Palace Secretariat (Chūshu Tsūji Shajin).

He was charged with drafting imperial edicts and managing state affairs. Although he was held in high esteem by the late sovereign for his literary talent, his character was rigid and upright, leading to a lack of harmony with the court officials.

At that time, Shi Wenqing and Shen Keqing were manipulating the administration through their sycophancy; consequently, Yishi (the subject’s name) was increasingly marginalized, and they [the two officials]... [colluded against him].

He slandered Yi Si, who had accepted gold from the envoy of Goryeo, and subsequently cast him into prison. While in prison, Yi Si submitted a petition vehemently criticizing the transgressions of the late ruler.
The late ruler was greatly incensed. Shortly thereafter, he dispatched an envoy to say to him, "I wish to pardon you;

can you reform your ways? He replied, "The heart of your servant is like his face; if the face could be changed, then the heart of your servant could be changed. The late ruler grew even more resentful.
The Emperor grew angry and subsequently had him executed in prison at the age of fifty-five. Three years later, the Sui dynasty extinguished Chen (according to the *Book of Chen*).

Zhi Guizi said: "Huiyan and Huida propagated the Dharma to assist in governance; Huilun protected living beings to preserve benevolence. The three He brothers withdrew into seclusion among the hills and gardens;
Daomao and Daoliu remained submerged in the marketplace and the court. As for the writings of the various sons of the Pei and Liu families—"

As for his character, his conduct surpassed his reputation; he possessed the refined style of a true gentleman. During the transition between the Liang and Chen dynasties, there were many among the scholar-officials who claimed to study Buddhism;
yet they often clung to their emoluments and preserved their positions, regarding the transfer of the imperial throne as if discarding spittle.
Alas! Could this not have been brought about by Buddhism? This is why I cannot forget him.
This is *Fu Zi*.
Wang Dashen said: "His entire being is the fragrance of sandalwood; there is nothing more that can disturb it.
His encomium is exceedingly elegant and correct, and one further perceives its wondrous depth as unfathomable.
The Biographies of Eminent Laymen, Volume Six:
The Biography of Prince Wenxuan of Jingling.
Prince Wenxuan of Jingling, Xiao Ziliang, was styled Yunying. He was the second son of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty. [He lived during the] Song...
In the third year of the Shengming era of Emperor Shun, he served as the Governor of Kuaiji, overseeing five commanderies and being enfeoffed as the Duke of Wenxi.

Since the time of Emperor Xiaowu, because the districts and counties had been slow in responding to urgent requisitions, imperial envoys were first dispatched from the central government; from that point on, public service became exhausting and disruptive.
Once the Qi dynasty had received the abdication of the throne, Emperor Wenxuan fully detailed these abuses and requested their abolition. In the second year of the Jianyuan era, because his mother...

Yu resigned from his office and subsequently served as the Governor of Danyang. He opened his private granaries to relieve the poor in the subordinate counties and petitioned for the restoration of ancient dikes, reclaiming several thousand *qǐng* of wasteland.
Emperor Gao accepted his proposal, but the matter was shelved due to his subsequent transfer of office. Upon the accession of Emperor Wu, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jingling.
In the second year of the Yongming era, he served as General of the Guard and concurrently held the rank of Minister of Education (*Sìtú*). In the fourth year...
He was promoted to the rank of General of the Chariots and Cavalry (*Cheqi Jiangjun*). At that time, as floods and droughts occurred out of season, he petitioned for the remission of overdue rents.

He further requested that punishments be lenient, labor services be suspended, taxes and corvée be lightened, and that the military expedition against Jiaozhou be terminated. In the fifth year, he was formally appointed as Minister of Education (*Situ*).

He moved his residence to the Western Mansion on the western side of Mount Jilong, where he summoned renowned monks to lecture on the Buddha-dharma. He composed new melodies for the chanting of sutras and hymns. Emperor Wu...

Originally, he was fond of hunting pheasants. Emperor Wenxuan admonished him to desist. Toward the end of the Yongming era, when he was about to hunt pheasants again, Wenxuan submitted another memorial, saying:
"I have suddenly heard public rumor that you intend to hunt pheasants once more. As a subject, my feelings are trembling with agitation; my heart is filled with anxiety and dread."
Now, in the preservation of life and the maintenance of health, humans and beasts are no different; in cherishing one’s person and loving one’s body, self and other are no different.
Thus, the *Book of Rites* says: "Upon hearing its cry, one does not eat its flesh; seeing it alive, one cannot bear its death.

How can the dignity of a sovereign of ten thousand chariots be lowered to conform to the pleasures of a commoner? To kill innocents is to wound benevolence and harm fortune. A Bodhisattva does not kill, for [it shortens] their lifespan.
One’s life-span is prolonged; those who receive one’s gifts dwell in peace and security, free from fear; they do not afflict sentient beings, and their bodies are free from illness and suffering.
Your servant, observing these fruits of retribution, therefore exerts himself day and night, strenuously disciplining his body to serve the Dharma.

While Your Majesty has constantly relinquished wealth to cultivate merit, my private heart has long looked up with longing yet still regretted that it was insufficient; how could I have expected to witness such a thing today? First.

"To diminish one's meritorious karma and then suffer regret is difficult to remedy. I pray that Your Majesty will illuminate this sincerity of mine and graciously consider it with threefold reflection.

Although the Emperor did not fully accept his request, he held him in deep favor and esteem. He and Crown Prince Wenhui shared a common devotion to the teachings of Śākyamuni and were very close as brothers.
Wenxuan’s reverence and faith were particularly profound; he frequently held vegetarian fasts within the gardens of his residence and assembled the high officials of the court for these occasions.
The monastic community was assigned the tasks of distributing food and serving water, or he personally attended to these matters himself.

One night, he dreamed that the Heavenly King Tathāgata of the World of Universal Radiance in the East preached the Dharma-gate of the Pure Abode and Pure Conduct. Consequently, he composed the *Jingzhuzi* (Treatise on the Son of Pure Abiding).

"Pure Abiding" (*jingzhu*) is the Sanskrit term *poṣadha*, which means to abide in purity of body, speech, and mind according to the precepts. The work consists of thirty-one chapters in total. Its...
The Gate of Faith and Devotion states: "The Tathāgata takes pity on sentient beings, loving them as if they were his only child.

Therefore, he manifests a form sixteen feet tall to display his numinous countenance, so as to inspire joy and longing in sentient beings for the sight of him. Those who hear his voice realize the Way; those who behold his form attain liberation.
Although we today receive his spiritual essence, our delusions are heavy and our obstructions profound. Advancing, we do not behold the majesty of his marks and signs; retreating..."
That you do not hear the eightfold musical tones of eloquent discourse must be due to the extreme gravity of your karmic offenses and the firm entrenchment of your afflictions (*kleśa*).
You harbor deep anxieties regarding the miserable realms (*apāya*) from which there seems no way to escape; how could you permit yourself to remain complacent and indifferent?

If you do not fortify your resolve, forgetting your own body and casting aside your life to withstand toil and endure suffering, and if you do not bear your grief with profound compassion, I fear there will be no means to extinguish the blazing fires of your afflictions.
It is extinguished. The profound darkness of ignorance has not yet seen the end of its clearing. It is like a heavy prisoner in a dungeon enduring manifold sufferings:
bound by long shackles and great fetters, wearing golden clamps and bearing iron chains, with festering sores, filth, and putrid stench enveloping him from all sides;
yet he wishes to use this bed to seek an audience with the sovereign or his noble ministers. Though he may apply himself with single-minded diligence, by what means could he possibly succeed?

Why is this? Because one who is possessed of various evils and does not depart from the instruments of suffering cannot appear spontaneously before the King even if his shackles are removed, his chains cast off, and he is cleansed of filth and dressed in fine garments;

such a person remains obstructed by the King. Now, those who wish to turn to faith in the same manner and desire to behold the Tathāgata’s marks, signs, and radiant light must first purify their body, speech, and mind, washing away the defilements of the heart and the six sense-objects.

When passionate attachments are forever extinguished and do not arise, and the heavy obstacles of the ten non-virtues are purified until nothing remains, one’s karmic burdens having been eliminated and both inner and outer self being pure, one may then direct luminous contemplation toward Kapilavastu and establish a clear mind within the Jewel Land. Having cast off all worldly toil, one enters the gate of faith;
thus, one will surely behold the foundationless Dharma-body by looking upward with reverence. One should pay homage to all Buddhas and seek their compassion through repentance.
After having repented, one should constantly practice a mind that is supple and harmonious, a mind capable of endurance, a mind of non-negligence, a mind of tranquility,
a mind of true correctness, a mind free from distraction, a mind without greed or stinginess, a superior mind, a great mind, and a mind of compassion, kindness, and peace.

With a mind of excellent joy, a mind that transcends all [worldly] minds, a mind that protects sentient beings, a mind free from the notion of "mine," and the mind of a Tathāgata—one should give rise to such vast, supreme, and wondrous minds.

One should single-mindedly seek extensive learning, cultivate the concentration of detachment, uphold the precepts with purity, remain mindful of the debt of gratitude, always maintain a state of gladness, and never abandon sentient beings. Regarding the gateway of self-reproach for body and mind, it says: "The body..."

This is the root of suffering. Created and accumulated by oneself, it further increases evil karma within the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, one must especially and deeply reproach oneself. As the sutra says:
"When seeing the faults of others, one must not speak of them; when one has evil within oneself, one should confess it. The Book of Documents says:
"The gentleman extols the beauty of others and does not boast of his own goodness. Thus, the fundamental principle of both internal (Buddhist) and external (Confucian) teachings is the same.
The same applies here. As for why they are called "internal" and "external," these are fundamentally not distinctions of physical form; they arise solely from differences in the mind.

If a person who has left the household life contemplates emptiness and impermanence, feels weary of and seeks detachment from birth and death, and practices the supramundane Dharma, this constitutes the "internal. To deviate from this is the "external."
For those living as householders, to take refuge in and revere the Triple Gem, to uphold the precepts, cultivate goodness, and practice propriety and righteousness—this constitutes the "inner.

To act contrary to this is the "outer. If one wishes to practice cultivation, one must first reproach oneself. One should know that seeking progress is a provisional designation, whereas withdrawing for self-examination is the true Dharma.
When the darkness of folly is extinguished, the light of wisdom emerges; when the four marks [of conditioned existence] are transformed, the virtue of the precepts becomes manifest. Thus we know:
Integrity and withdrawal are the omens of advancement; greed for advancement is the sprout of decline. That which is obtained through seeking is empty;
when the mind clings to something, one grasps at it, resulting in the suffering of peril and downfall—this is the way of external paths. To withdraw and yet obtain is substantial;
because the mind has no attachments, one attains the eternal peace of the bliss of nirvana—this is the way of the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, one should know that the critical examination of mind and speech is the path of the Eightfold Noble Path, and the inspection of bodily conduct is the track of liberation.
Regarding the gateway of shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*), the Sūtra says: "When shame and remorse are fully possessed, one is able to extinguish the obscuration of darkness. It also says:

Shame and remorse are like iron hooks; they can restrain people from what is unrighteous. If one lacks shame and remorse, there is no distinction between such a person and the various birds and beasts.

The meaning of shame and remorse takes non-transgression as its foundation. Now, since this principle is subtle and difficult to refine, even for a single moment of thought, one may turn away from it in every direction and commit immeasurable transgressions. Because the transgressions are immeasurable, shame and remorse should likewise be immeasurable. Its...

The various branches of this school cannot be described in detail; let me briefly cite one aspect. The urgency of sustaining life lies in food and clothing. Consequently, the toil and turmoil involved in obtaining these are extremely profound.
Among the silks, floss, leathers, and hides required, there is not one that does not involve the destruction of life and the taking of living beings.
One nourishes one’s own skin and flesh by wearing the skin and flesh of others. Even down to the consumption of a single grain of food, it cannot be obtained without the expenditure of effort.
Entering through the mouth, one deliberates upon previous efforts and speculates about one’s own belly; food constantly flows in and out without ceasing.
Within it, one selects the refined and the fatty, ingesting what is soft and smooth while craving delicious flavors.

Devoid of shame or modesty, it undergoes transformation in an instant until it becomes a foul odor that cannot be approached. What wise person would give rise to greed for such food? If greed should arise, it is a great [delusion].
One must feel shame; how does this differ from the beasts and animals? Regarding the gate of enduring great insults, it is said:
"The Way arises from suffering and not from the fruit of pleasure; virtue is established through effort and is not something accumulated by the passions. Thus, a sutra says:
"Patience is the foremost path, for toward all sentient beings the mind is without obstruction. This is because when one dwells in suffering, there are many obstructions and much affliction.
One gives rise to unwholesome karma. That one now attains non-obstruction is truly because one cultivates non-obstruction while remaining within obstruction;
thus, though obstructed, one does not become obstructed. Since there is no obstruction within obstruction, is this not brought about by the power of patience?
The Sūtra states: "The Sahā world is a realm of the five turbidities, where the five pains and five burnings prevail, and all manner of evil retributions are present.

For this reason, those who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna come to this land in great numbers; they take the salvation of suffering as their provisions and the uprooting of affliction as their essential practice."
In this land, practicing virtue for a single day is superior to doing so in other pure lands for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Now, one who wishes to give rise to the vast mind and practice the bodhisattva path must inevitably tread upon perils and traverse treacherous terrain, undergoing all manner of hardships.

One must step through blazing fires and pass through frost and snow, encounter bitter suffering, and endure agonizing pain. Only those who can patiently accept such myriad sufferings may reach the site of enlightenment.
[To] practice. If these afflictions did not exist, from what would patience arise? It is by relying on these afflictions that my various virtues are produced;

that is to say, the host of worldly defilements constitutes the seed of the Tathāgata. You should know that patience possesses power and is the foundation of the merits of great beings—namely, enduring itching and pain, enduring discursive thoughts, enduring illness, enduring the suffering of hunger, enduring fatigue, and enduring cold and heat. Enduring...
Enduring sorrow and grief; enduring heat and affliction; enduring abuse without feeling shame or humiliation; enduring blows without resentment or obstruction; enduring desire without attachment;
enduring pride without turning away from the Path; enduring that which is difficult to endure; enduring that which is difficult to practice; enduring that which is difficult to do;
enduring that which is difficult to accomplish—one who can act in this way may truly be called one of great forbearance (*mahākṣānti*). As for the exhortation to increase [this virtue]:...
Entering the hall, one says: "The act of exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*) is the height of earnest devotion. Because such earnest devotion is aroused, the sentiment of wishing for goodness becomes profound.
There are two kinds of exhortation: exhorting sentient beings to practice the precepts and virtues so that they may possess the roots of all merit;
and exhorting the Buddhas to protect and deliver sentient beings, teaching the Dharma so that it may endure for a long time. Regarding the four evil realms throughout the ten directions, I now..."
I exhort all of you to practice the various precepts and observances, thereby attaining human birth.
To all people throughout the ten directions, I now exhort you all to cultivate the ten virtuous actions and attain rebirth in the heavens.

To all devas and humans throughout the ten directions, I now exhort you all to enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and escape the evil realms. To all learners (*śaikṣa*) throughout the ten directions, I now...
I now exhort all of them. To awaken from and examine all afflictions, and swiftly ascend to the stage of no-more-learning—I now exhort all the Arhats of the ten directions.
Knowing that this is not the ultimate state, but that there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle—I now exhort all the Pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions.
Having perfected the wisdom of great compassion to transform and teach all sentient beings—I now [exhort] the multitudes of humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles.
I now exhort all Bodhisattvas to realize the Tathāgatagarbha and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva;
I now exhort all Bodhisattvas to practice the ten perfections and swiftly ascend to the ten stages.

I now exhort all Bodhisattvas in Tuṣita Heaven to constantly turn the non-retrogressive wheel and swiftly descend to deliver all sentient beings. For those Bodhisattvas whose wisdom is not yet clear, I now...

I universally entreat all the Buddhas of the ten directions who have newly attained perfect enlightenment—the Vajra-destroyers of defilements who manifest the true nature—to turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
I now take refuge and entreat all the Buddhas of the ten directions who wish to relinquish their life-span: may you remain long in this world. Thus, to these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I now...
All [beings] exhort and entreat [the Buddhas], giving rise to such earnest and diligent resolve; therefore, I prostrate in worship. Regarding the gateway of rejoicing in the myriad doors of goodness:
because sentient beings are deluded by ignorance, they harbor much envy and a mind of superiority.

Consequently, when they see others practicing virtue, they conceive malicious thoughts, seeking to destroy and ruin it so that it does not reach fulfillment. Yet, the person before them has not necessarily suffered any loss in their practice.
Yet those who are envious falsely increase their afflictions and feverish distress; they augment delusion and karma, so that birth and death continue without end.

For this reason, the sages regulate the mind and control the will, practicing this sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). They likewise exhort all sentient beings to practice according to what has been taught.

All the subtle virtues possessed by the entire multitude throughout the ten directions—benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, filial piety, nourishment of parents, humility, reverence, and compassionate harmony—[are all rejoiced in].
As well as love and respect, integrity, and pure conduct—if there be such virtues as these, I now rejoice in them all.

Those householders who have renounced desire and uphold the Tathāgata’s precepts—the three refuges, the five and eight precepts, the ten wholesome precepts of the bodhisattvas, and all pure codes of discipline—those who have distanced themselves from ill repute: in all such merits, I now rejoice. [I offer] this meal to the Saṃgha.
Bestowing Dharma robes; bathing to remove the defilements of affliction; rescuing and gathering in those who are destitute, those suffering from hunger, cold, and exposure;
and providing medicine for those in the misery of illness and peril—such meritorious deeds as these, I now rejoice in them all. Making fine wells by desolate roads;
crossing people and goods with bridges and boats; and giving gardens, groves, ponds, flowers, and fruits to the Buddha and making offerings to the Saṅgha for those who are parched and exhausted.
They eliminate feverish affliction; their merit is truly immeasurable. Such virtues as these, I now rejoice in with all my heart.

Those who transcribe the sutras to circulate the Dharma teachings, light lamps to give rise to the clarity of wisdom, practice recitation and chant, or thoroughly resolve the various meanings and purports—if they further explain them to others, their hearts of joy increase manifold.
In such virtues as these, I now rejoice in with all my heart. May they be established.
All stūpas and shrines, halls and palaces, as well as jeweled spires; painted images and wooden statues, made of gold, silver, copper, stone, and the like;
those that transmit and depict the various marks and signs—manifesting the Dharma-body—I now rejoice in all such merits.

If there are those who construct monastic dwellings, providing beds, curtains, and bedding, so that those who have stilled their minds may find peace within the forest of meditation, whether entering or departing...
The gateways of suffering and emptiness, the sequential contemplation of cessation—such merits as these, I now rejoice in all.
The Tathāgata, with great compassion, has skillfully expounded all dharma-gates; may this act of generating rejoicing cause us to practice and study.
I rejoice in all śrāvakas who endure suffering to cross over birth and death; I rejoice in all bodhisattvas who do not abandon the sufferings of the evil realms. I rejoice.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, the fearless Honored Ones among devas and humans, are able to draw forth all sentient beings from the prison of the three realms.
May they cause all classes of sentient beings to fully attain the Buddha-way; therefore, I rejoice and prostrate in homage to all Buddhas.
Regarding the gate of dedication to the Buddha-way, it is said: "Dedication" has the meaning of non-attachment. It originates from all sentient beings cultivating [the path] completely...

Although one may practice the myriad deeds and sacrifice body, life, and wealth, the reason one fails to attain liberation from birth and death is that one remains attached to karmic retribution and is unable to relinquish it.

If one can refrain from clinging with the mind and practice the means of gathering and delivering others, dedicating even the slightest merit toward the path of the Buddha for the sake of all sentient beings, then one will no longer give rise to attachment toward karmic retribution; thus, regarding birth and death—
One is thus serenely liberated. Therefore, a sutra says: "Practicing according to what has been taught and dedicating [the merit] constitutes great benefit.
For this reason, all virtuous deeds performed should be dedicated; furthermore, one should exhort sentient beings not to cling to karmic rewards.

Whatever subtle roots of goodness practiced by sentient beings throughout the ten directions—such as benevolence, filial piety, humility, respect, loving-kindness, gentleness, and so forth—as well as loyalty and rectitude in cultivation [should likewise be dedicated].
Ritual propriety and wisdom; showing compassion by providing for the orphaned and the destitute—such worldly virtues as these are all dedicated toward the Buddha-way.

All the various ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists, such as scorching the body with the five heats, leaping from cliffs, plunging into water or fire, binding oneself in reverse, and other such acts of suffering—these immeasurable false views are now all dedicated so that they may together return to the path of perfect enlightenment. All purity...

Lay devotees take refuge in the precepts and practice the ten wholesome paths of action; even women are able to cultivate merit and skillfully expound the Dharma, transforming and developing manifold sublime blessings.
They dedicate these merits to all living beings so that together they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

All the assembly of disciples, upon hearing his voice, immediately attain realization and understanding; they cry out, "Welcome! and become bhikṣus, attaining the fruits of the four stages of the path through skillful means.
First, one contemplates emptiness, suffering, and impermanence; these are also dedicated for the sake of all sentient beings so that they may together proceed toward the unsurpassed path.

The Pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions, who have spontaneously attained the state of an enlightened one, deeply realized the truth in past lives and clearly understood the law of dependent origination.

They manifest or remain hidden to transform sentient beings, dwelling alone in the bliss of sublime tranquility. In this same manner, one dedicates all such merits, including those of all beings, entirely toward the Buddha-way. The [Pratyekabuddhas] of the ten directions...
Bodhisattvas, please recite the sutras and the Dharma. To those entering and emerging from meditative concentration, they exhort them to practice all manner of wholesome deeds.
These three types of goodness and all other roots of virtue are likewise dedicated to sentient beings, so that they may turn toward the Unsurpassed Way.

All such virtues, up to and including the fruits of the noble ones, cannot be fully exhausted by one who understands emptiness; for existence and non-existence have not yet been simultaneously transcended. May all [beings] be made to share [in these merits].
All [beings] alike enter the truly wondrous realm; those with minds attached to the marks of existence are all led toward the path of liberation.

Such are these bodhisattvas, whom I now exhort to dedicate [their merit]; having given rise to this mind free from attachment, I therefore prostrate in worship. Other passages are not recorded in full here.

Once the writing was completed, a banquet was prepared on a grand scale, and scholars and commoners were gathered to establish a lecture hall, where discussions were conducted with earnest and thorough exchange.
Everyone was moved to tears and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. In the ninth year, a great flood struck the capital, with the region of Wuxing suffering the most severe damage.
Emperor Wenxuan opened the granaries to provide relief to the poor and the sick; he established an infirmary north of his residence to care for them, providing both clothing and medicine.

In the tenth year, he was appointed Minister of the Secretariat (Shangshu Ling) and Governor of Yangzhou, while retaining his previous titles. Shortly thereafter, he was again appointed Minister of the Secretariat, with the addition of the title of Palace Secretary (Zhongshu).

[The] Record: Emperor Wu was unwell. An imperial edict appointed Wenxuan to assist in the administration of state affairs. Wenxuan had long been disinclined toward worldly affairs, so he recommended Xichang Hou Luan;
an edict was issued appointing Luan as his assistant. In the first year of the Longchang era, [Wenxuan] was promoted to the position of Inspector of Nanxu Prefecture.

That same year, his illness became critical, and he said to those around him, "There must be something unusual outside my gate. He sent someone to look, and they saw that the fish in the Huai River had all...
Suan floated upon the water toward the city gate and soon passed away at the age of thirty-five (*Qi shu*, *Guang hongming ji*).
Zhiguizi said: "I have once examined the practice of hunting; it was not seen during the eras of the ancient emperors. The *Yushu* says:"
"Who will bring order to my [realm's] flora, fauna, birds, and beasts? The *Shangshu* says: "As for the birds, beasts, fish, and turtles, let them all be at peace.
When benevolence toward things is such as this, how could it be his heart to drive them away and kill them? I have observed the debates among rulers and ministers during the Qi and Liang periods;
they often possessed a compassionate heart that loved all creatures. If this mind were fully developed, it would surpass the subduing of the violent and the abolishing of killing.

It is not difficult to encounter those who possess such [virtues]. As for Wenxuan’s *Jingzhu zi* (The Son Who Abides in Purity), his vows and practices are profound and pure, and he is fully endowed with both compassion and wisdom.
How long he has wandered within the ocean of the Buddhas cannot be fathomed by worldly intelligence.
Therefore, I have selected and recorded those words of his that are most essential, placing the treatise "A Remonstrance Against Hunting" at the beginning.
Wang Dashen said: "The preface and treatise possess the eye of great compassion. Among those who studied Buddhism during the Qi and Liang periods, figures such as Xiao Ziliang were truly rare;
his 'Gate of Reproaching Body and Mind' is especially a vital point of the Dharma."
Yunchu recently sent me a letter in which he described his own great power of aspiration from days past—to transcend the Buddhas and the Patriarchs.

It turned out that he had merely lost his mind and did not know how to seek it; only recently has he come to believe that for all the thousands of sages and ten thousand worthies, there is no dharma-gate that does not emerge from the single phrase:
"seeking the lost mind. This is the third [turning] of the cycle of birth and death for sentient beings.
This is the verification of resting when the realms are utterly exhausted. Nevertheless, I do not dare hastily join in his joy, for Yunchu’s mind of seeking was exceedingly deep and heavy;
with a mind of seeking, he sought a mind of non-seeking, searching for the mind by means of the mind.
Seeking and seeking again, you further employ countless stratagems and fabricate innumerable demons and spirits;
is this not an excessive indulgence of the mind? Your letter addresses both Confucianism and Buddhism with equal weight: on one hand, you cannot abandon Buddhism;
on the other, you cannot abandon Confucianism. As Confucianism and Buddhism contend within you, Zhu Xi once diagnosed this as a "hidden, subtle, and deeply chronic ailment."
"Alas! This is a great illness of the dissipated mind. Will Yunchu be able to awaken to it? Yunchu’s temperament is irascible;
he always delights in clutching a talismanic tablet and chanting, 'Swift as the Imperial Decree!
Who knows that he does not regard Mencius as the Supreme Lord Lao, stubbornly seizing upon some object to hold fast as a means of self-protection?"
This is indeed a great matter that deceives the mind. It is not merely a case of letting one's own mind go astray;
as for the various ailments mentioned above, I have already calculated them all through for Yunchu. How would I dare to join in congratulating him upon such things?
I then reflected upon this according to the Dharma; it was neither too light nor too heavy. To accord with what Yunchu had previously calculated, I produced the character "retreat" (tui).

Yet, fearing that Yunchu might have merely grasped at echoes in the void, I recently examined Ziliang’s transmission, which stated that the causal conditions of that episode are extremely essential to the Dharma.
It directly demarcates the boundaries between the paths of the heterodox and the Buddha, distinguishing them most clearly.
Illumination. I have therefore resolved to assist Xi by adding the character "tui" (to withdraw) [to his name].

In leaving behind this segment of karmic connection for future generations to develop further, the first essential point is to clarify the method for seeking the settled mind and the place where one gains entry. Zhu Xi spoke well on this:
it is not a matter of using the mind to seek the mind; it is simply that when a single thought is struck with awe, the mind is immediately present.
This is it. It is the point where one penetrates from beginning to end. Chengzi spoke well when he said:

"The myriad words of the sages and worthies are simply intended to lead people to take back their wandering minds and place them within the 'cavity' [of the heart], so that they may naturally seek the upward path.
If you can penetrate these two cases, the ailments mentioned above will suddenly vanish.
"Kill it! Kill it! Yun-chu, Yun-chu! What you said regarding that single phrase, 'seeking the lost mind,' is the very crux of studying the Buddha.

You have spoken with authentic lineage. Look at the Great Śākyamuni down to the various masters beginning with Bodhidharma—they made every kind of enemy and adversary of all demons and heterodox teachers."

What is the meaning of the Way? It is simply because all demons and heterodox teachers have lost their minds, causing them to wander through the three realms and transmigrate within the six paths for ten thousand kalpas of long night. Therefore, you masters have earnestly and piteously exhorted them to study and learn.
The Buddha spoke as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; the Patriarchs said not a single word was established. This is solely to bring about awakening.
It is simply their original mind. When the various demons and heterodox practitioners suddenly awaken to their own original mind, they are immediately Buddhas; they are immediately Patriarchs.

Originally, they are members of one and the same family. Why do you take such pains to let them go out and create trouble, becoming demons or heterodox practitioners and thus inviting for yourselves this wretched state of long nights? Is what Yun-chu said not indeed based on a genuine lineage?
However, it is essential that, as Ziliang has judged, one must distinguish between the Buddha-way and the external paths; only then will the boundaries be clear.
Both the demonic path and the external paths consist of those of supreme intelligence. Yet their very intelligence leads them astray.
Because they pursue progress without ceasing, they lose their true mind. *Tou!* This is the demonic. *Tou!* This is the externalist. This is the Old Śākyamuni.
Once he lost his mind and, driven by insatiable greed for progress, walked straight on until he reached the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. "Alas, you outsider!
he cried, and with a single thought of sudden alarm, he abruptly withdrew from that state back to his original mind, whereupon it was finally revealed.
This is why Ziliang said that seeking progress is a provisional name, while withdrawing to examine is the true dharma; this is truly the essential point of the Dharma. You—
Look at Old Śākyamuni: he has not only made himself the sworn enemy and adversary of all demons and external paths;

he has also, within his own single body, made himself the sworn enemy and adversary of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense faculties (*indriya*), the six objects of perception (*viṣaya*), and all mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
What is the meaning of this? It is simply because the five aggregates are the great surging waves of the mind’s attachments.
"Disciple! Go, go! Go toward the six sense faculties. Go, go! Go toward the six sense objects. Go, go!
Go toward all mountains, rivers, and the great earth. Go, go!
Go toward the cycle of rebirth within the three realms and the wandering through the six paths. Our Buddha felt compassion for this, and therefore—
With bitter grief and piteous lamentation, he exhorted him to study and sought to turn his ears toward the truth.
When the talkative old man had spoken thus, Yunchu’s old ailment flared up again; he beat his belly in frustration, thinking:
"The Elder Śākyamuni serves as the eyes for all humans and devas. Truly, he is the Great Compassionate Father, the Great Benevolent Teacher, the Great Sage of Buddhist Learning!"

Yet, you have penetrated it thoroughly. I now urge you, Da-shen and Qiu, to cast aside worldly perceptions and devote yourselves single-mindedly to honoring Śākyamuni and seeking the awakening of a Buddha.
*Du!* Yun-chu has once again lost his mind. Have you not seen how Huineng spoke well?
"The Buddha-dharma exists within the world; it does not depart from worldly awakening. To leave the world in search of Bodhi..."
Ti! It is just like seeking the horns of a rabbit. Right view is called "transcending the world," and wrong view is called "the world.
When both the wrong and the right are completely cast aside, the nature of Bodhi is perfectly manifest. *Du!* (A shout of realization)
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Seven:
The Biography of Master Fu.
Master Fu’s name was Xi; his courtesy name was Shanhui. He was a native of Yiwu. He was born in the fourth year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty.
He lived in the home of Fu Xuanzi in Shuanglin Township. At the age of sixteen, he took as his wife a woman of the Liu family named Miaoguang, and they had two sons, Pu Jian and Pu Cheng.
It happened that a Śramaṇa from India named Song came to visit him and said, "I and you both made a vow together before the Buddha Vipaśyin.
Now, the robes and bowl in the Tuṣita Heaven remain there; on what day shall we return? Thereupon, he ordered [Pu Jian] to go to the water's edge.
As he gazed at the reflection, he saw a circular halo and a jeweled canopy. The Great Being smiled and said, "The forge produces many pieces of dull iron;
the gate of a skilled physician is filled with the sick. Saving sentient beings is the urgent task—why dwell on that pleasure? Huisong pointed to the summit of Mount Song and said:
"This place is suitable for dwelling. The Great Being personally tilled the soil and resided there.

When someone stole beans, wheat, melons, or fruit, the Great Being would immediately give them away, placing the items in a basket or carrying-net for the thief to take. He engaged in manual labor by day and practiced the Way at night.

There, he beheld the three Tathāgatas—Śākyamuni, Suvarṇapuṣpa, and Dīpaṃkara—emitting light that enveloped his body. He considered himself to have attained the Śūraṅgama-samādhi and practiced asceticism for seven years.
Desiring to guide the multitudes of beings, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, he dispatched a disciple to present a letter at the imperial court, saying:
"The Great Being of Future Liberation, Śākyamuni (Śubhamati), beneath the twin śāla trees, addresses the Sovereign, the World-Saving Bodhisattva:

I offer these teachings of superior, middling, and inferior goodness, hoping that you may accept and uphold them. As for the superior goodness, it is briefly based on the empty mind and takes non-attachment as its core principle, with formlessness as its..."
Taking *nirvāṇa* as the fruit, the superior summary of these teachings takes the cultivation of the self as its foundation and the governance of the state as its core principle.

As for the rewards of peace and happiness in the heavens and among humans, the inferior summary takes the protection and nourishment of sentient beings as its aim—overcoming cruelty and abolishing killing—and universally causes all the people to observe the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa*).
Now, hearing that Your Majesty honors the Dharma and desires to expound upon its principles, [I have] not yet fulfilled my long-held aspiration.
Huai sent his disciple Fu Yang to announce his presence. He Chang, the Director of the Grand Music Bureau, presented his letter. By imperial decree, he was summoned to the palace.
Emperor Wu asked, "From whom have you received instruction? Whence do you come? He replied, "I have come from nowhere; I have come from no one."
The Master’s conduct was likewise so. On another day, Emperor Wu invited him to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

As soon as the Great Being ascended the seat, he struck the lectern once with a ruler and then descended. The Emperor was astonished. The Great Being asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not."
The Great Being said: "Once, when the Great Being had finished preaching the sutra, one day during the course of his lecture, the Emperor arrived.

The assembly all rose, but the Great Being remained seated upright without moving. The assembly reported, 'His Majesty has arrived here; why do you not rise? The Great Being replied, 'If the ground of the Dharma were to move, all things would be unsettled.
He subsequently returned to the Double Grove (Śāla-vana) and composed the *Inscription on the Mind-King*, which says: "Contemplate the mind, the empty king, originally wondrous..."
Inconceivable. Formless and signless, it possesses great spiritual power capable of extinguishing a thousand calamities and accomplishing ten thousand virtues.

Although its essential nature is empty, it can bestow the Dharma rules. When observed, it has no form; when called upon, it has sound. It serves as the Great General of the Dharma, transmitting the scriptures through the mind-precepts.
Like the taste of salt in water or the presence of lacquer-blue within color, it is definitively existent, yet its form is not seen. This is the Mind-King.
It is likewise. Dwelling within the body, entering and exiting through the gateway of the face, it responds to objects and follows conditions with sovereign non-obstruction;

all that it does is accomplished. One realizes the fundamental consciousness-mind; the consciousness-mind sees the Buddha. This mind is the Buddha, and this Buddha is the mind. In every thought-moment, there is the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha.
If you wish to achieve success early, let the mind of precepts govern yourself. Purify the precepts and purify the mind; the mind is then...
This is the Buddha. Apart from this mind-king, there is no other Buddha. If you wish to attain Buddhahood, do not defile yourself with a single thing.
Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and anger is real. Upon entering this Dharma-gate, one attains Buddhahood while sitting upright.
Having reached the other shore, one obtains the *pāramitās*. A true seeker of the Way observes their own mind; knowing that the Buddha is within, they do not seek it outwardly. This very mind—

This is precisely the Buddha; this is precisely the Buddha, which is precisely the mind. When the mind clearly recognizes the Buddha, it thoroughly understands the mind. Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no mind.
That which is not the Buddha cannot be fathomed; it is incapable of any function. Clinging to emptiness and lingering in stillness, one drifts and sinks therein.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace in this. The Great Being who clarifies the mind awakens to this primordial resonance. The nature of body and mind is wondrous; its functioning is without limit.

It changes. Therefore, the wise person lets the mind rest in its natural freedom; do not say that the mind-king is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, for it can cause the physical body to act either erroneously or correctly.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, appearing and disappearing without fixed certainty. The nature of the mind transcends emptiness; it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely.
For this reason, I urge you: guard yourself well. Every moment of action leads once again to drifting and sinking. [Only through] purity...
The mind and intellect are like the gold of the world; the Dharma-treasury of Prajñā resides within both body and mind.

This treasure of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is neither shallow nor deep. Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have realized this original mind; those who encounter it through the right conditions do so beyond the categories of past, future, and present.

Furthermore, there is a verse that says: "Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; Morning after morning, one rises together with him. Whether rising or sitting, they are ever相随 (in constant accompaniment); In speech and silence, they are one."
In their dwelling, they are not separated by even a hair’s breadth, like a shadow following a form. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of speech.
He also said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally solitary. It can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet it does not wither along with the four seasons.
He further said: "Empty-handed, one grasps a hoe; walking, one rides a water buffalo. When a person passes over a bridge...
[The Master] passed away. As the bridge was crossed, the water did not flow. In the first year of the Taizhuan era, Sengtouduo entered *parinirvāṇa* at Lingyan Temple on Mount Ke.
The Great Being said, "Master Seng has been waiting for me in Tuṣita; I must not remain. On the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"This body is a collection of manifold sufferings and is utterly loathsome. One must be cautious regarding the three karmas and cultivate them with diligence."
The Six Perfections. "If one falls into hell, it is extremely difficult to escape. The disciple asked, "May I hear of the Master’s original departure [from his previous life]?
He replied, "I have come from the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven to deliver you all; I am next in line to succeed Śākyamuni. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"There is a bodhisattva who comes from Tuṣita Heaven, whose faculties are sharp and keen, and who swiftly accords with Prajñā"—this refers to my own person.
"So it is. Having spoken these words, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away at the age of seventy-three (*Wudeng Huiyuan*, *Fozu Tongzai*). Master Zhigu said:

"When the First Patriarch entered the Liang dynasty, his spiritual capacity was not in accord with the Emperor's. He departed for Shaolin; people take this to mean that Emperor Wu of Liang regretted losing him.
However, at that time, figures such as Master Baoci and Great Master Fu both transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal and propagated the Great [Dharma]."

The Vehicle of Multiplication. Wandering amidst the rafters, Emperor Liang clung to the causal conditions of merit and sin, coveting minor fruits and becoming intoxicated by conditioned Buddhist rites;

he remained mired in them without awakening. A single speck of dust strikes the Milky Way, obscuring the original truth; the bright sun stands in the sky, yet the overturned basin receives no light. Is this not tragic?
Out of the Bodhisattva’s profound compassion for sentient beings who are deluded and inverted, [this work was written] regarding the Transmission of the Great Being.
It is worth contemplating.
Wang Dashen said: "A person from within the house speaks the words of those within the house; reading this, every pore of one's body breaks into laughter.
Zhu Xi indeed found much to admire in the verses of the Great Being (Mahāsattva). How could I not go to visit?
In the school of Master Zhu (Zhuzi), were they not sated day and night with the talk of everyday domestic life? When the Five Houses flourished, their preaching was like thunder.
To the one who said "mind is Buddha," he gave a punch; to the one who called himself the "Lord of the Myriad Phenomena," he gave a kick.
Thus, even the Great Master Fu ended up as a "granny Chan" practitioner. Let those outside the gate try to guess it! Finished.
Ultimately, they are both the same and yet distinct.
*The Biography of Layman Jingshan*, the eighth in the *Biographies of Laymen*.
The Layman of Mount Jing, Lu Fahe, was a man of unknown origins. During the Qi and Liang dynasties, he lived in seclusion on Baili Island in Jiangling.
His clothing, food, and dwelling were in every respect identical to those of a monk observing the precepts. Elderly residents had seen him since childhood;
his countenance was always serene, and no one could fathom his nature. He later resided at Mount Zishi in Gao Yao County, Jingzhou.
He departed without cause. Shortly thereafter, there was the barbarian rebellion and the surrender of Hou Jing to the Liang dynasty.
The Layman addressed Yuan Ying of Nanjun, saying, "I, a poor monk, shall assist you, my patron, in striking them down. Yuan Ying replied, "Hou Jing is achieving merit for the state."
"Why did you strike him? [He] did not understand. When Liu Jing besieged the Tai City, the Layman was at Mount Qingxi at the time.
Yuan Ying went to ask him, "What is the situation regarding Liu Jing? The Layman said, "When an ordinary person gathers fruit, they should wait for the proper time of ripeness;

it will fall of its own accord without being plucked. Donor, simply wait for the time when Jing ripens; why trouble yourself to ask? Yuan Ying pressed him further, and he replied, "He will also be defeated."
He was likewise unable to prevail. Emperor Jing dispatched his general Ren Yue to attack Prince Xiangdong at Jiangling.
The Layman (Jushi) then went to Xiangdong to request military support. Ren Yue summoned eight hundred youths of the various Mian tribes and swore an oath with them at Jiangjin;
he then set out for Xiangdong. Furthermore, Hu Sengyou was sent to lead over a thousand soldiers to augment his army. The Layman laughed and said, "As for my troops and horses..."
It was extremely formidable. "What need is there for this? [he said]. In Jiangling, there were many shrines to spirits, and people’s prayers were invariably efficacious.
However, since the Layman’s army set out, no prayers have been answered. People believe that all the deities have followed him into the field. Upon reaching Chisha Lake, he faced Yuan Yue.
The Layman boarded a light boat, unarmored, and descended with the current. When he was one *li* from Yue’s army—
He returned and said to his officers and soldiers, "I observe that the dragon-army of the enemy remains asleep and motionless, while the dragons of my own army are leaping with vigor.
We shall attack them immediately. He then launched fire-ships ahead, but the wind blew against them. The layman (gṛhapati) took up a white-feathered fan and fanned the wind.

The wind immediately turned back. When Huiyao saw the Liang soldiers walking upon the water, his army was utterly defeated; everyone threw themselves into the water to their deaths, while Huiyao fled and his whereabouts remained unknown. The lay devotee said, "At noon tomorrow, you shall find him. When the time arrived and he had not been found, people asked about it. The lay devotee replied, "Previously, when the waters of this island were receding, I erected a pillar there and told the donors: 'If you see the pillar, you will know where he is. At noon, they went to look and indeed saw the pillar. They followed its direction and found Huiyao, who was hiding in a cave. He was brought out and returned to the capital. The lay devotee said, "I have already seen him. People asked, "How did you know? He replied, "When I first saw the pillar, I knew at once that he would be here. The people marveled at this and spread the word far and wide. Later, the Emperor summoned him to the palace and bestowed upon him the purple robe and the title of Master of the Dharma (Fashi). He lived in seclusion for many years and passed away at the age of seventy-nine. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Venerable Senglang. The lay devotee died at the age of ninety-six. He was from Wuxing and his secular surname was Chen. He was a man of profound wisdom and great virtue. During the Yongming era, he was granted the title of Great Master of the Dharma (Dafashi). His disciples numbered over a thousand. The lay devotee’s name was Zhang Rong; he was a man of the Jinling area and his secular surname was Xu. He was a man of exceptional intelligence and character. He served as a high official under the Qi dynasty, yet he always maintained a humble demeanor. He deeply revered the Triple Gem and was devoted to the practice of giving. He built monasteries and provided for the Sangha with great generosity. He was a contemporary of the Master of the Dharma, and the two were close friends. When the Master of the Dharma was about to pass away, he entrusted his disciples to Zhang Rong. Rong cared for them with all his heart until they reached adulthood. He died at the age of eighty-one. He was a man of exceptional intelligence and character. He served as a high official under the Qi dynasty, yet he always maintained a humble demeanor. He deeply revered the Triple Gem and was devoted to the practice of giving. He built monasteries and provided for the Sangha with great generosity. He was a contemporary of the Master of the Dharma, and the two were close friends. When the Master of the Dharma was about to pass away, he entrusted his disciples to Zhang Rong.
