"Although this is indeed the actual thief, it is merely a signpost for him. Why do you not seek him out beneath that signpost?
Following these words, he indeed saw the thief in the water, clinging to the signpost with his arms and holding his head up; as soon as the thief’s nose emerged, he seized him.

When the thief saw the lay devotee (upāsaka) and begged for his life, the lay devotee said, "The King has a karmic connection with you; there is certainly no cause for other concerns. Furthermore, the King shall surely obtain you as a patron (dānapati)."

[This was] due to his power. Xiangdong indeed released him and appointed him as the Governor of the Commandery. When the Wei army besieged Jiangling, he joined forces with Yuao to provide relief, fighting with great vigor;
it was just as the lay practitioner had said. After the lay practitioner had pacified Yuao, it happened that the Shu rebels were about to arrive.
He requested to guard Wuxia to await them, whereupon he led all the troops there and personally hauled stones to fill the river. For three days, the water did not flow.
He laid iron chains across [the river]. When Prince Ji of Wuling indeed dispatched Shu troops to cross, the situation at the mouth of the gorges became desperate;
they could neither advance nor retreat. The Layman engaged in battle with Wang Lin and utterly destroyed them. As for the Layman’s character, his words rarely issued from his mouth.
Whenever he engaged in debate, his eloquence was unrivaled. Throughout his life, there were many miraculous occurrences.

Once, beneath a large tree north of the city of Xiangyang, he marked out a square of two chi on the ground and ordered his disciples to dig there; they unearthed a tortoise measuring one and a half chi in length.
He struck him with his staff and said, "You wish to leave, but you cannot; you have been here for several hundred years. Had you not encountered me, would you ever have seen the light of heaven?

He then conferred upon him the Three Refuges. When he first entered the layered mountains, there were many people afflicted with malignant diseases. The lay practitioner gathered medicinal herbs to treat them;
usually, they were cured after no more than three doses. They immediately requested to become his disciples. Within the mountains, there were venomous insects and fierce beasts.

He was granted the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), whereupon he ceased biting and stinging. Whenever his ship moored along the shores of rivers or lakes, he would always post a notice saying, "Releasing living beings at this spot.
Fishermen who arrived there found nothing at all; if they did catch something, a great wind and thunder would immediately arise, but once they released it, the weather would settle.
When leading troops, he strictly prohibited fishing and hunting among his soldiers. Should anyone secretly violate this, fierce beasts would appear in the middle of the night.
He wished to bite [the boy], or perhaps he had lost his boat. A junior disciple playfully severed the snake’s head. Later, they went to the lay practitioner (upāsaka).
The practitioner asked, “Why have you killed a snake? The disciple was startled. Pointing [at the head], the practitioner said, “Is this not what you killed?

Only then did the disciple see that the snake’s head was biting the crotch of his trousers; he shook it, but it would not fall off, which terrified him. The practitioner ordered him to perform repentance for [his deed].

The snake performed meritorious deeds. Furthermore, there was a man who tested his sword on an ox, severing its head. He then went to a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), who said, "An ox with its head severed has come to claim its life from you;
the summons is extremely urgent. If you do not perform meritorious deeds for it, the retribution will arrive within one month.
The man did not believe him. A few days later, he indeed died. When Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty ascended the throne, he [honored] the lay practitioner...
He was appointed as the Commander-in-Chief (Dudu) and Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Yingzhou, enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiangye County. Subsequently, he was promoted to Minister of Education (Situ).
His several thousand followers were collectively addressed as his "disciples. He transformed others solely through spiritual arts and techniques, rather than through legal punishments.

As for his method of collecting market taxes, he placed an empty casket with a lock between the roads; it had a single opening at the top to receive money, and merchants calculated their goods to pay the tax. From this point on—
He entrusted [the items] to a chest. At evening, the officials opened the chest and sorted its contents; the tax items were then sent to the treasury.

At that time, the lay practitioner (居士) was amassing a great fleet of warships at Jiangxia with the intent to raid Xiangyang. He also intended to enter Wuguan Pass, but Emperor Yuan sent someone to stop him.
The lay practitioner said, "Fahua is one who seeks the Buddha; he does not even aspire to the seat of Śakra or Brahmā, so how could he plot for the throne?"
"I merely had a karmic connection through incense offerings with the Buddha Śūnyarāja during the time of my former lord.
Seeing that retribution must surely come upon my lord, I came to his aid. Now that you have been suspected, your karma is fixed and cannot be altered.
When the Wei army mobilized, the lay practitioner went from Ying to Hankou, intending to head for Jiangling. Emperor Yuan again sent someone to stop him, saying: "In this region..."
"He can defeat the rebels; however, he need only remain stationed in Yingzhou and need not move. The lay practitioner (jushi) then returned to the prefecture.

He plastered the city gates and donned a coarse white cotton shirt, trousers, and a slanted cap, with a thick rope bound around his waist. He sat upon a reed mat all day long before finally removing them.

Upon hearing that Emperor Yuan had been defeated and extinguished, he placed the mourning garments for the deceased at his chest and wept as he received condolences. Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty sent...
Prince Yue of Qinghe led troops to attack Wei and rescue Liang. Upon the fall of Jiangling, the Layman (Jushi) submitted the entire province to Qi.
Emperor Wenxuan appointed him as the Grand Marshal (Dadu du) over the military affairs of ten provinces and the Duke of Taiwei.

When the Layman entered court, he did not address himself as a subject, but simply called himself "The Layman of Jing Mountain. Emperor Wenxuan personally hosted a banquet for him and bestowed upon him one million coins and a thousand articles of goods.
He possessed one hundred *qǐng* of prime farmland and two hundred male and female slaves; his living resources and household goods were commensurate with these.

He emancipated all the slaves he had acquired as a layman, saying, "Each may go according to their own conditions. His money and silks were distributed in alms until they were exhausted in a single day.
He converted the residence granted by the government into a Buddhist temple and lived in a single room himself. Within three years, he served twice as Grand Minister (*tàisǒng*).

The Commandant [Wang] was free from illness, yet he announced to his disciples the date of his death in advance. When that time arrived, he burned incense, paid homage to the Buddha, sat upon his corded bed, and passed away.
After the bath and prior to the enshrouding, the corpse had shrunk slightly to about three chi in length. Later, by imperial decree of Emperor Wenxuan, the coffin was opened to examine it;
it was found to be empty. The lay practitioner possessed prophetic utterances that anticipated events of the Qi dynasty, all of which were subsequently verified (Beishi).

Zhiguizi said: "The man from Wu, Mr. Wang, says that while the Layman [Zibo] was within the Buddha-dharma, he attained the pleasure of 'singing in the wind and playing with the moon'—the same aesthetic interest as that of Zihan and Zhonggong.
Lu Sheng of Ruijin agrees with Mr. Wang's words. Yet some would claim that the Layman was startled by supernatural wonders. How tragic!"
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume IX:
Biography of Prince Zhaoming, Tong.
His courtesy name was Deshi. He was the eldest son of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty. His mother was Lady Ding, the Noble Consort. He was compassionate and magnanimous.

He was respectful and frugal, serving the Buddha with devout sincerity. He habitually maintained a vegetarian diet. On the day he received the precepts, sweet dew descended before the hall. He was able to penetrate the meanings of the sutras;
all offerings and gifts he received were used entirely for religious services. He passed away in the seventh year of the Putong era. His crown prince was born intelligent and wise;
at three years of age, he received the *Xiaojing* and the *Lunyu*, and by five, he had read all five classics. This was in the first year of the Tianjian era.

He was established as the Crown Prince. On the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year, Emperor Wu presided over the Xuan hall and performed the capping ceremony for the Crown Prince at the Dajidian.
At that time, Emperor Wu greatly propagated Buddhism, and the Crown Prince also deeply believed in and honored it, perusing all the various scriptures.

Within the palace, he established the Huiyi Hall (Hall of the Meaning of Wisdom) and invited renowned monks to engage in discourses. He once composed a treatise titled *Explaining the Meaning of the Two Truths*, stating:
"The methods for clarifying the Way are not of a single kind. To summarize the essentials, they do not transcend the objects [of cognition] and wisdom.

At times, the meaning is clarified through the objects; at other times, practice is manifested through wisdom. As for the two truths, this refers to clarifying the meaning by way of the objects. If...
If one is deluded regarding their direction, the three realms of existence will not cease. If one attains their wisdom, all myriad entanglements are cast off. As for what is called the Two Truths:

the first is the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), and the second is the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya). The Ultimate Truth is free from both existence and non-existence; the Conventional Truth is both existence and non-existence.
"Existence and non-existence are both provisional names; departing from existence and departing from non-existence is the Middle Way. This true Middle Way takes non-arising as its essence.
Since the conventional is a provisional name, it takes arising phenomena as its essence. Huichao asked: "That which is floating, false, and conditioned is called the conventional;
that which is free from existence and non-existence is called the ultimate. I do not yet understand whether this floating and falsity..."
Are they identical with reality, or should they be considered different? The answer is: that which is known by worldly people has "arising" as its essence;
that which is known by those who have transcended the world has "non-arising" as its essence. When formulating a treatise based on human conventions, one should speak in this manner.

However, if one discusses reality itself, it is precisely emptiness; in the conventional sense, one points to emptiness and calls it existence. Clarified according to this principle, they cannot be distinct from one another. Furthermore, [the questioner] asks: since the ultimate and the conventional...
[The questioner] says: "You speak of them as being of one essence. I do not yet understand whether the True Truth (paramārtha-satya) also possesses movement and activity.

Is it that movement and activity are unrelated to the True Truth? He answers: "The True Truth is quiescent and devoid of any characteristic of movement or activity. It is the deluded consciousness of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) that falsely perceives movement. Again he asks: "I do not yet understand:
is it that there is movement and ordinary beings falsely perceive it, or is it that there is no movement and ordinary beings falsely perceive it? He answers: "If there were movement..."
If there is movement, it cannot be called "transverse vision" (*pārśva-darśana*). It is because there is no movement that vision is transverse. [Xiao Ya] asked:
"If dharmas have no arising or movement, then there should be only one truth (*satya*. He replied: "This principle is eternally quiescent; this itself is one truth.

Transverse vision and the arising of movement are likewise one truth. There should be only two, and one cannot say there is only one. Xiao Ya asked: "The True Truth (*tattva-satya*) is called 'true'."
"Is this truly real or not? He replied, "It attains the reality of true reality. Again he asked, "When a Bodhisattva realizes suchness, does he forget both the mundane and the real?
He replied, "Because he forgets both the mundane and the real, it is called 'realizing suchness. Again he asked, "By forgetting both the mundane and the real, how can one attain true reality?
He replied, "If one were to preserve the mundane or preserve the real, how could that be called 'true reality'? It is precisely because both are discarded that [true reality is attained]."
This refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Fayun asked: "The realm known by the sages is the ultimate truth;

I do not yet understand whether the wisdom that knows it is itself the ultimate truth or the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). He replied: "That which knows is wisdom, and that which is known is the realm.
When wisdom comes to merge with the realm, it may be said to be identical with the ultimate. Fayun asked again: "Is the person who possesses this wisdom the ultimate truth, or..."
"This is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). He replied, "If one calls a person of wisdom [a 'person of truth'], that is conventional truth.
Again he asked, "I do not yet understand how a person of conventional truth could possess the wisdom of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). He replied, "The sage is able to forget the conventional;
therefore, they are able to attain ultimate truth. Fapeng asked, "If ordinary people perceive existence while sages perceive non-existence, then it should follow that..."
Ordinary people see only that which exists according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); sages should see the great void and non-existence. The answer is:
even the "great void" is not what the sage perceives. The name "great void" arises from mutual dependence; since it is produced through dependence, it is likewise something seen by ordinary people.
Again he asked: "Ordinary people perceive both emptiness and existence; can it be said that these two are one? He replied:

"Speaking from the perspective of ordinary people, existence is truly different from non-existence; speaking from the standpoint of the sages, there is nothing that is not identical to existence. Jingtuo asked:
"I do not yet understand whether the sages who perceive the Truth see it gradually or see it all at once. He replied: "They see it gradually. Again he asked: "The signless and empty mind is one..."
Seeing this principle, one realizes that the myriad phenomena are simultaneously quiescent. I do not yet understand for what reason the realization of the Truth (tattva) must proceed gradually.

The answer is: From the state of an ordinary person to that of a sage, there are varying depths of understanding. While the Truth itself is inherently empty and still, this does not preclude the possibility that its realization occurs gradually. Furthermore, I inquire:

Once the signless (animitta) is attained and all myriad existents are forgotten, is it the case that everything is entirely forgotten, or not? The answer is: Once the signless is attained, the myriad...

There is total forgetfulness. The explanation of the meaning of the *dharmakāya* states: "The *dharmakāya* is empty and tranquil, far removed from the realms of existence and non-existence, and uniquely liberated beyond cause and effect.
It cannot be known by cognition, nor can it be discerned by consciousness. How could it be something that can be discussed or debated through names and designations?
Yet, wishing to manifest this principle, one cannot remain silent. In India it is called *dharmaśarīra*; in this land [China], it is called..."

Regarding this *dharmakāya*: if one considers its actual substance, it is a designation for self-nature (*svabhāva*); if one considers it through verbal expression, it is a name established through mutual dependence.
"Dharma" has the meaning of a norm or rule as its essence; "kāya" has the meaning of having a body or substance. Because it is the substance of the norm, it is called the *dharmakāya*.
To state its substance briefly: it is the eternally abiding body; it is the diamond body (*vajrakāya*). If one subjects it to further rigorous investigation: its...
It is not so. If it were definitively a vajra, it would become a name and a mark; if it were definitively permanent, it would become a spatial location.
What is called "permanent" is originally a provisional name, and what is termed "vajra" is originally a metaphorical description. As for discussing its actual substance:
Thus, their nature is identical to non-arising. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall among all phenomena. Hence, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The body of the Tathāgata is not a body, yet it is a body; it is immeasurable and boundless, without footprints, without cognition, and without form."
It is ultimately pure. It is pure in its lack of cognition, yet it cannot be said to be non-existent; it is called "wondrous existence," yet it is not existent.

It is free from both non-existence and existence—this is what is called the Dharma-body. Dharmamegha asked: "I do not yet understand whether this eternally abiding Dharma-body is something obtained through the myriad practices.
He replied: "Within the realm of names and forms, it is that which is obtained through the myriad practices. He asked again: "Since it is [attained] by means of the myriad practices..."
"What has been attained—how could this be without marks (*animitta*)? If it were necessarily without marks, how could it be attained through the myriad practices?
The answer is: "Nameless and markless—how could there ever have been attainment? It is by means of names and marks that we provisionally say there is attainment. Again, [the questioner] inquires:

"If the myriad practices truly exist and the fruit of Buddhahood is truly attained, how can you say that being markless means there is absolutely nothing attained? The answer is: "The questioner’s mind remains fixed [on these dualities]."

In reality, there are the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*). Now, it is said that these ten thousand practices are themselves empty; how then could there be any real fruit to be attained? Again, [the interlocutor] asks:

"There are currently sentient beings who cultivate the ten thousand practices; I do not yet understand why you categorically claim they do not exist. The answer is: "What ordinary people perceive, they call 'existent.

When examined according to principle, however, the ten thousand practices are in fact non-existent. Again, [the interlocutor] asks: "The sutras speak of the eternal abiding (*nitya-sthiti*). [The Master] says: "It is taken as..."
"Sublime Existence. As it is a provisional designation, what is meant by "sublime existence"? The answer is: it is spoken of as "sublime existence" by relying upon names and marks;

yet in principle, it transcends names and marks—what "sublimity" and what "existence" could there be? Fapeng asked: "I do not yet understand whether the title 'Dharmakāya' refers solely to the sublime source, or if the golden form of sixteen feet is also the Dharmakāya?
The answer is: "If discussed from a comprehensive perspective, both the fundamental and the manifested [aspects] are..."

This is so. To speak of them separately, [the Buddha] abides only in the eternally present (*nitya*). Again, it is asked: If he abides only in the eternally present, he should not have a physical body.

If one takes the *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) form as being inclusive, why would it be called the Dharma-body? The answer is: Since the eternally present exists, how could its wondrous essence be without a body?

Even the *zhànglù* form is able to serve as a model for sentient beings; therefore, it may be universally designated as the Dharma-body. Again, it is asked: If the eternally present is free from all burdens...

Only then can it be called the *dharmakāya*. If one possesses the constraints of the six-foot form, how can it be called the *dharmakāya*? He replied: "Sentient beings look up with devotion and thus falsely perceive the six-foot form.
The six-foot form does not truly exist; if it were real, what constraint would there be? In the fourth month of the first year of the Putong era, sweet dew descended upon Huiyi Hall.
The Crown Prince was profoundly filial and respectful toward his parents; whenever he sat or rose during his leisure time, he did not dare to act [otherwise].

Facing south, whenever he was summoned to enter, he would sit upright and remain so until dawn. When Lady Ding fell ill, the Crown Prince attended her morning and evening, his robes never loosened from his waist.
Upon her death, he took no food or drink; every time he wept, he would faint from grief.

Following the Emperor’s command, he was forced to take food and drink, yet by the day of the burial, he had consumed only one *sheng* of wheat gruel and had not tasted any vegetables or fruit. His constitution was naturally...
In his maturity, he reduced [the administration] by more than half. Since his investiture with the cincture, Emperor Wu had him oversee the myriad affairs of state.

As petitions from the various offices piled up before the Crown Prince, he became proficient in all matters of governance; he analyzed right and wrong with such precision that even the finest details were made clear.

When there were errors or transgressions, he would calmly instruct them to be corrected, never once accusing or impeaching a single person. In adjudicating legal cases, he frequently granted full pardons or leniency. He departed...
He occupied the palace for over twenty years without maintaining singers or performers; he merely summoned scholars of literature to discuss the classics.
At a time when the imperial army was campaigning in the north and grain prices in the capital were high, the Crown Prince wore coarse clothing and reduced his meals.
Whenever heavy rain or deep snow persisted, he dispatched his attendants to travel the roads to inspect the homes of the poor. To those who were destitute and wandering, he secretly provided relief.
He was granted further rewards. He also provided large quantities of cotton and silk to make short jackets and trousers for distribution to those suffering from the winter cold;

for those who had died and lacked the means for burial, he prepared coffins and shrouds. Whenever he heard that the common people, both near and far, were burdened by the hardships of taxation and corvée labor, he would immediately assume a solemn expression.
In the second year of the Datong era, an imperial edict was issued to mobilize the people of Wu Commandery, Wuxing, and Yixing to dredge the Great Channel in order to drain the Zhe River.
Because Wuxing was afflicted by floods, the Crown Prince requested that Emperor Wu temporarily suspend these labor services. The Emperor responded with a gracious imperial decree.

In the third year, in the third month, he fell ill; knowing that he would not recover, he ultimately did not report his condition to the throne. He passed away in the fourth month at the age of thirty-one.
His posthumous title was bestowed as *Zhāomíng* (Śrīprabha). (*Liangshu*, *Guang hongming ji*).
Zhiguizi said: "In my observation of Prince Zhaoming’s treatise, he may truly be called one who has clearly perceived the Buddha-dharma;
it is something that the rulers and ministers of the Liang could not have attained. The Prince was benevolent, filial, magnanimous, and wise, and his every action conformed to the rules of propriety.

Had he been entrusted with the legacy of the Liang and diligently bestowed its bounty upon the four quarters, a wind of pure harmony might have been awaited daily. Yet, the course of heaven is now fraught with difficulty."
The morning star suddenly fell; with the uprising of a single man, the state of Jiang crumbled like a collapsing embankment. How tragic!
Wen Zhongzi said, "The Qi and Liang states perished despite their cultivation of ritual purity and fasting; it was not the fault of Śākyamuni. It was simply because of fixed karma.
Even Heaven could not grant its pure protection to the Crown Prince. How lamentable!
Wang Dashen said: "His conduct corresponds quite closely with the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*. Zhaoming was truly a seed of the Buddha. I do not value his Buddhist teachings;
I value his benevolence, filial piety, magnanimity, and clarity—these constitute the seed of the Buddha.

When it comes to discussing the Dharma to its most subtle and profound depths, it is merely the ignorance of what is known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). It is a pity that he did not encounter [the patriarchs] from Bodhidharma downwards."
The great masters of old pricked them with needles of acute pain to strip away the ignorance of "knowable objects.

Yet, while they sought only to transcend existence and non-existence, they remained stuck, as before, on the very ground of existence and non-existence—uttering nothing but "zhi-hu-ze-re" (the empty particles of Chinese rhetoric).
When these "zhi-hu-ze-re" reach a point where there is no other way, one must ascend to compose a tower of blue, yellow, white, and black; this is precisely where it lies.
The disposition of a literary man is not the seed of a Buddha; how could he possess the karmic fortune of a celestial son, and how could he achieve the great deeds of an emperor?
This is because his heels remain planted within the ranks of scholar-monks, causing him to become merely a hollow and empty figure.
Alas! With a disposition of benevolence, filial piety, magnanimity, and clarity, and having once studied the Classic of Filial Piety...
As for the *Sūtras*, the *Analects*, and the Five Classics, they have been left at the end utterly disorganized; is this not a pity?
Why is it that Wang Dashi (Wang Dashen) delighted in practicing the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Heart Sūtra*, the *Gāthās of the Seven Buddhas*, and the *Platform Sūtra*?
Zhu Xi once judged them all to be right—ten thousandfold right—saying: "The Buddhist learning of the Six Dynasties people was merely talk."
These are merely matters of refined talk; when spoken of, they appear so ethereal and empty as to be wearying.
This is why Bodhidharma came to China and swept all such things away; it was only upon reaching Huineng that there was finally a place to begin the actual work of practice.
It is a pity that so many exceptionally brilliant and resolute seekers find it difficult to enter this gate.
Furthermore, upon entering this gate, there are thorns reaching to the heavens; one by one they fall into them and cannot emerge.

They are left utterly disarrayed, with every ailment and every pain arising solely because those who practice the Way merely shift between movement and stillness, while those who discourse on principle merely dwell in existence.
The Unsurpassed One holds up his flower; everyone takes the finger for the moon—when have they ever truly known the moon?
To enter this gate is no small matter; throughout a thousand lives and ten thousand kalpas, one must achieve total realization here, with nothing remaining unresolved.
If one does not understand this, there will be no end to it throughout all future kalpas. How can one simply stop once they have managed to speak well or act with a pleasing appearance?
If it were merely a matter of being able to speak well or acting with a pleasing appearance, that would be the end of it.
Among the children of this village, people such as these are as numerous as hemp and millet. There is no need for your honor’s illustrious presence within this gate.
Nevertheless, as it is said that matters cannot be viewed from only one side, since you have already graced us with your presence, we shall not refuse to open the gate of expedient means.
We invite you to come and play within it once. If you wish to play within this Dharma-gate, [please do so].
By all means, do not shift between movement and stillness. There is no picking up or putting down of existence or non-existence. Movement and stillness are merely objective conditions;
existence and non-existence are merely the conjectures of the mental faculty (*manas*). They have no connection whatsoever with the Mind.
If you possess great power, strike one blow for movement, one blow for stillness, one blow for existence, and one blow for non-existence. Strike!
When there is neither movement nor stillness, all the "brain-bags" of the various demons are rent asunder;
not even a shadow is seen. The light of the mind naturally manifests. *Duh!* Even that light of the mind is struck with one blow. *Lai!* One has leaped out of the sphere of the mind (*cittamātra*);
the sphere of the mind can no longer constrain him. Is this worthy guest not indeed transcending the Buddhas?
"Is he not a man who has transcended his ancestors? This old fellow here treats people with a light and disrespectful mind.
I wonder how you, a refined scholar, could bring yourself to such a hand. Stop, stop, stop! For now, let us employ a minor expedient.
Go, and do not concern yourself with whether it is mind, object, or the faculty of consciousness. When you encounter..."
When in a state of stillness, look only at where the mark of stillness resides. When encountering movement, look only at where the mark of movement resides.
When encountering non-existence, look only at where the mark of non-existence resides.
When encountering existence, look only at where the mark of existence resides. Looking thus, one becomes dazed and vacant.
Utterly topsy-turvy! Meeting people, you do not know they are people; seeing things, you do not know they are things.
Once this moment has passed, you will be delivered to the gate of a great master to receive a blow of the staff. You, sir, must now prepare yourself.
"This is the business of the Radiant Dharma-gate. Master Wewen Xiucai and the other monks consulted one another, saying:
"If Linji’s staff and Deshan’s rod were placed in the hands of Wang Dashi, they would surely blind the eyes of all people under heaven.
Truly, these words are true!
Biographies of Lay Practitioners, Volume Ten:
Liu Ming, Liu Yu, Liu Xiang, and the Biographies of Feng and Li;
Liu Lingyu, whose courtesy name was Qiu. A native of Nanyang, he moved his residence to Jiangling. During the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he served as the Magistrate of Dangyang.
Having resigned from office and returned home, he was summoned by the Prince of Yuzhang to serve as his *biexia* (deputy) in Jingzhou, but he did not accept.

In the third year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, he was summoned again to serve as a *tongzhilang*, yet he likewise declined. When the Prince of Jingling heard that Lingyu was profoundly versed in the Buddhist teachings, he sent a letter to convey his intent.

Summarizing his departure toward the east, he said: "I have left behind the traces of my service and the dust of the jade and silk ribbons; my heart has long sought solace in the rivers and lakes. Though we have not met, we are as close as kin;

hearing of your reputation was like meeting you in person from olden times. Yet the thought of your turning back your carriage fills me with anxiety; though I wish to observe the ritual of honoring one at their gate, there is no means to do so. You stand out as uniquely remote and noble."

Truly difficult to uproot, his cultivation of both the substantial and the refined was brilliant and discerning. There were those who spoke of the "man who has forgotten words," capable of discussing the boundary between the celestial and the human;
yet how could they have anticipated this soaring like a phoenix or wheeling like a crane, with a mind so focused and gathered, observing the mysterious wandering of one who shoots at the Hao River?
To bend the Dharma-friends of the *Kucī* and *Gṛdhra* mountains, to expound the Three Vehicles to the destitute sons, and to awaken the Two Truths for those in ignorance—this is the cause.

How magnificent it is! The reply states: "Though my dragon-like limbs lie prostrate with illness, I have attended to the irrigation during three seasons. I let forth the lingering echoes of the Dharma in the mountains and marshes, entrusting my twilight sentiments to fish and birds.
Is this not surely due to the profound grace of Yao and Shun, and the vast bounty of the Duke of Zhou and the Marquis of Shao? Far... [text ends].

Once the marshes had been drained, his benevolent regulations were first established; he did not dare harbor any suspicion regarding the gathering of firewood or grazing, respectfully fulfilling the duty of reporting the presence of frogs to the carriage.

At home, he wore coarse cloth garments and observed the perpetual fast while worshipping the Buddha. He annotated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and lectured on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Dīrgha-āgama* and *Madhyama-āgama*.

Because the western sandbars of Jiangling were distant from the population, he moved his residence there. In the second year of the Jianwu era, an imperial edict summoned him to serve as a National Preceptor.
The Doctor did not accept [the invitation]. That winter he fell ill. At midday, white clouds hovered about the eaves and doors;
the fragrance filled the room, and the sound of a stone chime resonated clearly from the air. He passed away on that day at the age of fifty-eight (*Nan Qi Shu*; *Guang Hong Ming Ji*).
Mingxiu was a monk of renowned virtue. A native of Geguo in Pingyuan, he was twice nominated as a *xiucaoi* (excellent scholar) during the Yuanjia era.

At the transition between the Song and Qi dynasties, he lived in seclusion to teach, declining repeated summons to serve. He subsequently resided at Sheshan. Having heard of Sengyuan’s long-standing reputation for moral integrity, he went to visit him at Dinglin Temple.
When Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty wished to see him at the temple, Sengyuan asked Mingxiu: "If the Son of Heaven..."
"Come, layman! How would you respond to this? He replied: "A man of the mountains and marshes should simply carve out a hollow in a brick wall to escape.

If I decline and yet do not receive permission, I shall follow the precedent set by Dai Gong. Formerly, when Dai Yong remained in high retirement and refused to rise, the imperial court bestowed upon him the attire of a mountain recluse.
Thus it was said: 'He withdrew and returned to Mount She,' where the Emperor bestowed upon him bamboo."

He wore a crown made of bamboo shoots and leaves that were as pliant as his will. When he first arrived at the mountains, an old villager admonished him, saying, "The mountains abound with venomous snakes and fierce tigers;
you cannot dwell here. Xiu Lie replied, "Among poisons, none is more virulent than the three poisons. A person of loyalty and integrity can tread upon fire and water;
what power do snakes and tigers have to harm me? Thereupon, he settled there. He dwelt in a state of tranquil stillness for some twenty years. At that time...
The Daoist Gu Huan composed the *Yixia lun* (Treatise on the Barbarians and the Chinese), intending to suppress Buddhism and promote Laozi. Xiu Lie commented on it, saying:

"As for those who take learning as a mirror for living beings and establish teachings in the midst of heaven; who observe the celestial patterns to gauge transformations and maintain them without further discourse—this is the profound depth of governing the world, the ultimate reach of Confucius and Laozi.
Yet, to act before things have yet come to be, to fully illuminate and exhaustively examine conditions, to see that diverse beings share a common principle, and to refine away the false..."

Returning to the truth is the rectitude of divine efficacy and the magnificence of Buddhism. Thus, the Buddha clarified its fundamental principle (*mūla*), while Laozi perfected the preservation of life.

Those who merely cling to life remain obscured, whereas those who clarify the fundamental principle attain penetration. Nevertheless, when one rests in stillness within the Great Way, even if obscured, one is not deluded.

When movement proceeds from its fundamental source, principle becomes pervasive and illumination reaches its ultimate limit. Thus, when one’s study attains what is truly to be learned, one can provide sustenance for all living beings and establish a teaching honored within the realm.
By acting through non-action, one may extinguish habitual tendencies, reverse the flow [of samsara], and transcend both humans and devas.
Once, while lecturing on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* with Chan Master Fadu, he suddenly beheld gold in the middle of the night.

The light illuminated the chamber; within the light were pavilions and manifested Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. In the seventh year of the Yongming era, he donated his residence to establish Xixia Temple.
He dreamed that a Buddha was emitting light from between the cliffs; though he intended to construct [a statue], he passed away before completing it.
Subsequently, my [disciple] Zhongzhang, together with Fadu, fashioned a three-zhang-one-foot-plus image of Amitāyus Buddha and concurrently established an Avalokiteśvara [sanctuary].
Yin Shi-zhi completed his father’s aspirations with a statue. His younger son, Shan-bin, styled Xiao-ruo, was able to carry on his family’s legacy.
During the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, he rose to the rank of Court Gentleman Attendant (Sanqi Changshi).

At that time, Fan Zhen authored the *Shenmie lun* (Treatise on the Extinction of the Spirit), which Xiao Chen and Cao Siwen both challenged with formal arguments. Emperor Wu also issued an edict to refute Zhen’s treatise, ordering Shi Fayun to present [his rebuttal].
There were twenty-six individuals in total, including princes, dukes, and nobles, each of whom wrote a reply expressing their conviction that the spirit is not extinguished.

Among them, Shan Bin’s letter was the most profound in its meaning. His text read: "I am honored by your gracious communication and the imperial decree you have shown me, in which Your Majesty examines the *Discourse on the Extinction of the Spirit*.

Its origins are deep and its purport far-reaching; how could it be fathomed by the likes of deer or rabbits? Each receives understanding according to their kind, and perhaps each rejoices in what they perceive."

I have seen it and received it with full devotion; I am overcome with joy, as if dancing for delight. Those who debate are limited by their own sight and hearing; how could they reach such vast and distant truths?

With eyes that see but a hundred years, their minds remain deluded regarding the three periods of time. To claim that once the physical form and soul have perished, the spirit and consciousness are likewise extinguished—this is both far removed from the Buddhist scriptures and contrary to the teachings of Confucius.
How can one discuss the Ultimate Way or speak of subtle principles with such a person? Indeed, as for clarity...

Thus, there are rites and music; in the unseen realm, there are ghosts and spirits. For this reason, Confucius established a model by responding to inquiries about death with knowledge, and King Wen of Zhou founded his teachings so that his many talents might continue after his passing.
The *Shi* praises the "Three Sovereigns dwelling in heaven," and the *Shu* records that the "ancestors have arrived.
These are all matters set forth in the historical records, clear and manifest. Now, because things are conditioned and dependent, they must perish; yet karma—

Because they are created, they are impermanent. Thus, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) combine and dissolve together like smoke; the four subtle elements (*catvāraḥ paramāṇavaḥ*) are hollow constructs that vanish like fire being extinguished.
I venture to say that the Way of the Divine Intelligence is neither karma nor conditions. Because it is neither karma nor conditions, though it undergoes transition, it does not perish.

Because it can condition and can perform karma, suffering and joy result in distinct retributions. This is the sublime proclamation of the Buddha (the Able One), which those in official robes [should uphold].

Furthermore, although the teachings follow divergent paths, their underlying principle remains one and the same. Your Majesty’s wisdom encompasses both emptiness and existence, and your insight reaches the ultimate source of the divine.

Thus, you have given expression to your sacred intent by personally inscribing these imperial calligraphies, extensively extolling the supreme teaching to awaken those in deep ignorance and ensuring that students forever cast off doubt and confusion.
That you have shown such boundless favor and left none behind is truly a matter of both joy and sorrow. Later, he served as Acting Governor of Beiyanzhou under the command of the *jie*.
He died in office. He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Secretary (Zhongshu Ling) and conferred the posthumous name Zhi (Nanshi;

Hongming ji). Liu Shiguang, whose given name was Xiao, was a native of Pingyuan. At the age of eleven, upon reading the "Xiaoyao" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, he was immediately able to explain its great principles to his guests.
As he grew older, he became widely learned and accomplished in literature. Subsequently, he devoted himself wholeheartedly to the study of Buddhism and remained celibate.
He did not serve in office. The divine monk Zhigong encountered him at Xinghuang Temple and rose in surprise, saying three times:
"Retire from the world to study the Way; remain pure to ascend to the truth. At the age of thirty-one, he composed the *Gechong lun* (Treatise on the End of the Leather [Body]).
Its summary states: "As for the physical form, it is a substance devoid of consciousness. As for the spirit, it is a nature endowed with consciousness. Consciousness does not exist in isolation."
Relying on ignorance, they establish themselves; thus, the body is but a lodging for the spirit—a mere inn. When death arrives, the spirit departs from here to go elsewhere.
Once the spirit has departed from here, what use is there for the lodging to remain? Once the spirit has gone elsewhere, what is there to sacrifice at?
Is it not for this reason that the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius were otherwise? Indeed, the rise of ritual and music—
The emergence of sacrificial vessels and ritual offerings arises from a decline in sincerity; the arrangement of ceremonial ranks and formations stems from the corruption of customs.

To spread the spirit-tablet, to set out the inner and outer coffins, to present funeral offerings, and to construct burial mounds—these are intended merely to provide a place for the filial son to express his remembrance.

Now, one should prune away what is cumbersome and elaborate, striving instead for frugality and simplicity, so as not to wound the feelings of those who remain and to accord with the Way of the Supreme Person. When the breath has ceased, there is no need for...

The soul is restored. Having washed the hands and feet, the body is encoffined. One thousand coins are used to purchase a coffin, a single shroud, an old skirt, shirt, robe, headcloth, pillow, and shoes.
Beyond these items for the funeral procession, the usual contents for the coffin, and the supplementary offerings set aside for the ritual, not a single thing shall be bestowed.
Once the encoffining is complete, the body is placed in an open carriage and returned to the ancestral mountain. A site is obtained as it may be; once the ground is sufficient, a pit is dug. The pit—

The coffin shall be large enough to accommodate his feet; there is no need for broad tiles, nor is it necessary to labor over mounds or plant trees. Do not provide sacrificial feasts, nor set up couches or mats.

As for the ancestral sacrifices and the succession of descendants, these matters have been severed by my likeness [the image]. Let the rites cease with my own person; this will not harm the teachings of the world.
In the spring of the following year, someone planted a persimmon tree in his courtyard. Shìguāng said, "I shall not live to see its fruit. When autumn arrived...
He passed away. His relatives and friends composed a eulogy for his conduct and conferred upon him the posthumous title "Master of Upright Integrity" (Zhengjie Xiansheng).

His cousin Yan-du, whose given name was Jie, lost both parents while still young; his grief and emaciation nearly extinguished his very nature. Upon reaching adulthood, he served his paternal grandparents and elder siblings with profound filial piety and fraternal devotion.
By nature, he loved cleanliness and purity. When his elder brother had already chosen a day for his marriage, Yan-du heard of it and fled, whereupon the matter was abandoned by the local commandery.
He was appointed as a clerk (zhubù), but did not accept. When the official in charge insisted that he take up the post, he hung the summons upon a tree and fled once more.
Yandu deeply believed in the Buddha-dharma; he had previously listened to lectures at various temples on Mount Zhong with Shi Guang.

Consequently, they built a hermitage together by the eastern stream of Songxi Temple, with the intention of spending their final years there. In the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era, he passed away at Shi Guang’s residence.
At the age of thirty-one, he left a testamentary instruction that no successor be appointed. His funeral rites and mourning period were largely similar to those of Shi Guang.
His fellow disciples jointly inscribed a stele with his epitaph, and he was posthumously titled Chushi Yuanzhen (Retired Scholar Yuanzhen). (Liangshu)
Yu Yanbao, whose name was Xin, was a native of Xinye. He was widely learned in the classics, histories, and the auxiliary sciences of astronomy and divination (*weihou*).

By nature, he valued tranquility and simplicity, and was particularly fond of forests and springs. His ten-mu estate had mountains and ponds occupying half its space; he lived on vegetarian food and worn clothing, never engaging in commercial enterprise.
Once, while returning from a mountain retreat in Juzhong by boat, he was carrying one hundred and fifty *shi* of rice when someone [encountered him].
He entrusted thirty *shí* of grain to be carried for him. Upon arriving home, the person who had been entrusted with the load said, "You have thirty *shí*, while I have one hundred and fifty *shí*.
Yǎnbǎo remained silent and allowed him to take as much as he wished. A neighbor was falsely accused of theft and recklessly implicated Yǎnbǎo.
Yanbao took pity on him. He therefore pawned his own collection of books for twenty thousand coins and instructed a disciple to feign being the man’s relative to pay the debt on his behalf.
When the neighbor was spared from punishment, he came to thank Yanbao. Yanbao said, "I took pity on an innocent person throughout the world; how could I expect a personal thanks?
Emperor Wu of Liang had been close friends with Yanbao since their youth. When the Emperor raised his army, he appointed Yanbao as the Secretary of the Pingxi Commandery.
He did not submit. During the Putong era, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, but he declined on the pretext of illness and did not rise to the post.

In his later years, he established a *daochang* (meditation hall) within his residence, where he performed prostrations and repentance rituals at the six periods of the day. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* once every day.
One night, he suddenly saw a Daoist practitioner who called himself Master Yuan; his demeanor was most extraordinary, and he addressed Yanbao as "Master Shangxing. He bestowed upon him—
He departed with incense in hand. In the fourth year of the Zhongdatong era, while napping during the day, he suddenly woke up and said, "I wish for Master Gong to come again;
I cannot remain here long. Having finished speaking, he passed away. The entire household heard a voice in the air proclaiming, "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Pure Land of Amitābha.
He was seventy-eight years old at the time. When Emperor Wu heard of this, he issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title "Master of Upright Integrity" (Nanshi).
Liu Xuanwen, whose given name was Huifei, was a native of Pengcheng. From his youth, he was widely learned and possessed literary talent.

He began his official career as a *xing canjun* (acting assistant commandant) in the Legal Office of the Prince of Ancheng under the Liang dynasty. Once, while returning to the capital, he passed through Mount Kuang and met the reclusive scholar Zhang Wenyi.

They took great pleasure in each other's company, and Liu developed the intention to spend the remainder of his life there. He subsequently resided at Donglin and further constructed a garden on the northern side of the mountain, which he named...

He resided at Ligou Garden (Líjiù Yuán), where people of the time called him Master Ligou. He devoted himself to the meticulous study of the Buddhist scriptures and was skilled in both seal and clerical scripts.
While in the mountains, he transcribed over two thousand scrolls of Buddhist sutras by hand; those he regularly recited numbered more than one hundred scrolls.

Day and night he practiced the Way with tireless diligence, earning the admiration of those far and near. When Emperor Jianwen governed Jiangzhou, he sent him a footstool and a staff. Commentators [have said]:...

It is said: nearly three hundred years after the passing of Master Yuan, there first arose the flourishing era of Zhang and Liu. [Liu Xiaoxiu] died in the third year of the Datong era; his writings are lost.
His name was Xiaoxiu, and he was a native of Wan in Nanyang. He served as a regional secretary (zhongcóngshìshǐ) and later moved to Xunyang.

By nature he was straightforward and resilient against cold. He was fond of Buddhist scriptures and strictly observed the monastic precepts. Residing at Donglin, he worked diligently in the fields to provide for the mountain community.
Whenever a monk committed a transgression, he would immediately assemble the community before the Buddha to perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) and flog him;
many repented their faults. He passed away in the third year of the Putong era. Within his chamber, an extraordinary fragrance was perceived. At the same time, there was Ruan Shizong.
His name was Xiaoxu. A native of Chenliu, he was also renowned for his pure reclusion. In the final years of his life, he abstained from meat and alcohol, serving the Buddha with devout sincerity.
He regularly made offerings to a stone image that had previously been damaged; wishing to repair it, he prostrated himself with the utmost devotion.
One night, it was suddenly restored (Nan shi).
The layman Xiang left behind his name; he was a man of the Northern Qi. He dwelt in seclusion among the forests and wilds, eating from trees and drinking from mountain streams.

Having attained a silent resonance with the Dharma of the mind, at the beginning of the Tianbao era, hearing that the reputation and teachings of the Second Patriarch, Master Ke, were flourishing, he sent him a letter, saying: "The shadow arises from the form..."
Arising, the echo follows the sound; playing with shadows, one tires the body. Not realizing that form is the root of the shadow, one raises the voice to stop the echo;
not knowing that sound is the source of the echo. To eliminate afflictions while seeking *nirvāṇa* is like removing the form to extinguish the shadow;

to distance oneself from sentient beings while seeking the fruit of Buddhahood is like silencing the voice to seek the echo. Thus we know that delusion and awakening are one path, and folly and wisdom are not two.
Distinctions arise where there is no name; by giving names to things, right and wrong are born. Principles arise where there is no principle; by positing principles, disputes begin.
Illusions are not real—whence comes "right" and whence "wrong"? The false has no substance—what is empty and what exists?
Know, then, that gain is nothing gained and loss is nothing lost. Before I have had the honor of paying my respects in person, I venture to set forth this meaning. I prostrate myself.
I look forward to your reply. The Second Patriarch spoke again in verse: "I have fully observed the intent of your coming, which is entirely as it truly is;
the principle of the profound mystery is ultimately no different. Originally, you mistook the mani-jewel for a mere pebble, but now you have suddenly awakened to its true nature.
Ignorance and wisdom are fundamentally not distinct; you should know that all phenomena are thus. Out of compassion for those who cling to these two views, I shall set forth my words."
Setting down my brush, I have composed this writing: "Observe that one's own body and the Buddha are without distinction; why need one seek that which is beyond remainder?
When the layman received this verse, he immediately went to pay his respects and receive the master’s seal of transmission (from the *Wudeng Huiyuan*).

Feng Yan was a native of Jizhou during the Northern Qi dynasty. Having been recommended as a Confucian scholar to enter the imperial academy, he heard that Dharma Master Huiguang was propagating the teachings in Ye City.
He thought to himself, "I have already extensively studied both the Daoist and Confucian traditions, yet regarding the Buddhist school, I have not yet developed deep faith.
I shall go to visit Huiguang to choose whom to follow. Upon his arrival, he encountered Huiguang delivering a lecture; he listened with rapt attention for a long time.
His doubts and obstructions were instantly dispelled. He struck his head in prostration and vowed to take refuge for the rest of his life, subsequently becoming a disciple.

He investigated the essentials of the Dharma with all his heart and constantly engaged in self-examination. When others came to him for instruction, he administered medicine according to their ailments, often moving them to tears.
He would say: "Practitioners must not trust this ignorant and deluded mind to seek out the long and the short; you must recognize it as a deceitful thief."

If you seek out the faults and evils of others and do not inquire after their virtues, then the sense of self will gradually subside. You must constantly observe the mind; for one's own transgressions are many.
Though dwelling in the world, there is no true flavor therein. This mind leads me upward as far as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, yet brings me back down to the hells.
It constantly entices and deceives me like an enemy, or like a beloved slave. How can I ever nourish this thieving mind and allow it to seek fame?
This is like creating a carbuncle or a woodworm; it is merely a profit. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Always take the mind as your teacher, do not take the mind as your teacher.

To be able to recite [the scriptures] at eight years of age but fail to practice them at a hundred years of age does not save one from the urgency of the moment. At that time, there were those who transmitted and copied these words, which the world calls the *Pǒngxīn Lùn* (Treatise on Supporting the Heart).
While at Guāngmén, Chōng kept his head bowed and restrained his breath, daily preparing rice gruel. Once he had finished serving the monks, he would personally wash the vessels.
He stayed overnight before the hearth. He took one and a half bundles of mugwort, using half as a cushion for his back and half as a seat.

Just as the light of dawn began to stir, the porridge was already cooked. After midday, he carried the food to deliver it to those prisoners in the jail. Wherever he passed on his way there and back, those who recognized him cleared a path for him.
Even when he encountered large crowds, they would be the first to provide him with whatever he needed—whether water or fire, or brooms for sweeping—according to his requirements.
There was nothing that he did not fully prepare for his duties. When he had a little leisure from his work, he would preach the Dharma according to his speech, never complaining of fatigue.
Thus he passed away at Kuangmen (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
Li Yuē’s courtesy name was Mínqiān. He was a native of Píngjí in Zhàojùn. Having lost his father while still a child, he served his mother with filial piety.

At the age of twelve, he was appointed as a Counselor to the Secretariat by Wáng Zàn, the Prince of Guǎngpíng of the Wèi dynasty. From the Qi dynasty through the Sui, he was repeatedly summoned but did not respond.

Upon the death of his mother, he grieved so deeply that he became emaciated until his bones were visible. After the mourning period ended, he donated his residence to establish a *gānlán* (monastery) and withdrew from worldly life to travel for study, reading extensively.

Regarding both internal and external scriptures and teachings, he took refuge in the Buddha Vehicle. Throughout his life, he neither drank wine nor ate meat, and his speech was never harsh or violent.

When relatives and guests gathered, he would set out the sacrificial vessels and, sitting upright all day long, he inspired such solemnity among the young and old that none dared to be lax or indolent.
Later, they said to one another, "Now that we have seen this noble person, we finally realize the lack of virtue in our own ranks. He was benevolent by nature.

He was fond of practicing charity. When there were disputes in the district over the unequal distribution of property, Ziyue would provide his own wealth to supplement the shares of those who received less, making them equal to those with more;
the brothers felt inward shame and subsequently yielded to one another in mutual deference. Once, while out walking, he happened to see thieves cutting his vegetables, so he silently avoided them.
A servant caught someone stealing grain, but Ziyue comforted the thief and sent him away, saying, "You are destitute..."
This was caused by his own distress; he could not be held accountable. Once, during a year of famine, he lent several thousand *shí* of millet to his fellow villagers.

When they were unable to repay it, they all came to express their gratitude. Ziyue prepared wine and food to entertain them, then took up the contracts and burned them before the villagers, saying, "The debts are settled.
I hope you will not take this to heart. The following year, when the harvest was bountiful, the debtors vied with one another to repay the grain.
He did not accept it. Later, there was a great famine, and he provided gruel to feed the starving; those whom he saved numbered in the tens of thousands.
He established a large burial mound to collect and inter the corpses of those who had died on the roads. When spring arrived, he distributed grain and seeds to the impoverished.

The people of Zhao were grateful for this, and when they spoke of his descendants, they said, "These are the ones saved by Officer Li. A guest remarked that Ziyue possessed many hidden virtues (*yin-de*), to which Ziyue replied: [I have done nothing].
What is called "hidden virtue" (yin-de) is like tinnitus: one hears it alone, and no one else knows of it. Now, what I have practiced you all know;
how can this be called "hidden"? The guest spoke again: "Master Yue, as for the doctrine of retribution, Buddhist scriptures record it, yet why is it absent from the secular classics?
Master Yue said: "The accumulation of good brings remaining blessings; the accumulation of evil brings remaining calamity. High...

Waiting at the gate for the seal of office; sweeping the graves and awaiting the arrival of the funeral procession—is this not retribution? The Buddhist scriptures state that the cycle through the five realms of existence has no end;
is this not what Jia Yi meant when he spoke of "a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, never beginning to reach an ultimate limit"?

As for such cases as Gǔn becoming a yellow bear, Wàngdì becoming Dùyǔ, Bāojūn becoming a dragon, Niú'āi becoming a beast, and Péngshēng [becoming a boar]—are these not manifestations of the same principle?

The Yellow Mother became a pig; Xuanwu became a turtle; Deng Ai became an ox; Xu Bo became a fish. Is this not what is meant in the Buddhist tradition by the transformation and reception of different forms?
The guest said, "Xing Zicai once asked: 'How could the latter incarnations of pine and cypress transform into the common *chū* and *lì* trees?
I believe this to be so. Subi Yue said, "This is a discourse on things that are not analogous. Transformation—"
"Because of the mind. Since wood has no mind, the guest was unable to raise further objections. He passed away at his home in the eighth year of the Kaihuang era at the age of sixty-six.
Among the men and women of Zhao, there were none who did not weep, saying, "How is it that we have not died, yet Officer Li has died?

Those who attended his funeral numbered more than ten thousand. His wife was of the Lu clan of Fanyang; she possessed virtuous character and was a widow when her son Yao passed away. [He received] funeral offerings.
He gave away [the grain] without accepting anything in return. He said to the elders of his district and village, "The Army Commandant was always fond of practicing charity.
Although he has now passed away, how can we allow his will to be thwarted? He then distributed five hundred *shí* of grain (from the *Sui Shu*).
Zhiguizi said: "In my compilation of the accounts of the various gentlemen from Liu Ming onwards, I have traced their deeds;

for the most part, they left behind the world and its fetters, soaring beyond the realm of material things, resting their minds in the domain of purity and stillness, and exerting themselves on the path of compassion and patience."
Truly, he was sufficient to still the restless and compete with those at the periphery of the stream; he disseminated the pure wind for a hundred generations.

As for Layman Xiang, his realization arose from his own fundamental mind, and he profoundly penetrated the ancestral Way; he was one who transcended all categories and peerless, whose wondrous distance was unfathomable.

If one were like Yan Zhitui, Wang Gu, Yao Cha, Xu Xiaoké, and their ilk—though they were able to dwell in detachment and maintain their practice without interruption—they nonetheless served with compromising flexibility within a chaotic court, attending to successive dynasties.
They attempted to emulate Yang Xiong’s composition of the *Fayuan* while feeling as much shame as Zhuangzi did at having to drag his tail through the mud.
I have no regard for such men; let later scholars be careful regarding what to abandon and what to pursue, and examine with care the distinction between the pure and the turbid.
To distinguish the turbid from the pure, to strictly observe the *vinaya*, and to transcend the accumulation of worldly defilements— this may be called crossing over all doubts and slanders,
and repaying the profound kindness of the Buddha.
Biographies of Laymen, Volume Eleven:
Biographies of Zhang Hongzhen, Zhang Tinggui, and Xin Tefou.

Zhang Hongzhen, whose given name was Huipai, was a native of Jiumen in Changshan. His learning was refined in the Three Rituals (*Sanli*), and he was also proficient in the Spring and Autumn Annals (*Chunqiu*).
He studied the doctrines of the hundred schools during the autumn [of his youth]. He served in the Wei court as an Adviser on Remonstrance (*jianyi dafu*).

Whenever there were major deliberations at court, he invariably cited the principles of the Classics to present his arguments repeatedly, never yielding even slightly. At that time, Emperor Xiaoming did not personally attend court audiences;

matters concerning the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples were entirely delegated to the relevant officials, while the construction of monasteries and statues proceeded without pause. Daohong submitted a memorial, saying: "Your servant has heard..."

The virtuous sovereign honors the ancestral sacrifices; Tang the Completer illuminated his six-hundred-year mandate. With a reverent father paired with Heaven, Confucius said, "The Duke of Zhou was such a man.

Thus, his fragrant influence was heard afar, and his blessings were transmitted through distant ages. We humbly observe that Your Majesty, continuing the radiant legacy of the imperial line, is reverent, enlightened, and wise.
Your thoughts are aligned with Heaven and Earth, and the hundred deities await your favor. It is therefore fitting that you should earnestly honor and elevate the rites of sacrifice. All...
The ranks [of officials] lack clear regulations; thus, the rites of announcing the month and the court visit to the ancestral temple are not personally performed at the Mingtang.

The seasonal sacrifices of *chang* and *di*, as well as those to Heaven, Earth, and the spirits of the soil, are mostly delegated to the presiding officers. This fosters urgentless and obscure undertakings while diminishing the vast resources of the common people.

Stipends are reduced and labor is diminished to provide for monks who serve no purpose. Cloud-palaces are lavishly adorned to seek rewards for benefits yet to come. The ministers, prostrating themselves at the break of dawn—
While monks of primordial stillness roam within, their transgressions of propriety and defiance of the times leave both humans and spirits unsettled.

I, a fool, believe that rather than seeking the fruits of *kalpas* through causes cultivated from morning to evening, it would be better to first employ the joyful hearts of the myriad nations to serve one’s parents, thereby bringing peace to the world so that calamities do not arise.
I humbly pray that you will be prudent and careful in your majestic demeanor. Ten thousand...

He established models for the state, personally attending with devotion to the rites of the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples, and personally presiding over the ceremonies on the first and fifteenth days of the month.

He performed the ritual offerings at the National University and exerted his heart in the thousand-acre fields [of agriculture]. When filial piety can communicate with the divine spirits and virtuous instruction can illuminate the four seas, then the sovereign alone enjoys auspiciousness and the myriad people depend upon it.
Thereafter, he diligently advanced the Three Jewels and placed his faith in the Tathāgata; thus, the Way flourished through the profundity of transformation.
Thus, all outflows (*āsrava*) may be exhausted; through the accumulation of merit in accordance with the Dharma and propriety, one may ascend to the further shore (*pāra*).

It is therefore appropriate to reduce the non-essential offerings to monasteries and restore the long-suspended ranks of the various officials. As for buildings already under construction, let them be completed with economy; as for future constructions, let them be temporarily suspended.

In this way, by practicing frugality and loving the people, both the clergy and the laity shall rely upon it. Subsequently, he was promoted to Right Minister of the Department of State Affairs (*Shangshu Youpuye*).

He served as a Vice Minister (*cheng*) and was subsequently appointed as the Regional Inspector (*cishi*) of Dongyuzhou. He died, and his posthumous title was Xuan Gong (according to the *Weishu* and the *Guang hongming ji*).

Zhang Tinggui was a native of Jiyuan in Henan. He was a man of noble character and high principles. During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, he was promoted through various offices to become a Censor-in-Chief (*jiancha yushi*).
During the Chang’an era, a tax was levied upon the monks and nuns of the empire to raise funds for the construction of a temple at Baisima Pass.
He proposed the construction of a great Buddha statue. Wang Tinggui submitted a memorial to remonstrate, saying:
"Now, the Buddha takes awakening and knowledge as his defining characteristic; he is realized through the mind and cannot be perceived through physical marks. A sutra says:
'If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, such a person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. This fruit of True Suchness (Tathatā) is not to be sought externally."
Furthermore, Your Majesty has with a sincere heart taken refuge and made great vows to magnify the pagodas and temples and expand the sacred images;
this has already pervaded the world for a long time. Yet, to practice giving while dwelling upon signs is not the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma.
As the Sūtra says: "If a person were to fill the three-thousandfold world system with the seven treasures and distribute them as an offering..."
If one were to give alms, even giving away as many bodies and lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, the merit would be exceedingly great.
Yet, if a person were to receive, uphold, and expound for others even a single four-line verse from this sutra, their merit would surpass that of the former.

As the Buddha has said, even if Your Majesty were to exhaust the wealth of the four seas, expend the labor of ten thousand men, and use every tree from the mountains to construct a stupa, it would reach its ultimate limit—yet [the merit of the Dharma] remains superior.
To smelt metal and cast it into an image involves great toil and incurs vast expense, yet the merit obtained does not exceed that of a single commoner who builds a meditation hall.
A Bodhisattva practicing the accumulation of merit should not be greedily attached to such things; for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are not worthy of high esteem.
This is especially true when the undertaking of construction is so extensive—excavating earth and wood, leveling the ground, and erecting lofty foundations.

As they ascend the steps, they trample over insects and ants by the billions. How could this not contradict the Buddha’s teaching on the meaning of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), which out of compassion for all wriggling creatures forbids the harming of their lives?
Furthermore, it is improper to employ spirits while neglecting human beings alone. When calculating the total number of craftsmen, most are impoverished;

driven morning and evening, their sinews are exhausted and their bones are worn out. They subsist on a single basket of rice and a ladle of soup, cooking at dawn and eating under the stars, suffering from hunger.
Afflicted by the maladies brought about by thirst, with various eruptions breaking out all at once—how could the Buddha have intended for this to be a practice of mere physical toil?

Would he not have pitied the beasts and been unable to bear the exhaustion of their strength? Furthermore, as for the expenses of construction, the monks and nuns are the ones taxed. Although these funds are obtained through begging, those who are poor and destitute are still many.
When the prefectures and counties demand payment with the urgency of a shooting star, some find themselves with no means of planning, while others must sell their possessions.

The cries of resentment fill the roads, and the harmony of the breath of life has not yet prevailed. How could this be in accord with the Buddha’s teaching on the meaning of *anumodana* (rejoicing), which takes pity on the ignorant and deluded, and would never bear to deprive them of their property?
Furthermore, as the frontiers and the north have not yet been pacified, military equipment must be supplied daily; thus the empire is exhausted and the realm within the seas is worn out by toil.
We humbly entreat Your Majesty to regard this with caution and gravity, to contemplate the practice of *bodhi*, and to act for the benefit of all.

All sentient beings should practice giving in this manner; then their merit would be as immeasurable as the emptiness of the south, west, north, east, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Why, then, labor so diligently to dwell upon signs, thereby withering the livelihoods of the common people and exalting urgentless pursuits?
When I evaluate this by the standards of current governance, it is appropriate to prioritize the defense of the borders, replenish the treasuries, and nourish [the people].
Regarding human effort, when judged by the teachings of Śākyamuni, one ought to rescue others from suffering and calamity, extinguish all [dualistic] marks, and honor non-action (*avivikta*).

I humbly entreat Your Majesty to examine this humble servant’s folly and carry out the intent of the Buddha: to take principle as your primary concern and not to reject words because of their speaker.
"How fortunate, how fortunate! Then Tiantian summoned him for an audience and comforted and praised him deeply. At that time, the Chancellor of the National Academy Li Jiao also remarked:

"There are currently more than one hundred and seventy thousand strings of cash from the funds for casting images. If these were distributed as alms to the poor, each person would receive two thousand."
He saved more than one hundred and seventy thousand households, alleviating hunger and cold and reducing labor services.

This accorded with the compassionate heart of all Buddhas and fulfilled the sovereign’s virtue of nurturing all beings. Thus, both spirits and humans were delighted, and his merit was inexhaustible; even the Emperor could not fully recognize it.

At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, Wang Tinggui served as Minister of Rites (Libu Shilang) and once responded to an imperial decree by offering a thorough critique of current affairs. He was subsequently promoted.
He served as an Attendant Censor of the Yellow Gate. Later, he retired from office with the rank of Director of the Office of the Imperial Household. He died at the age of over seventy.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works and conferred the posthumous name Zhenmu (Tang Shu).
Xin Tefou was a native of Wannian in Jingzhao. During the Jinglong era, he served as the Left Reminder (Zuo Shiyi).
At that time, Emperor Zhongzong was extensively promoting Buddhist temples; the common people were exhausted by labor, and the state treasuries were depleted. Xin Tefou remonstrated, saying:

"As for the teachings of Śākyamuni, they take purity as their foundation and compassion as their core. Therefore, they always embody the Way to save all beings, never seeking personal gain at the expense of others."
One should eliminate the self to preserve the truth and refrain from adorning the body to the detriment of the Teaching. As the Sūtra says:

"If a Bodhisattva’s mind dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing. Truly, to reduce the expense of carving and ornamentation in order to relieve the poor and lowly is to possess the virtue of the Tathāgata;
to cease the suffering of digging and excavating in order to preserve insects is to possess [the virtue of the Tathāgata].
"Regarding the benevolence of Your Majesty: you have treated what is urgent as non-urgent and what is non-urgent as urgent; you have lost the reality for the sake of hoping for the void.

I privately lament this. His memorial was not accepted. During the reign of Emperor Ruizong, he earnestly discussed current affairs and was promoted to Right Palace Attendant Censor of the Court of Judicial Review.
He passed away at the beginning of the Tianbao era (Tang Shu).
Zhiguizi said: The Sūtra states, "If bodhisattvas accord with sentient beings, they are thereby acceding to the worship of all Buddhas;
if they honor and serve sentient beings, they are thereby honoring and serving the Tathāgatas. Why is this?
Because all Buddha-Tathāgatas take great compassion as their very essence. Yet the rulers of this degenerate age impose heavy taxes and are corrupt...

To employ soldiers and exhaust the people for one’s own indulgence, yet desire to exhaust the labor of building works and dazzle others with the adornment of gold and jade in hopes of attaining blessings—how vast indeed is such a grave transgression! How excellent are the words of Mencius: "If by practicing one act of unrighteousness or killing one innocent person one could gain the empire, he would not do it. This is what may be spoken regarding the pure precepts. The Book of Documents also says: [The wise kings] did not consider their own persons as precious; they considered the people as precious. To harm the people for the sake of one’s own body is to lose both. How much more so when one loses both the body and the state! It is said that the Way of Heaven is retribution; it does not wait for the next life to punish the wicked. If one commits evil in this world, how can one hope for blessings in the next? Therefore, the wise king was cautious in his conduct and did not dare to be negligent. He feared the calamities of Heaven and did not dare to be remiss.
