Biographies of Lay Practitioners XII:
Jiang, Liu, Zhang, Sima, Li Yuanwan, Zhu, the two Wus, Peng, and Gao.

Jiang Hanjie, courtesy name [Mì] Pi, was a native of Kaocheng in Jiyang. His father, Jian, served as the Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (*Guanglu Dafu*) under the Liang dynasty. Hanjie...
At the age of thirteen, his father fell ill with an eye disease. Hanchie attended to him with such purity that for nearly a month he did not even remove his sash from his waist.
One night, he dreamed of a monk who said, "One suffering from eye disease will surely recover if they drink the water of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

His uncle, Lu, was on good terms with the Dharma Master Zhizhe of Cudang Monastery; he went to visit him. Zhizhe said, "The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: 'The wisdom-eye perceives the truth and is able to [see]...'"

[The Emperor] crossed over to the other shore. Zhìqiān then, together with Zhìzhě, submitted a memorial. They proposed to donate a residence in Niútún Village, Xià County, to establish as a monastery and requested that it be granted an auspicious name.
The imperial decree stated: "The 'Eye of Wisdom' (huìyǎn) is one of the five eyes; it may be used as the name."
When the temple was completed, he drained the water from an old well; it was exceptionally clear and pure. He then realized that this was what he had dreamed.

He took the water to wash his eyes and used it to boil medicine, whereupon his illness was cured. When the Prince of Nankang governed the southern region, he summoned Senghanjie to serve as Chief Clerk.

Senghanjie was quite fond of the *Laozi* and *Zhuangzi*, and was especially skilled in Buddhist doctrine. He took no pleasure in official advancement. Upon the death of his father, he lived in a grass hut at the tomb. After some time—
[This concludes the entry from] the *Book of Liang*.
Liu Shixuan, whose given name was Ji, was a native of Pingyuan. During the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, he began his official career as a *fengchaoqing* (court attendant).

He was subsequently appointed as the *zheng* (magistrate) of Jiankang, but soon retired on the grounds of illness. His mother, Lady Ming, fell ill; although Liu Shixuan was already fifty years of age, he attended to her day and night.
For seventy days, she recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* ten thousand times. At night, she dreamed of a monk who said to her, "The lady’s allotted lifespan has been exhausted;
because your sincerity is so profound and earnest, it shall be extended by several decades. She subsequently passed away after more than sixty days.
While observing the mourning period, she lived in a hut beside the grave, where a pair of white cranes circled above the dwelling. She died before the period of mourning had ended (*Liang shu*).
Zhang Xiaoshi, whose given name was Yuan, was a native of Rucheng in Hebei. His grandfather, Cheng, served in the Zhou dynasty as the acting Governor of Pingyang Commandery.

His father, Yanjun, served successively as the Director of Retainers and the Chief Clerk of various prefectures and commanderies. By nature, Xiaoshi was benevolent and filial, and he revered and believed in the Buddha-dharma.
When he was a child, seeing a discarded puppy on a village road, he took it in and raised it. His paternal uncle scolded him, saying, "What use is this?"

[The Emperor] asked. He replied: "Among all classes of living beings, there are none who do not cherish their own life and nature. For Heaven to have bestowed them upon us and for humans to then cast them aside is contrary to the Way.
To see them and not take them in is a lack of benevolence. His grandfather lost his sight three years ago;
when Xiao Shi was sixteen, he recited Buddhist scriptures and prostrated himself day and night to pray for blessings. Later, while reading the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*, he saw a blind man..."
Having obtained this instruction, Yuan invited seven monks to light seven lamps for seven days and seven nights to recite the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*.

He proclaimed, "Yuan was unfilial toward his grandfather, causing him to lose his sight. Now, by universally bestowing these lamp lights upon the Dharma-realm, I pray that my grandfather’s eyes may be restored to sight.
Yuan’s transgressions are deep and heavy; I pray that my own eyes be blinded. On the seventh day, he dreamed of an old man who...
He scraped his grandfather’s eyes with a golden hairpin. Three days later, the grandfather’s eyes were indeed restored to sight.
Yang Yu, the County Doctor, and others reported his filial conduct to the throne, and an imperial edict proclaimed his family’s gate. (Beishi)
Sima Qiaoqing was a native of Henei. During the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, he served as the District Magistrate of the Revenue Office in Yangzhou.

Upon encountering the mourning period for his mother, he emaciated himself through grief and pierced his chest, writing out one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with his blood. On the mourning hut where he resided, two stalks of *zhicao* (mushroom) grew.
After nine days, it grew to a height of one chi and eight cun. It had green stalks and crimson caps; each day it yielded one sheng of juice.

When eaten, its flavor was like honey. Once exhausted, it grew back again, and this occurred four times in succession. At that time, many officials and gentlemen spread word of this as a marvel (*Fayuan zhulin*).
Li Guan was a native of Longxi. During the Xianqing era, while residing in Yingyang, he encountered the death of his father.

He drew blood to transcribe one scroll each of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. A wondrous fragrance emanated from his courtyard, lingering intensely for many days.

Xiang and his neighbor. (From the Fayuan zhulin. Note: This Li Guan is distinct from the person recorded in the Tang Shu whose courtesy name was Yuanbin; their chronological distance is considerable. However, the Faxi zhi and the Jintang lu combine these two into a single individual.)
This is not so. Yuan Zizhi, whose given name was Dexiu, was a native of Henei. During the Kaiyuan era, he passed the jinshi examinations. Upon the death of his mother, he lived in a hut by her grave;
he abstained from salt and curd, and used no mats or bedding. He drew blood to paint Buddhist images and transcribed sutras. Subsequently, he held office in Lu.

Shan Ling completed his term of service and returned home, carrying a single roll of silk and driving a cart laden with firewood. He took a liking to the mountains and waters of Luhun and settled there.
His household had no servants or concubines; during years of famine, he would sometimes cook but once a day. He amused himself by pouring wine and playing the *qin* lute.
Throughout his sixty years of life, he never once looked upon the beauty of women. He passed away in the thirteenth year of the Tianbao era (*Tang Shu*).
Wan Jingru was a native of Hefei. After his parents passed away, he lived in a grass hut beside their tomb for eighteen years. He drew blood to transcribe Buddhist sutras;

having severed two fingers of his hand, they grew back again. Emperor Xuan honored his family by issuing an imperial edict and renaming his residence Chengxiao Township (The Fortress of the Buddha-Dharma).
Zhu Kangshu, whose given name was Shouchang, was a native of Tianchang in Yangzhou. By virtue of his father’s official rank, he served as a Director of the Directorate of Works (*Jiangzuo Jian*).

During the Zhiping era of the Song dynasty, he held successive posts as the Prefect of Langzhou and the Military Commissioner of Guangde. When Kangshu was seven years old, his father was serving in Chang’an and sent his mother, Lady Liu, away to marry into a commoner family.
Once Kangshu entered government service, he traveled throughout the four quarters in search of her, yet he rarely encountered her even at places where she ate and drank.
He abstained from wine and meat. Every day before the Buddha, he would cauterize his arms, burn the crown of his head, and draw blood to transcribe scriptures, hoping to fulfill his aspiration.

At the beginning of the Xīníng era, he resigned from office and traveled to Qín. He took leave of his family, vowing not to return until he had seen his mother again. While traveling through Tóngzhōu, he found her.

Kāṅshǔ, mindful of repaying his mother’s kindness and wishing to deliver all beings from suffering, examined various teachings and found that the *Zhòu* [scriptures] were most essential and proximate.

It arrives. Nothing compares to the *Cānfa* (Repentance Method) composed by Emperor Wu of Liang; however, its prose is voluminous and its meaning esoteric, such that readers cannot fully comprehend it.
Therefore, I have re-cast it into rhymed verse so that all people may sing and praise it together, thereby obtaining both merit and benefit. Su Zizhan spoke the following gāthā:
"The elder lost his mother and constantly thought to himself: 'My mother originally gave birth to me, yet I have now given birth to my mother.'"

I departed. To have a self and yet no mother is not as bad as having no self at all. I vowed that throughout this life, from birth to death, if my mother were not seen, I too would perish along with her.
Among the multitude, I was like a madman, wandering aimlessly day and night for over forty years, until finally I saw my mother.
At first, I could not recall her height or stature, nor her size, whether she was fat or thin; how could I—?

Upon seeing her, one immediately knows she is one's mother; the natural affinity between mother and child is a spontaneous, profound resonance, like a magnet and a needle that meet without prior consultation.
Before I saw my mother, there was nothing to seek; once I had seen her, there was nothing further to seek.

You are certainly capable of being loyal to the point of forgetting yourself, public-spirited to the point of forgetting your private interests, and devoted to the state to the point of forgetting your family. Is this not so?
Take those sour-souled scholars from the Confucian gate and those shaven-headed donkeys from the Chan gate;
even when their thoughts of fame, beauty, or victory stir, they must still maintain a solemn expression on their faces. Thus, they are made into "serious" people.

There is great use for this head. If you are willing to take the matter seriously, as described above, when you bring forth this ten-thousand-aeon-long burning heart and this heaven-shaking blood-nature, it will be beyond measure. Why is it beyond measure?
When Li Shizheng comes to pay his respects, you shall sit upon the crest of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff and bring down a great club from above, striking him right onto the edge of that precipice.
This will ensure that this man’s wretched life is spared not even a single thread.
However, if this man is clever enough to claim he is a disciple of the Institute of Righteousness, take the point he has just argued and use red ink—
Ge'er copied out a composition in the style of a *shiwen* (examination essay).

Having learned that he was serving as a private tutor at the residence of Wang Dashen, he respectfully presented it for correction. You then took up a worn-out brush and returned it with this verdict:
"A person who truly practices his craft; not a single word can be altered. One reward and one punishment.
How clear and distinct this is! To what extent have you, with your passionate temperament and blood-hot nature, applied these qualities with such propriety?
Why do you suffer by using them for the sake of lust, fame, and victory, thereby becoming an ordinary worldling and causing Old Master Li to expose your ugliness?
Great Scholar has now manifested his body to preach the Dharma; let all ordinary worldlings listen.
It is further said: "The method of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) is not merely the fundamental framework of the Tiantai teachings;
it is, moreover, the great *dhāraṇī* (total retention) of both Confucianism and Buddhism. Yao, Shun, and Yu transmitted to one another, saying: 'Be refined and singular, and truly uphold the Mean.
'Being refined' is *vipaśyanā*; 'being singular' is *śamatha*; 'truly upholding the Mean' is the equality of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Tang said: 'The sage’s reverence ascends day by day.'"

"Sage" refers to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). "Reverently abiding" refers to quiescence (*śamatha*). Taken together, they signify the equality of quiescence and contemplation. The text says: "In the brightening [of virtue], reverently abide.
"Brightening" refers to contemplation; "reverently abiding" refers to quiescence. Taken together, they signify the equality of quiescence and contemplation.
The transmission between Confucius and Yan Hui states: "When there was something not good, he never failed to know it; having known it, he never again practiced it. "Knowing" refers to contemplation.
It has never been that they were practiced separately; taken together, they constitute the equality of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

Mencius, who transmitted the teachings of Zengzi, proclaimed the learning of Confucius, saying: "To rectify the mind and to cultivate sincerity" is *śamatha*; "to extend knowledge and examine things" is *vipaśyanā*.
It is said that "illuminating the good" is *vipaśyanā* (contemplation). It is said that "sincerizing the person" is *śamatha* (calm abiding).
It is said that "the sincere one" is *śamatha*. It is said that "one who seeks sincerity" is *vipaśyanā*. Taken together, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are equal.

If one extrapolates from this, the teachings of the great Confucian masters of the Liang, Luo, Guan, and Min schools all harmonize without exception. I have seen very few Buddhist texts; what I recall is even less.

Briefly, regarding what is seen and what is remembered, as stated in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "How does one subdue the mind? This refers to *vipaśyanā* (insight). "How does one abide?
This refers to *śamatha* (calm abiding). It says: "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. "Dwelling nowhere" is *śamatha*; "giving rise to the mind" is *vipaśyanā*.
Taken together, they signify the equality of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This is explained in full detail in the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*.

Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* speaks of entering samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, while the *Heart Sūtra* describes Avalokiteśvara proceeding from contemplation to cessation;
these layers of depth do not, in total, transcend the dharma-gate of śamatha-vipaśyanā. Inferring from this:
The myriad scriptures and ten thousand classics naturally find no contradiction [within it]. By this, I know that the Tiantai school is truly vast.
However, regarding the texts of the Tiantai school, I have truly never set eyes upon them beyond the *Wenyang Song* (Verses of Yongjia).

From where could I have obtained them? I obtained them from reading the writings of Zhu Xi. Zhu Xi spoke of "preservation and cultivation" (*cunyǎng*), which is *zhǐ* (stopping); he spoke of "examination and investigation" (*shěngchà*).

This is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). It means that the practices of preservation, nourishment, examination, and investigation are brought forth together and mutually stimulated; thus, *samatha* and *vipaśyanā* are equal. This reiterates the emphasis on reverent attentiveness (*jing*).
This refers to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. It involves earnestly applying the功夫 (kung fu) of investigating things and exhausting their principles.

One enters the three samādhis through hearing, reflection, and cultivation. All phenomena are subsumed within the single character "sincerity" (*cheng*). This is the Unsurpassed, Perfect, and Complete Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
When I read the writings of Zhu Xi, every sentence and every word serves as a golden needle for the school of Confucius, and furthermore, as a golden needle for the Śākya clan.
When I read the scriptures of the Śākya clan, every sentence and every word serves as a mind-seal for the school of Confucius, and likewise, as a mind-seal for Zhu Xi.
What differs between Confucius and Zhu Xi is merely their outward traces; later scholars [have failed to see this].
Many have debated Zhu Xi’s doctrine of "investigating things" (*gewu*).
Might his teaching not be what Śākyamuni criticized as "exhausting emptiness without reaching its end"? Śākyamuni’s being Śākyamuni consisted simply in exhausting emptiness to its ultimate limit.
My Master Confucius’s being Confucius consisted simply in exhausting principle (*li*) and exhausting human nature (*xing*) until one reaches destiny (*ming*).
Thus it is said. Former scholars have remarked that Yanzi was separated from the Sage by but a single interval, precisely because his mind was still coarse.
If this is so, then those who still harbor residual dust regarding their studies are likewise merely coarse in mind. Alas!

While *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) constitute the Great Dhāraṇī, the method of insight is especially vital; there is no one who can achieve *śamatha* without being profound in insight.
Furthermore, to cease without contemplation—even if one were granted eighty thousand kalpas—ultimately results in falling into emptiness and oblivion. Is this not something to be deeply heeded?
Therefore, in the learning of the Confucian school, the investigation of things (*gewu*) is essential; in the learning of the Buddhist school, the contemplation of phenomena (*guancha*) is essential.
Zhu Xi was refined in the investigation of things, while the Great Being Avalokiteśvara was refined in the contemplation of phenomena. Thus, they are the [exemplars] of Confucianism and Buddhism.
This is my selection. Alas! Some may regard these words of mine as a strange tale, while others may deem them a far-fetched argument;
neither, however, reflects my true intention. My heart’s desire is simply that all beings, whether gods or humans, should seek the ultimate, true meaning and find no pleasure in the midway stages.

It is further said: "Those who use daily without knowing are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Those who know how to reach the ultimate and thus reach it, and know how to bring the process to its conclusion and thus conclude it, are Bodhisattvas.
Those who penetrate both day and night and possess such knowledge are Tathāgatas. Wénzhōngzi remarked:
"That *yuan*, *hēng*, *lì*, and *zhēn* operate without exhaustion is the achievement of wisdom; in this regard, it is almost like the *Yījīng*. How magnificent!"
Regarding the *Yuanjue jing*, it is like the *Book of Changes* (*Yijing*) among texts; in both, one can perceive the fundamental principles.
Furthermore, it is said that these three gentlemen were those who possessed a refined balance of literary elegance and substantive substance within the Buddhist tradition.
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume 14:
Li Fan, Niu Yu, Shang Zheng, Ma Lu, and the Biography of Li Shanlong.
Li Shanlong was a native of Fengyi. During the early Tang dynasty, he held the office of Gatekeeper Commandant (Jianduan Jiaowei). In the Wude era, he died suddenly, yet his chest...

He experienced a slight fever. His family members waited for him, and he soon regained consciousness. He spoke of his own accord that after death, an official had led him to the residence of a Prince.
In the courtyard were several thousand prisoners, all wearing neck-collars and shackles, standing facing north. The Prince sat upon a high couch, surrounded by a magnificent retinue.
Once Shanlong had reached the foot of the steps, the Prince asked, "What meritorious deeds did you perform throughout your life? He replied, "Whenever my fellow villagers..."
He established a vegetarian feast and constantly provided material offerings to assist him. The king asked again, "What wholesome deeds have you performed?

He replied, "I recite two fascicles of the Lotus Sūtra every day. The king said, "Excellent! He immediately invited him to ascend the steps to the high seat; the king then moved his own seat to face him.
The *Shanlong kai jing* states: "The Lotus Sutra, Chapter One: Introduction. Upon hearing this, the King requested that Shanlong descend from his seat.
As Shanlong descended, all the prisoners in the courtyard suddenly vanished. The King said, "The merit of your recitation of the sutra benefits not only yourself;
since all these prisoners have been liberated upon hearing the sutra, how excellent! I now release you and allow you to return. He then addressed his officials.
[The King] said, "Take this man and lead him through all the hells. The official led him eastward for over a hundred paces;
they passed an iron city, which was said to be the dwelling place of the offenders. Shanlong, filled with compassion, recited "Namo Buddha. Continuing on, they saw a large cauldron.

The fire was fierce and the boiling water seethed. Beside it sat two men. When Śāla asked them about them, they replied, "We have received this cauldron of boiling water as the retribution for our sins.
Because we were blessed by the worthy one’s recitation of 'Namo Buddha,' the prisoners in hell have obtained a day's rest.
Śāla then recited "Namo Buddha" himself and returned home; seven days had already passed since his death. At that same time—
There was a man named Shi Sha who lived on the southern outskirts, in the shade of the Fushui River. He recited the Lotus Sūtra without ceasing, whether walking or standing still.

Serving as a clerk for the district magistrate, he always took the small paths when entering or leaving the city walls; with a humble demeanor and a pleasant countenance, he maintained continuous mindfulness.

Throughout his life, he never once rode a horse, for he followed the sutras in showing compassion for all beings. At the time of his death from illness, the fragrance of his body wafted for a distance of one *li*.
Ten years later, his wife died; when they were buried together and the tomb was opened, his tongue remained as if alive. Furthermore, there was one Xue Yan, who served as the Sima of Zhongzhou.
He maintained a lifelong fast and honored the Buddha, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* thirty times every day. When he reached the age of... [text ends]
When the seventy-second [day] was drawing to a close, banners and canopies descended from the sky of their own accord, and celestial music filled his ears.
His wife saw Yan slowly ascending into the air and departing; a wondrous fragrance, pungent and intense, filled the room, which none of the family members failed to perceive.
(From the *Mingbao ji*, *Fayuan zhulin*, *Xu gaoseng zhuan*, and *Baoying ji* [Āśī or alternatively Ādān]).
Fan Yuanzhi was a native of Anding. From his youth, he was fond of the Way. Residing south of the capital, he relied upon the Venerable Du Shun.

Du Shun instructed him to take the study of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary practice and, in accordance with the scripture, to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra. Whenever he recited the sūtra, śarīras frequently emerged from his mouth;
over time, there were several hundred grains. At times, when he recited at night, his mouth emitted a brilliant light that illuminated a distance of forty li.
The surrounding villages, both near and far, were struck with wonder. At the age of ninety-two, he passed away without illness.
During the cremation, his teeth transformed into *śarīra* relics; more than a hundred grains were obtained, all of which emitted light that did not cease for several days.
Monastics and laypeople erected a stupa as an offering (*Huayan jing shu chao*, *Huayan ganying zhuan*).

Niu Siyuan’s fame spread far and wide; his place of residence is unknown. From youth, he possessed extraordinary character, being profound, serene, and reticent in speech. In his early years, he attained the rank of *jiedu* after mastering the classics.
During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, he was demoted to the post of Sub-prefect of Jian’an in Zangke because his maternal uncle, Pei Yan, had been convicted of a crime.
The Vice Minister Cui Cha sought to harm him, but he was granted a divine incantation by a supernatural being and thus escaped. He subsequently became a devoted believer in the Buddhist Way;
though married and holding official rank, he lived like a monk observing the precepts—his speech never strayed into falsehood, and his gaze never wandered toward improper sights.

While in Zangke, he widely disseminated the teachings of Śākyamuni and established several *dharma-śālās*. The local tribespeople were all deeply transformed by his influence. After three years had passed, Zhuang Zhou...

The Liao people rose in rebellion and advanced into Zangke, slaughtering everyone far and near. The local officials responded [with resistance], and the great local warlords of Jian’an raised an army to plunder them.
Sengsiyuan sat beneath a tree; as they were about to execute him, a bystander suddenly appeared with a blade and severed the heads of the guards.

He placed Sengsiyuan in a carrying cage and fled. Once the unrest was quelled, he returned to his official duties. Later, he governed several districts, always accepting his salary only according to the number of days served.

Yu Feng was renowned for his integrity, and people all admired his purity. He subsequently resigned from office and devoted himself wholeheartedly to Buddhist teachings until the end of his life (*Jiwen*).

Yu Chang’s place of residence is unknown; during the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, he served as the Registrar of Pingzhou. By day he adjudicated official affairs, and by night he presided over the courts of the underworld.

He would often foresee calamities and disasters, making secret preparations for them. This continued for six years, after which he encountered the mourning period for his mother and took up the practice of the *Vajra* [Sūtra].

He made it his daily practice for many days and was no longer summoned by the officials of the underworld. At the age of eighty-four, as he was about to pass away, he suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance.
He immediately said to those around him, "The Sage of the West has come to welcome me," and he passed away while facing westward, repeatedly chanting the name of the Buddha (from the *Baoying ji*).
The layman Shang left behind his name; he was a native of Sanhe County. At the age of seven, he was able to master Buddhist scriptures.

Later, he lived in seclusion within a field to the west of the county, where there were several hundred thousand scrolls of Buddhist texts. He read and recited them without ceasing for even a single day.
Those who followed him as disciples numbered in the hundreds. Whenever he walked, his skeletal frame rattled like the sound of jade being struck. He lived to over ninety years of age.
One day, having prepared his bath and donned his cap and sash, he summoned all his disciples to a meal and told them, "I shall die this morning or evening;
you must cremate my remains. Be careful not to contravene my wish. That evening, he sat upright and passed away. Three days later, he was cremated.
When his bones were examined, they were found to be linked together like a chain of hooks. Thereupon, the villagers erected a stupa to enshrine them.
(*Xuānshìzhì*). Zheng Mùqīng was a native of Xíngyáng.
His entire family practiced the pure karma (*śukla-karman*). During the Kāiyuán era, when he was critically ill, someone urged him to consume fish and meat, but he refused.
Holding a censer in his hand, he focused his mind while facing west. Suddenly, a magnificent and extraordinary fragrance wafted forth, and he subsequently passed away. His...
His maternal uncle was Su Ting, a Minister of the Imperial Secretariat. He dreamed that a precious lotus flower blossomed, upon which Mu Qing sat (Fozu Tongji).

Ma Ziyun’s place of residence is not clearly known. He was recommended as a filial and incorrupt official (xiaolian) and served as the Magistrate of Jing County, where he was assigned to oversee the grain transport for his prefecture.

He was appointed to oversee the transport of grain to the capital. His boat capsized and sank, drowning ten thousand *hu* of rice. He was imprisoned, during which time his son Yun focused single-mindedly on reciting the Buddha’s name.
After five years, he was released upon encountering a general amnesty. He lived in seclusion at a mountain temple in Nanling, maintaining a fast of one meal per day.

In the tenth year of the Tianbao era, he passed away at Jingxian. Addressing others, he said: "Because my fortune was ill-fated, I have consequently applied myself with diligence to the Inner Teaching (Buddhism). Now, my karma for the Western [Pure Land]..."
"It is accomplished; you shall be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. On the following day, he bathed, donned new robes, and sat upright with palms joined.
Suddenly, a wondrous fragrance filled the room. Ziyun said, "The Buddha has arrived," and then he passed away (from the *Jiwen*).

Lu Kangcheng’s place of residence was unknown. While serving as a legal officer (facao) in Jingzhao, he suddenly saw a former subordinate whom he had already dismissed from office standing before him holding a case file.
Startled, Kangcheng said, "You have already passed away; how could you come here? The man replied, "These are the records of the underworld office;
they concern all those who will die by the blade next year. Kangcheng asked, "Might there be anyone among them who am I? The official searched the documents and showed them to him.
Kang Cheng looked startled and asked, "What should I do? The official replied, "Only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* can be entrusted to you;
I offer it specifically for your protection. Having spoken, he vanished. Kang Cheng then took up the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and recited it several dozen times every day.

The following year, Zhu Ci rebelled and appointed him as a Censor. Kang Cheng rebuked Zhu Ci, saying, "You treacherous minister dares to interfere with a man of national caliber! Zhu Ci was enraged and ordered—
Several hundred horsemen surrounded him and shot at him. Kangcheng silently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the arrows could not penetrate him. They eventually desisted.
Kangcheng departed for Mount Zhongnan, where he lived out his years in seclusion (*Baoying ji*).
Li Zhiyao was a native of Chang’an. He was deeply devoted to the Pure Land and led the assembly of faithful followers in the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) in five sessions.
Late in life, he fell ill; suddenly he said, “The Master has come! He washed his face, put on his robes, lit incense in the burner, and went out of the hall to prostrate himself in worship.
A voice from the air was heard reciting a verse, which said: "I inform you, Li Zhiyao: merit accomplished, fruit naturally invited;

I shall lead you to be born in the Pure Land, and carry you across the Golden Bridge. Thereupon, he sat upright upon his bed and passed away in stillness. A wondrous fragrance filled the room, and everyone present smelled it (from the *Jingtu wen*).
Zhi Guizi said: "I have observed the records of the hundred schools, and their accounts of matters concerning resonance and response (*yinggan*) are detailed.

Yet some consider these things strange. Now, all phenomena are one mind; self-resonance and self-response are like food satisfying hunger or drink quenching thirst—how could they be considered strange?
By observing the deeds of the various lords from Shanlong downwards, we truly know that the power of the mind is inconceivable."
It is thus deliberated. Those who speak of the Buddha yet do not believe are perhaps those who lack confidence in their own minds. Wang Dashen said:
"The light of the mind is obstructed by the power of karma, and thus there arise such things as the hells;
when the power of karma is shattered by the light of the mind, then the hells and such matters are instantly resolved. One must cultivate the mind with diligence and uphold the Buddha.
After a long time, the light of his mind spontaneously manifested, enabling him to rescue all from suffering. This biography was composed by Zhiguizi;
his resolve to deliver others from suffering and his heart of exhortation reach the ultimate pinnacle of sincerity. I humbly pray that the benevolent ones will listen to it with reverence.
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume 15:
The Biography of Master Li.
Master Li, whose name was Tongyuan, was a scion of the Tang imperial clan. He possessed a handsome beard and mustache, with bright eyes and brows. His complexion was ruddy...
His lips were purple and his skin was radiant. By nature he was extraordinary, and in his studies he had no fixed teacher; his traces were unfathomable.

From his youth, he applied himself to the Way of the *Yìjīng* (Book of Changes), exhaustively mastering its subtle principles. In his early forties, he devoted himself exclusively to the Inner Canon (*Nèidiǎn*).

Once, while traveling to Mount Wutai, he entered the Shanhu Monastery and encountered a strange monk who transmitted to him the great essentials of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. As they were about to part, the elder asked, "Where is the Master going? The monk—
He pointed toward the summit of Beifeng Peak. That night, he saw from afar a firelight on the northern peak stretching across the sky. The elder took up his staff and ascended;
there he saw the aforementioned monk amidst the firelight, raising a purple-gold banner and surrounded by several hundred people wearing imperial crowns.
The elder surged forward into the scene, prostrated himself, and then rose. Suddenly, the previous vision vanished. He then sat upon a cliff for three days. Thus it was.

He then descended the mountain and resolved to propagate the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra. During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, when the eighty-fascicle new translation of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra was completed, he carried it to Taiyuan and stayed at the home of Gao Xiannu.
He consumed ten jujubes and one *bǎoyè* (ginkgo leaf) pancake daily.

After residing there for three years, he moved to the ancient Buddha Hall of the Ma family, where he remained for ten years. He then again took the sutra upon his back and departed, traveling for two...
Ten *li* away, he encountered a tiger blocking the road. The Elder patted it and said, "I am about to compose a treatise to explain the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;
you should find a dwelling for me. He then placed his sūtra bag upon the tiger's back, and they proceeded until they reached a clay grotto at the foot of Mount Shenfu.
The tiger crouched beside the grotto, and once the Elder had entered, the tiger departed. There was originally no [human habitation] in the mountains.
Water. That evening, wind and thunder uprooted a pine tree in front of the niche. A spring gushed forth, its water clear, cool, and sweet.
The mountain dwellers consequently named it "The Elder’s Spring" (Chángzhě Quán). At night, it emitted white light to serve as a lamp. The two women did not know from where it came;
every day they drew water for the Elder, lit incense, and provided paper and ink. At mealtime, they prepared pure food and set it out.
The elder stepped forward. When the meal was finished, [the bowl] was removed. From the seventh year to the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he completed the writing of this treatise.
The two maidens also subsequently departed and were no longer seen. The elder himself composed the preface to the treatise, stating:
"Now, as for the root of sentient beings, it relies upon the ocean of wisdom as its source; the stream of conscious beings takes the Dharmakāya as its substance. It is only because emotions arise..."

Wisdom is separated [from ignorance], and as thought transforms, the substance becomes distinct. When one penetrates the fundamental, emotions vanish; when one knows the mind, the substance is unified.

This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Great Vaipulya Buddha-Flower Adornment, clarifies the primordial limit of sentient beings and reveals the source of the fruition of all Buddhas. As for its being the "fundamental": [it is so because it is the root of all phenomena].
It cannot be accomplished through merit. As for its source, it cannot be attained through practice. When merit ceases, the foundation is revealed; when practice is exhausted, the source is perfected.
The source and foundation are inherently without merit. One who is able to act with sovereign freedom according to conditions is precisely this Vairocana.

Taking the fundamental nature as primary, wisdom responds to the capacities of beings, and great compassion rescues all things; it is by virtue of this that he is so named. He abides in accordance with this very nature.

Having established the bounty of his teachings, they flow forth throughout the Dharma-realm to nourish all living beings. Thus, he took up residence in the four heavens and manifested his form through the eight stages of enlightenment.
Within the site of Bodhi, he appeared in an araṇya to mark the beginning of his realization; in the Hall of Universal Light, he dwelt in the great mansion of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The elder Samantabhadra displayed the fruits of his virtue within the *guhyakāya*, while the young Mañjuśrī first initiated the process of awakening.

Golden-hued, he manifests his numinous presence throughout the Dharma-realm by means of the Sea-Seal Samādhi; through the Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye, he beholds the oceans of lands within a single speck of dust.
The two retributions—the primary and the secondary—interpenetrate as body and land; the two gates of cause and effect mutually penetrate as essence and function.

With the precious net of Śakra-devendra, the multilayered majesty of the ten lands is revealed; with the stainless *maṇi* jewel, the ten bodies of the Buddha are made manifest in their profound depth.
Boundless realms of the worlds—self and other—are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip;
the ten periods of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from the present moment of thought. As for its vastness, it takes empty space as its measure; as for its minuteness...
Abiding within the ultimate atom yet leaving no trace; though the ten directions are uncontracted, even the minute marks are not diminished.

Without expanding even a speck of dust, it encompasses the ten directions without obstruction. Within the ocean of wisdom, the fruits of virtue manifest their distinct divisions through the gates of the five stages.
Permanently dwelling in the Hall of Dharma, they demonstrate the practice of advancement atop the nine heavens. As it is here, so it is in all ten lands. Thus, the Sage...

The assembly is like clouds; they enter one another within the ocean-like gathering. Wisdom and the mundane do not obstruct each other, resembling many mirrors that receive all forms without mutual interference, like a thousand lamps sharing a single room.
The essential point of this discourse clarifies that the nature of sentient beings is identical to the nature of the Buddhas:

when deluded, one is an ordinary being; when awakened, one is a Buddha. It is simply a matter of being able to believe and enter [this truth]. From the initial generation of the mind, it is the principle of Mañjuśrī.

The conduct of Samantabhadra is suddenly and instantaneously impressed [upon the mind], like bestowing the precious throne directly upon an ordinary person. Looking back at the world, it is like a dream of a thousand years;

once awakened, it vanishes accordingly. Therefore, regarding the explanation of the ten kinds of generating the mind, in the "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*), starting from the stage of an ordinary being, one takes faith as the foremost and resolutely seeks the great bodhi of the Buddha; thus, from the ground of an ordinary being—
Because one believes that the Immovable Wisdom of the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions is no different from the wisdom of one’s own mind;
it is only because of being deluded by ignorance that this occurs, yet ignorance and the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions have been fundamentally non-dual from the beginning.

From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes that the fundamental wisdom of the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions is no different from one’s own body. Why is this? Because they are all...
There is one Dharma-nature body and one fundamental wisdom, just as from a single root of a tree many branches and leaves grow.
Due to causes and conditions, the formation and destruction on that single tree trunk differ.

Therefore, from the stage of an ordinary person, I believe that I am fully capable of practicing the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the ten stages of the Tathāgata. Why is this? Because I recall that [I have] no...
In the beginning, when one was carried away by the current of the ocean of suffering, one still performed useless deeds;
how much more so now, when a Bodhisattva performs the myriad practices to save sentient beings—how could one not be able to do this?

From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes that all Buddhas of the ten directions are born from samādhi, and thinks, "I, too, shall attain it. Why is this? Because the samādhis of all Buddhas arise from the Tathāgata.
Born from the skillful means of intrinsic nature, I too possess the pure nature of the Tathāgata’s own body and am equal to the Buddhas.
From the stage of an ordinary being, I shall also attain all the supernatural powers of the Buddhas of the ten directions through faith. Why is this?
The supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of all Buddhas are attained by relying on true wisdom. I rely solely upon the wisdom of true nature (*dharmatā*), wherein there are no afflictions or ignorance;
thus, wisdom is perfected and all karma is extinguished. Therein exists only the wisdom of compassion, which transforms beings with sovereign ease.

From the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one should believe that the wisdom of the Buddha can likewise be attained. Why is this? Because all Buddhas have come from the state of being ordinary persons.

Therefore, from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one believes that the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Buddhas universally covers all beings, and thinks, "I too shall attain this.
Why? Because the great compassion of all Buddhas arises from their great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*); I too, like the Buddhas, have given rise to great vows.

From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes in the sovereign power (*vaśitā*) of the Buddhas, and thinks, "I too shall attain this. Why? Because the sovereign power of all Buddhas arises from the *dharmatā* of the nature of phenomena (*prakṛti*).

Whether born from eggs, moisture, or by transformation, all sentient beings—if they plant even a single seed of roots of goodness—will ultimately achieve the fruit of Buddhahood.

I do not slight you; do not slight yourselves. The verse of repentance says: "Throughout kalpas without beginning, whatever sins have been committed—whether light or heavy, great or small—I seek their characteristics within and without, yet find them utterly non-existent. This is called repentance. Thus he spoke.
The Vow Verses say: May afflictions depart; may Nirvana abide. May I ascend the ten stages; may I deliver the four modes of birth.
When a Buddha appears in the world, may I be able to attend him personally, being the very first to request that he turn the Wheel of Dharma.

When a Buddha passes into extinction, may I encounter him, being the very last to make offerings and receive the prediction of Bodhi. He passed away in the sixth year of the Huichang era at the age of seventy-five.

His final instructions were that he should be shrouded in a single set of garments and escorted by a single carriage; no ceremonial procession was to be used for his burial, nor were blood offerings to be made in sacrifice.
He was not to be granted a posthumous title by the Grand Music Bureau (Taichang), nor was a stele for the Divine Way to be erected.

He was to be buried beside the stupa of Chan Master Rimian at Mount Xiangshan. His family followed these instructions. As he had no son, his lineage was continued by his great-grandson. (From the *Tang Shu* and the *Changqing Ji*).
Zhi Guizi said: "Mokṣagupta (Wang Mojie) and Lü Zithou both resounded with their literary arts during their lifetimes and were transmitted to posterity.
Yet, upon examining their lives, they fall short when compared to Master Bai. 'The *miyang* grass, the *miyang* grass—do not harm my path.
This is what caused grief to the ancients. Mokṣagupta shed his burden at Wǎngchuān; Zithou stirred his sincerity before the Sea God. How startling!"
When the defilements of the mind have shed their husks like a cicada, one becomes pure and ethereal; possessing such causes of purity, it is only natural that one should attain liberation.
Yet you, Sir, continue to linger amidst worldly delights; even establishing a reputation for intimidating others and getting drunk—why do you alone act thus?
Wang Dashen said: "The three men transmit the same teaching, yet they take Master Bai as their ultimate goal. This is the point where this biography leads the reader into the marvelous.
While the principles of Wang and Liu are exquisitely subtle, Master Bai’s vow-power (praṇidhāna) is firm.
He further said: "As for Zhiguizi’s praise, those who already possess the 'single eye' will see it through; the two men were ultimately unable to [achieve their aims] throughout their lifetimes."
As for those who lack a sense of shame, have you, my son, ever investigated the reasons for this?
It is because these two individuals possess the seeds of literary talent. Such seeds are of the least practical use.
Recently, I have still taken pleasure in the writings of masters such as Gui Zhenchuan, Hou Chaizong, and Wang Dunweng, as well as those of Tang Linchuan, Hong Fangsi, and Qu [Yuefu].

It is truly lamentable that you do not succeed in your endeavors. A genuine student of the Way should have only the internal and external scriptures, the writings of the ancient sages and virtuous masters, the historical records of successive dynasties, and the poetry and prose of Han Yu, Ouyang Xiu, Li Bai, and Du Fu upon his desk;
not a single word from these should enter the realm of the dead. Remember my words! It is even better to linger over the divine flavor of their expressions, for it is precisely because of them—
The root of one's destiny lies solely in the ears. The root of destiny also derives from the root of the written word.
That he became a spirit is because Zi Hou was upright throughout his life. If one discards the pursuit [of fame] and preserves that uprightness, one will be reborn in heaven.
Take my words to heart.
Biographies of Eminent Laymen, Volume 20:
Biographies of Yang Dainian and Li Gongwu.

Yang Dainian’s name was Yi. He was a native of Pucheng. From his youth, he was capable of literary composition. At the age of eleven, Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty summoned him for an examination.

He composed poetry and prose. He was appointed as a Corrector (Zhengzi) in the Secretariat (Bishusheng). During the reign of Emperor Zhenzong, he was successively promoted to Left Censor-in-Chief (Zuosiyan).

In the Xianping era, an imperial edict summoned high-ranking officials to deliberate on the matter of whether to abandon or retain Lingzhou. Yang Dainian submitted a memorial vehemently describing the hardships of military service and arguing that abandonment would be beneficial.
When Zhenzong established Empress Liu as his consort, her lineage was of humble origin; court officials deemed this improper. Zhenzong wished to...
When Wang Dainian received the imperial decree for his composition, the Emperor dispatched Ding Wei to convey his instructions. Dainian demurred, and Ding Wei said to him, "Make an effort to do it;
you need not worry about not attaining wealth and honor. Dainian replied, "Such wealth and honor are not what I desire.

He then entrusted the task to Chen Pengnian and soon thereafter feigned illness to return home. Originally, Dainian had no knowledge of Buddhism; later, he was exhorted by Li Wei of the Hanlin Academy.
Through the encouragement provided by the ritual phenomena of the Zen school, he consequently gave rise to deep faith and composed a *Pranidhāna* (Vow Text), stating:

"To all the Buddhas who eternally abide throughout the ten directions, the true, pure, and wondrous Dharma, and the noble ones of non-arising: I pray that you, with your eye of reality and your wisdom of reality..."
Truly equal and impartial, do not abandon your vow, but grant your compassionate grace.
I deeply contemplate all sentient beings, numbering as many as the dharma-realm, who since beginningless and vast kalpas have neither known the Buddha, nor encountered the Dharma, nor met the Sangha.

From that interval until this very day, they have pursued the dust of the mundane while turning their backs on awakening; they have lost their original mind and closed the gate of liberation. Having traversed...
In the path of saṃsāra, the net of views is spread wide; the hive of delusion is bustling with clamor. One hoists the sail of craving and desire, and beats the waves of ignorance.
Drinking the wine of pride, one becomes intoxicated in the land of suffering. Failing to rely upon sincere devotion for refuge, one remains mired in the traces of cause and effect.
Such faults are known by the Buddha alone and seen by the Buddha alone; whether light or heavy, they are all equally subject to the Dharma.
May all sentient beings throughout the realms who possess such transgressions together repent. May their offenses be extinguished.

By means of the roots of goodness accumulated over billions of eons, may they be dedicated at this moment to the *tathatā-bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality). Relying upon the power of the fundamental vows of all Buddhas and their great, majestic, and fierce power.
With supreme power of mindfulness and protection, until the end of the future and up to unsurpassed bodhi, may I serve as the basis for all environments and beings, and as the adornments thereof;
may I be the gateway to liberation for all self and others, the gateway to all samādhis, the gateway to all dhāraṇīs,
and the gateway for establishing all sentient beings— each equal in measure to empty space and the dharma-realm— and in every instance, may there be my own body.
Arousing a courageous mind, I shall relinquish body, life, and wealth to perform great Buddhist services and bring about great benefit for sentient beings.
May all sentient beings who see my form or hear my name all resolve to attain bodhicitta and dedicate their merit together with me.

May the supreme bodhicitta never regress. I vow that for myself and all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm who have not yet realized this mind, may they open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and awaken to their own original mind.
May they manifest illumination in a single thought, such that all environments become purely serene.

Whether going or coming, sitting or standing, seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing—may all these be in accord with the wisdom of reality (yathābhūta-jñāna), without contradiction. From this moment until the end of the future, may it be so.

In the future, may the bodhicitta continue without interruption; may the benefits one performs always manifest before one; may one make offerings to all Buddhas and bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings;
and only when all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood shall one attain perfect enlightenment, even if space were to come to an end.
My vows are boundless; the Dharma-realm has its limits. My vow-mind is infinite. When the illness arose, he was appointed by the Secretariat Director to govern Ruzhou.
He went to visit Master Guanghui and asked: "A cloth drum is struck before the hall; who is the one who understands it? Guanghui said:
"The wind that comes is clearly discerned. Dayan said: "If that is so, then when Zen guests meet, they simply snap their fingers. Guang—
Guanghui said, "The gentleman may enter. Dayan responded with an assent. Guanghui remarked, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated.
During their conversation at night, Guanghui asked, "With whom have you had discussions lately?
Dayan replied, "I once asked the Chief Administrator Yunyan Liang, 'When two great tigers bite each other, what then? Liang said, 'A unified form. I [said], 'I only..."
"Watch closely. I wonder if you can speak in such a manner? Guanghui said, "I do not. Dayuan said, "Please, Master, turn another phrase for me.
Guanghui made a gesture with his hand as if pulling a nose and said, "This beast will leap about even more!
At these words, Dayuan was suddenly liberated. He spoke a verse: "The octagonal millstone runs through the void; The golden-maned lion..."
The Master transformed himself into a dog, intending to hide his body within the Northern Dipper; yet he further had to join his palms behind the Southern Dipper.
Thereafter, he associated closely with Guanghui (Guanghui) day after day and eventually inherited his Dharma. He once wrote a letter to Li Weimian, saying:

"Since meeting Master Guanghui, I have sought instruction in every possible way. My delusions and obstructions were suddenly dispelled; after half a year, I was vast and free from doubt. It was as if...

In a moment of forgetfulness, it was as if waking from a dream; that which had long obstructed his chest fell away with a sudden burst, and matters unclarified for kalpas of accumulation appeared before him in vast clarity.

The conditions for his succession to the lineage lay herein. In the fourth year of the Tianxi era, serving as Hanlin Academician, he submitted a memorial on behalf of Kou Jun requesting the Crown Prince to oversee the state affairs and denounced the wickedness of Ding Wei. When Ding Wei heard of this—
He harbored a deep resentment toward him. That year, he fell slightly ill. Chan Master Huan went to visit him. Da-nian said, "My four great elements are about to separate;
how can the Great Master save me? Huan struck his chest three times. Da-nian said, "Fortunately, I have encountered a master craftsman."
Huan said, "How many years have you studied the Buddha-dharma, yet your worldly airs are still not removed? Dadian replied, "Calamity does not come alone. Huan made a sound of sighing.
Dadian wrote a verse and sent it to General Li, saying: "The arising of bubbles and their extinction—these two dharmas are fundamentally equal.
If you wish to know the place of true return, look to the east or west of Zhaozhou’s monastery. When the General received the verse, he exclaimed, "Mount Tai!"
He went to visit him while the latter was selling paper money in the temple, but Da-nian had already passed away.
He was forty-seven years old at the time of his death and was posthumously granted the title "Wen" (Wuyi Ji; Wudeng Huiyuan; Song Shi).
Li Gongwu, whose given name was Zunxu, was a native of Shangdang. He passed the jinshi examination and married Princess Wanshou Chang as a Fu-ma duwei (Prince Consort).
He served in successive offices until he reached the rank of Commander-in-Chief of the Zhen’guo Army. By nature he valued simplicity and possessed a sense of integrity and principle.
During the Tiānshèng era, he petitioned for the Empress Dowager to return the administration to the Son of Heaven; commentators deemed this act praiseworthy.
In his daily life, he constantly explored the essential tenets of the school without regard for cold or heat. He attained the Dharma-heart from Chan Master Gūyǐn.

He once composed a verse which says: "To study the Way, one must be an iron man; Upon touching the heart-mind, one makes the judgment. Directly hasten toward unsurpassed Bodhi; Pay no heed to any right or wrong."
The Duke did not take pleasure in official service and requested to retire to the mountains and forests, following the precedent of Wei Sili of the Tang dynasty; this was not permitted.
He formed a close friendship with Yang Dainian and Chan Master Ciming within the Buddhist community. When Dainian passed away, he observed the prescribed mourning rites for him.
In the year of his passing, he sent a messenger to invite Ciming to Tangming. Once Ciming had arrived, more than a month passed before Gongwu fell ill.
As he approached death, he drew a circle and composed a verse, saying: "The world has no support; mountains and rivers offer no obstruction.
The great ocean is but a speck of dust; Mount Sumeru fits within a mustard seed. Picking up my head-wrap and unfastening my belt—if you seek birth and death, ask this."
Pidao. Cimeng asked, "What is the original Buddha-nature? Gongwu replied, "Today is as hot as yesterday.
Cimeng followed up by asking, "What about that one phrase at the moment of departure? Gongwu said, "Originally there is no obstruction."
He accommodated himself to any situation, whether square or round. Gong Wu remarked, "I am extremely weary by evening; I shall no longer engage in conversation. Thereupon, he passed away peacefully.

His second son, Zhongzi Duanyuan, held the rank of Grand Marshal (Daweï) and was likewise devoted to the Way of his ancestors. He built a dwelling in the rear garden and invited Chan Master Daguan to reside there.
Day and night, he consulted and studied with him, even forgetting to sleep or eat. One day, he asked Daguan, "Heavenly Paradise..."
"Are the hells ultimately existent or non-existent? Da Guan replied: "The Buddhas speak of existence within non-existence—this is like seeing flowers in the empty sky with one's own eyes.

Your Excellency seeks non-existence within existence—this is like reaching out your hand to grasp the moon in the water. It is truly laughable that you see the hells before your eyes yet do not avoid them, while hearing of paradise beyond your mind and desiring to be born there.
You fail to realize that joy and fear reside in the mind, and that good and evil constitute the external environment."
The Grand Marshal said, "I simply wish to understand my own mind; then naturally there will be no delusion. Da Guan asked, "How does one understand the mind?
He replied, "Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all. Da Guan asked, "After ceasing to deliberate, where does the mind go? Da Guan said, "For now, please return to your residence, Grand Marshal.
He asked, "As for when a person dies, where does the mind go? Da Guan said, "If you do not yet know life, how can you know death?"
[Daoguan] said, "Death. [Enduan] replied, "Life is already known. Daoguan asked, "From where does life come? Enduan prepared to answer.
Daoguan struck him in the chest and said, "It is right here. What is there to contemplate? Enduan said, "I understand. I only knew how to hurry along the journey, unaware that I had missed the way.
Daoguan pushed him away and said, "A hundred years are but a single dream. Enduan spoke a verse, saying: "Thirty..."
At eight years of age, he was ignorant and bewildered; when he eventually attained knowledge, how did it differ from his ignorance?
The waters of the Bian River flow on, and the embankments of Sui remain faintly visible. Master, you must return! The arrow-like waves rush eastward. Duan Yuan stood in court with upright integrity;
he retired from office as Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince and passed away (from the *Wudeng Huiyuan* and the *Song Shi*).
Zhiguizi said: "The two masters Yang and Li did not abandon the toil of the mundane world yet suddenly realized their original nature, thereby transcending the threshold of birth and death.
How magnificent! Yet beginners among students often weary of movement and seek stillness; when stillness cannot be attained,"
When afflictions assail from within and the bonds of karma grow ever stronger, it is difficult indeed to falsely hope for liberation.
How then can one not take the two masters as mirrors?
Wang Dashen said: "Guanghui and Daguan both attained the functional pivot of Linji; this is why they were able to resolve matters."
This is a matter of great importance for people. Lately, those who pursue intellectual understanding merely ask, "How is it?
or "What is it like? or "In what way? Consequently, those who are already leaping about continue to leap, while those who are rushing toward their goal continue to rush.
Look at them—when will they ever reach the end? How tragic!
Biographies of Laymen, Volume 21:
Biographies of Chao Wenfu, Zhang Zhao, and Chao Mingyuan.

Chao Mingyuan, whose given name was Hui, was of the Chao clan and was originally from Qingfeng. His father, Jian, moved the family residence to Pengmen. Mingyuan was able [to achieve spiritual realization] while still young.
His biography states: In the fifth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he passed the jinshi examination. At the end of the Zhi Dao era, he served as a Hanlin Academician.

By nature, he was easygoing, pure, and steadfast; his devotion to the Way was profound. Throughout his various official posts and the affairs he encountered, he never once allowed personal bias to harm others.
Emperor Zhenzong frequently praised him as a man of integrity. Initially, he studied under Liu Haichan and acquired the arts of refining the physical form and ingesting vital breath (*qi*). Later...
He studied the teachings of Śākyamuni, taking *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as his primary doctrine. While sitting with his colleagues within the Imperial Park, a water-carrier passed by in haste.
He remarked to his colleagues, "One whose contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is fully matured sees no whole person before their eyes.

His written works include the *Daoyuan bieji* (Separate Collection from the Monastic Garden), which extensively elucidates the principle of emptiness. One passage therein states: "In the course of a human life in this world, there are countless dreams."
There have been countless dreams, each of which called itself "I. Is not each of these "I"s empty? Throughout the succession of kalpas, one's bodies have been countless;
each of these countless bodies called itself "I. Is not each of these "I"s likewise empty?
Since dreams are empty, the body is likewise like a dream; why then do you become deluded and attached? Moment by moment, you struggle with emptiness. Furthermore, it is said:
"A person has a body, and only thereafter does a name arise. Yet every person individually clings to their own body and name, regarding them as their own self.
Since beginningless time, we have undergone countless births, deaths, appearances, and disappearances.
One does not know at what time or in what place one’s body was taken as the "self," nor at what time or in what place one’s name was left to endure imperishably.

Reflecting quietly on those who cherish their posthumous fame—is it not indeed a far-reaching and fleeting pursuit? Furthermore, one should perform the seven examinations: first, the examination of all deluded thoughts.
1. Are you able to still [the mind]? 2. Are all external conditions somewhat simplified and reduced? 3. Can you remain unmoved by all sensory objects?
4. Can you be prudent and discreet in all speech? 5. Have all dualistic distinctions between black and white been extinguished?
6. Is there no inversion within your dreams? 7. Do you find tranquility and joy within your heart? Write this upon your seat.

Thus, for the rest of his life, he examined himself to verify his power of the Way. After Emperor Renzong ascended the throne, he retired from office with the rank of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
Residing in the Shao-de Ward, the neighborhood named his hall "Congji" (Tranquil Stillness). There, he frequently practiced *ānāpāna* meditation, lashing his mind to enter into the principle.
By day he recited the *Heart Sūtra*, and by night he practiced counting the breaths. He strictly forbade his family members from making any requests on his behalf. His wife secretly observed him.
He saw him sitting upright with eyes closed, his beard and hair swaying in the wind, as motionless as a wooden puppet.

One night, Mingyuan dreamed that he traveled to a land in the northwest and entered a mountain cave where a multitude of monks were seated in rows reciting sutras; Mingyuan joined his palms and paid them homage.

He looked up and saw a Daoist priest bowing toward Mingyuan; he hurried away to avoid him. One month later, Mingyuan passed away at the age of eighty-four, posthumously honored with the title Wenyuan.
Later, Li Changling recorded the story of Mingyuan, stating that in his previous life he was in fact the Lord of the Pure Abode (Netravati).
(From the *Dongdu shilüe*, *Daoyuan lu*, and *Fazang suijin*: "The Extraordinary Account of Wenyuan.")
Prince Zhengming Sui was a native of Heyang. He passed the jinshi examination with distinction and served successively as the governor of various prefectures and commanderies.
In his administration, he was stern outwardly yet lenient inwardly. Constantly admiring the character of Lord Pei (Pei Xiu), he was appointed as Censor-in-Chief to govern Qiantang.
There, he visited Master Xiaoshou at Xingjiao Temple; their spiritual discourse reached perfect accord, and from that time forward, he devoted himself to the practice of Chan.

As the days deepened, he ultimately clarified the Great Dharma. At that time, when Master Changshui’s disciple, Fazhun, had completed his commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, his son Zheng was commissioned to write the preface. The preface states:

"The *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa-artha-guhyahetu-nītārtha-śūraṅgama-sūtra* is the grand paradigm of India and a precious scripture within the garden of the Dharma. Formerly, the Sage of Nengren [Śākyamuni], having emerged from the five..."
Heavenly One, uniquely honored throughout the three realms, you relinquished the golden wheel to enlighten all beings and manifested the jade-white brow-hair to respond to the world.

Observing that the four types of birth suffer in pain, you bestowed compassionate aid upon all things; pitying that the various capacities of beings had not yet awakened, you exerted yourself to provide virtuous guidance.
Thus, you contemplated the ultimate truth and proclaimed the subtle words, opening the gate of great compassion and broadening the ocean of True Suchness.
All phenomena arise solely based on deluded thoughts; all sentient beings do not exist apart from causes and conditions.
Thus one comes to know that the cycle of birth and death has craving as its root, while the cultivation and realization of eternal bliss take meditative wisdom as their essence.

By means of this sutra, one can discern various demons and destroy the seven realms of existence. This refers to the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), through which one cultivates perfect enlightenment.

The wondrously luminous mind, having given rise to the truth and returned to the source, realizes the supreme and ultimate Way. How magnificent! Prajñā translated its meaning, and the Chancellor Fang recorded its prose.
Now, Master Shi Xuan, whose learning and knowledge are both eminent and whose eloquence is unimpeded, has taken this sutra as the timely teaching for this era;
he has divided its wondrous principles into ten sections. His merit rescues the great trichiliocosm, and his Way—
The non-dual [teaching] has been transmitted. To believe and accept it is to become a bridge for the world; to awaken to it is to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Thus, I have titled this scripture and composed a commentary (*śāstra*). Through the commentary, the principles are clarified; thereby, prior doubts may be dispelled and subsequent obstructions resolved. One may strip away the clouds of delusion and behold the sun of wisdom.

While my aspirations lie in external protection [of the Dharma], I am ashamed of my lack of internal study. Having had the opportunity to read and examine [this work], I have ventured to record these reflections.
Preface. Taking refuge in the Dharma Jewel, may you diligently investigate the true expositions; extolling the Buddha Vehicle, may its supreme fruits universally benefit all.
I have previously edited and compiled the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) into the *Yu Ying Ji* (Collection of Jade Blossoms), which has been circulated in the world.

During the Ming Dao period, while serving as a Participant in State Affairs (*Canchizhengshi*), he wrote this verse at the time of his death: "The lamp in the painted hall does not go out; pointing my finger, to whom shall I speak? Departing and abiding are fundamentally..."

Ordinary. "The spring breeze sweeps away the lingering snow. Presented to the Grand Secretary (Zhongshuling). Posthumous title: Changhui (from *Dongdu shilüe*, *Wudeng huiyuan*, and the *Preface to the Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*).

Wen Kuānfú, whose given name was Yànbó, was a native of Jièxiū in Fénzhōu. He served through four successive reigns—those of Rénzōng, Yīnzōng, Shénzōng, and Zhézhōng—for over fifty years, holding various positions as both general and minister, until he attained the rank of Tàishī.
He once concurrently served as the Imperial Commissioner for Translating and Polishing Buddhist Scriptures and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lù.
When he was first stationed at Běijīng, the Elder of Huáyán Cave came to bid him farewell. Kuānfú said, "The Dharma Master is old..."
"Where will he go now? [The other] replied, "He has entered *parinirvāṇa*. Kuanfu took this to be a jest. After [the monk] had departed, Kuanfu sent someone to observe him;
it was indeed true that he had entered *parinirvāṇa*. He marveled at this greatly. When the cremation took place, he went in person to oversee it.
Placing a glass bottle before the seat, he made this vow: "If the Buddha-dharma is truly efficacious, may the *śarīra* enter my bottle. Immediately, smoke descended from the sky.
He poured it into a bottle and obtained an incalculable number of śarīra relics. Thereupon, he took refuge in and believed in the Buddha-dharma.

In his later years, he applied himself even more diligently to the Way, single-mindedly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha. Whether walking or sitting, morning or evening, he never slackened for even a moment.
He made this vow: "May I always be diligent and zealously cultivate all virtues; may I realize the essence of the mind and widely deliver all sentient beings. He resided in the capital.
Together with Dharma Master Jingyan, he gathered one hundred thousand people for a Pure Land assembly. He passed away at the age of ninety-two.
His posthumous title was Zhonglie (as recorded in the *Dongdu Shilüe*, *Linjian Lu*, *Fozu Tongji*, and *Fofa Jintang*).
Fu Yan’s courtesy name was Bi. He was a native of Henan. During the Qingli era, he served as Chancellor alongside Wen Kuanfu;
they were collectively known as "Fu-Wen. He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zheng. Zhao Yuedao once sent him a letter of counsel, saying:

"Your Excellency has reached the pinnacle of wealth and honor, and your moral cultivation is most flourishing. Yet, that which you have not yet given much heed to is the Tathāgata’s Great Matter of Causality."

"Enough. I wish for you to strive even more. Yan Guo agreed with this. While serving as the Governor of Bozhou, he heard that Chan Master Xiu Yong was presiding over Touzi Temple, so he went there to pay his respects.
Upon seeing him, Xiu Yong called out, "The Excellency has already entered; Fu Bi is still outside.

Yan Guo broke into a sweat that soaked his back, and he attained a realization. He immediately invited the master to his residence and stayed there for two months, during which time [the master] daily provided him with instruction.
Ming later presented a letter to Yong, saying: "I, Bi, have encountered the Master; that which has been forgotten since beginningless time has suddenly been recognized.
From this point forward, I must certainly pull myself out of the ocean of birth and death. This is no ordinary debt of gratitude; though one exhausts their strength, it cannot be fully expressed.
He passed away at over eighty years of age. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, he was posthumously granted the title of Taishi (Grand Preceptor) and the posthumous name Wen (Civilized).
(Zhong [in the *Dongdu shilüe*, *Wudeng huiyuan*, and *Xianghu yelu*]). Zhang An Dao, whose given name was Fangping, was a native of Songcheng.
He served successively as Grand Preceptor to the Crown Prince and held office both at court and in the provinces, commanding great prestige throughout his generation.
During the Qingli era, he served as the Governor of Chuzhou. While traveling on Mount Langya, he arrived at a monastery and happened to see the *Lengyan*...
He took up and examined the *Ga* Sūtra; suddenly, it was as if he had recovered an old possession.

Upon reading the passage, "The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky," his long-standing karmic obstructions melted away like ice, and he finally clarified the essential point of the mind. He composed a verse, saying: "A single thought remains within arising and ceasing;

A thousand mechanisms bind one to existence and non-existence. Where the divine blade is lightly raised, It passes through and escapes like a bead rolling off a platter. In his later years, he transmitted this sūtra [to others].
Su Zizhan provided three hundred thousand coins to have [the text] printed and distributed throughout the Jianghuai region.
Wang Jiefu asked An Dao, "More than a thousand years after the passing of Confucius and Mencius, why is it that there has been no one [to equal them]?
An Dao replied, "How could it be that there were no people? There have even been those who surpassed them. Jiefu asked, "Who were they? An Dao replied, "Mazu Yi and [Yunmen] Wenyan."
Yang Wenyu, Xuefeng Cun, Yantou Quanhuo, Danxia Tianran, and Yunmen Wenyan—Wang Anshi did not yet understand them.

Fan An Dao said, "The Confucian school is so austere and desolate that it cannot hold them; they all return to the followers of Śākyamuni. Wang Anshi sighed in admiration. Later, he spoke of this to Zhang Tianshu.
Tianshu struck the table and said, "How profound is this argument! He was eventually posthumously titled Wending (Slope). (From Dongpo)
[From] the *Wenji* (Collected Works) and the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs):
Zhao Yuedao, styled Bian, was a native of Xian County in Quzhou. His bearing was pure and refined; he never allowed his joy or anger to manifest on his countenance.

During the reign of Emperor Renzong, he served as an *yushi* (Censor). He was upright and fearless in his speech. During the reign of Emperor Shenzong, he was promoted to *Chanzhi Zhengshi* (Vice President of the Council of State).

He repeatedly presented the harms of the New Policies (*xinfa*). Having served as the governor of various prefectures, the people cherished his benevolence. At over forty years of age, Yue Dao cast aside worldly pleasures and sounds;
