The self-nature of Amitābha is precisely what is called "purity of nature. Because the nature is pure, it is called the "Pure Land.
Amitābha has made all the great vows for the sake of sentient beings because the nature of all sentient beings is pure. He exhorts them...
As for all sentient beings who attain rebirth: from the very beginning they are unborn and there is nothing that can be extinguished.
That sentient beings can attain rebirth by means of this very body and mind is because this very body and mind are illusory births.
That one is exhorted to leave the defiled for the pure is likewise because this very body and mind are illusory births. There are nine grades of rebirth.
This is because illusions have both that which is exhausted and that which is inexhaustible, and likewise, karmic retribution and merit have both that which is empty and that which is non-empty.
For sentient beings who resolve to cultivate the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, they must attain a hundred-thousandfold degree of faith in the first phrase concerning Kāśyapa Buddha;
only then will they know that Amitābha was not a mere fabrication, for his nature is fundamentally thus. All sentient beings...
The nature of birth is pure. When one reaches the utmost degree of conviction in the second phrase, one will know that rebirth is not a product of deluded thought;
birth is fundamentally thus. From the beginning, there has been no birth and nothing that can be extinguished.
When one reaches the utmost degree of conviction in the third phrase, then attachment to the present body and attachment to the mind can be shattered. Regarding the...
In the fourth phrase, when faith reaches its ultimate perfection, one may ascend to the highest of the high grades of rebirth.
How great indeed is the meaning of Kāśyapa Buddha’s verse! It is the great pivot of the Pure Land.
The method for practicing the Pure Land lies entirely within the gate of mindfulness; one must be able to break through it and enter. This is the method for entering the gate of mindfulness.
What is essential? The words of Caoxi are ultimate: "True Suchness is the substance of thought;
thought is the function of True Suchness. True Suchness gives rise to thought from its own nature; it is not the eyes, ears, nose, or tongue that can think."
True Suchness possesses the nature [of awakening], which is why thoughts arise. Alas! This exhausts the matter.
From the *Biographies of Laymen*, Volume 23:
The Biography of Zhang Pingshu.
Zhang Pingshu, originally named Bo’end, later changed his name to Yongcheng and took the sobriquet Ziyang. He was a native of Tiantai.

During the Xining era, he traveled to Sichuan where he met Liu Haichan, who transmitted to him the methods of the Elixir (Dāna). After a long time, he thoroughly penetrated the source of the Dharma and composed the *Wuzhen neiwai pian* (Inner and Outer Chapters on Realizing Truth).
The preface states: "In the birth of a person, it is all due to deluded emotions that one possesses a body; possessing [a body]..."
The body is subject to affliction; if there were no body, from where would affliction arise? Now, those who wish to escape affliction do nothing better than embody the Ultimate Way (*tīdào*).
To embody the Ultimate Way, one does nothing better than clarify the Original Mind. Thus, the mind is the substance of the Way, and the Way is the function of the mind.
If a person can examine the mind and observe its nature, the substance of perfect luminosity will manifest of itself.
The function of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is spontaneously accomplished without relying on the exertion of effort; it is to suddenly transcend to the other shore.
Were it not for this clarity of mind and realm, wherein the divine pearl is vast and luminous, how could one cause all phenomena to be suddenly detached and remain untainted by even a speck of dust?
How else could the source of the mind be sovereign and definitively non-arising? Thus, for those who clarify the mind and realize the Way, the body cannot burden their nature.
When the objective realm cannot disturb one’s truth, how could weapons and blades cause injury? How could tigers and rhinoceroses inflict harm? How could great fires or vast floods pose any threat?
The mind of the person who has attained realization is like a clear mirror: it reflects without grasping; it responds to things according to circumstances, harmonizing without initiating.
Thus, they can overcome all things without being harmed. This is what is called the supreme, ultimate, and wondrous truth.
It is the Way (*dharma*). Originally, this Way has no name; it is only the Sage who gives it a provisional name. Originally, the Way has no words; it is only the Sage who provisionally speaks of it.
Yet, if names and words were silent, the stream of time would have no means to recognize its essence and return to its truth.
Therefore, the Sage established teachings and formulated words to manifest the Way. Alas, this Way is most wondrous and most subtle; how can the people of the world—?
Their faculties and natures are deluded and dull; they cling to the existence of a self and loathe death while delighting in life. Therefore, it is ultimately difficult for them to attain awakening.
Huang-Lao, pitying their greedy attachments, employed the arts of cultivating life to accommodate their desires and gradually guide them.

He held that the essence of cultivating life lies in the Golden Elixir (*jindan*), and the essence of the Golden Elixir lies in the Divine Water and Flower Pond. Thus, the *Daode jing* and the *Yinfu jing*...

Thus, his teachings came to flourish widely throughout the world. However, his words were obscure and his principles profound; though scholars might recite his texts, none could comprehend their meaning.

Had they not encountered a supreme person who bestowed upon them the oral instructions, even if they had employed a hundred kinds of conjecture, they would ultimately have been unable to realize their efficacy or accomplish their purpose. In the past, during the year of Jǐyǒu, I met the Master in Chengdu.
He was granted the method of the Cinnabar Elixir (Dandan). Thereafter, he transmitted it to others three times; on each occasion, he encountered calamity within no more than twenty days.
He then reflected upon his former transgressions and resolved that from this day forward he would always keep his mouth clamped and his tongue tied, never daring to speak of it again.

This work contains all the subtle principles regarding the medicinal ingredients and the firing process (huohou) of the Great Elixir as they are celebrated in the *Wuzhen pian* (Canticles of Realization), leaving nothing incomplete. Those who seek the Way should study it with diligence.

Those who possess the skeletal constitution of an immortal from an early age will find their wisdom and discernment naturally clarified upon observing this; this is a gift from Heaven, not something I have arbitrarily transmitted.
As for the verses at the end of the work that discuss the method of realizing one's nature, these are precisely what was referred to above as the Way of Unconditioned Sublime Enlightenment.
However, the Way of Non-action takes the equalization of all things as its core principle; though it reveals the most profound and secret essentials, [it remains beyond conceptual grasp].
In the end, there is no fault. Alas, ordinary beings have karmic conditions that vary in thickness and natures that differ in acuity;

even upon hearing a single sound, they produce diverse views. If there are those of sharp and keen faculties who see or hear this treatise, they will know that I have attained the sublime essence of the Supreme Vehicle (Ekayāna) of the Dharma-ghoṣa patriarchs, and may realize ten thousand things through a single word.
This is the Dharma. If residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) still remain, one will revert to views of the Small or Middle Vehicles; this is not my fault.

There are thirty-three verses in the "Outer Section" (Wai-pian), but as the text is extensive, I have not recorded them all. I record here the "Verses on Mindlessness," which say: "How laughable is my mind!
It is as stubborn and base as it is dull and distracted. Stolidly and aimlessly, I surrender myself to things as they come. I do not understand how to practice cultivation, nor..."
I have committed transgressions. I have never benefited others, nor have I pursued my own private interests. I do not maintain the precepts, nor do I observe prohibitions.

I know nothing of ritual and music, nor do I practice benevolence and righteousness. Among the capacities of worldly men, I possess not even one hundredth of a part. When hungry, I eat; when thirsty, I drink.
When weary, I sleep; when awake, I move about. When hot, I wear a single garment; when cold, I cover myself with a quilt. I am without thought.

Be without concern. What is there to worry about, what is there to rejoice in? Do not regret, do not scheme; have no thoughts and no intentions. The honors and disgraces of this life are merely a transient lodging.
They may be compared to birds perching in the forest trees: they come without being invited and depart without staying.

One neither avoids nor seeks them; there is neither praise nor blame. One does not loathe the ugly and evil, nor does one envy the good and beautiful. One does not dwell in quiet chambers, nor does one distance oneself from...
In the bustling marketplace, do not speak of others' faults, nor boast of your own rightness; do not favor high officials, nor despise the lowly and young.
Whether toward kinsmen or enemies, the great or the small, those within or without, sorrow or joy, gain or loss, honor or contempt, and the perilous or the easy—let the mind behold no duality.
Be serene and uniform in all things. Do not be the precursor of fortune, nor the initiator of calamity. Respond only after being moved; arise only after being pressed. Do not fear.

How could a sharp blade fear tigers or rhinoceroses? One responds to things according to their names; why be constrained by designations? The eye does not go toward forms, and sound does not come to the ear.
All phenomena that possess marks belong to the realm of falsehood and delusion. The forms and sounds of male and female are neither fixed entities.

When essence and marks are without mind, they are neither defiled nor obstructed. Thus one is free and at ease, such that no thing can cause entanglement. The light of wondrous enlightenment is perfect and round, reflecting and penetrating all.
Manifest and hidden, it envelops the six extremities; there is nothing far or near. Its radiance is not light, like the moon reflected in water.

Since it is difficult to grasp or reject, how can it be compared to anything? To comprehend this wondrous function is to transcend all else entirely. If one asks what its fundamental principle is, this is it.
At the age of ninety-one, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Following the *caitya-vibha* (cremation) rites, over a thousand *śarīra* relics were obtained. Great!

He was like a water chestnut; his complexion was entirely a deep azure-blue. During the Chunxi era, he once returned home and sat upon the seat of honor, speaking with his family members in great detail about matters after his transformation.
At that time, his grandson was not present; by the time he returned, the boy had already departed far away.
Among his disciples was one named Wang Bangshu, who had followed Pingshu for nine years without understanding the essentials of entering the Way.
One day, they arrived at Luofu Mountain, where Pingshu asked him, "You have followed me for a long time; why do you not seek the Way?"
He replied, "I did not dare to do so. I considered myself ignorant and feared that I had no lot [in this Way].
Pingshu said, "Alas! The Way resides within our hearts; everyone possesses it. The wise do not possess more of it, and the foolish do not possess less.
For you to speak thus is to conceal your own inner light. How truly lamentable! At these words, Bangshu’s tears flowed down to his chin, and he bowed until he could not rise. Pingshu—
He said, "You should withdraw for a while and reflect deeply upon this. When you have some realization, come quickly to inform me.
Bāngshū took his leave and entered his room to meditate in stillness. When night fell, Píngshū went to visit him. Bāngshū opened the door and came out.
Píngshū smiled and said, "I sought you once and immediately beheld your head and face. Why is it that you cannot find that which is inherently yours? Thereupon, he extinguished [the lamp].
Taking the candle he held, he departed. Bāngshū was greatly distressed; sitting there until the fifth watch of the night, he attained great awakening, and sweat flowed from his entire body.
Waiting for dawn, he presented this verse: "The moon shines upon the long river, wind and waves are stilled; Fish and dragons hide their traces, the waters are level and calm.
Who sings within this realm? A true immortal; His voice fills the void, and all the myriad pipes are clear. Bāngshū read it and asked, "Who sang that?"
"Who listens? Bangshu recited once more: "Ask not who; ask not who. One voice rises high, another falls low. Who sings? Who listens?
Across the vast expanse of the great chiliocosm, it cannot be fully described. The Master has the intention to ferry those lost across the ford."

Suddenly striking the Lingtai (Numinous Terrace), he set up the Precious Mirror. The mirror was bright, clear, and still; the myriad conditions were empty. A hundred thousand strands of light permeated everywhere.
As the Dipper turned and the stars shifted, the man slept peacefully. When he awoke, the red sun was exactly at the zenith.

Pingshu then produced the *Jindan tu* (Diagram of the Golden Elixir) and bestowed it upon him. He remained on Mount Luofu, where thirty years later he passed away while seated in meditation (*Tiantai zhi*, *Wuzhen pian*, *Qinghua biwen*).

The Master Zhigu said: "Among those in the world who study the arts of the immortals, there are many who mistake illusions for reality and seek existence within emptiness, thereby losing their way regarding the true and eternal.
For kalpas upon kalpas amidst the dust of the world, they have wandered astray; the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* has rebuked them most severely.
Although Cui Pingshu aspired to the Golden Elixir, his writings often accord with the great purport of the Westward Transmission. Among the followers of Laozi, he may indeed be called..."
To those who possess right knowledge and vision, I have therefore set this forth.
Wang Dashen said: "I have briefly examined his writings; he is truly one who practices the path within the traditions of Buddhism and Daoism.
Yet, when viewed by those with clear eyes, could it not be that he remains seated within the confines of the inner chambers, merely practicing his exercises?"
The Biographies of Eminent Monks (Kōsōden), Volume 24: Zhongli,
Sun, Lu, Zhang, Sun, Ma, Zuo, Fan, Hu, Sun, Zhu, the two Wangs, Wu, Zhang, and Li.
Lu Yan, Qian Zan, Wu Chen, and Zhongli Jin of Kuaiji.
Their mother was Lady Ren, who had diligently cultivated pure practices. At the age of ninety-eight, her daily activities remained as usual.
One day, she suddenly admonished Jin, saying: "Every person has their own Amitābha; alas, how can you cast him aside? She passed away while sitting upright.
"There is no place that is not the Land of Ultimate Bliss. You do not understand how to return there. I am about to depart; you must keep this in mind.

On the following morning, he rose early, burned incense, and recited the names of the Buddhas. After a short while, with palms joined, he passed away. From then on, Jing was moved and inspired; every day he performed twenty acts of benefit for others.

Later, while serving as the magistrate of Jishui County, he was about to marry off his daughter and intended to provide her with a concubine. Upon investigation, it turned out she was the former magistrate’s daughter.
She was a daughter. She then informed her in-laws that she requested a delay in the wedding date, but first sent word to her former magistrate relative, saying:

"How can you alone act as a gentleman? I have a nephew for whom I am currently choosing a bride. Would it not be appropriate for us to share the dowry equally so that we may welcome the bride together?
They agreed to this. That night, she dreamed that the former magistrate came to thank her, saying: "Your humble son has benefited from your great kindness; he has already—"

He presented this to the Emperor, who decreed that his descendants should enjoy official emolument for ten generations. Subsequently, he served as an official in Western Zhejiang, where he discussed the "Essentials of Rebirth" with Master Shishi of Ciyun;
his pure cultivation became even more earnest. Lady Ren possessed a sandalwood Buddha image which she had long worn upon her head while practicing the Way.
When Huijin was now paying homage to it, several grains of *śarīra* suddenly burst forth from between its eyebrows. Shortly thereafter, he learned that [the image] had opened.
He sealed his chambers. At midnight, he suddenly rose and said to his family, "My lady has informed me that the time for my rebirth has arrived.
He then sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. On the day before, the entire family had dreamed that Jing was riding upon a blue lotus flower, surrounded by celestial music.
He ascended into the air and traveled westward. His son, Jingrong, who held the official rank of Chaoqing Dafu, moved his residence to the side of Dongyuan in Yizhen.
He constantly recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and practiced the *nienfo samādhi*. He once said: "If one does not recognize Amitābha, Amitābha remains beyond the Western Quarter;
if one recognizes Amitābha, Amitābha is found right within one's own home. One night, he invited a monk...
Miaoying recited the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra" (Puxian Xingyuan Pin). Having finished listening while burning incense, he performed mudrās with both hands and passed away.
His great-great-grandson, Song, held the rank of Chaoqing Dafu and served as the Director of the Chongdao Abbey in Taizhou; during the Qiandao era, he resided in Suzhou.
He formed a religious society with Master Baoji Shigong to cultivate the Pure Land practice. Those who joined numbered nearly one hundred.
At the age of eighty-six, he passed away without illness (Fozu Tongji; Lebang Wenlei).
Sun Liang was a native of Qiantang. He lived in seclusion to study the Tripitaka and attained a profound mastery of the essential principles of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
He once received the Bodhisattva precepts from Vinaya Master Dazhi and daily recited the names of the Buddhas ten thousand times; he did not cease this practice for twenty years.

Suddenly, he instructed his family to invite monks to chant the Buddha’s name. After only half a day, he joined his palms toward the sky and said, "The World-Honored One and the Bodhisattvas have already bestowed their grace upon me."
He descended [into samādhi], whereupon he withdrew from his seat and passed away (*Fozu tongji*).

Lu Jun was a native of Qiantang. In his youth, he served as an official, but after a long time, he abandoned that life. He joined the "Recollection Assembly" at West Lake, taking Pure Land as his ultimate refuge.
Whenever he performed repentance before the Buddha, his voice and tears would flow together. Occasionally, when meeting with friends, he would speak of it...

Regarding the causes and conditions for the Pure Land, he was never without feelings of profound grief and sobbing, fearing that he might not cross over in this life and that his pure karma would be difficult to accomplish.
At the end of his life, he requested the Dharma Master Yuanjing to expound the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.

As they recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* up to the chapter on "Birth in the Highest Grade," Yuanjing said to him, "It is time to depart now. Xun replied, "The assembly of sages has not yet gathered; let us wait for a moment."
After waiting for a short while, he rose and sat upright facing west upon a bamboo bed. Within moments, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).

Zhang Di was a native of Qiantang and served as a Teaching Assistant (*Jiàozhù*). He received the Bodhisattva precepts from Master Yuanjing and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land.
Before the Buddha, he burned his arm as an offering and a vow; whenever he recited the name of the Buddha, his voice was so forceful that it continued even until his vocal cords failed.
He did not cease his practice. Once, while in a quiet chamber, he saw a white *piṅgala* bird dancing before him.
There was also a green-haired youth who joined his palms in greeting. Three years later, he passed away while facing west and reciting the Buddha’s name (*Fozu Tongji*).
Sun Shierlang, whose name was Zhong, was a native of Mingzhou. From an early age, he admired the Western [Dharma], abstaining from meat and observing the precepts.

He constructed a hermitage east of the prefectural city, excavated two ponds to plant white lotuses, and built a pavilion overlooking them. He gathered the assembly monthly to hold a *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) assembly.
Once, he saw the Buddha’s body appear in the sky; he rushed out and called his two sons to join him in prostrating before it. After a long while, it finally vanished.

Later generations consequently named that place Zhufu Xiang (Buddha-Stationing Lane). In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, the monk Kejiu traveled spiritually to the Western Land for three days before reviving.
He said that on a golden terrace in a pond, the name of Kejiu was inscribed, followed by that of his grandson.
He was the twelfth brother. He subsequently passed away. After some time, the twelfth brother fell ill. He invited a hundred monastics and laypeople to hold a *nienfo* assembly.
Suddenly, looking up at the void, he joined his palms in greeting and, forming a double mudrā with his hands, passed away with a serene expression.
The entire city heard celestial music and extraordinary fragrances gradually vanishing toward the west. His two sons were able to carry on his legacy; they, too, headed west.
*Sitting Transformation* (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Ma Zhongyu, whose courtesy name was Wu, was a native of Hefei in Luzhou. His father was Duke Liang, the Marquis of Zhongsu.

While the Duke was serving as the Governor of Hangzhou, Master Shikong Ciyun instructed him in the Dharma-gate of Pure Land. Consequently, the entire family came to revere the Buddha. During the Yuanfeng era, Zhongyu encountered...
At the beginning of the Guangchu era, Sengguang obtained the *Ten Doubts on the Teachings of Tiantai* and said with joy, "I have now found my refuge.
He subsequently followed the method of the Ten Recitations and Dedication of Merit according to Ciyun, practicing it for over twenty years. Later, he further corresponded with Wang Minzhong.
He redoubled his diligence in the practice of *nienfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) and constantly took the liberation of living beings as his Buddhist service.

Having served in succession at Zichuan and Xinding, he governed with benevolence and compassion. He established a daily routine of reciting sutras and dharanis while visualizing the Western Pure Land.

At that time, the consort of the Prince of Jing was practicing the Pure Land path together with her handmaidens. After one of the handmaidens passed away, she appeared in a dream to the consort and led her [to the Pure Land].
While wandering by a lotus pond, he saw someone dressed in court robes sitting upon a flower. [The deity] said, "These are Ma Xu and Yang Jie.
At that time, Jie had already passed away, while Zhongyu was still hale and hearty. In the first year of the Chongning era, he fell ill;
having bathed, changed his clothes, and sat upright reciting the Buddha’s name, he passed away. A vapor like a blue canopy rose into the sky. Shortly thereafter, at home—
Ten or so people shared the same dream, in which Zhongyu said, "I have already attained rebirth in the Pure Land in the highest grade.

That autumn, a maidservant fell ill while lying in bed; she too recited the Buddha’s name and passed away. His son, Yongyi, also practiced the method of ten recitations and cultivated the sixteen contemplations.
After more than thirty years had passed, he fell ill. He then beheld Amitābha Buddha and two Bodhisattvas coming to welcome and guide him.

He formed mudrās and passed away in peace; a fragrant aroma filled the room. Once he was encoffined, five-colored flowers grew upon the coffin, their radiance brilliant and resplendent (from the *Lèbāng wénlèi*).

Zuo Shen was a native of Tiantai who lived by the sea. He received the Bodhisattva precepts from the Dharma Master Shenzhao and subsequently fashioned images of the Three Sages of the West in his quest for rebirth in the Pure Land.
He recited the Lotus Sūtra three thousand four hundred times and the Diamond Sūtra twenty thousand scrolls.
In the autumn of the second year of the Shaosheng era, he fell ill and instructed his son, the śramaṇa Jingyuan, to chant the opening verses of the Lotus Sūtra.
Title. Shortly thereafter, he dreamed of three majestic figures standing on the riverbank. They summoned Shen to board a boat and requested that a monk recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Suddenly, [the figure] said, "I have already seen the light of the Buddha," whereupon he sat upright, formed a mudrā, and passed away (*Fahua chiyen ji*;
*Fozu tongji*).
Fan Yan was a native of Renhe. He lived his life on a regular vegetarian diet and remained unentangled by worldly ties, saying, "A hundred-year sojourn is all there is;
what more is there to seek? Daily he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and transcribed a copy with his own hand, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
During the Daguang era, he suddenly saw Samantabhadra riding a six-tusked white elephant emitting golden light, who said to Yan: "You have constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*."
"Because I recited the name of Amitābha Buddha and attained birth in the Pure Land, I have come to inform you. One night later, he beheld the various sages extending their hands;
he took his seat, joined his palms, and passed away (Fozu Tongji).

Hu Da-fu, whose name was Yin, was a native of Qiantang. He held the official rank of Xuan-yi-lang. By nature he was straightforward and easygoing, fond of composing poetry and traveling among mountains and waters;
he also placed his faith in the Buddha-dharma, though he had not yet entered its depths. In his later years, having retired from office, he associated with the Vinaya Master Qingzhao.
One day, he fell ill, and his son invited Qingzhao to visit him. Qingzhao said to him, "Throughout your life, Da-fu..."
Huiheng and [Da]fu were good friends. [Huiheng] asked, "How can one not know that this is the great matter at the end?
Da-fu said, "I thought that if the mind is pure, then the land is pure. Qingzhao asked, "Da-fu, is there no defilement from discursive thoughts at any time?
He replied, "I am not yet able to do so. Qingzhao said, "If it is like this, how can you have a pure mind and a pure land? Da-fu said, "The sutra says..."
To recite the name of Amitābha Buddha once can extinguish the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. Why is this?
Qingzhao said: "Amitābha Buddha possesses great vows and great majestic virtue; his radiant spiritual power is inconceivable, as fully described in the sutras.
Because of this, by reciting his sublime name even once, the defilements of sin naturally vanish, just like the blazing sun at its zenith."

"What does frost and snow matter? Da-fu was profoundly enlightened by these words. He subsequently devoted his whole heart to reciting the Buddha’s name and requested monks to assist him for several months.
Finally, when Qingzhao arrived, Da-fu said, "Why have you come so late? You and Guanshiyin and Dashizhi have already descended to grace me for a very long time.
Qingzhao and the assembly of monks together chanted the Buddha’s name, and Da-fu passed away peacefully (in the Land of Bliss).

[From the *Wenlei*]. Sun Bian was a native of Qiantang. He styled himself the Layman Without Strife (*Muzheng Jushi*). In his youth, he studied the *Yi Jing* (Book of Changes) and sighed, saying: "To exhaust principle and exhaust nature—this is the teaching of the *Yi*.
What use is there for official emolument? Thereupon, he closed his door to hide his traces and dwelt apart from worldly affairs. The śramaṇa [Shou]...
He would rather associate with him, saying, "Bai Lektian cultivates his person through Confucianism and governs his mind through Buddhism; have you heard of this?
Te-buan was moved to reflection and subsequently read the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vajracchedikā*, and other sutras daily, taking the Pure Land as his ultimate refuge.
His mother, Lady Gong, recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and held the Buddha’s name day and night without ceasing. She once fell ill and invited the Vinaya Master Qingzhao.
The Master directed her to return to the West. Before his preaching was finished, he sat upright and passed away. The old maidservant Yu also devoted herself to reciting the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly, she dreamed that Gong told her, "I have already attained rebirth in the Pure Land;
you shall follow me in seven days. When the time arrived, she indeed passed away. Shortly thereafter, Yuan dreamed of reaching a lotus pond and saw Qingzhao by her side. Beside...

A person handed him a sheet of paper with characters in the Sanskrit script (Brahmī), which he did not recognize. That person said, "I am merely requesting that you observe the fast for thirteen days.
At that time, it was still the twelfth month. When the appointed day arrived, he suddenly fell ill. A monk came to inquire after his health and wished to perform prayers on his behalf.

Baoyun said, "Birth and death are already determined; why pray? He then informed Qingzhao, saying, "I must now depart from you for a while," and finally sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), forming the mudrā, facing west.

He passed away while seated. On the following day, Qingzhao arrived; he preached the Dharma for him and sealed his coffin. Three days after returning to his hermitage, Qingzhao also passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
The name of the Jinshi (Bachelor of Literature) Zhu has been lost. He was a native of Suzhou who once visited Tiger Hill Monastery to listen to Chan Master Foyin.
While lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he reached the verse on the "six kinds of likeness" and experienced a moment of joyful realization.

The following day, while dozing off, he dreamed that a ghost official was supervising five men walking along, with himself following behind them. They arrived at a house where a blue cloth curtain was hanging;
the ghost official lifted the curtain and they all entered. Reaching the kitchen, they saw a bucket filled with soup, and the five men each went to drink from it. Zhu Fang, however, was thirsty.
He also wished to drink it. A ghost official rebuked him, saying, "Those who listen to the Dharma may not drink this. Startled, he woke up.
He walked casually to investigate and indeed found a house exactly as he had experienced in his dream. The man there said that six dogs had recently been born in the kitchen.
One of them died. Zhu Da was terrified and said to himself, "I have not heard the Buddha-dharma, yet I have become such a beast.

How perilous! Thereupon, he severed all worldly affairs and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily. At the age of eighty-nine, on the full moon of the eighth month, he invited his fellow practitioners to bid them farewell.
He entered the rear garden, climbed to the top of a tree, and spoke this verse: "Zhu Gong, at eighty-nine years of age, with both hands..."
He split the void asunder; with both feet treading upon white clouds, he manifested his passing to the east of the Bodhi tree.
Having spoken these words, he passed away in a state of dignified composure (*Jingang Zhengguo Lu*).

Wang Wugongmingtian was a native of Cixi, Mingzhou. Having failed to pass the jinshi examination despite two attempts, he lived in plain clothes and subsisted on vegetarian food. He traveled extensively to attend various lecture halls.
In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of the *nienfo* samādhi and composed the *Jingtu Zixinlu* (Record of Self-Confidence in the Pure Land).

Its preface states: "The great sages of antiquity established their words and transmitted their teachings, which have reached down through a hundred generations. Yet, there remains that which is suppressed and..."

Having perused all the sutras and deeply sought their essential intent, I can summarize the merit of rebirth in a single phrase: it lies simply in the ordinary person attaining non-retrogression.

Why is this? Because practicing in this land, one must reach the first stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) or the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle (*xiǎoshèng*) before such attainment is possible.

In humans, the three poisons of false views never arise again. This constitutes the severing of delusions and the awakening of realization; one has newly entered the stream of the sages and transcended the cycle of rebirth.

Even among ordinary beings, although delusions may be suppressed and awakening attained, once a Bodhisattva undergoes the extraordinary transformations of birth and death, they forget what was realized.
Because of what has been cultivated, there are those who, upon encountering adverse conditions, may regress and still fall into the realms of suffering.

However, as for the Pure Lands where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, such as the Land of Ultimate Bliss and others, although they are contained within the three realms, they consist only of humans and devas;

Wang Zhong was a native of Jiahe. He resided on Gushan Island in Qiantang. During the Zhenghe era, he was nominated for the title of Recluse but did not accept.

He had once studied under Chan Master Xiaoben but had not yet attained realization. By chance, he heard a monk reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra* and was moved by it; he subsequently devoted himself single-mindedly to the Pure Land practice.
Every day he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* seven times and the Buddha’s name ten thousand times. For nineteen years, he never [failed to do so].

He lived in seclusion and established a Lotus Society at his residence; there was no distinction made between monastics and laity, nor between the noble and the humble, and all were permitted to join its assemblies.
One day, without prior illness, he bathed, faced west, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away (from the *Fozu Tongji* and *Lebang Wenlei*).
Wu Xinsou, whose given name was Bingxin, was a native of Mingzhou. During the Shaoxing era, he held office at court; having come into conflict with Qin Gui, he was branded a partisan and dismissed.
Upon returning home, he built a hermitage south of the city wall and practiced seated meditation day and night. He fashioned a coffin and slept within it every night.
At the fifth watch, he ordered a youth to knock on the coffin and sing: "Wu Xinsou, come back! There is no peace in the three realms;

one cannot dwell there. In the Pure Land of the West lies the lotus womb; come back! Upon hearing this chant, [the Master] immediately rose. He practiced meditation and recited scriptures for a long time until Huigui died.

He was then summoned as a Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites. At that time, the imperial decree regarding the suspension of ordinations for monks was in effect, and Xinsou requested [its reconsideration].

He sold ordination certificates (*duòdì*) to augment state revenues. While discussing the clique of Qin Gui, he was ultimately implicated by that very clique on charges of using devotion to Buddhism to seek personal blessings.
He was consequently dispatched as the Prefect of Changzhou. In the twenty-sixth year, he was summoned once more;
while sitting in the post station at Xiaoshan, he ordered his family members to listen quietly. They all heard the sound of celestial music, whereupon he said: "Within the realm of purity..."
His mindfulness failed him as he reached this point. Once the golden platform had arrived, he said, "I shall now proceed," and having finished speaking, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Zhang Lun did not know the origin of [this vision]. He served as the Vice Commander of the Western Zhejiang Circuit and was a devout practitioner of the Pure Land.

He once requested that Emperor Gaozong inscribe the two characters "Lotus Society" (Lianshe) to adorn his residence. The Emperor wrote a record for it, saying: "I, your servant, have often read of the Indian..."

There is no suffering of hunger, cold, old age, illness, birth, or death, nor the turbidity of the five realms of existence dwelling together. By means of these various supernatural powers and skillful expedients, he skillfully guides sentient beings so that they may joyfully give rise to faith.
If, within their daily lives, they can produce even a single thought to recollect the name of that Buddha, then—this very [act]...

Not only shall they be transmitted to Yunlin to celebrate this magnificent encounter of a thousand years, but I truly wish—
May all those throughout the world and in future generations who encounter this through sight or hearing universally attain the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation and ultimately achieve unsurpassed Bodhi.

How could the extent of such benefit ever be measured? I have therefore carefully engraved this upon metal and stone, to respond to and exalt the great and manifest auspicious mandate. (From *Lèbāng Wénlèi*)
Li Bing served in the inner court at the end of the Shaoxing era. Having served through three reigns, he held the rank of *Wugong Dafu* and managed the Imperial Pharmacy.
He subsequently requested a temple appointment to retire. In his prime, Li had admired the Chan school; he studied under Chan Master Zide of Jingci Monastery and attained realization.
After parting from Zide, he composed a verse on his staff and sent it to him, saying: "The staff obtained was originally priceless; [I] divide..."
"Entrusted to those with true understanding, may you uphold this well. A thousand miles apart, we share the same wind; there is nothing at all to say.

When night deepens and the moon rises upon the coral branches. Thereafter, he turned his heart toward the Pure Land. He carved a copy of the *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (The Treatise on the Pure Land from Longshu) to exhort the world.

He was diligent and earnest in his recitations for more than thirty years. His son, Yuanzhang, together with several like-minded companions, established a Pure Land Society at Chuanfa Temple. [He] maintained this practice...
In the autumn of the fourth year of the Jiatai era, he fell ill. He reduced his food and declined medicine, yet his countenance remained increasingly alert.
When winter arrived, he suddenly saw Amitābha manifest within his dreams. At dawn on the seventh day thereafter, he saw golden flowers filling the room.
He called his two sons to support him as he rose, bid farewell to his relatives and friends, and requested a brush to write: "Sixty-one years spent in confusion; this slight glimpse of the truth."
"Yet it is well. Now, proceeding directly toward the West, may we be eternally free from the aging of birth and death for ten thousand kalpas.
Having set down his brush and adjusted his hands, he formed a mudrā and passed away (*Lèbāng wénlèi*).

Lu Ziyuan, whose given name was Yuan, was a native of Shanyin, Kuaiji. He passed the examination for the Ministry of Personnel twice as the first-ranked candidate and served as the supervisor of the Imperial Chancery in the Temporary Capital and the supervisor of the Six Departments of the Ministry of Rites.
In his official duties, he maintained an air of aloof independence; he adhered to integrity and would not flatter those in power.

Upon completing his term of office, he was promoted to the rank of Assistant Director of the Grand Court (Dafusi Cheng). He was subsequently transferred to an external post and served as the Commissioner for Maritime Trade (Tijū) in Fujian.

Due to the mourning period for his mother, he returned home. Following the accusations of his colleague Zheng Xingyi, he incurred official censure and lived in seclusion; his family resided on the banks of the Hengxi River in Mingzhou.
Whenever a guest arrived and the conversation turned to the matter of Zheng, he would invariably say: "Yuan and Zheng have been enemies for kalpas. I must resolve this through the wholesome Dharma;
otherwise, our mutual exchanges will never come to an end. He regularly upheld the Lotus Sūtra.
Upon rising at dawn, he would bathe and burn incense, first chanting a verse that began: "Washing my hands at early dawn, the *palm-leaf* [scriptures] unfold... [He did not seek anything else...]
The Buddha does not perform rituals to avert calamities. Where worldly conditions are severed, he follows that severance; amidst the flames of the kalpa-ending fire, he dances once.

Thereafter, he opens his scroll and reads, neither too slowly nor too hurriedly, with a voice like a string of pearls. He recites one fascicle daily in this manner for thirty years. Upon reaching the age of eighty, he increases his reading to three fascicles.
There is no aspect of either the doctrinal or the ritual traditions that he has not researched. Furthermore, he recites the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing* (Lotus Sūtra).
He recited the name of the Buddha with single-minded devotion, his thoughts constantly directed toward the West. At the age of eighty-five, he bathed, donned ceremonial robes, and passed away.

From his mouth and nostrils issued the fragrance of lotus flowers, which remained pervasive for an entire day before finally subsiding. This account is recorded in the *Shaoxi Five Years* (contained in the *Wei-nan Wen-chi*, *Fa-xi Zhi*, *Record of Miracles in Upholding the Lotus Sutra*).

Yan Bangrong was a native of Jinyang in Chizhou. In his middle years, he once encountered a monk who exhorted him to cultivate the Pure Land practice and to recite the *Wǎngshēng zhòu* (Rebirth Mantra).
He subsequently abstained from meat and blood. Every morning, he would face west and recite the mantra a thousand times; he also led his sons and daughters to recite it together with one voice.
After twenty years had passed, on the first day of the first month of the first year of the Shaoxi era, while reading the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, he sighed and said:

Human life is but a dream and an illusion; why should I harbor any attachment? On the first day of the third month, a wondrous fragrance was perceived, its sweet scent pervading for an entire day without ceasing.
His son dreamed that Amitābha Buddha emitted a great radiance, which illuminated the hall and its contents until they all became the color of gold.
Five days later, he rose at dawn. Having finished his regular recitations, he looked at his family and said, "I shall depart today; be careful not to disturb me.
He then faced west, closed his eyes, and sat in the full lotus posture. After midday had passed, he suddenly rose and said, "I am going.
He stood up, walked a few steps, extended his hands in a mudrā, and passed away with a smile (*Lèbāng Wénlèi*).
Qiantong Bo, whose name was Xiangzu, was a native of Taizhou. His grandfather, Duanli, served as a State Councilor. [Bo] once attained a realization while attending upon Master Huguo Yuan;
he subsequently investigated the ultimate purport of the Chan school to its depths. At the time of his death, he wrote: "This floating world is empty and illusory."
Fundamentally, there is no coming or going. The four great elements and the five aggregates must ultimately reach their end; they are merely the temporary gathering of earth, water, fire, and wind.
One must not mistakenly regard them as one's own possession. A great man should maintain firm grasp when acting;
wherever he stands, all is true, and his coming and staying are free and at ease. This is the path of liberation and the gate of nirvana for all the sages of antiquity. I am now like this...
"Indeed! How joyful this is! Having set down his brush and closed his eyes, he passed away. Tong Bo was appointed Court Vice Director of the Grand Music Bureau (*Taichangcheng*) by imperial favor.
During the Kaixi era, while serving as State Councilor, he opposed the plan of the Chancellor Han Moxiu to wage war against the Jin dynasty.
Consequently, he was dismissed from office and assigned to a provincial post. Later, he was reinstated and conspired with Shi Miyuan to execute [Han].
Mao Qizuo. The world relied upon him. In the second year of the Jiading era, he was appointed as the Left Prime Minister, but soon retired.

Subsequently, he turned his heart toward the Pure Land. During his tenure in Jinling, he established ten reception monasteries in his native region, all of which he named after the Ultimate Bliss of the Pure Land.
He founded Zhi-an, where he stayed among eminent monks, remaining there until his retirement from official service.

Thereafter, his practice became even more powerful. In the fourth year of the Jiading era, he happened to fall slightly ill. He wrote a verse, saying: "The fragrance of the lotus comes from the Buddha-land;
Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, not a speck of dust remains. My own mind is pure and transcends that place; Today, I know from afar that one flower has blossomed.
When a monk came to inquire after his well-being, he replied: "I do not crave life, nor do I fear death. I shall not be reborn..."
He will not be reborn among the gods or among humans, but shall surely be reborn in the Pure Land. Having finished speaking, he sat cross-legged and passed away.
At that time, celestial drums resounded and a wondrous fragrance wafted through the air. The people of the commandery all dreamed of a voice from the sky saying:
“The Chancellor Qian shall be reborn in the Western Pure Land as the Bodhisattva Ciji” (from the *Fozu tongji*, *Xugangmu*, *Wangsheng zhuan*, and *Taizhou zhi*).
Zan Shengzhai, whose courtesy name was Dingguo, was a native of Mingzhou. He served as a tutor at the local prefectural school and constantly cultivated the practices of the Pure Land.

He established a "Western Rebirth Society" (*xiguoshe*) and, in the early JiaTai era, founded the Jingtu Monastery at Huiguang on Xiaojiang. He constructed stone stupas by the pond to serve as places for the local people to enshrine their remains.
On the twenty-eighth day of every month, he would assemble monks and laypeople within the monastery to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the Buddha’s name.
He drew a diagram divided into grid-like sections and exhorted people to recite the Buddha’s name. There was an ironworker named Mr. Ji who was nearly seventy years old and had lost his sight.

Having received this diagram of the Buddha-recitation from him, he recited it until he reached the fourth section, at which point both his eyes became clear. He continued in this manner for three years until he had completed all seventeen sections.
One day, while in the midst of reciting the Buddha’s name, he suddenly fell into a stupor for half a day and then revived. He said to his son: "I have already..."
He saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Western Quarter. Zan Xueyu was the leader in exhorting him; one should divide the six illustrations and present them to him, while also conveying my thanks.
He sat facing west and passed away. In the fourth year of the Jiading era, Shengzhai dreamed that a young attendant told him:
"The Buddha has now informed you that in three days you shall be reborn in that land. On that day, he bathed, changed his clothes, and quickly recited [the Buddha's name].
The Buddha’s name was [Endowed with] Dignity; he passed away while sitting upright (*Fozu Tongji*).
Wu Fuzhi, whose courtesy name was Keci, styled himself the Layman of Kai’an. He resided in Pujiang, Wuzhou.

Having studied the *Zhouguan* (Rites of Zhou) in his youth, he conceived a profound ambition to benefit the world. When his aspirations were not realized, he withdrew to live in seclusion at Zuoxi, where he suffered from chronic eye disease.
Someone urged him to pray to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara. Fu replied, "One who remains unchanging in the face of peril is a true man of honor.
Another cited the words of Du Qi Gong: "If you have not read Buddhist scriptures, how can you know that [the Buddha] does not surpass Confucius and Mencius?

Fu then tried to hold the name of the Great Being; his illness was quickly cured, whereupon he gave rise to profound faith and read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* until reaching the passage on Śāriputra’s mind.

Within, it was like clouds vanishing into the vast clarity of the Great Void; his ignorance was suddenly dispelled. Having read the *Zongjing lu*, he met Master Shigong Baoji, who said to him, "This book lacks formal structure;
it would be better to study the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), taking the two characters 'Contemplating the Object' (*jingguan*) as your staff and crutch.
After he had taken this advice to heart, he indeed attained realization and sighed, "How profound is the saying regarding formal structure! It is truly what is meant by..."
"Is it not by means of the ultimate square that one squares what in the world is not square, and by means of the ultimate circle that one circles what in the world is not circular?

He then composed the *Fahua Shujian* (The Pivot of the Lotus Sūtra) and dedicated the merit toward rebirth in Sukhāvatī, saying: "Without reading the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is no way to clarify that the wondrous Dharma is inherently present within my own mind.
Without being born in An-yang (Sukhāvatī), there is no way to realize that the wondrous Dharma is inherently present within my own mind. Thus did the Tathāgata exhort us repeatedly.

He instructed his disciples thus: "The wise are earnest in their expansive exposition of the sutras; the Buddhas and Patriarchs have bestowed their compassion, and from the beginning there has never been a divergent path.

During the Qiandao era, while residing in Suzhou, he established a Lotus Society with Master Shi and commissioned artisans to paint illustrations of the ten realms and nine grades upon the two corridors.
First, he demonstrated that all phenomena are mind-only; second, he pointed out the direct path to the Western Land. His fellow practitioner Zhongli Song composed a record for him.
In the winter of the seventh year of the Jiading era, he passed away at Baoshan. By his final instructions, he was cremated according to the rites for a monk.
He was seventy-five years of age (*Fozu Tongji*, *Lebang Wenlei*).
Chen Junzhang was a native of Huangyan. Born during the Yuan dynasty, he turned his heart toward the Buddha-dharma at the age of forty.

Together with his wife, Ye Shi, he recited the Lotus Sūtra and dedicated the merit toward rebirth in Sukhāvatī. After twenty years had passed, when his illness became critical, he ordered his son, Jingxing, to help him sit up and said, "I am returning home.
Jingxing asked, "Where are you going to return? He replied, "To where there is no place to go," and then he died.
Later, he followed the *śramaṇa* method of cremation; with palms joined, he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha and passed away (*Wangsheng ji*).

Zhi Guizi said: "During the Song dynasty, the imperial winds [of devotion] flourished greatly, and those at that time who transmitted the Tiantai teachings always took the Pure Land as their ultimate refuge.
Thus, those among the scholar-officials who were dedicated to the Western Paradise exceeded those of the Tang era in their renown. Sigh!

Alas! A hundred years pass like a flash of lightning; the six realms of existence revolve like a ring. Having been born within this world, if one does not return to the Pure Land, where else will one find rest in the end?
Wang Dashen said: "This single volume is a text of ice and snow. As I read it over and over again day by day, how can my heart remain at ease?"
Thus it is said: "When one recites the Buddha’s name and translates the sutras, if lotus fragrance issues from both the mouth and the nostrils, then the pure karma has been accomplished.
With every thought one recollects the Buddha; with every thought one plants lotuses. When the mind opens, one perceives the nature; when the flowers bloom, one beholds the Buddha.
This is the Land of Ultimate Bliss."

Liu Xingchao, whose courtesy name was Jingchen, is unknown as to his place of residence. He was over thirty years of age when he encountered Donglin Zhaojue.

"Then one sees it as if it were present before one's eyes; when in a carriage, one sees it leaning against the crossbar. One looks for it in front, and suddenly it is behind.

whether it be a moment of silence, a single word, a sigh, or a smile—even down to all manner of skillful means, these are all intimate acts for the sake of others. Yet, precisely because they are so intimate, many people are left at a loss.

My study must seek self-realization before it may cease. Fortunately, one night I attained awakening; regarding everything seen by my eyes and heard by my ears—
I have heard that whatever the mind conceives, whatever the mouth speaks, and whatever the hands and feet move—none of these are not wondrous.
Having attained this for a long time, it increasingly manifests before me; yet whenever I attempt to impart it to others, they are unable to receive it.

Only then do I realize that this wondrous Way truly cannot be transmitted through written words. Alas! This Way is transmitted when there is a person worthy of it; if there is no such person, it remains untransmitted.

His family resided on the eastern shore of Donghu Lake in Yuzhang. Cherishing the Way and delighting in reclusion, he did not rise from his seat despite the joint recommendations of high officials since the Jiayou era.
He amused himself with the lute and books, styling himself the "Pure and Recluse" (Qingyi Jushi). He once sought instruction in the Way...
Under Master Nangong of Huanglong, he attained the secret meaning. One day, Nangong’s disciple, Master Yuankong, visited him while he was tuning his lute.
Yuankong remarked, “Even at such an advanced age, you are still playing with these strings.
He replied, “I must play so that it sounds. Yuankong said, “It is not enough. He replied, “How many people can truly know this?”—Juefan Hong.

He inscribed the inscription for the portrait as follows: "The treasury of Vairocana’s non-arising; a vessel of the Way in Zhendan. Discoursing on the wondrous meaning, he borrows this body for his tongue;
upholding the great thousandfold world, he takes his hands for the earth. His spiritual acumen was no less than that of Pangyun, yet he understood the Chan of letters;
his conduct and withdrawal were largely like those of Layman Ruzi, yet he encountered an era of peace and brilliance. Although King Shu urged him [to leave], he could not be persuaded. His spirit...
I examined the matter thoroughly and found that he did not rise; this is something heard by all the scholar-officials of the world.
Yet, how could you, Master, have stopped at this alone? (From *Shimen Wenzici* and *Jintang Zhengwen Lu*)

Xu Shujing was a native of Suzhou. He passed the jinshi examination and gained renown during the Yong and Xian reigns. He served as the Director of the Shrine Department (Cibu Langzhong) in the Ministry of Personnel (Shangshu).
Later, he was appointed as the Prefect of Hongzhou, where he studied under Dongshan Xiaocong and attained the True Dharma Eye (*samyak-dharmacakṣus*).
He once composed a poem for Xiaocong, which included the lines: "Sitting through the night upon the cloud-connected rocks; planting spring pines amidst the rain. One day, while with Letan Cheng...

While Shanglan Pu was seated for a short while, Letan asked him, "When you were sitting through the night by the Cloud-Connected Rock, and planting pines in the rain during spring, what words did you offer to Dongshan at that time?

Shujin replied, "Today the office has been dismissed early. Letan said, "I heard you answered regarding the saying, 'The Great Sage of Sizhou appears in Yangzhou'—is that correct? Shujin said, "Please bring some different tea. Letan [nodded].
It is said that his reputation was not unfounded. Shujing asked, "When will the Master return to the mountain? Letan said, "Today you have been seen through by Shanglan.
Shanglan then gave a shout. Letan said, "Only after this can you begin. Shujing said, "What can one do with a boat? Break the dipping-scoop!
Later, he rose to the rank of Transport Commissioner and died posthumously honored as Minister of Rites (from *Wudeng Huiyuan*).
(From the *Suzhou Zhi*):
Guo Gongfu, whose given name was Xiangzheng, was a native of Dangtu. His mother dreamed of Li Taibai before he was born. Upon reaching adulthood, he became skilled in poetry.
During the Xining era, he served as the magistrate of Wugang County and as the acting administrative secretary for the Baoxin Military Command, after which he retired from office.
He lived in seclusion among the green mountains, styling himself the Layman Jingkong. He crossed the river to visit Master Baiyun Wenzhun of Shuzhou.
When Baiyun ascended the hall, he said: "Last night, while upon my pillow, I composed a verse to express my gratitude for Gongfu’s diligent journey from afar.
I must present it to you all, so as to strip away the flesh-and-blood sweat-shirts of every monk with nostrils throughout the world."
"Do not say that I have not spoken," he said. Then he recited: "The Great Man above; Qiu Yi-ji; transformed three thousand;

seventy scholars; you, the young student; eight or nine disciples; well-cultivated benevolence; one may know propriety. Guofu had harbored doubts about this, but later, upon hearing a child reciting it, he suddenly attained realization.

He wrote to Baoyun to report this, and Baoyun replied with a verse: "To hide one's body, one need not shrink; To manifest one's form, one need not expand. If you wish to see the Master’s face, Look at the child reciting the text."
Head! Why need you withdraw your traces or pull back your feet? The golden crow stirs the heavens at midnight;
the jade hare cannot catch it. One day Baiyun asked, "Is the ox pure? He replied, "It is pure. Baiyun scolded him. Gongfu stood with his hands folded. Baiyun said, "Pure! Pure!
Then he presented him with this verse: "The ox comes into the mountains; Water is sufficient, grass is sufficient."
The ox leaves the mountain; it touches the east and touches the west. Once he arrived at Yunju, he invited Foyin to ascend the seat.
Holding up the incense, he said: "Meeting on the ground of awakening—how early! The foul-smelling monk’s robe is now cast off. If you wish to know the one mysterious word of Yunju, take care:
the donkey eats grass in the back garden. He then addressed the assembly, saying: "This single portion of incense perfumes the heavens and scorches the earth."
[Chang] Gu went out. Foyin said, "Today I did not have the advantage; I have been smeared right in the face by this fellow.
He then struck him and said, "Thank you, sir, for coming from a thousand li away to visit. We shall converse together on the deep bamboo path of Mount Dongshan.
I lend you a dragon to ride out of the cave; if you encounter a drought, let it bring down the rain. He threw down his staff and descended from the seat. Gongfu bowed and rose; Foyin [continued].
Foyin asked, "Have you caught the dragon? Gongfu replied, "It is already here. Foyin asked, "How do you ride it?
Gongfu made a waving gesture, danced, and then departed. Foyin clapped his hands and said, "Only this fellow has some measure of comparison."

Later, he was again appointed to serve as the Prefect of Duanzhou, but he soon resigned and departed. He spent his later years at home (according to the *Dongdu shilüe* and the *Wudeng huiyuan*). Chen Tichang, whose courtesy name was Yi, lived at Zuo Yan on the left bank of Cai Xi.

From his youth, he was fond of learning and had a comprehensive mastery of the classics and histories. At the beginning of the Xining era, he took the imperial examinations but immediately abandoned them.
He engaged in discussions with Buddhists regarding the supramundane dharma (*lokottara-dharma*). He once composed a verse which said: "Sitting in secret retreat, one investigates..."
To the very end, one must forget one's own cleverness; there is nothing that even the Buddhas and Patriarchs can transcend.

How could there be any distinction between enemies and kin, or between compliance and opposition? Though this vivid, solitary luminosity is still recognized as a shadow, and though this towering, solitary manifestation still wears a robe—yet I sigh for those who claim they have attained the brilliant spirit, saying they have reached the ultimate goal in their ordinary daily lives. The second verse says: "The true point within this..."
Who knows? Those who know are rare when they return. To see and hear is immediately to misunderstand; to depart from sound and form is to become further estranged.
Mountains are green and waters are blue—this clarifies the primordial intent; cranes cry and monkeys shriek—this reveals the wondrous mechanism.

If you have a mind to seek it, you will never encounter it; if you are without mind, you meet It everywhere. During the Chongning era, he was nominated as a man of hidden talent; he was nominated again.
The Eight Practices. Guo Zhong, the Prefectural Governor, extended formal courtesy to invite him. Tichang replied in a letter, saying: "In my youth, I roughly cultivated the Eight Practices;

in my later years, I have simply realized the One Mind. Since the mind is fundamentally non-existent, how could there be any practices? Throughout my life, I have never looked askance at anyone nor uttered a false word.

When speaking of the general principles of Laozi, Zhuangzi, and the Buddha, I would discourse tirelessly, forgetting all weariness. In the eighth year of the Xuande era, he sat in the lotus position...
He passed away while sitting in the lotus posture (*yu yin cong hua. fa xi zhi*).
Wu De-fu, whose name was Xun, his native place is unknown. In the first year of the Yuanfeng era, he served as the legal magistrate (*fa cao*) of Yuzhang.
At that time, the regional commander Wang Shao invited Chan Master Huìtáng into the city and lodged him at Dafàn Monastery, where [Wu] consulted him regarding the Great Dharma.
Dedefu also went there to seek instruction. Huìtáng said, "I shall not ask about the doctrinal understandings you have acquired throughout your life;
rather, bring me a single phrase for the time before your parents were born. Dedefu was unable to respond.

One day, while reading the *Chuan Deng Lu*, he came upon the account of Dèng Yīnfēng, who passed away while standing upside down, his robes remaining aligned with his body without falling off. This left him deeply perplexed, so he hurried back to question [Huìtáng] again.
Huìtáng laughed and said, "As you stand here attending me now, is this following the natural order, or is it contrary to it? Dèfú replied, "It is following the natural order.
Huìtáng asked, "Do you still have doubts? Dèfú said, "I have no doubts. Huìtáng said, "Since you yourself have no doubts, why do you doubt that other thing?
At these words, Dèfú attained great enlightenment and immediately spoke a verse: "Alas! This worldly fellow of much knowledge, Has chewed through all the public cases of the past and present!"
Case: Suddenly, amidst a heap of refuse, he picked up a dung-ball made by a dung beetle. It was clearly not worth a single coin; ten thousand taels of gold could not buy it.
He casually picked it up and showed it to others, simply because it was difficult to watch a ball roll away.
At that time, Xuefeng Chao also attained the Dharma from Huìtáng and composed this verse: "By day I forgot to eat, by night I forgot to sleep; holding the dragon pearl..."
Ascending to heaven, he cast everything down upon himself; the four corners resting flat on the ground, perfectly round.
Later, Master Hedfu rose to the rank of Secretariat Director (*Wudeng Huiyuan*, *Linjian Lu*).

Zhi Guizi said: "Observing the questions and answers of these worthies, as well as their writings and treatises, one finds that they are profoundly clear regarding the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*).
Tracing the circumstances of their entry into and departure from the world, it appears they were generally unattached to material things; is this not a testament to their realization?
When compared with those such as Xia Song and Lü Huiqing, who unworthily joined the ranks of the *Denglu* (Lamp Records), how vast is the difference between them?"
Wang Dashen said, "Vividly solitary and luminous; towering and sitting alone. Lately, have there been any such figures among you laymen?
If there are, tell them to come to Dashen’s door to see the arrow."
Biographies of Laymen, Volume 26:
The Biographies of Su Zizhan, Huang Lushi, and Chao Wujou.
Su Zizhan, whose given name was Shi, was a native of Meishan in Meizhou. His mother was Lady Cheng. While she was pregnant with him, she dreamed that a monk came to her door.
He subsequently fathered a son, Zhan. When Zhan was seven or eight years old, he frequently dreamed that his own body was that of a monk.

As he grew up and read the *Zhuangzi*, he sighed and said, "In the past, I had a vision within my mind that I could not express with words; now, seeing this book, I have found my own heart. He passed the jinshi examination.
At the beginning of the Xining era, he served as the Director of the Office of Official Announcements. At that time, Wang Anshi was in power and implementing the New Policies. The Emperor...
Emperor Shenzong summoned Su Zhiyan for an audience and asked, "How can you assist me?

He replied, "I believe Your Majesty seeks to govern with excessive urgency, listens to counsel too extensively, and promotes men too precipitously. I pray that Your Majesty remain calm and wait for things to come forward, and only then respond to them.
Shenzong said with a start, "What Your Excellency has said, I shall reflect upon in detail. Whenever Su Zhiyan had a discourse...
Lüe frequently disagreed with Ānshí. When he was appointed as the Judicial Commissioner (tuīguān) of Kāifēng, he submitted a memorial vehemently denouncing the harms of the New Policies (*xīnfǎ*).
Ānshí became increasingly displeased, so Lüe requested and was granted an external post as the Vice Prefect (*tōngpàn*) of Hángzhōu.

At that time, the Vinaya Master Yuánzhào of Qiántáng was just beginning to open the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land (*jìngtǔ*). Zīzhān consequently commissioned an artisan to paint an image of Amitābha Buddha for him.
To offer merit to his parents, he composed this verse: "The Buddha, with his Great Perfect Enlightenment, fills worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Yet I, through inverted conceptions, drift in and out of birth and death. How can I, by means of a single thought-moment, attain rebirth in the Pure Land?

The karma I have created since beginningless time originally arose from a single thought; since it arose from a single thought, it shall likewise be extinguished by a single thought. [Birth and extinction...]
In the state of cessation, I am one with the Buddha; like water cast into the sea, or like bellows blown by the wind, even with the great wisdom of a Sage, one cannot distinguish them.
May my former parents and all sentient beings find the West wherever they dwell, and may all they encounter be the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
May every person attain Infinite Life, where there is neither going nor coming—this alone is what I know.
In Huzhou, the Censor impeached him for slandering the state through his poetry. He was arrested and sent to the imperial prison, where his fate seemed uncertain.
Emperor Shenzong secretly dispatched someone to observe him; Su Zhan was then fast asleep, the sound of his snoring reaching outside the door.
The Emperor remarked, "I know that there is truly nothing on Su Shi’s mind. Consequently, he was demoted to the rank of Vice Commandant of Huangzhou Garrison. Su Zhan—
Since his release from prison, he has observed the precept against killing. Passing through Qiting, he visited his old friend Chen Jichang and composed a poem for him, saying:
"I pity the frog in the basket, Closing its mouth to guard its remaining juices. I also pity the fish in the net, Opening its mouth to spit out its scant moisture.
To carve open their bellies would afflict both; To go beyond this limit, what could I possibly gain? We have met, yet have not yet exchanged pleasantries; I urge you to observe this most [of all]."
In haste, he failed to see Lu Huai-shen; he steamed a duck in a jar, and all the guests suppressed their laughter until the lid was suddenly lifted to reveal nothing but a shaven head.
When Wang Wuzi was not present, the knife on his table would always be stained red; a steamed piglet sat upon a *liuli* vessel, its center white with human milk.
Lu Gong was truly haggard and unrefined, his thinning hair barely holding a full cap. Though Wang Wuzi was a man of grand extravagance, even before he died, his spirit had already departed.

I weep. You have offered ten thousand pieces of precious jade to the Master, yet you seek to protect the flaw of this single ant. One year becomes a single dream; a hundred years are truly but a passing guest.

Do not let this verse fall into neglect; it shall be included in the collection of Du Fu’s poems. By the time he reached Huangzhou, he built a residence at Dongpo and styled himself the Dongpo Recluse.
Having obtained the An-guo Temple, a refined retreat south of the city, he would go there every once in a while to burn incense.
He sat in silence, subduing himself and repenting his transgressions. After a long time, both body and mind became empty;
he searched for the marks of sin and defilement, but they were utterly unfindable. After five years, he moved to Ruzhou and traveled to Gao'an.

Before parting from his disciple You, on the evening of their departure, You, Zhenjing Wen, and Shousheng Cong shared a single bed and slept together; all three dreamed that they were welcoming Chan Master Wuzu Jie.
Shortly thereafter, Zizhan arrived. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, he served as Hanlin Academician; in the fourth year, he was appointed to govern Hangzhou.
Hangzhou was suffering from a severe drought and an epidemic. Zizhan devised methods to provide relief, saving many lives.

He dredged the two lakes of Maoshan and Yanqiao and restored the Six Wells, which greatly benefited the people, who subsequently erected a living shrine for him. In the sixth year, he returned to the capital to serve as Hanlin Academician.

He received the imperial decree and was promoted to the rank of Academician of the Duandian Hall, concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy. In the eighth year [of Shaoxing], he was sent out to serve as the Governor of Dingzhou.
At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, when the calamity of factionalism broke out, he was exiled to live in Huizhou. Upon his arrival there, he wrote in a letter to Wang Dingguo:
"I have been here for eight months; I came with only my youngest son. In all matters, our needs have not gone unmet, and the local climate and customs are not particularly harsh."
It is distressing. Because of this, I have completely cast aside worldly affairs; both body and mind are at peace, and my young son has likewise transcended the mundane world.

It is not that such a son would not be born unless he had such a father. Whether we go north or south, dwell here or there, is determined by destiny; thus, I do not even harbor thoughts of returning home.

Next year, I shall purchase land and build a house to become a resident of Huizhou. Furthermore, I wrote to Li Gongze: [...]* *I have omitted the final sentence as it was not provided in the source text.*
I have received your new poem, which is filled with the sentiment of longing and desolation at our impending separation.
Although your affection for me is profound, I have always regarded you with an iron heart and stone entrails; why then have you become like this?

Though we are old and impoverished, the Way and its principles run through our hearts and livers, and loyalty and righteousness fill our very marrow. We must simply be able to laugh and talk even at the moment of life and death. If one sees...
When I am in distress, I feel a sense of despondency; thus, I am not far removed from those who have not studied the Way.

Although I harbor a sense of frustration regarding my circumstances, whenever there is a matter by which I might honor my lord and protect the people, I forget my own person and act for it. I entrust fortune and misfortune, gain and loss, to the Creator.
Were it not for you, brother, how could I have even conceived such a thought? After three years had passed, regardless of whether people were wise or foolish—
Having won the hearts of all, he was subsequently transferred to Changhua. He carried a single scroll of an Amitābha Buddha image with him, saying, "This is my *gong'an* for rebirth in the Pure Land.
When firewood and rice were not available, he would eat taro and drink water. He composed writings and often walked through the fields singing while carrying a large gourd;
looking up and down with a vast air of composure, he found his own joy therein. At the beginning of the Yuánfú era, a great amnesty was proclaimed.
He returned north and was again appointed as the Court Honorary Official (Chao-feng-lang) overseeing the Jade Bureau Observatory (Yuju Guan) in Chengdu.

Falling ill, he stayed in Changzhou and submitted a memorial requesting retirement, which was granted. At the time of his death, his disciple Qian Shixiong urged him, saying, "Master, having reached this point in your lifelong practice, you should exert even greater effort.
He replied, "To exert effort is precisely the error. With these words, he passed away. During the reign of Emperor Gaozong, he was posthumously honored with a title.
Wenzhong. Ziyou’s name was Che. While he was in Gaoyang County, Chan Master Quan of Huangbo encouraged him to study Chan.
Finally, upon visiting Chan Master Shun of Hongzhou, he attained realization. He served successively as Hanlin Academician and Vice President of the Department of State Affairs.
He died, and his posthumous title was Wending (based on the *Sudōpō Nianpǔ*, *Wénjí*, *Chūnzhǔ Jìwén*, *Lóngshū Jìngtǔ Wén*, *Sòngshǐ*, and *Wǔdēng Huìyuán*).
Huang Lüzhi, whose given name was Tingjian, was a native of Fennings in Jiangxi. He once visited Shanshu Valley Temple in Qian and Wanzhou and took great delight in it;
consequently, he styled himself the "Shangu (Valley Mountain) Hermit. During the Zhiping era, he passed the jinshi examinations and thus had a penchant for composing erotic verses.
Master Chan Faxiu rebuked him, saying: "By means of your flowery rhetoric, you stir up the lustful hearts of people throughout the world; do you not fear [the consequences]?"

He entered hell. Lu Zhí was struck with awe and repented his errors, subsequently resolving to study the Buddha-dharma with vigor. While serving as the magistrate of Tàhé County, he governed with equanimity and simplicity.
After more than a year, he was transferred to serve as the supervisor of Dèpíng Town in Dézhōu. Passing by the Sengqiā Pagoda in Sīzhōu, he made this vow:
"The Bodhisattva, the Lion King, takes the pure white Dharma as his body; within the valley of ultimate emptiness, he displays his majestic prowess."
And with a roar, he contemplates the bow and the brilliant, sharp arrow; clad in the armor of compassion, unshaken by the power of patience, he directly shatters the army of Māra.
He constantly delights in samādhi, takes ambrosia as his fine food, and takes the flavor of liberation as his drink.
He sports within the three vehicles and abides in all-knowledge, turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. I now praise him—praising that which accords with his true nature.
Through body, speech, and mind, I deliberate and examine, and thus perform confession according to reality.
From the past until now, due to ignorance and craving, I have drunk wine and eaten meat, increasing my thirst for desire and entering the forest of false views, failing to attain liberation.
Now, before the Buddha, I make this great vow: from this day forth, throughout the entirety of the future world, I shall no longer engage in sexual desire. May it be so from this moment on...
Day by day, throughout the entirety of future worlds, I shall no longer drink alcohol. From this day forth, until the end of the future, I vow never again to eat meat.
Should I ever again succumb to lustful desire, may I fall into hell and dwell within a pit of fire for immeasurable kalpas.

For all sentient beings who must undergo the retribution of suffering due to their licentiousness, may I receive it all on their behalf. Should I ever again drink alcohol, may I likewise fall into hell.
In hell, they drink molten copper for immeasurable kalpas. Because all sentient beings have become perverted by alcohol, they ought to undergo this retribution of suffering;
I shall receive it all on their behalf. Furthermore, if one eats meat, one shall fall into hell and swallow hot iron balls for immeasurable kalpas.
Because all sentient beings have committed killing, they ought to undergo this retribution of suffering; I shall receive it all on their behalf. May I...
By this means, throughout the limits of the future, through the vows of patience, the sense bases and objects are purified, and the ten kinds of patience are fully realized.
Without relying on the instruction of others, one enters all-knowledge and accords with the Tathāgata, manifesting Buddha-works within the realms of immeasurable sentient beings.
I reverently contemplate the Ten Bodies, which penetrate and illuminate the adornment of myriad virtues; may they bear witness for me in every land and at every atom of dust.
Even if I were to pass through a kalpa of existence, should I forget my original vow, may you graciously bestow your protection and disperse the clouds of my delusion.
I prostrate myself with a pain as vast as space. Having arrived, the local official, Zhao Tingzhi, sought imperial favor and wished to implement the market-exchange system (shi-yi fa) in the town;
Lu Zhi remarked that the town was small and the people poor, and thus it was discontinued. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, he was appointed to the post of School Inspector (Jiao).

He served as a Secretary of the Library (Shūláng). He compiled the Veritable Records of Emperor Shenzong and was subsequently promoted to Assistant Director of the Court of Imperial Annals (Zhuōzuò Zuóláng).

When his mother fell ill for many years, he watched her facial expressions throughout the night, never removing his sash from his waist. Upon her death, he escorted her funeral home; so consumed by grief that he emaciated himself, he nearly died.
