After she was buried, he lived in a hut at her tomb until the completion of the mourning period. Once the mourning was over, he was appointed Vice-Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Chéng). At the beginning of the Shaosheng era, he requested a transfer to a provincial post and was appointed Governor of Xuancheng, later transferred to Ezhou.
In the province, as the disaster of the factional strife broke out, Zhang Dun and Cai Bian argued that the *Shenzong Shilu* (Veritable Records of Emperor Shen-zong) contained many falsehoods.

Consequently, Lu Zhi was demoted to the position of *biejia* (assistant magistrate) in Fuzhou and relocated for house arrest to Qinzhou. Initially, Lu Zhi had gone to Master Haitang to inquire about the Way.
Haitang said, "The *Lunyu* states: 'Do you think, my disciples, that I have something hidden from you? I have nothing hidden from you. How do you usually understand this?"
Lun. Lu Zhi presented his understanding, to which Huìtáng replied, "Not so, not so. Lu Zhi remained in a state of persistent confusion.
One day, while attending Huìtáng on a mountain walk when the *mùzhī* (muguet) was in full bloom, Huìtáng asked, "Do you smell the fragrance of the *mùzhī*? He replied, "I do."
Huìtáng said, "I have nothing hidden from you. Lǔzhí was suddenly enlightened and immediately prostrated himself before him.
Later, having visited Chán Master Sīxīn, he entered the meditation hall with the assembly. Sīxīn opened his eyes wide and asked, "Sīxīn is dead; the scholar is dead.
Once we are burned into two heaps of ash, where shall we meet? Lǔzhí was unable to answer. Sīxīn dismissed him. Upon arriving in Qián, it happened that—

He clarified the questions posed by Sīhamati and replied with a letter, saying: "In the past, I have often been exhorted by your bitter words, yet for a long time I remained as if in a drunken dream, lingering vaguely within the shadows of light.
This was because my state of doubt was not exhausted and the root of my life-destiny was not severed; thus, I retreated, looking back at the precipice.
While napping on the road in Southern Quan, upon waking, it suddenly became vast and clear. I then reflected that I had been deceived by the old masters throughout the world..."
"How many people have the Master deceived? Only the Venerable Sishin refused; that was truly the highest form of compassion.

When Emperor Huizong ascended the throne, [Dahui] was appointed to oversee the taxes of Ezhou. Although he repeatedly received summons from the court, he declined and did not go. He requested to be stationed in Zhi-tai-ping.
When Zhao Tingzhi became Prime Minister, he harbored a long-standing resentment toward Lu Ji (Ru-zhi) because the latter had not aligned himself with him. Consequently, Zhao falsely accused Lu Ji of—

His writings slandered the state, and he was consequently stripped of his official title and placed under house arrest in Yizhou. The family that provided him lodging was summarily punished by the authorities; he therefore took up residence in a guard tower.
There, amidst the rain above and the wind around him, he sang freely and with self-satisfaction. In the ninth month of the fourth year of the Chongning era, he passed away due to illness.
His close friend Jiang Wei arranged his funeral and escorted his remains back to Jiangxi. During the reign of Emperor Gaozong, [he was posthumously honored].
His posthumous title was Wénjié (contained in the *Shānyù Wénjí*, *Sòngshǐ*, and *Wǔdēng Huìyuán*).
Cháo Wújiū, whose given name was Bǔzhī, was a fourth-generation descendant of Cháo Míngyuǎn. He was skilled in literary composition and was close friends with Sū Zǐzhān and Huáng Lǔzhí.

His official career reached the rank of Director of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù Lángzhōng*), concurrently serving as a compiler for the National History (*Guóshǐ Biānxiū*). He served successively as the governor of various prefectures and commanderies, leaving behind benevolent deeds.
Zheng lived in Qizhou and once saved several thousand displaced people. At the age of twenty-something, he turned toward the True Dharma and gained deep faith in cause and effect.
He associated with various Chan masters, such as Yuantong Juehai, seeking the ultimate matter of transcendence.
In the second year of the Chongning era, a commoner in Wei Prefecture slaughtered a pig; a dog then took the pig’s head bone in its mouth and departed, barking loudly for four days without eating.
Or perhaps they were different and he dissected them; within the hollow of a left male tooth, he found a piece of flesh shaped like a thumb, bearing the likeness of the Tathāgata.
Its topknot had a grain-like protuberance like a pearl, its eyes were deep blue, and it sat in the full-lotus posture, complete with every mark of adornment.
Wujiu’s younger brother Cai personally witnessed this event and recorded it on stone to show Wujiu. Wujiu said: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas vow to save sentient beings, even unto..."
Out of love for others, he gave his head, eyes, marrow, and brain to deliver both humans and animals from immeasurable suffering.
Yet, ordinary people bound by all fetters continue their slaughter for the sake of gain and offerings; they shall all fall together into the great fiery pit of intense suffering.

To warn such a lot, the Buddha and Bodhisattvas stir their majestic spiritual power, so that through fear they may give rise to faith. Thus, from within the boiling cauldron of scalding water, a lotus flower emerges, and one repents the taking of life with the precepts.
Harmful! One should universally perform dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). By this, the causes for the profound *prajñā* increase, and one is protected and remembered by all Buddhas;

how could this not be superior? Thereupon, he composed a hymn of praise, saying: "I observe the birds and beasts that take various fleshly forms—with mouths like hooks and teeth like saws, as cruel and fierce as *rākṣasas*.
Such beings as these, whether strong or weak, are driven by the power of karma to devour others."
To nourish oneself is to encounter food; having died, one is able to be reborn. Yet you instead seek to exact retribution for it, as if saying, "You have devoured me.

As you ply the wooden formers up and down the wall, there is no end to the labor. This karma is profound and cannot be transcended even by a Buddha. Oxen and horses eat grass; their mouths are square and their teeth flat.
Their karma is shallow and easy to transcend, and they suffer no further retribution. Humans are not oxen or horses; our teeth are even like shells or gourd seeds, and we eat grain.

Fruits and vegetables: their forms are naturally so; why then would it not be the same? It is said that while oxen and horses differ from other beings in lacking predatory muzzles and tusks, they nonetheless possess sharp hooves as weapons;

whereas hawks and tigers receive retribution for their inherently predatory forms. Thus, although human and Buddha-forms are not naturally cruel like those of hawks and tigers, when humans die and receive retribution, it is even more severe than that of horses and oxen.
I recite these words to universally exhort all who have eyes: because blood enters their teeth, they kill living beings.
Without ceasing. The Perfected Person is without [discriminating] mind; they regard all with equal benevolence and look upon all as one. They view others as themselves and view pigs as humans.
Yet humans themselves do not know what these pigs truly are, nor the causes for their kinsmen in previous lives. How is it that through ignorance they daily slaughter their own kin?
They pierce their hearts to take their blood, which flows like a vast abyss; they boil them alive to scald their bristles, which form a heap as high as Mount Sumeru. Thus do they die.
He did not abandon them; ten thousand pigs constantly followed him. "Do not brandish your knife," he said, "thinking that pigs are lowly creatures.
Within this mass of warm blood, there exists a body sixteen feet tall. Namo Buddhāya. Namo Saṃghāya. I dare not kill.

Before all the Buddhas, all sentient beings—whether flying or running, whether submerged or burrowing, large or small, beautiful or ugly—each possesses [a Buddha-nature] within their flesh and blood."
One Buddha. How can you see the Buddha and yet wish to brandish a knife? You who wish to kill this pig should reflect thus:
When the King of Kaśmīra killed the Venerable One, before he had even laid down his blade, his arm fell off and white milk gushed forth, causing the earth to quake in six ways.
This pig is just like that; its brain is shattered and the Buddha emerges. The Buddha is not outside; the Buddha is not inside. The Buddha is not...
He abides in emptiness; the Buddha does not reside in form. This pig did not die; that Buddha remained solemnly present.

With a mind of worldly discrimination, he claimed for himself human nobility, yet said that the karma of sheep and pigs was originally intended to provide for humans. "Since they have come here by reason of their own karma, why should I accept them?

To accept them would mean that the karma of sheep and pigs returns to my own person. Long ago there was a great boar who, from birth, did not eat filth but fed on mint grass, and he delivered the herd.
"A pig of karma! By the majestic spiritual power of a Bodhisattva, he manifests entry among the various species. You possess but the physical eye; by what means could you recognize a pig?

Withdraw your blade and do not strike the head of this pig. Within my molar grinder sits one who dwells in the full-lotus posture. I bow my head to the World-Honored One who resides within my grinder;
I dare not treat him with arrogance. Here there is neither pig nor man. I only pray that he appear before me. May all who see and hear it be like a Bodhisattva."

I vow: in every thought-moment, do not harbor doubt. By means of these supreme causes, universally dedicate [merit] to parents, teachers, and elders of the three periods of time, whether they be enemies or kin.
May they transform their hearts to become supple, abandon their poisonous and harmful intentions, cast off the flow of hot blood, and obtain the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*).

May the ocean of suffering dry up entirely, and all be brought together in peace and security. Furthermore, he once composed a text on *yansuo* (seated meditation), which says: "When sitting in quietude during ordinary times, close the eyes and withdraw [the senses]."
He constantly spoke these words: "Your body now is neither male nor female; it is neither descendant nor ancestor; it is without past or present, without coming or going.
It is pure and fundamental by nature, yet through delusion a realm of land arises. When consciousness is defiled by dust, the sense organs then coalesce.
This has been so for a long time and cannot be washed away, like a garment that has absorbed a stain. Thus there is a delusory physical form and a delusory name—this is Zhang, this is..."

Li. Whether male or female, since you are not this [body], this [body] is also not you. It is like the example of an oyster that, being adhered to a rock, mistakes the rock for its self and suffers for a thousand kalpas. This meaning is not so. I have a parable:

it is as if the self were like space, which is nailed down by a nail. Space is not a material thing; the nail has no place to adhere. Thus, one immediately attains liberation and departs from both "self" and "the self."
At such a time, look with clear eyes. A single thought in accord [with reality] is the path to nirvāṇa.

During the Daguang era, he served as the Administrator of Sizhou and died at the age of fifty-eight. His younger cousin, Shuozhi, whose courtesy name was Yidao, held the office of Imperial Archivist (Weiyou Ge Dazhi).
He once visited Master Mingzhi of Hunan to study the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school. In his later years, he recited the *Dharmapada* daily.
The *Huajing buzhue* (Uninterrupted Flower Sutra) states (in the *Song Shi*, *Jilei Ji*, "Buddhism as a Golden Bulwark"):
"The Master Zhiguī said: 'The three gentlemen Su, Huang, and Chao were all literary men who swam in the ocean of the Buddha’s teachings.

The vastness of Zizhan (Su Shi), the sharp vigor of Lüzhi (Huang Tingjian), and the profound earnestness of Wujiu (Chao Buzhi)—examining their writings, each was truly a reflection of his own character.'"
Regarding the person [in question], his poems on Qíngtíng have attained the level of the *Dàfó zàn* (Praise of the Great Buddha), and their purport is increasingly expansive.

Do those who consume meat perhaps also harbor such things within? I am merely surprised that Lǔzhí, having initially composed a "Text of Self-Vow," completely destroyed the prohibitions he had maintained by the time he resided in Qián;
since this is repeatedly seen in his poetry, I cannot understand the reason for it. Alas!
"Alas! Pure karma is difficult to accomplish; habitual fruits are easy to indulge. How can one not be cautious?
How can one not be cautious? Wang Dashen said: "Suzhou Dongpo’s life was like a house full of scattered coins. From where could they be gathered up?
This biography has been transcribed so that each item is strung together one by one; it possesses extraordinary ingenuity and spirit. [Suzhou] Dongpo traveled...

He played among men; compared to the gatherings in the mountains and valleys, he was somewhat more lively. Regarding Zen, both involve the path of principle, yet Dongpo was somewhat more expansive and leisurely.
It is further said that Wujiu’s transmission should be regarded as equal to the Verses of the Seven Buddhas, the Heart Sutra of Prajna, and the names of the Buddhas of the Western Paradise.
Recite [the mantra]. Morning and evening, hold the one-hundred-and-eight-bead rosary, ensuring that mind and mouth are in accord.
If within one, two, or three years you do not enter the Way, may I suffer the retribution of having my tongue cut out.
Biographies of Laymen, Volume 27:
The Biographies of Zheng Jiefu, Zou Zhiwan, Jiang Minbiao, and Chen Yingzhong.
Zheng Jiefu, whose given name was Xia, was a native of Fucheng in Fuzhou. From his youth, he applied himself with diligence to learning. During the Zhìpíng era, he was promoted...

He passed the jinshi examination in the first rank. He was appointed as Judicial Assistant (Sifa Canjun) in Kuangzhou. Upon completing his term, he entered the capital and supervised the Anshang Gate.
During the sixth and seventh years of the Xining era, the two river provinces, the Guanzhong region, and the capital suffered from a great drought and locust plagues;

furthermore, the people were distressed by the New Laws, and those fleeing in exile filled the roads. Jiefu painted what he had witnessed into a scroll, detailing the harms of the New Laws in extreme detail, and stated: "Your Majesty is implementing my..."
...these words. "If it does not rain within ten days, I beg that you execute me to punish my crime of deceiving the sovereign.

He falsely claimed the matter was urgent and sent it via the postal relay service to the Silver Terrace Office (Yintaisi). When Emperor Shenzong examined the diagrams and the memorial, he was deeply moved.

The following day, eighteen matters of the New Policies were abolished, and an edict of self-reproach was issued. Three days later, it indeed rained heavily. Wang Anshi was dismissed from his post as Chancellor. Lü...
Huiqing succeeded him and continued to implement the New Laws as before. Jiefu again submitted a memorial, speaking of them with extreme severity.
Huiqing considered this to be slanderous criticism of the administration and banished him to become a commoner, placing him in Yingzhou. He resided at Mount Daqing.

Ying’s disciples and younger brothers were drawn to his virtue, and many among them flourished in their studies. [Jiefu] composed the "Preface to the Layman of Daqing," which states: "The Layman was originally a Confucian."

He took the school of Confucius as his primary foundation; he attained the teachings of Laozi to provide illumination, and it was only after encountering the teachings of Śākyamuni that they became truly great and clear.

Beyond these three schools, regarding the records of the hundred philosophers, the histories of successive dynasties, and even medical prescriptions and minor tales—whatever might offer even a hair’s breadth of benefit to the people and all things—he paid heed to them all.
Such was his learning. He considered [these teachings] as the principles for the relationship between father and son and ruler and minister.
The relations between husband and wife, elders and juniors, or friends are like the single wing of a cicada;
when the six directions—above, below, and the four quarters—are joined together, they form but a single entity, and it is merely this. Such is their understanding.

They believe that their own right and wrong, praise and blame, as well as the calamities or blessings of ghosts and spirits, and their promotion or demotion by the court, are all interconnected and correspond to one another. Therefore, even when facing their wives...
No one dares to exaggerate the virtues or vices of others. In the deep darkness and silent seclusion, no one deceives themselves.

Above, they do not flatter high officials; below, they do not seek favor from their local communities. Though one might step into fire or water, their principles cannot be swayed. This is their steadfastness.

May you alone become a Yao or a Shun, and let the people return to the Great Antiquity. Then, with every meal and every garment, those ten thousand *li* in all four directions shall share in the same abundance and warmth.
One grieves and one rejoices; ten thousand *li* in the four directions share in this joy and sorrow alike.

From the remote antiquity above to the infinite future below, from the vastness of heaven and earth down to the smallest of scaled and shelled creatures, it remains thus. Yet there is no presiding agent for these deeds, nor any repository for these things—this is their intent.
In their view, the past and present, the ancient and the modern, are equal; they regard themselves as equal to others, and all sentient beings as equal.
He was equal to the Buddha, and the Buddha was equal to sentient beings. There was not a single thing to be grasped or rejected; he was neither identical to nor separate from them.

Taking great purity and perfect integration as his dwelling place—this is what is called being a "lay practitioner" (*jushi*). When Emperor Zhezong ascended the throne, he was restored to his official rank. He returned to his hometown and did not emerge from there again.
In the first year of the Yuanyfu era, he was exiled once more to Yingzhou for his previous offenses. When Emperor Huizong ascended the throne, he was granted amnesty.

He returned home. He was subsequently appointed as a Professor (Jiaoshou) in Quanzhou. Upon the completion of his term, he returned home again and took the sobriquet "The Layman One-Broom" (Yifu Jushi).

In the first year of the Xuanhua era, he dreamed of a guest who called himself the Iron-Cap Daoist (Tiéguan Daoshi) and presented him with a poem; upon examining it, he found it to be a poem by Su Zizhan.
Upon waking, he sighed and said, "I am about to depart. At the end of his life, he composed a poem: Throughout my entire life, I have relied solely on Heaven;
Better than a passing bird amidst the clouds and mist. Now, by my side there is not a single thing; I have won the right to sleep upon a pillow in this empty hall.
He entrusted [his affairs] to his grandson and passed away at the age of seventy-nine. During the Jiading era, he was posthumously honored with the title Jie (Yutang Ji; Song Shi).
Zou Zhawan, whose given name was Hao, was a native of Jinling in Changzhou. He passed the jinshi examination and served in various offices, eventually becoming a Professor at Xiangyang.
During the Yuánfú era, he was summoned for an audience and appointed as the Right Rectifier of Speech. At that time, Zhang Dun was monopolizing power; Zhawan submitted three memorials impeaching him.

Dun had not yet submitted his report when an imperial decree was issued to establish Empress Liu. He again submitted a memorial to contest this, whereupon Dun accused him of arrogance and recklessness, leading to his removal from office and demotion to Xinzhou.
Upon the accession of Emperor Huizong, he was summoned back to his former post and promoted to Censor-in-Chief. He subsequently served as Vice Minister of the Ministries of Personnel and War.

When Cai Jing came to power, he was once again dismissed and appointed as District Magistrate of Hengshan, then transferred to administrative detention in Yongzhou, where he was again stripped of his rank and placed under house arrest.

In Shaoyang Prefecture, he was transferred to Hanyang Commandery. Previously, while Zhigan was serving as an official in Xiangzhou, he dreamed of visiting a great monastery where he saw the White-Robed Bodhisattva personally preaching the Dharma to him.
Upon waking, he painted an image based on what he had seen. Later, while he was in Shaoyang Prefecture, his veneration of the image became increasingly devout;
one day, as he knelt before the image reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, śarīra relics emerged from the sleeve of his robe, and they grew behind the image.
There were three bamboo poles, their branches hanging down and covering [the space]. This was no different from the bamboo on Mount Putuo depicted in secular paintings.

Having read the *Huayan jie lun* (Comprehensive Commentary on the Avatamsaka), I composed a verse, saying: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Avatamsaka, With compassion and wisdom, pervade all things.

They widely open the gates of skillful means, With leaders and attendants mutually responding to one another’s requests. Within the state beyond words and speech, They preach the Dharma in immeasurable quantities. I have finished reading and reciting it.

Reflecting thus, I have attained entry through the faculty of faith. Like encountering the Lamp that Illumines the World in the darkness, or meeting the medicine of the Snowy Mountains when ill, I have suddenly found a priceless great jewel within my garment. May I, until the end of the future, fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra;
before every Teacher, I shall offer worship one by one; before every sentient being, I shall bring benefit one by one. I uphold this sutra...
There was a man who, wishing that all might share his aspiration, styled himself the Layman Daoxiang (Dweller of the Way Village). He composed the "Song of Daoxiang," which says:
"If you wish to know the location of Daoxiang, it lies within a single speck of dust. It does not establish boundaries or frontiers; it takes no account of the two polarities of cold and heat.
The sun and moon constantly radiate their brilliance, and birds and beasts come in droves to dance in harmony. Its customs are free from both praise and blame."
The people there have neither joy nor anger; they constitute a distinct kind of heaven and earth, entirely different from the climate and soil of the Nine Provinces.
Even Master Kuang, straining his ears, could hear nothing; even Li Lou, rubbing his eyes, could see nothing. Who would know that there exists such a realm of profound obscurity?

Treading upon its primordial gateway, one enters without moving the soles of one's feet; one dwells there without recording the passing of years. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, all is done with serene composure.

In form, sound, odor, and taste, he was simple and unrefined; yet by chance, he conformed to the rules and standards of propriety. He had never been a rat or a tiger; let others speculate as they will, whether from any angle.
He was utterly detached from the mechanisms of taking and giving. Among men and in the heavens, he had no peer. It may be said that from this day until antiquity, [he stands alone].

In the first year of the Daguān era, he again served in the Longtú Gé (Dragon Diagram Pavilion). He requested leave to return home to care for his parents. Six years later, he passed away at the age of... [years].
52 (Song Shi, Daohuang Ji, Yuyin Conghua). Jiang Minbiao, whose courtesy name was Gongwang, was a native of Yanzhou.
He passed the jinshi examination and, in the first year of the Jianzhong Jinggu era, was appointed as the Left Palace Counselor (Zuosi Jian).
He vehemently discussed the calamity of factionalism during the reign of Emperor Zhezong as a warning for the future. At that time, within the Inner Garden...

He kept a few rare birds and exotic beasts. When the people’s representatives brought this to his attention, Emperor Huizong took the throne and released them. After he was appointed to govern Huaiyang Commandery, Cai Jing came to power;

resentful of those who submitted petitions, he exiled him to Annam by means of administrative detention. There, he regularly maintained a vegetarian fast with his wife, Lady Yu, cultivating the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
He composed the "Essay on the Expedient Means of Buddha-Recollection," which states: "Regarding the mundane and supramundane..."

Regarding the method for accomplishing this with ease: nothing is better than binding the mind to a single object. For instance, when reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, there is a skillful expedient:
one need not move the mouth nor produce sound. One merely uses the tip of the tongue to lightly strike the front teeth, while the mind’s recitation corresponds accordingly.
The sound is distinct yet does not exceed the nasal cavity; the faculty of hearing is inwardly integrated, and the mind...
The seal [of the teaching] activates the tongue-faculty. This faculty withdraws the root of discursive thought, entering the stream from hearing and turning the hearing back toward one's own nature.

These three [hearing, nature, and self] merge; every moment of thought becomes perfectly penetrating. After a long time, this eventually results in the contemplation of consciousness as being solely mind.

If one is a person of keen faculties, then in every moment of thought nothing arises, and in every state of mind there is nothing to be grasped. The six sense-faculties become profoundly still, all consciousnesses are eliminated, every phenomenon is entirely true, and every gateway is cut off.
Wait. In an instant, you will suddenly achieve the True Observation of Reality (*yathābhūta-parīkṣā*).

For beginners and those of recent study, if they single-mindedly collect their thoughts upon the Tathāgata—even while performing domestic chores and various tasks—these activities will not obstruct one another.

By completely gathering the six sense faculties and maintaining pure mindfulness in succession, within no more than ten days or months, one will attain samādhi. This is what is called "the Buddha made by one's own mind; one's own mind is the Buddha."

The Buddha. [Jiang Gongwang] saw the Buddha within his own mind. His son had died young and appeared to him in a dream, requesting that he petition the people to have the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* recited at Tianning Temple to pray for rebirth in a good realm.
Furthermore, the son said he had seen a golden inscription on a stele in the underworld which stated:

"Master Jiang Gongwang, though occupying a position of official censure, aspired to the principles of suffering and emptiness; he personally attended to the practice of incense burning and cultivation, his mind free from attachment, whether in motion or stillness."

He opposed the Buddha-dharma; yet, as his speech and silence were in accord with the spirit of the school, he was said to have already escaped the dark barrier. His body would surely return to the Pure Land.

Later, upon encountering a general amnesty, he was permitted to return home and passed away without illness (from the *Song Shi*, "Section on the Textual Categories of the Land of Bliss," *Buddhadharma Jintang*).
Chen Yingzhong, whose given name was Guàn, was a native of Shā County in Jiànzhou, South China. By nature he was serene and refined, never contending with others.

When he observed the shortcomings of others, he never rebuked them face-to-face; he would merely offer a subtle hint to serve as a warning. He passed the jinshi examination and served as the Left Palace Attendant during the reign of Emperor Huizong.
In his deliberations, he maintained impartiality and strove to uphold the fundamental principles of statecraft. It was only when it came to Cai Bian and Cai... [he spoke out most forcefully].
Jing, Zhang Dun’s crime was that he ultimately could not be tolerated for his upright path. Shortly thereafter, he was sent out to serve in the provinces.

Subsequently, he returned to serve as the Vice Director of the Right Bureau and acted as the Acting Censor-in-Chief. He spoke out on the failings of current administration and offended Chancellor Zeng Bu, leading to his dismissal and appointment as the Governor of Taizhou.
During the Chongning era, he was placed under house arrest in Yuanzhou, and later transferred to Tongzhou. There, he authored the *Zunyao Ji* (Collection in Veneration of Yao) to clarify [the truth].

Wang Anshi submitted his slanderous "Daily Records" [to the Emperor], and [Foyin] was subsequently exiled to Taizhou. Initially, Yingzhong had been fond of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and styled himself the "Avataṃsaka Layman.
Upon meeting Dharma Master Mingzhi, he inquired about the fundamental tenets of the Tiantai school.

Mingzhi instructed him on the "Inconceivable Realm" of the *Zhi guan* for those of superior faculties, wherein cultivation is subsumed by nature to achieve the practice of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). He attained a profound resonance with this teaching.
Entering. The *Verse on the Gate of the Three Thousandfold Existence* states: "The inconceivable provisional is not a partial provisional;
this provisional inherently possesses all phenomena. True emptiness is not empty of itself; the perfect Middle is perfectly complete, not merely the Middle.
Therefore, the first of the four gates is precisely the inconceivable provisional. The first gate is three, and the three are one; it is neither one nor [three]."

Third, it is also not four [as the wise explain four gates: first, the gate of existence; second, the gate of emptiness; third, the gate of both emptiness and existence; fourth, the gate of neither emptiness nor existence].

One, two, three, and four fingers all point to the single moon; though the four points appear distinct, they are but a single emptiness. Gate after gate, each is the *dharmadhātu*, encompassing all phenomena without exception.
If one does not contemplate through the wondrous gate of provisional existence, who would know that the *dharmadhātu* is fully endowed with all phenomena? Hearing and reflection.

There is nothing that is not perfected through cultivation and realization, for the mind is able to contemplate this inherent endowment. If one contemplates only the mind and does not contemplate this endowment, then within a single contemplation two schools are divided.
One school’s method of contemplation differs from other teachings; yet although these teachings differ, their contemplation of the self-nature is one and the same.

Those who are deluded regarding the single mind that possesses all dharmas fall into the sequence of the general and the particular. They give rise to things in succession and sever them in succession;
how could they know that the ten realms are originally one? That the three thousand worlds are fundamentally one is likewise so; none of these can be distinguished by worldly numeration.
The wondrous realm is from the beginning neither empty, provisional, nor middle, yet it is not separate from emptiness, provisionality, and the middle. Emptiness is itself the mind.
If this is form (*rūpa*), that which is neither form nor mind is called the Middle. Where form and mind are transcended, the reality of the Middle manifests;
it is fully present within the essence of each and every phenomenon. When the ordinary person’s mind is complete, it is the Buddha’s completeness.

If one grasps and clings, it is not complete; only the single word "complete" reveals the essence of our school. Those who enter this school are extremely rare. Furthermore, he wrote a letter to discuss this with Mingzhi.

The Commentary states: "The verses of the *Yǒumén* (Gate of Existence) merely follow the ancient intent; I have been honored by your perusal of them. Looking up at the Master’s handling of these notes with such ease, I see your mastery.
Your recent communication stated that you titled it 'Existence' fearing that those of dull faculties might not grasp it—this is indeed just as you feared.

However, the Wise Ones regard the Gate of Existence as the characteristic of the Perfect Gate (*yuánmén*), and further maintain that within this characteristic, all four gates are wondrous and devoid of coarseness."
The Gate of Existence subsumes all phenomena within the Dharma-realm; how much more so the three gates, whose dharmic characteristics are equal and devoid of superiority or inferiority?
Therefore, if one discusses the fullness of the Buddha-dharmas, then the provisional nature of view-delusion and thought-delusion is itself the Dharma-realm.

If one discusses the causal conditions of the dharma-nature, then the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise a causal condition. This wondrous gate is designated by the name "Existence," and it is precisely this that gives rise [to all things].
The existence of death is the existence of the true aspect (*dharmatā*). All phenomena (*dharma*) tend toward existence; existence is itself the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Beyond the Dharma-realm, there is nothing further to be discussed. This is the great purport of the Gate of Existence (*yu-men*) within *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and it is the intended meaning of the "wondrous provisional" (*miaojia*) in your previous letter.

As for what was said—that these three thousand natures are the Middle Way, where principle is neither existent nor non-existent, and existence and non-existence are simply as they are—this is precisely that point.

This is the subtle discourse on the perfection of wisdom elucidated by the ancient masters. Now, that which is neither existent nor non-existent is the sublation of the single attachment that stands outside of the wondrous.
That existence and non-existence are such as they are is the opening of the single wondrousness that is free from attachment. Within existence, it is the wondrous existence.
In the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is true non-existence. True non-existence is empty yet not empty; wondrous existence (*pranītasat*) exists yet does not exist.

Existence and non-existence are thus of themselves, not [merely] existence and non-existence. When in the provisional (*prajñapti*), it is fully present as the provisional; when in the empty (*śūnya*), it is fully present as the empty; when in the Middle (*madhyama*), it is fully present as the Middle.
There is nowhere it is not, and nothing it does not fully possess. Thus, how could the existence of the wondrous provisional be a product of deluded attachment? Provisional...
It does not depend on emptiness; it is utterly extinguished and without counterpart. Whether one speaks of existence or non-existence, neither depends on nor is it severed from [this reality].
Furthermore, when a single thought-moment arises, there are three thousand worlds: one thousand lands consist of mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so forth;

one thousand worlds of the five aggregates consist of all phenomena of form and mind, both defiled and pure; and one thousand worlds of sentient beings consist of the six realms of ordinary beings and the four... [sages].

This is the "holy provisional designation. When a single thought-moment arises, the three thousand [realms] arise; nature and characteristics arise simultaneously. When a single thought-moment ceases, the three thousand cease;

nature and characteristics cease simultaneously. Outside of the thought-moment, not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma can be found; outside of dharmas, not even a hair’s breadth of a thought-moment can be found.
This is the primordially abiding, non-transmigrating reality. This non-transmigrating reality is the essence of the perfectly luminous Middle Way. This essence...
He is mindful in accordance with reality. His lifespan is immeasurable; originally he has no name, yet he does not lose all names.
His land is named Sukhāvatī, and his body is named Amitābha. Body and land interpenetrate, merging into a single wondrous harmony.
Thus, the sound of his preaching the Dharma does not leave that land, while the mark of his broad and long tongue is fully perfected and all-pervasive. Its equipment...
It is thus. To proceed toward the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one must go by way of not going; within the sphere of skillful means (upāya), what prevents one from returning after having departed?
When the capacity [of the practitioner] matures and conditions deepen, the task must certainly be accomplished. This is how I, Guàn, have attained the meaning of the Patriarchs’ intent.
Since entering Tàizhōu, Yíngzhōng has discarded his books and no longer composed writings, devoting himself exclusively to the cultivation of the *nienfo* samādhi.
After five years, he was again granted the title of Chengshilang and transferred to Chuzhou, where he resided near Mount Lu.
He once said to his close associates, "In my past years, when I encountered hardships and calamities, my only fear was death; now, both life and death are cast beyond my considerations.

He subsequently passed away at the age of sixty-five. At the beginning of the Jingkang era, he was posthumously honored with the title of Jianyidafu; during the reign of Emperor Gaozong, he was further bestowed [with honors].
Posthumous title: Zhongsu (according to the *Dongdu shilüe*, *Fozu tongji*, *Lengzai yehua*, and the *Li Zhongding ji*). Zhi Guizi said:
"I observe that the four gentlemen—Zheng, Zhou, Jiang, and Chen—cultivated the *māyopama-samādhi* (the samādhi of illusion-like practice).

They remained detached and equanimous amidst the vicissitudes of fortune and misfortune, as well as the threshold of birth and death. As the sutras state, 'The host of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes the seed of the Tathāgata. Is this not so?"
How true it is! Yingzhong has indeed grasped the essence of the Tiantai teachings;
regarding the single gate of the Pure Land, he is like one who catches cicadas—picking them up with ease.
Wang Dashi said: "Existence is non-existence; non-existence is existence. This principle is very clear, and I too can speak of it.
What is difficult is to sever emotional views (*qingjian*). Once emotional views are severed, let you say 'existence' or 'non-existence' as you please;
it is all the Treasury of Radiance (*prabhāsvara-garbha*). If you harbor even a trace of emotional views, then even if you speak in accord with the Tathāgata..."
All these are, in essence, the very roots of birth and death. Yingzhong’s loyalty and righteousness mean that his severing of emotional attachments and views must be courageous;
his words are naturally worthy of being treasured. This is not true of Yingzhong alone; Zheng, Zhou, and Jiang were all men of loyalty and righteousness.

It is precisely because they were courageous in entering the Way that they were able to sever emotional attachments and views. Most especially, it is the literary men and sons of talent who cherish fame.
Such people cannot accomplish the task. As soon as this matter is mentioned, they already understand it; yet they do not realize that this is merely an interpretation based on emotional views.
They deceive themselves through thousands of lives and ten thousand kalpas, merely reciting "fine" phrases regarding the head-word within birth and death.
Biographies of Eminent Laymen, Number Twenty-eight:
The Biography of Zhang Tianjue.
Zhang Tianjue, named Shangying, styled the Layman Wujin (Inexhaustible), was a native of Xintan in Shuzhou. As a man, he possessed... [the text continues].

His temperament was unconventional and bold; he looked upon the world with an air of superiority. When he first served as a district magistrate of Tongchuan, he once entered a temple and saw that the volumes and fascicles of the Tripitaka were perfectly arranged.
He sighed in frustration and said, "The books of our Sage Confucius do not even come close to this. Upon returning home, he brooded deeply and could not sleep through the middle of the night.
When his wife, Lady Xiang, asked him the reason, Tianjue said, "I was just about to compose a 'Treatise on the Non-existence of the Buddha. Lady Xiang...

Xie said, "Since there is already no Buddha, what is there to discuss? Tianjue was skeptical of his words and consequently desisted. Later, while at the residence of a colleague, he saw a copy of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Upon reading the passage, "This illness is not the earth element, yet it is not separate from the earth element," he sighed and remarked, "Can the words of these foreigners also be so profound?
He then borrowed the text and returned home to complete his study of it. When Xie saw this, he said to him:
"You should read this thoroughly before composing your 'Treatise on the Non-existence of the Buddha. " Tianjue was struck with awe and subsequently developed deep faith in the Buddha-dharma.

During the Shenzhong era, he was summoned to the inner court upon the recommendation of Wang Anshi; he was subsequently promoted to the rank of Acting Censor of the Court of Judicial Review. Soon thereafter, he was exiled to the provinces due to certain affairs.
During the Yuanyou era, he was appointed as the Commissioner for Criminal Justice of Hedong. While staying at Qingliang Mountain to observe a fast, he lodged there overnight.
He prayed to Mañjuśrī, and on several occasions beheld the radiance of golden lamps as bright as day. A manifested Bodhisattva appeared in the sky;
subsequently, he fashioned a statue of Mañjuśrī to enshrine in a mountain temple. He composed a vow-text which says:
"In all places is the Golden World, for true wisdom has no fixed location; yet in the northeast lies the Cool and Precious Mountain, for illusory conditions have their manifestation."
When there is no fixed location, not even a single speck of dust can be established; when there is a place of abiding, the three realms gaze upon it in unison.

Therefore, with my five limbs prostrated in refuge, I shed two streams of tears in sorrowful longing. I humbly reflect that in the past, while in the Inner Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-prabhāsa*) or perhaps in the eastern part of the City of Great Fortune (*Mahābhāga-pura*), a single thought of deviation caused me to drift through the four modes of birth. Thus have I emerged and submerged within the three thousand worlds, entangled in the ten [directions].

Second, regarding the sense organs and their objects: having encountered these superior conditions of the present due to past virtuous causes, one bears the skillful means of a single moment to open the light that has been obscured since beginningless time.
Yet, as the defilements of the mundane world have already become deep, I fear the veiling banners still remain.

Entrusting this to an earthen image, I clarify this wheel of aspiration: the three realms are empty, and my own nature is likewise empty; what is real and what is false? The ten directions are illusory, and my...
Form, too, is an illusion. How can it differ, and how can it be the same? I humbly pray that the Bodhisattva may lead me into the palace of compassion and receive me back into the hall of wisdom;
that I may establish the feet of faith upon the summit of Mount Sumeru and draw the river of resources from the pool of Anavatapta.

Vowing to exhaust this body of segmented existence, I shall further manifest rare and wondrous deeds. Shortly thereafter, during a severe drought, he entered the mountains to pray for rain; three times he prayed, and three times his plea was answered. Thus...
Having reported this at court, he returned three hundred *qǐng* of temple lands to the monastic community. He was subsequently appointed as the Transport Commissioner (Yùnshǐ) of Jiangxi.

There, he visited Chan Master Zǒng of Dōnglín; Zǒng interrogated him regarding his insights and found them to accord with his own, and thus approved him. Having completed his term, he was assigned to Ning province.
He encountered Chan Master Doushuai Yue, who said to him, "I have heard that you are skilled in literary composition.
Yue replied, "As for me, I am the ninth-generation descendant of Linji. To discuss literature with an official like you is just like your discussing Chan with someone like me.
Tianjue did not agree with these words; he merely praised Donglin in Yue's presence. Yue was unwilling to concede. As the night grew deep, Yue said:

Donglin had already certified the Commissioner. Donglin asked, "Do you have even the slightest doubt regarding the words and teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? He replied, "I have doubts concerning the stories of Xiangyan’s 'one-legged head' and Deshan’s 'bowl-tossing. Yue said, "If you have doubts about these, how could you possibly be without them regarding the rest? As for Yantou’s 'final word,' does it exist or not? He replied, "It exists. Yue said:

"Since you say it exists, why do you not understand that it is precisely because it exists that it cannot be grasped? It is like a person who, having been struck by a sword, falls to the ground; if they were dead, they would not feel the pain, and if they were alive, they would feel the pain.

Now, tell me, was he dead or alive when he felt the pain? If you can answer this, then you will understand that the final word exists. Furthermore, if you wish to see the Buddha, you must first see your own nature; if you wish to see your own nature, you must first see the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha and your own nature simultaneously, then you will know that the final word exists. But if you still harbor doubts, you will never be able to escape the net of delusion."
Xuedou laughed heartily and returned to his quarters, closing the door behind him. That night, Tianjue could not sleep peacefully;

at the fifth watch, he got out of bed and accidentally knocked over his urinal. Suddenly realizing the meaning of Xuedou’s previous words, he went immediately to knock on the door of the abbot’s quarters and said, "I have already caught the thief!
Xuedou asked, "Where is the stolen property? Tianjue was speechless. Xuedou said, "Commissioner, you may go for now. Come back tomorrow."
They met. On the following day, [Xuefeng] presented a verse, saying: "The drum is silent, the bell has ceased; returning with the alms bowl, A single thrust from Yantou was like thunder.
Truly, you shall live for only three more years; Could it be that you have received his prediction? Yue then said to him:
"The reason one studies Chan is precisely because the life-root has not been severed. To produce interpretations based on words—such as what you have said—you have already deeply realized this."

Without knowing or perceiving it, one falls into the realm of conditioned existence at the point of extreme subtlety. Thus, he composed this verse: "In the ordinary course of action, every step is as it should be;
though dwelling amidst sound and form, how could one linger in being or non-being? The single mind is without difference, and the myriad dharmas are not distinct.

Cease distinguishing essence from function; do not select the refined from the coarse. Unimpeded when facing critical moments, responding to things without constraint—this is the state beyond the emotions of right and wrong."
When both the mundane and the sacred are exhausted, who gains and who loses? What is near and what is distant? To take the head for the tail is to mistake the real for the false;
to turn one’s back on the realm of demons and set foot upon the path of heterodoxy. When there is nothing of the contrary or the compliant, no effort is ever violated.
Tianjue then invited Xue to Jianchang; along the way, he composed ten verses, to which Xue also composed ten verses in response. Tianjue...
He was at odds with the high officials of the Yuanyou era. At the beginning of the Shaosheng era, he served as the Left Censor-in-Chief and submitted a memorial denouncing Sima Guang;

public opinion held him in low esteem for this. During the Chongning era, he was promoted through successive ranks to the position of Vice President of the Department of State Affairs (Shangshu Zuocheng).

As his policies conflicted with those of Cai Jing, he frequently disparaged him, leading to his dismissal and appointment as the Prefect of Bozhou. Subsequently, he was sent into exile to the two prefectures of Gui and Xia. [Doushuai]...
Yue once saw that Shi-sang’s attendant Qing-su had attained the "last word," which he then related to Tian-jue.
Later, while Tian-jue was at Xia, he told Chan Master Jiao-fan Hong:

"In the past, when I was with Zhen-jing at Gui-zong and we were discussing the 'last word' of Dou-shuai, before I had even finished speaking, Zhen-jing suddenly burst into a rage and scolded me, saying: 'This blood-spitting baldy is full of deceptions!'"
This is false speech; do not believe or cherish it. Zhenjing did not know this. Hong said, "You only know the 'final word' transmitted orally by Doushuai.
When it came to the moment when the True Medicine appeared before Master Zhenjing, you were unable to discern it. Why was this?
Tianjue suddenly saw the scope of Zhenjing’s function beneath those words, whereupon he took out the portrait of Zhenjing kept at home, prostrated himself before it, and inscribed upon it:"
The Emperor said: "Yun’an Gangzong was capable of both function and illumination; with his cold countenance and stern gaze, his divine light shone uniquely.

Who transmitted his essential teaching? Only Diliu was his true likeness. Before him were Yue and Hong; like Rong and Zhao, he was a man of great vision. In the fourth year of the Daguan era, when the Chancellor resigned from the capital, [Gangzong] was appointed as Academician of the Zizheng Hall.
Shortly thereafter, he was appointed Minister of the Secretariat. At that time, those both within and outside the court were collectively indignant.

Regarding what Liang Ji had done, Tian Jue was seen to be able to establish his own distinct reputation; they were both acclaimed as worthy men. Emperor Huizong, following public opinion, appointed him as Grand Chancellor (Shangshu Zuopuye).
At that time, there had been a long drought and a comet appeared in the sky. On the day the imperial decree was issued, it rained heavily, and the comet vanished from sight.

Emperor Huizong was delighted and inscribed the two characters "Shanglin" (Rain of Shang) to bestow upon him. He extensively reformed corrupt administration and changed the currency minted by Liang Ji.
He set the exchange rate so that ten *dang* coins were equivalent to three, thereby leveling the currency.

He further rotated the grain in the state granaries to eliminate direct transport costs, implemented the salt-certificate system to facilitate commerce, and remitted arbitrary levies to ease the burden on the people.

He exhorted the Emperor to curb extravagance and cease construction projects, while suppressing favoritism. Emperor Huizong held him in great awe; once, when repairing the Shengping Tower, he cautioned the officials in charge:

When Chancellor Zhang Dao passed by on horseback, [Wang] hid beneath the stairs of the artisan’s tower. Having served as Chancellor for over a year, he was again resented by his colleagues, who incited the censors to fabricate charges against him.
He was consequently sent out to serve as the Governor of Henan Prefecture, but was soon thereafter demoted and exiled to Hengzhou.

When Cai Jing became Chancellor once more, the students of the Imperial Academy composed a eulogy for his grievance, and he was restored to his former rank. On a morning in the eleventh month of the fourth year of the Xuande era...

Lying upon his bed, he dictated his final testament with his mouth and commanded his disciples to write it down. He composed a verse, saying: "My illusory body has worn the court robes for eighty-one years;
Like bubbles arising and bubbles perishing, who can know what lasts? Having shattered the void, I depart; The iron ox enters the sea, leaving no trace.
Suddenly, he took up his pillow and struck the door and windows with a sound like thunder, whereupon he passed away. His posthumous title was "Wenzhong" (Literary Loyalty). (From the *Zongmen*).
(*Wuku*, *Luohuye lu*, *Song shi*, *Qingliang tongzhuan*, *Faxi zhi*). Zhin gui zi said:

"In his early years, Tianjue was fond of official emolument and advanced with impetuous haste; he did not distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and for a time he nearly lost himself—how perilous!
Yet, in his later years, he walked the path of rectitude and was not cowed by the many crooked ways of the multitude. Is this not what is called..."
Those who reform their faults are indeed gentlemen; they know where to direct their efforts regarding the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground. Alas!
Those of limited intelligence, upon entering the Chan school, act with total disregard and lack of caution. They cast aside cause and effect and fall into the pit of ignorance;
those who do not know how to exert themselves for themselves—these are the sinners against Tianjue (Heavenly Awakening).
Wang Dashen said: "The First Patriarch entered the Eastern Land and transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal; he swallowed it all at once.
From that point on, the successive patriarchs transmitted mind-to-mind until, reaching Caoxi, it was fully expressed without remainder.
Later generations came to view this as something easy, passing it from mouth to mouth, yet it remained nothing more than a scholastic study. Thus, [the lineages of] Nanyue and Qingyuan..."
The patriarchs of the later generations were deeply apprehensive of this; thus, they reopened the gate of expedient means (*upāya*) and exhaustively perfected the subtleties of the smith’s forge.

They cherished these secrets in successive layers and cleared away all obstacles with fierce resolve. Employing an extraordinary form of guidance, they utilized the staff and the shout as the primary strike.
Their words were often strange and their discourse seemed like the ravings of a madman—all of which were the bitter efforts born of necessity.

A true student opens up the school’s tenets and clarifies its fundamental meaning; they must exhaustively investigate and diligently research the机缘 (ji-yuan) and recorded sayings (fa-yu) of the First Patriarch and the Sixth Patriarch.
One must truly see that there is no school outside of the mind. Any externalizing of the mind-school belongs to false views.
No matter how much others may claim to have seen it as reaching the limits of heaven and earth, it is merely a mass of empty vapor—a single speck of darkness.
Only through this can one see with clarity and precision. For many lifetimes, the doubt-mind has been difficult to sever and the aggregates and elements difficult to wither.
Now, the gate of expedient means is opened once more and the power of the forge and bellows is raised again.

From Caoxi downward, one must investigate door after door until the doubt-mind is severed and the aggregates and elements are withered; only then is it truly resolved. Yet, in all cases, it does not go beyond the initial [awakening].
These are the records of the karmic encounters and Dharma discourses of the Patriarch and the Sixth Patriarch.
Should there be any further path to pursue beyond this, it would constitute a great falsehood—a vision of the Great Pāpīyan.

Since the time of the Sages has long passed and those of the final age rarely possess authentic lineage transmission, those who seek the Way often do no more than read "The Great Man" (Shàng dà rén) before immediately harboring strange and novel words within their hearts.
In the midst of this, their intention is to transcend the Buddhas and surpass the Patriarchs; yet in the end, every one of them turns out to be a base, deluded demon. How painful, how painful!
Within these transmissions there is so much that is extraordinary, yet even after reading them, I remain as before in doubt. Fortunately, the fundamental path has long been clear to me;
though I doubted, I was not deluded, for I have already gained the conviction that no other way exists to travel. ○ [The phrase] "to overturn by contact" [is here].
The *Jingping* (Pure Vase) [case]: Zhang Tianjue was buried alive. His snoring was like thunder; Tianjue appeared at the end of his path—what more is there to doubt?
*Jushi Zhuan*, Volume 29.
The Biography of Li Boji.
Li Boji, whose given name was Gang, was a native of Shaowu. His father, Kui, held the office of Dragon Diagram Attendant (Longtu Dazhi).

Initially serving as a magistrate of Songxi, he maintained a close relationship with the Chan Master Qingyu of Dazhong Temple and devoted himself to the study of Buddhist teachings. At that time, Minister Lü...
While in exile in Jian’an, Longtu (Lǚ Gong) maintained a formal relationship with Qìngyú because of their former connection as Dragon Diagram (Lóngtú) officials.

One day, Qìngyú ascended to the hall, sat in the full lotus posture before the assembled crowd, and passed away. Just then, Lǚ Gong was traveling at Wǔyí; he returned in haste to view the body, only to find that one full day and night had already elapsed since Qìngyú’s passing.
Lǚ Gong wept bitterly, lamenting that he had not lived to personally pay his respects while Qìngyú was still alive. He went to the place where [Qìngyú] had been.
Zheng Longtu said, "Why not offer a sincere prayer? If you can return, Master Lü should burn incense, prostrate twice, and strike the small chime several dozen times.
Qingyu suddenly opened his eyes and smiled, saying, "We have already parted; why do you need to do this? I shall remain for you for seven days.
He then descended from his seat. Master Lü consulted him on the essentials of the Way and requested that Qingyu stay once more.

He ascended the Dharma hall to preach the teachings, for which Longtu composed a preface whose words and meaning were exceedingly beautiful. When the appointed time arrived, he again ascended the seat as before and passed away.
Later, Boji visited Jian’an to seek out the remains of Longtu’s legacy and recorded these events to encourage those who study Buddhism.
In the second year of the Zhenghe era, Boji passed the jinshi examinations and served in official positions both at court and in the provinces during the reigns of Emperors Huizong and Qinzong.
The Emperor Gaozong entrusted him with the相位 (prime ministership) three times. His solitary loyalty was trusted by both the court and the commonalty; his grand strategies surpassed those of his age.
In the brief span of a moment’s glance, he intimidated powerful enemies and sustained a precarious state. The officers and commoners relied upon him as their very life.

Yet, obscured by a consensus of the wicked, he was repeatedly summoned and repeatedly dismissed. Passing through perilous circumstances, his inner heart remained vast and resolute. At that time, Wu Yuanzhong Min and Boji were already [well-known].
Later, when he held the reins of government, he took the restoration [of the dynasty] as his personal mission. Before long, both were exiled to distant lands.

They exchanged letters back and forth on numerous occasions, refining their understanding of great principles with passionate intensity; he compared himself to Zhongsun Shu, yet, finding no way to personally demonstrate his resolve, he remained frustrated.

He then resolved with fervor to seek the supramundane Dharma and studied Buddhist scriptures. Having heard that Boji was well-versed in both the *Yījīng* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, he sent a letter from Lei Yang inquiring about the similarities and differences between these two texts.
Boji replied, the gist of which was as follows: "The *Yījīng* establishes images to exhaustively convey its meaning;
the *Avataṃsaka* relies on phenomena to manifest its principles. Fundamentally, there is no duality in their underlying truth; likewise, there is no duality between the mundane and the supramundane."
The Way. Why is this so? The fundamental nature of heaven, earth, and the myriad things is entirely subsumed within the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*).

When these are extended and elaborated, their manifestations become infinite. This is precisely the mutual inclusion of one another within the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein the one becomes the immeasurable and the immeasurable becomes the one; the great appears within the small, and the small appears within the great. Such is the Dharma-realm.
Formation and destruction are the arising and ceasing of a single bubble. The closing and opening of heaven and earth are the filling and emptying of a single breath.
The *Yi* has its seasons; in the *Avataṃsaka*, these are the worlds. The *Yi* has its capacities; in the *Avataṃsaka*, these are the Dharma-gates.
I have often observed the ten locations and nine assemblies: though he ascends to the celestial palaces to preach the Dharma, he never departs from the Universal [Dharma-realm].
In the Hall of Radiant Light, although he manifests universally before all sentient beings, he always remains upon the seat of enlightenment.

At every assembly, there are Buddhas and Bodhisattvas from the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm who come together to pay homage, bearing identical names and manifesting identical deportment;
they offer consolation and praise with identical speech, even down to the Buddha they serve and the land from which they have come—all of which are without exception the same.
What is the principle behind this? It is like mirrors reflecting one another, layer upon layer, entering into one another without end.

Therefore, the ten billion worlds of heaven and earth are the Qian and Kun hexagrams; the ten billion suns and moons are the Kan and Li hexagrams; the ten billion mountains and seas are the Gen and Dui hexagrams.
When yin reaches its extreme and yang is born, the Way of the Gentleman flourishes—this is the appearance of a Buddha in the world. When yang reaches its extreme and yin...
The birth of the noble person signifies the waning of the Way; this is the passing away of the Buddha. The alternation of the firm and the yielding gives rise to transformation;
the arising and ceasing of the world are mutually dependent. The six lines circulate in an endless cycle; the transmigration of all things involves their alternating rise and fall.
Speaking from this perspective, is there any difference between the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka and the Qian and Kun hexagrams of the *Yījīng*?

I have observed that when Sudhana entered the Dharmadhātu, he sought instruction from fifty-three spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) without exception—whether they were boys or girls, non-Buddhists, immortals, physicians, diviners, or ship captains; whether on the peaks of Mount Sumeru, along the seashore, in the wilderness, or within cities.
There is no village or hamlet he does not reach. Mañjuśrī leads him from the front; Samantabhadra shows him from behind.
With a snap of the fingers, the pavilions open; with the gathering of the mind, the Buddha-realm appears. The significance of these symbolic teachings is subtle indeed.
Nevertheless, that which constitutes the Bodhisattva path and the practice of the Bodhisattva way is nothing other than the various *pāramitās* and such dharmas. (60)
The four hexagrams represent spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). The noble person contemplates their images; this is like Sudhana’s universal pilgrimage.

There is no aspect of the hexagrams that is not drawn upon, and there is no principle the noble person does not take as a model. To be self-strengthening and never- ceasing, accumulating the small into the great—is this not diligence?

To illuminate one’s own bright virtue and to deliberate at the outset of every undertaking—is this not wisdom? To turn back upon oneself to cultivate virtue and to practice frugality—[is this not discipline?]

To open up the way for the virtuous and avoid difficulties—is this not patience (*kṣānti*)? To weigh things and distribute benefits equitably, extending one’s emoluments to those below—is this not generosity (*dāna*)?
To restrain anger, suppress desire, be cautious in speech, and moderate in eating—is this not ethical discipline (*śīla*)?

To stand firm without wavering in one’s words and to possess constancy in action—is this not meditative concentration (*samādhi*)? His teachings were inexhaustible and his protection of the people was boundless; he responded magnificently to the seasons to nurture all things.

The myriad things are what is called compassion (*maitrī*). To deliberate on legal cases and grant reprieves from death, applying punishments with clarity and caution while not allowing prisoners to remain in detention, is what is called pity (*karuṇā*).

To enjoy food and drink in feasting and music, and for friends to study together, is what is called joy (*muditā*). To stand alone without fear and to live in seclusion without resentment is what is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The images that form the hexagrams all derive from *Qian* and *Kun*; when the noble person contemplates these images, they...
One attains ease and simplicity; when ease and simplicity are attained, the principles of the world are mastered.

Viewed from this perspective, is there any difference between the Dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka* and the Dharma-gate of ease and simplicity in the *I Ching*? When the *Appended Statements* discuss the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*), they necessarily take them as wondrous through the Divine (*shen*).
These Eight Trigrams are the Bodhisattvas—such as the so-called Mañjuśrī, the Youngest Son, and Samantabhadra, the Eldest Son.
It is of this nature. The "Spirit" (shen) is the Buddha; it is as the so-called Vairocana. That which brings about birth after birth is called Change (yi).
The alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way (dao). The unfathomability of Yin and Yang is called the Spirit (shen).

This is analogous to the Buddha possessing the Pure Dharma-body (dharmakāya), the Perfect Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya), and the thousands of billions of Transformation-bodies (nirmāṇakāya). When the Eight Trigrams (bagua) are employed, there is Change, yet no [fixed] pattern.
Thus it is said: When all the Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma, the Buddha remains silent.

If one analyzes the body of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī attains his principle, Samantabhadra attains his practice, Avalokiteśvara attains his compassion, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta attains his wisdom. When these are unified, they constitute the Buddha.

When their dispersed and changing natures are considered, Qian attains its vigor, Kun attains its docility, and the six children attain their movement, stillness, penetration, attachment, joy, and entry.
When these are unified, they constitute the *Yī* (the Book of Changes). The spirit has no fixed locus; the *Yī* has no fixed form. The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm;
there is nowhere it does not exist and nothing it does not accomplish. There is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that is not filled with emptiness.
Within a single speck of dust there is no Buddha-body; yet even the fluttering insects and wriggling creatures are all the wonders of the spirit.
Even the grasses and trees, their fibers and knots, are all the manifestations of the transformation of things (*yì*).

When one turns back to contemplate this, the great trichiliocosm Dharma-realm and all the heavens, earths, and myriad things are contained within my own square inch of heart-mind. Therefore, Mencius said: "The myriad things are all complete within me. Turn back to yourself and...
Sincerity—there is no joy greater than this. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "All things that exist within the world are none other than the wondrously luminous, original mind of bodhi.
The essence of this mind is all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions. Turn back and contemplate the body born of one's parents."
It is like a single mote of dust blown within the empty space of the ten directions—whether it exists or perishes, one cannot trace its origin or destination;

or like a single bubble floating upon a vast, tranquil ocean, arising and ceasing without a source. This is the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*citta-bhūmi*). To explain it in simpler terms, it is said:

"Does he not restore [the state] by which he beholds the Heart of Heaven and Earth? By means of this, one washes the mind and withdraws into the profound mystery, sharing in the fortune and misfortune of the people.
Regarding the shared affliction, the teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* states: "One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm; all things are created solely by the mind.
If one skillfully employs this mind, one will obtain all supreme and wondrous merits. The mind is tranquil and luminous, vast and expansive, empty and penetrating, still and numinous.
It establishes the myriad dharmas and acts as their sovereign. Yet, when it is obscured by external objects, its luminosity [is hindered]."

The dark becomes bright; the great becomes small; the unobstructed becomes obstructed; the numinous becomes dull-witted. This is what is meant by "maintaining it through effort and losing it through negligence.
Therefore, the *Yijing* establishes images to exhaustively convey its meaning, and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* relies on phenomena to manifest the Dharma;

both do so by pointing toward that which is inherently possessed, rather than bestowing upon one that which was previously non-existent. To embody this Way, nothing is superior to sincerity. When one reaches the state of ultimate sincerity, then—
It rests. When it does not rest, it becomes enduring. Being enduring, it becomes broad and substantial. Being broad and substantial, it becomes lofty and brilliant. Therefore it is said:
"Only the most sincere in the world can fully realize their own nature. Being able to fully realize one's own nature, one can then fully realize the nature of others.

To be able to exhaust the nature of humanity is to be able to exhaust the nature of all things. To be able to exhaust the nature of all things is to be able to participate in the Three Powers of Heaven and Earth.
This is the realization of sincerity such that heaven, earth, and the myriad things are attained within a single mind.
Those of old who set forth the Unsurpassed Way began with the Ten Faiths; therefore it is said: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit; it nurtures and grows the One."
It cuts through all roots of goodness, severs the net of doubts, and emerges from the flow of craving; it reveals the unsurpassed path to Nirvana.
Through this, one is fulfilled as the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the ten stages, culminating in the attainment of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
It is like nurturing an infant until they become an adult, or cultivating a sprout until it becomes a mature tree; its bones, joints, branches, and trunk are already fully formed.

It is simply a matter of expanding upon this. Their compassionate vows are profound; with courageous and vigorous diligence, they enter the various evil realms for the sake of all sentient beings and undergo all manner of suffering without their resolve ever wavering.

The Master expounds verses on the Pure Land; in his hand he holds the mechanism of the ancient Buddhas, its beads numbering as many as the recitations.
Each verse consists of four lines, and in every line the meaning is fully revealed. Though the number of characters exceeds three thousand, in reality there is not a single word.

He remained constantly by the Emperor's side, providing counsel on numerous occasions and extolling the Way of benevolence and righteousness of the sovereigns. He exhorted the Emperor not to rely exclusively upon military force and penal law.

It was further stated that "in the world there are no two paths, and the Sage has no dual mind. At that time, among the court officials, only Ye Jìnglǎn was able to deeply accord with the Emperor’s intent.

Thereupon, he reverently remained silent while contemplating the Way, dwelling in solemn purity; without a second thought, he took Heaven as his companion.

Having finished, he handed it to Tao Kai, the Minister of Rites. Kai received it and proceeded along the Yellow Road to exit through the Wumen Gate, where he placed it [upon the throne].
Within the dragon carriage, equipped with ritual implements and accompanied by the sounds of drums and flutes, Wanjin was escorted to Mount Jiang’s Tianjie Zongchi Monastery.

They descend upon the court, surrounded and escorted by the assembly of majestic spirits. Reaching down even to the dark, numinous beings, they come to partake of and enjoy the offerings.

Wang Dao'an, whose given name was Er'kang and courtesy name Xinghai, was a lay practitioner (jushi) from Luling. His father was Yu Ren, who served as the Magistrate of Fuzhou.

In the twenty-ninth year, he retired from his post due to illness and returned home. He resided at the Zhaoti Monastery, serving the assembly.

Xue Yuanchu, whose given name was Dachun, was a native of Bozhou in Fengyang. He was the grandson of Langzhong Xue Hui.

It has no interior and no exterior; it neither diminishes nor increases. It is naturally filial and fraternal, naturally intelligent and clear-sighted. Within joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, there is not a single thing.
Being moved, it thereby penetrates the affairs of the world. Sentient and insentient beings are united as one body. Before they have donned their physical shells, there is only this.
The Sage uses this to cleanse himself and retreat into concealment; there is only the perfect circle by which it can be described.
What is contained within the treasury? What is named within the enclosure? Most refined and singular, it is the heart of heaven and earth.

Tracing this true mind back to its source, it makes no distinction between the ignorant and the wise; the leaping fish and the soaring hawk each fulfill their own function. Yet, in my clouded existence, I busily toil and destroy myself.
One hews down oneself and ruins oneself; one deludes oneself and goes mad. One builds up one's own walls and fortifies one's own barriers.
One casts oneself loose in the field of sorrow, lamentation, extravagance, vulgarity, parsimony, greed, and envy, yet remains unaware that these are not the true and eternal.
Alas! What kind of mind is this, going forth and never returning? At midnight, with a single cry, the Heavenly Mind is revealed—after the dream, it is the Duke of Zhou in the temple.

One must practice so that what is masculine becomes loathsome; one must practice so that what is fragrant becomes loathsome;

This is the gradual gate. However, if you encounter a friend who is impatient by nature, please instruct me as to how it should be done.

Be extremely urgent; do not hesitate to turn back your head. Regard this mark of self (*ātman*) as a close relative and seek it with all your might.

The Biography of Yan Minqing (Lu Yusheng).
Yan Minqing, styled Nü, was a native of Changshu, Suzhou. He passed the jinshi examination in the twentieth year of the Jiajing era and served as an official in the Hanlin Academy.

Lin Yuan served as a Lecturer at the Imperial Academy. During his tenure, the Three Wu regions were repeatedly afflicted by Japanese incursions, and the following year a great famine struck, leaving nearly half the population dead or displaced.

Following the corruption of the administration under Yan Song, the bureaucratic path had become defiled and chaotic; Minqing exerted himself to restore discipline and exhorted the court officials.

If one does not seek [the truth] within the mind, the more one seeks, the further one strays. The contemplations of the Three Sages were all merely external pursuits of signs; the Sage brought about [his teaching] because he was moved by the ailments [of the world].

Thus, those at the stage of "identity-in-principle" (*li-ji*) rely on *prajñā* to cultivate realization, thereby rescuing those drifting in the wheel of suffering. To speak of "mind-only":
this enables practitioners of contemplation to take the *dharmakāya* as their basis for liberation, beholding the Three Sages within the true and eternal. The Sugata...

Pointing out a treasure trove to others, the Great Mirror (the Buddha) opens it with the primordial key; the Great Mirror shows people the flower of causes, while the Sugata leads people to the ground of fruition.
To strip away the flower while discarding the fruit is equivalent to having no flower at all; to possess the treasury but be unable to open it is equivalent to having no treasury at all.
Those who serve the Land of Bliss are able to transcend the notion that [the Pure Land] is anything other than the Mind-only.
The past and present are the past and present of my own mind; they extend through the three periods of time without limit.
The world-systems are the world-systems of my own mind; they spread boundlessly without end.

Whether pure as the four classes of noble beings or defiled as the six realms of ordinary beings, these are the four noble ones and six ordinary beings of my own mind. If one does not say it is "mind-only," where else could one seek for them?
This is the Land of Bliss. Truly knowing that all is but mind, one must certainly not remain indifferent toward the Land of Bliss.

From time immemorial, these deluded sentient beings have falsely conceived birth within the unborn and clung to a self within the selfless; their habits of the three bonds and ten fetters have long been deeply ingrained.
Were it not for relying on the boat of vows for salvation to take refuge in the sacred realm of the sages, even Bodhisattvas would still be lost in the darkness beyond.

As for the "Shadows" (the five aggregates): there are Śrāvakas who are dim-sighted regarding their emergence from the womb; how could those of such inferior capacity expect not to fall back? Mañjuśrī is the guide of the seven Buddhas;
it is not that he has not realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), yet he receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of rebirth [in Sukhāvatī].
Sudhana brings to perfection in a single lifetime the fruit of kalpas of vast duration; it is not that he has not heard the primary truth (*paramārtha*), yet he makes vows to lead [others].
Returning home, if one does not serve the Land of Bliss, how can one cultivate to exhaust the wondrousness of the Mind-only?
The Amitābha Buddha within my own mind has, during the stage of causal practice, adorned the sublime land of my own mind as the Land of Bliss.
