Originally, I was no different from and non-dual with Amitābha Buddha; it was only I who became deluded and wandered astray, becoming [an object] within the Buddha’s mind.
As for these sentient beings, the Buddha awakens them and cultivates realization; he is simply the Buddha within the hearts of sentient beings.
My own mind is the Buddha-mind; though "I" cannot be apprehended, there is no "self. The Buddha-mind is my own mind; though the "Buddha" cannot be apprehended, there is no "other.
This Buddha, who cannot be apprehended as other, delivers sentient beings in every thought-moment without ceasing from his work toward me. Yet sentient beings cling...
Alas! That which cannot be attained is my illusory self. Turning my back on awakening and uniting with the sensory dusts, I labor in vain, utterly deluded within the three realms.
Therefore, to cultivate the Land of Bliss to the utmost is to cultivate my own mind to the utmost.
To cultivate my own mind to the utmost is to distance oneself from inversion and realize that which I share in common with Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddhas have nothing else to realize; they simply realize the fundamental nature of sentient beings. Whatever Amitābha Buddha possesses, I also possess;
it is not separate from my own mind. Therefore, the Land of Bliss is not a set of external phenomena, and because it is my own mind, it is not empty.

The signless is itself the sign, yet it is not a sign. Therefore, being the sign yet not a sign, both the environment and its inhabitants are truly real; thus, sentient beings and Buddhas share the same essence.

Since both the environment and its inhabitants are truly real and sentient beings and Buddhas share the same essence, the World-Honored One, King Sound (Ghoṣarāja), of the past in that Land of Bliss has never entered extinction;
the World-Honored One, Mountain of Merit (Guṇakūṭa), of the future has long since attained Buddhahood; and the present Amitābha...

The Tathāgata is beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-fields, yet there is no separation between them. His eighty-four thousand secondary marks appear according to one's thoughts and perceptions.
My mind does not go to him, nor does that Buddha come here; it is like a lamp in a mirror or the moon in water.
The mirror does not grasp the lamp, yet the lamp appears of itself within the mirror; the moon does not enter the water, yet the water always contains the moon. It is present everywhere.
It is so. Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). The *ūrṇā-kośa* mark is constantly observed yet not observed; the jeweled terrace is unborn yet one is born there.
If this is so, should it be called "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*)? Or should it be called the "Land of Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*)? I cannot know for certain.

The Venerable Luting has carved into wood the *Lebang Wenlei* (Classified Texts on the Land of Bliss) compiled by Master Songxiao of the Song dynasty, and has requested a preface for its volume. Thus, I have examined it.

He was a leader among the Buddhas. He set forth his own views and established them during the Longqing and Wanli eras. During the Wanli period, Master Hongluo of Yunqi propagated the Dharma-gate of Pure Land;
Minqing served as his lay protector. In his hometown, he delighted in charity and gave generously. In his speech, he was ever cautious lest he should offend others.
When there was famine, he sent letters to those in authority requesting three successive remissions of land taxes; the people were deeply grateful for this, and he was thus praised.
He was posthumously titled Yan Laofu. He died at the age of seventy-four; he was granted the title of Vice President of the Board of Rites (Shaobao) and the posthumous name Wenjing.

His second son was named Cheng, styled Daocheng, with the sobriquet Tianchishan Qiao. From his youth, he possessed pure integrity. Once Minqing had entered the inner cabinet, Cheng returned home to serve his mother.
Whenever they passed through places where people offered him gold, Cheng said, "My father declined such gifts when he went to court; how can I accept them on the road?"
He firmly declined [the honor]. He served Master Guǎn Dōngmíng as his teacher and transmitted his learning. Subsequently, he engaged in the investigation of the Chan school with Qú Yuánlì.
By virtue of his family’s official status (yìn), he became a Zhōngshū Shèrén; his official career reached the rank of Prefect of Shàowǔ.

In his later years, he retired home to practice the teachings of Yúnqī. His son, Pǔ, was honest, prudent, and fond of doing good. At the age of twenty-five, he fell ill and was about to die. Tóngchéng said to him:

He said, "Do not harbor distracting thoughts; simply recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion. Puk replied, "Yes. Cheng further said, "From this day forward, I too shall recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion.
Puk said joyfully, "If it is truly so, my son has nothing to worry about. He then composed his countenance, joined his palms, and passed away.
Cheng then took the *Longshu Jingtu Wen* (Pure Land Text of Longshu) that Puk had carved and printed it, widely distributing it among his relatives and friends, and appended [a preface] to it.
The letter says: "I have been ill for some time and was nearly at the point of death. Unexpectedly, I have returned to life; yet though I merely endure, who knows what tomorrow holds?
Turning back to manage my worldly affairs, my old schemes seem like chewing wax. This single skin-bag must inevitably decay;
where can the shadows of the six sense-objects find any solidity? It would be better to cast off this ordinary mind and seek birth in the Pure Land, reciting a single phrase of Amitābha."

To extinguish boundless karmic offenses, I humbly offer this exhortation to express my sincere intent. He passed away at the age of seventy-eight. His younger brother was Ze, whose courtesy name was Kaizong;

he served as a Secretariat Drafter (Zhongshu Sheren). He was a man of noble spirit who could readily come to the aid of others in distress. At the time of his death, he wrote a verse of farewell, saying:
"The Great Trichiliocosm is vast and boundless; it is entirely a field for contending for fame and seizing profit. Today this old man casts off his hands and departs;

all conditions are purified, and he beholds the Empty King. Having thus set down his brush, he passed away. His courtesy name was Zeshi, and his style name was Zizhang. He was a jinshi of the seventh year of the Chongzhen era.
He served as the magistrate of Xinyang Prefecture and achieved merit in defense and protection. Upon entering the present dynasty, high officials submitted joint memorials [in his favor].
He did not emerge from seclusion despite recommendations for office. He constructed a small *Laṅkā* chamber beside the ancestral tomb on Mount Jinfeng to devote himself to meditation and recitation.
One morning, after rising and completing his worship of the Buddha, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away. His younger brother was Ji (style name:

Daohang), a student at the Imperial Academy who was skilled in calligraphy; a handwritten copy of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* by him still circulates in the world (*Ming Shi*, *Changshu Zhi*, *Yunqi Fahui*, "Postscript to the Pure Land Writings," and "Preface to the Lebang Wenlei").

Lu Yusheng’s courtesy name was Guangzu, and his style was Wutai Jushi. He was a native of Pingchao. In the twenty-sixth year of the Jiajing era, he passed the jinshi examination and was appointed as Magistrate of Jun County.

He was subsequently promoted to Director of the Bureau of Rites in Nanjing, and served successively as Director of the Bureau of Verification and Seals, then transferred to the Bureau of Merit and the Bureau of Personnel Selection.
During the Wanli era, he was repeatedly promoted to Grand Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel. This was Master Yusheng.

Loyal, upright, and thoroughly versed in historical precedents, he served successively in the Ministry of Personnel (*Li-bu*). He steadfastly upheld public opinion (*qing-yi*) and championed men of talent and distinction, never neglecting those of humble or lowly status.
Consequently, the expectations of the people gathered around him in great harmony; yet for this very reason, he was targeted by those who harbored resentment.

Repeatedly forced to retire and live as a private citizen, he devoted his heart to the Buddha-vehicle (*fo-sheng*), vowing to propagate and protect the Dharma. His mind remained unshaken by either slander or praise. He once...
Wenmu carved the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (The Compendium of the Five Lamps). Its preface states:

"When the Buddha-dharma flowed eastward, during the Jin, Song, Qi, and Liang periods, those who studied Buddhism vied with one another to exalt themselves through metaphysical principles and meditative contemplation, yet none investigated the fundamental nature of the mind’s wondrous luminosity.
It was only after the Great Being Bodhidharma arrived here that he first proclaimed the direct pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and achieve Buddhahood."

When the lineage reached the Sixth Patriarch, Master Neng, this school flourished greatly. Subsequently, the five schools were established side by side, their pedagogical styles becoming increasingly rigorous.
Their perfect mechanisms and subtle meanings cannot be understood through mere words nor sought through intellectual effort.

As for such acts as raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye, shouting, or striking with a staff, these were employed to reveal the true essence; they became ever more extraordinary as they emerged. Those who attained realization experienced it as if undergoing a piercing pain.
To encounter this while eating a fist is like a deaf person hearing a drum; those with superficial understanding may find it difficult to penetrate and disparage it as strange and eccentric.
This is because those of dull faculties fail to enter [the teaching], leading them to claim that the words of the Sage contain hidden meanings.
This is generally the case. However, after the Kaiyuan era, the teachings of the religion became brilliantly manifest.

From those above, such as the Emperor wearing his ceremonial crown and sable-earplugs, down to merchants and common women, many were able to respond to the profound words with resonance and move through the subtle mysteries of the Way like a blade. At that time, it was thus.

Seeing one’s nature and knowing the mind, they transcend the mundane and enter the sacred. Within several hundred years, spanning from top to bottom, there have been more than a thousand such individuals.
Since the establishment of the two polarities (Heaven and Earth), nothing has ever been as flourishing as this.

Why is it that the Confucian school is so sparse and desolate, while the Buddhist teaching is so widespread and numerous? This is truly because the Way has been lost amidst many divergent paths, and wisdom has become fragmented and pierced by bias.

It was excavated [from obscurity]. Since the passing of Zhongni (Confucius), the era has not returned; since the death of Yan Yuan, it has now vanished. When the official transmission was lost, it was sought among the four barbarian regions;
when learning was severed, it was transmitted beyond the outer limits of the world. That there has been one period of darkness followed by one of illumination is for this reason.

It reached the great scholars of the Song dynasty, Zhou Yuan-gong and Cheng Bo-zi, who extensively sought out the fallen threads of tradition and secretly elucidated the core of the mind. Someone asked:
Regarding the similarities and differences between Confucianism and Buddhism, Bozi said: "In the original state from which you come, are there still Confucians and Buddhists?

It was only late in his life that Yichuan studied the Buddhist scriptures; upon meeting a strange man, he finally clarified this learning. Kaotang also remarked: "Dharmatrāta completely overturned the conventional molds; this is truly sublime.
Thus we know that the disparagement of Buddhism and Daoism as heterodoxies is not the definitive doctrine of Cheng and Zhu. From this point forward...
Since the descent [of the Buddha], the time has been distant from the Sage; Confucians are ignorant of universal principles, and Buddhists are confined by sectarian studies.

Consequently, the sublime intent that came from the West has become a rare sound in the East. Fortunately, the single transmission outside the teachings is fully recorded in the five records of the *Chuan Deng Lu*.
Master Jie, considering those texts to be vast and extensive, abridged them into the *Huiyuan*. This is indeed what Zhuangzi criticized: "The Sages have already passed away..."
Yet, while only the dregs remain, those who seek the Way are able to use words as a fish-trap to exhaust the depths of principle;
they unravel them day by day and probe them night after night, until suddenly the saw reaches the end of the wood and it is severed, and the water arrives at the channel of its own accord.
This is what is meant by "using the finger to see the moon" and "borrowing a raft to cross the sea"—it is indeed easy.
Thus, this land and these books cannot be dispensed with for even a single day. Since my youth, I have admired the immortals, often encountering auspicious signs in my dreams;
having heard the teachings of Confucius, I learned to seek their source within the Six Classics. Later, upon encountering the Buddhist scriptures, I occasionally perused the Tripiṭaka. Gradually...
To be able to penetrate its single thread and unify its divergent paths—this I have achieved through my own deliberations, for there was no one to instruct me. Alas!
At the retreat of five thousand disciples, the Buddha lamented that arrogance is difficult to dispel; at the forty years of silence, he sighed that this embodied existence is easily exhausted.
I wish to join with those of like mind to together cultivate the causes for attaining the Way. I venture to request that you exert your strength alongside me in this work. In the past...
In the past, there were those who awakened to the mind upon hearing half a verse, or realized the fruit of enlightenment upon recognizing two characters;

how much more so for these living words contained in twenty fascicles, which are indeed a marvelous encounter once in hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Those who enter this Dharma-gate shall all become Buddhas.

Should there be any sagacious and talented individuals whose wisdom penetrates the subtle, or noble worthies of profound insight, let them completely renounce the "money" (the *adbu* coins) on their bedside tables and achieve worldly success.
This is a rare occurrence. May it inspire future generations to follow the path of those who came before; may one attain self-liberation and thereby liberate others—is this not truly magnificent?

I hope you will not remain mired in dogmatism. A pedantic scholar might say, "This is not the book of our Confucius. Yet, while observing the mourning period for his father, after the burial, he crossed the river to Mount Mao (Mòshān) to pay homage to the Buddha’s śarīra.

Upon his arrival, a monk emerged from within a stupa holding a suspended golden bell, which was... [capable of... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a historical or biographical account concerning a Buddhist figure, likely from the Six Dynasties or early Tang period, discussing the intersection of Confucian mourning rites and Buddhist practice.)
He measured it with his fingers and looked inside; the śarīra moved and rotated without fixed position.
At first it was like a pearl, then like a bullet, then like a melon, and suddenly like a chariot wheel. It manifested in five colors, its radiance dazzling the eyes.

At that time, some of his companions saw it as white as a *wú* seed, while others saw it as green as a bean. They were all amazed by this phenomenon. Consequently, he brought forth gold and constructed a stone stūpa.

A diagram was drawn and placed within the stupa, recording these events. [The author] requested the support of various officials and lay devotees (upāsakas), whereupon the stupa and its hall were restored.
Master Mìcáng Kāi led the initial fundraising for the carving of the Small Canon (Xiǎoběn Zàngjīng). Together with Shéngyǔ, Fēng Kāizhī, Chén Tínguǒ, and others, he exhorted them with great vigor.
Responding from both far and near, the project was ultimately completed. Kāizhī’s name was Mèngzhēn; he was a native of Xiùshuǐ.

He was a jinshi of the Wanli era and served as the Rector of the National University (Guozijiao). Upon his retirement from office, he took Master Zibai Ke as his teacher and made a vow to propagate and protect the Dharma.
He drew blood to transcribe one scroll each of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. Tingnuo has a separate biography;
in his later years, he also followed the Elder Zibai, studying with even greater diligence. Subsequently, he cultivated the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation.
When he lay ill, he remained as bright and alert as usual. With his left hand, he formed the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*), which he did not release for ten days.
When Zibo came to visit him, he marveled at the firmness and intensity of his mental power and spoke this verse for him: "The hand-seal is firmly maintained, visible to all;

Yet at the very beginning of the hand-seal, it cannot be fathomed by the mind. How could it be seen with the eyes? That which cannot be seen is precisely what is neither destroyed nor indestructible—this is wisdom."

This was perfectly clear. The multitude were struck with wonder and amazement. He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince (Taibao) and conferred the posthumous name Zhuangjian.

His son, Bozhen, whose given name was Jizhong, was able to carry on his father's learning. By virtue of his father’s official rank, he served as a Sibu (Office Clerk) in the Ministry of War and was subsequently promoted to Langzhong (Ministerial Official) in the Ministry of Justice.

It happened that Zibo had been falsely accused due to the "Seditious Book" (Yaoshu) incident and was imprisoned; having already delivered a gāthā and passed away, Bozhen composed a eulogy for his portrait, saying:
In the past, the late Master Zhuangjian was a golden fortress for the Dharma-gate; he widely sought out the "dragon and elephant" talents to serve as bridges and rafts for the Dharma.

Having encountered our Master, he declared him to be a true Dharma King. We took refuge in him and requested instruction, serving him with devoted and tireless reverence. Through the grace of my loyalty, I obtained the karmic conditions to attend by his side, providing his headcloth and water flask.
A lamp of wisdom in the dark alleys, a compassionate vessel across the sea of suffering, a fatherly mentor to the world, and a guide beyond it. To approach him is to feel awe;

to distance oneself from him is to long for him. At first sight he seems strange, yet as one draws near, he becomes increasingly compassionate. He reveals the essentials of the Way and awakens me from my delusion.
In the snap of a finger, I realized my former errors. Having abandoned the ocean to identify with a bubble, it is only now that I have come to know:

through the Master, one knows the Buddha; through the Buddha, one knows the Confucian Way. That the numinous clarity is vast and penetrating possesses its own stages and steps. The Master said, "Ho! Ho! These stages and steps are not it."
I have received his instructions with my own feet; as soon as he raised them, I reached his presence. I constantly reflect upon his profound compassion, moved to tears of gratitude.

The debt for the milk of the Dharma is difficult to repay; in death, I shall remain as one with him, without a second heart. Yet, alas, how meager was my karmic affinity, that I must personally witness the passing of my Master. Alas! The wisdom of this sage is truly inconceivable.

The light of his precepts and wisdom grew ever more intense as he encountered conditions. Wandering through halls of merit, he performed great Dharma-gifts; though passing through various sufferings and afflictions, his mental state remained serene.
Having fulfilled the royal law, he declared that his past karmic ties were exhausted. With palms joined and legs crossed in the lotus posture, his single sandal slipped away with a fluttering grace.

In the sixth month, the prison cells stand exposed to the wind and mist; they loom like mountains, their light overflowing onto the cheekbones. At West Spring, the summer burials have been submerged as torrential rains form rivers;
the city is tilted and houses swept away, with nothing remaining firm against the surging waves. I suspect that these earthen mounds are gnawed by the rain and pierced by the wind.
When the journey south began and the reliquary was opened, we beheld the Master’s countenance once more; his marks and signs were majestic and solemn, as if he were still alive.

We have heard that ancient sages and saints can come and go at will through the power of their concentration and wisdom, forming *śarīra* relics so that their physical bodies remain unimpaired even when entering fire or water.
I did not expect that, being so ignorant and dull-witted, I would behold such a marvel. It is indeed as the Master said; it was verified on the very spot where he closed his eyes.

Were this not a flesh-body Buddha, how could it have been thus? Bo-zhen later died in office (*Ming Shi*, *Ayu Shan Zhi*, *Zi Bai Lao Ren Ji*, *Wu Deng Hui Yuan Xu*, *Ping Hu Zhi*, and the appendix to *Mi Cang Chan Shi Yi Ji*).
Zhi Guizi said: "As for Minqing’s relationship with Yunqi and Reng’s relationship with Zibo, it was not merely one of external patronage.
Examining their discourse and fundamental principles, there were also subtle points of mutual resonance between them. Among the Yan and Lu families, there have been many eminent figures;
I have selected those who possessed a thorough understanding of the Buddha-dharma and recorded them here. Alas! As for hereditary rank—"
Among those who possess a household, many have met with ruin through arrogance. Were it not for being patterned by the Way, how could they endure?
Master Wang Dashen said: "The Buddha and sentient beings are fundamentally no different in their mind-nature. One who has passed the barrier may speak thus;
however, one who has not yet passed the barrier must ultimately take the phrase 'replacing the ordinary mind' as the means to break through the barrier."
Seizing the narrow pass and the essential point: What is the "ordinary mind"? It is the form-and-mind (*rūpa-citta*) of sentient beings.

Sentient beings rely entirely upon this form-and-mind to nurture the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), to bring peace and security to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and to experience the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
They indulge themselves, claiming to spend their days in happiness. Yet they do not realize that the original segment of luminosity has fallen into the midst of form-and-mind and the five aggregates.
It is buried away. The six sense faculties are intertwined, and the six sense objects are sealed and obscured.
You have allowed this very radiance of yours to be defiled throughout a thousand lifetimes, wandering through ten thousand kalpas without even a hair’s breadth of opportunity for liberation.
You must give rise to a mind of weary detachment and exchange it for something else. How can you exchange it? Those within the Zen school cast aside that which is meaningless.

The flavor of words remains within your belly; it is like an iron-acid condiment. No matter how much you chew and gnaw upon it, not a single speck of its color or essence can be nurtured or extracted.

When you have chewed until the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) become pitiable, the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya) fall apart, and the six sense objects (ṣaḍ-viṣaya) are extinguished—this is what is called the time when the family estate is ruined and the house is scattered. The family is already dispersed; the house...
It has already been defeated. This segment of radiance will naturally appear, pervading heaven and earth.
Those within the Pure Land invite a Buddha and place him within your belly; this is your true master. Maintain this mindfulness without interruption.
With single-minded devotion, make offerings. After making offerings for a long time, your recollection of the Buddha will gradually increase.
Form and mind gradually dissolve away of their own accord. When they have dissolved completely, these very five aggregates, sense organs, and objects are transformed into a Buddha-land.
What is called "the physical body of form and segments being transformed into a body of light" is simply the restoration of that original segment of light within you.
To replace the ordinary mind with this is the great critical pass of cultivation; once it has been replaced, [one attains realization].
This is the holy; that which cannot be exchanged for it is the ordinary. In this place, there is not even so much as a hair’s breadth of anything borrowed or artificial.
A practitioner must examine themselves. If you cannot pass this critical juncture, be careful not to vainly imitate those who have passed it by prattling about the mind and nature being one or two;
you will only waste a lifetime. Within the Confucian school, they speak with great earnestness of the "mind of the Way" (daoxin).
The mind is the nature of principle (li) and the nature of material force (qi); it is also the most vital point.
Only when one masters oneself can one transform the nature of material force and thereby achieve the perfected nature.

This is as certain as the coldness of water and the heat of fire; there is no room for doubt. If one has not yet applied diligent effort in this regard, it is merely talk about what is already accomplished.
"This one" refers simply to having formed an affinity with form and mind; it is nothing other than the single phrase: "one cannot abandon the nature of sensory desire.
Regarding Yan’s relationship with Yunqi and Lu’s relationship with Zibo, though they were far apart, their structural arrangements naturally entered the realm of the sublime.
Biographies of Eminent Laymen, Volume 41:
The Biographies of Yang, Tang, Go, Sun, Zhu, Guo, Hao, Du (two), Wu, and Zhang.
Yang Banghua, whose given name was Jiahui, was a native of Taihe County in Jiangxi. During the Wanli era, he was a provincial scholar (*zhusheng*). From his youth, he was fond of learning.

There was no branch of literature he did not explore. Subsequently, he devoted himself deeply to the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures). At the age of thirteen, he observed the precept against killing; even fleas and lice were never harmed by him.
When he reached his early twenties, he entered the National University (Guozijian) in Nanjing.

Shortly thereafter, he fell ill and dreamed that he traveled through the hells, where he beheld Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva in the Hall of the Living and the Dead. Upon awakening, he released all living creatures and invited monks to recite the sutras for him.
He chanted the Buddha’s name. Afterward, he said to those around him, "I am about to depart. Blue lotus flowers have appeared before me; is this not the realm of the Pure Land?
Thereupon, he chanted the Buddha’s name incessantly day and night. He instructed his attendant to extinguish the candle, saying, "I am always within the light;
there is no need for a candle. When asked what he saw, he replied, "Lotuses of four colors are blooming. When asked if he saw Amitābha, he replied, "Yes."
"No," he replied. "I saw Amitābha manifesting a body one thousand *zhang* tall. I asked about Avalokiteśvara, and [Amitābha] said his body was equal to that of Amitābha;

only Śrī-garbha (Śikhin) was not visible. Having spoken these words, he suddenly leaped up, offered incense, and said, "The merit of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is unspeakable, unspeakable, unspeakable.
I have already attained rebirth in the highest grade (*uttama-kula*). Then, in silence, he passed away. (From the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn*)
Tangti was named Mingtiren. He was a student at the local school in Lanxi, Zhejiang. By nature, he was pure and sincere, personally practicing filial piety and fraternal kindness.

Later, realizing that the world is impermanent, he devoted his heart to the Ultimate Way. He studied under Master Yunqi Hong and received the precepts for the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance, which he then practiced with great diligence.
For thirteen years, time passed as if it were but a single day. At the age of sixty, during the second month of winter—

On the eleventh day of the New Year, he said to his sons, "I shall depart on this day. When the time arrived, he washed and rinsed his mouth, adjusted his robes, sat upright, formed mudrās with his hands, and recited the name of the Buddha;
smiling, he passed away. This event took place in the thirty-first year of the Wanli era (as recorded in the *Wangsheng zhuan*).
Goyi was a native of Qiantang. He served Master Yunqi Hong as his teacher; his Dharma name was Guangtai. He was filial toward his parents and delighted in practicing hidden virtues.

In his later years, he served the Buddha with great devotion. Together with the monk Suanxue, he established two seasonal societies for the purpose of reciting the name of the Buddha and chanting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Subsequently, he said, "My time has come to an end; I must now prepare for my journey to the West."
He then closed himself in a room to practice meditation and recitation, never ceasing from morning until night. He set a specific date for his return home;

two days prior, when family members came to visit him, they were deeply moved by his sorrow. Dao’an said, "Birth must inevitably end in extinction; why grieve? I am merely concentrating my spirit on the pure realm."

He beheld Amitābha face-to-face. [The Master] said, "You all must not allow worldly attachments to disturb my right mindfulness. He then invited Xuansu to arrive so they might chant the Buddha’s name together.
When the appointed time came, he passed away (from the *Wangsheng zhuan*).
Sun Shuzi was a native of Tongcheng in Jiangnan. His father, Layman Jingwu, while reading Yunqi’s *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, sighed with admiration and said:

"How sublime is this wondrous function! It turns heaven and earth upside down. That which is called 'the ten ages of past and present never departing from the present moment'—is it not solely through the single gateway of Buddha-recitation? He then cast an image of Amitābha Buddha and, according to the four...
Adorned with the eighteen vows, the image was completed and sent to Yunqi. Consequently, he requested a Dharma name, which was Guangyu;
he addressed himself as the disciple Shu. At the age of twelve, [the boy] followed him and received the five precepts, receiving the Dharma name Dawu.

Upon returning home, he abstained from meat and alcohol, abandoned the pursuit of the civil service examinations, and practiced the *nienfo* samādhi. Diligent and arduous, he did not spare his own body or life. Suddenly, he saw...
Two bhikṣus holding lotus flowers stood before him and said, "Young man, well done! You have single-mindedly purified the Pure Land.

Furthermore, he saw transformed beings reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for a full day and night. Thereupon, he suddenly rose from his seat and said, "Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara have both come to welcome me.
He then formed the *vajra-muṣṭi-mudrā* and chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha several times, after which he passed away in profound stillness.
There is a "Song of the Twelve Hours" concerning the Pure Land that has been transmitted through the world. Within his chamber, auspicious *zhī* fungi were produced annually;

in the year of his passing, one as large as a peck (*dǒu*) appeared, its color sometimes like gold, sometimes like jade, and sometimes like a red or white wheel (from the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn* and *Yúnqī fǎhuì*).
Zhu Gang was a *gongshi* (tribute scholar) from Shuntian. He served as a District Vice-Commissioner (*futingzhi*) before his official career ended.

He devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, reciting the name of the Buddha thirty thousand times every day for fifteen years. One day, while sitting on his couch and holding a rosary to chant the Buddha’s name, a wondrous fragrance suddenly filled the room.
He exclaimed, "The Buddha has come! and then passed away (*Wansheng zhuan*).
Guo Dalin was a native of Tangyin. He also devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of the Pure Land.
At the age of seventy-six, one day he said to his son, "I shall depart at noon tomorrow. He passed away without illness (from the *Wansheng zhuan*).
Liu Tongzhi was a native of Shuntian. He was diligent and devoted in his recitation of the Buddha’s name. At the age of fifty-two, he fell ill; his mindfulness became even more earnest.
His dharma-fellow Bai Zhai had previously passed away. When Tongzhi fainted and then revived, he said to his family members, "Bai Zhai and I shall be reborn together in the Pure Land.
He has already moored his boat there to await me. Change my clothes for me and hang my prayer beads upon [the door]."
Xiang followed him and subsequently passed away (*Wengshengzhuan*).
Hao Xizai was a student from Qiantang who was loyal, trustworthy, and free from deceit; in his later years, he returned to the teachings and methods of Yunqi.
His name was Guangding. He practiced seated meditation and recitation at home without interruption. Later, he fell ill.

One day, he suddenly raised his head, looked out the window, and said to his son, "Today, a different world-system has appeared. At midnight, he said, "The Buddha is sitting upon a lotus pedestal before me;
I am going. Thereupon, he passed away. This event took place in the thirty-ninth year of the Wanli era (as recorded in the *Wangsheng zhuan*).

The layman Du left behind his name; he was a native of Shuntian, Wanping. He lived in seclusion for thirty years within the ancient *caitika-hall* beside Rui Guang Temple on the Western Hills, dedicating himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. When encountering others, he would only join his palms and chant the Buddha’s name.

Foreknowing that his end was near, he performed ritual repentance for nine days. Upon reaching the most earnest passages within the liturgy, he would suddenly shed tears and choke with emotion, after which he passed away.

He ate only a small amount of water each day. Upon completing his repentance, he passed away while seated. Ten days later, when the body was finally enshrouded for burial, his complexion remained as if alive.
Five-colored clouds swirled above his dwelling. Those living in the mountains spread word of this marvel (from the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn*).

Wu Daien was a native of Renshou County in Zhejiang. He was compassionate and fond of charity; he relieved the orphaned and destitute and protected living beings, earning him the praise of his fellow villagers.
Subsequently, he turned his heart toward the Buddha-dharma, reciting sutras and chanting the Buddha’s name morning and night.

One day, he took leave of the assembly and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). His countenance remained radiant, and a fragrant aroma filled the room. These events occurred in the fortieth year of the Wanli era (the *Wansheng zhuan*).
Wu Yongqing, whose given name was Jixun, was a native of Xin’an in Jiangnan. He was by nature grave and resolute, and he pursued the good with the intensity of one parched for water.

In his later years, he cultivated the Pure Land practice, reciting the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-mantra* and chanting the Buddha’s name with a fixed daily regimen. Once, he lost his footing and fell into the river;

a spirit supported him, and after drifting ten *li*, he leaped back onto a boat. The multitude regarded this as divine. Shortly thereafter, he suffered from a carbuncle on his back and continued his recitations.
He continued his recitation as usual. Suddenly, with right mindfulness, he manifested his passing (from the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn*).
Zhāng Àiwàn was a eunuch during the Wànlì period. In his later years, he upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

After several years, he died of illness and arrived before a king, who said to him, "You ought to receive a womb in the human realm. He replied, "I uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and pray [for rebirth in the Pure Land]."
She was reborn in the Pure Land and did not wish to undergo conception again. The King said, "Your merit from upholding this sutra is small; how can this be?

Miaolai replied, "I have heard that even ten recitations can achieve success, so what need is there to mention such long-term practice? The King said, "Let her go for now to listen to and continue upholding the sutra.
Once she had revived, she departed for Mount Xi, to Biyun Temple, where she specialized in reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Eleven years passed. One day—

He assembled the congregation and said, "By the power of upholding this sutra, I shall now depart for the West. Having bathed and changed his robes, he sat upright and passed away (*Record of New and Extraordinary Events of the Diamond Sutra*).
Zhiguizi said: "The preceding record is a compilation of the *Biographies of Rebirth at Yunqi*, with some additions and supplements.

For the most part, these individuals were inspired by the influence of the Yunqi style. As for other scholars and gentlemen whose integrity and reputation were brilliantly manifest, they have separate biographies.
Alas! Since the time of Donglin, there has been none where the transformation of the Land of Bliss has flourished more than here. As Mencius said:
His spirit vibrates through a hundred generations; those who hear of him, whether from a hundred generations past or future, cannot fail to be inspired.
How much more so for those who have personally basked in his presence! I say the same of Master Hong.

Wang Dashen said: "Now, this is a different world altogether. As for those who speak as they are, who speak truly, and who do not speak deceptively—if one has not reached such a stage, their cultivation still lacks sufficient verification.
How can it be known that one speaks as they are, speaks truly, and does not speak deceptively? By observing them through the ten realms of existence, they are seen to be ten distinct [realms]."
Heaven and Earth. The Buddha-dharmadhātu is the heaven and earth of the Buddhas. The Bodhisattva-dharmadhātu is the heaven and earth of the Bodhisattvas.
The Pratyekabuddha-dharmadhātu is the heaven and earth of the Pratyekabuddhas. The Śrāvaka-dharmadhātu is the heaven and earth of the Śrāvakas.
These are the dharmadhātus of the four types of noble ones; they constitute the heaven and earth of the four noble ones. The Deva-dharmadhātu is the heaven and earth of the devas. Cultivation...
The dharma-realm of asuras is the *qián-hún* (heaven-earth) of asuras. The dharma-realm of humans is the *qián-hún* of humans. The dharma-realm of animals is the *qián-hún* of animals.
The dharma-realm of hungry ghosts is the *qián-hún* of hungry ghosts. The dharma-realm of hell-beings is the *qián-hún* of hell-beings.
These are the dharma-realms of the six classes of ordinary beings; they constitute the *qián-hún* of the six classes of ordinary beings. Thus one practices.
When one reaches the stage of transcending the mundane and entering the sacred, the realm of the sages naturally manifests before one.
Is this not, indeed, a separate heaven and earth? How may its verification be clarified? By observing the causes of the ten dharma realms:

when a single thought arises within the sphere of the ten evil states, the mind produced therein is the cause for the hell realm; if these thoughts continue without interruption, [the other realms follow accordingly].
One immediately completes the cosmic order of hell. To give rise to thoughts within the realm of stinginess and envy is the cause for the hungry ghost realm;

when these thoughts continue uninterrupted from moment to moment, one immediately completes the cosmic order of the hungry ghosts. To give rise to thoughts within the realm of ignorance and lust is the cause for the animal realm;
when these thoughts continue uninterrupted from moment to moment, one immediately completes the cosmic order of the animals. Regarding the five...
To give rise to the mind upon the object of the precepts is the cause for the human realm; when this continues uninterrupted from moment to moment, one completes the cosmos of the human world.
To give rise to the mind upon the object of the lower grade of the ten wholesome actions is the cause for the asura realm;
when this continues uninterrupted from moment to moment, one completes the cosmos of the asuras. To give rise to the mind upon the object of the higher grade of the ten wholesome actions is...
The cause for the celestial realm is that when one gives rise to thoughts within this state without interruption, one thereby constructs the celestial universe.
When one gives rise to thoughts within the sphere of the Four Noble Truths without interruption, this is the cause for the Śrāvaka realm; one thereby constructs the Śrāvaka universe.

When one gives rise to thoughts within the sphere of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination without interruption, this is the cause for the Pratyekabuddha realm; [one thereby constructs the Pratyekabuddha universe without interruption.]
Having completed the creation of the kalpa of the Pratyekabuddhas, to give rise to the mind within the sphere of the six perfections is the cause for the realm of the Bodhisattvas;

when this continues uninterruptedly from moment to moment, one completes the creation of the kalpa of the Bodhisattvas. To give rise to the mind within the sphere of unsurpassed *bodhi* is the cause for the realm of the Buddhas;
when this continues uninterruptedly from moment to moment, one completes the creation of the kalpa of the Buddhas. Contemplating it in this way...
If one’s mind is directed toward the Land of Bliss, with every thought and moment uninterrupted, how could there be anyone who does not attain rebirth?
If there were anyone who did not attain rebirth, it must be because the cause they have produced was not genuine, or because their practice of reciting the Buddha's name has been interrupted.
Therefore it is said: "Those who have practiced for only a short time already possess signs of realization. This statement is praised for two reasons:
first, to strengthen the resolute mind of others; second, to inspire the mind of diligence in others.
Biographies of Laymen, Part 42:
The Biographies of Yin, Chen, Gu, Zhu, Zhou, Cai, Yu, Huang, Zhuang, and Bao.
Yin Shixun, whose courtesy name was Mai and sobriquet was Qiuping Jushi, was a native of Yingtian. In his youth, he pursued his studies at Nanjing.
While serving at the Guozijian (National Academy), he associated with He Shanshan of Jiangxi and heard of the teachings of Wang Yangming.

He further received instruction from Ouyang Nan’ye, the Director of Studies. Thereupon, he withdrew to dwell in mountain temples, turning inward to seek the truth within his own mind, vowing to attain self-realization.
In the twentieth year of the Jiajing era, he passed the jinshi examination. He was appointed as a Director of the Ministry of Revenue (*hubu zhushu*).

He subsequently served as Vice Commissioner for Education (*tixue fushi*) in Guizhou before requesting leave to return home. At the beginning of the Longqing era, he was recommended and reinstated as Vice Commissioner for Education in Zhejiang, later being promoted to High Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud (*nantai puqing*).
However, he again cited illness to remain at home. At the beginning of the Wanli era, when Zhang Juzheng was in power, he sought to recruit him to assist his administration.
At that time, he was serving as the Surveillance Commissioner for the Yangtze River (Chaojiang Du Yushi). When Wang Zhuan went to his residence to convey his greetings, Shi Xun did not respond.
Later, he said to his son Shi Qing, "Lord Zhang is too overbearing and will surely meet with misfortune. Wang Zhuan is no upright man; one must not form an alliance with him.

After some time, he was appointed as the Southern Metropolitan Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Nan Taichang Qing), and shortly thereafter served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites (Libu Shilang) while concurrently acting as the Chancellor of the National University in Nanjing (Nanjing Jiaojushi).

He repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement and was granted his leave. By nature, he was pure and detached; although he held a high and important office, he could not endure social formalities and communicated with others only through strict decorum.
Of his total tenure, he served in office for thirteen years and remained on leave for seventeen. During his leisure time at home, he devoted himself to Buddhist scriptures.

Having attained enlightenment through the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the "Dry Wisdom" (*kenghui*) chapter of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he authored a single volume titled *Zhuoyan* (Supplementary Remarks) to discuss the essential meanings of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. Furthermore...
Regarding the various commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, those that directly express the realization attained through the mind take the *Wenling* commentary as the most excellent.

It consists of ten volumes of the *Wenling Yaoyi Jibuzhu* (Essential Commentary with Supplements). While serving as the Director of the Court of the Imperial Stud, he resided at Qiyun Lou in Chuyang and composed a verse which says:
"The spring gloom shrouds my secluded chamber; Only at dawn does it clear and brighten. The spring breeze comes leisurely, And a rain of flowers fills the courtyard. Furthermore:

It is said: "A hundred thoughts arise from within stillness; they turn back and vanish within that same stillness. Had I known earlier that birth is immediately followed by extinction, I would have believed from the start that their arising is but toil.

It is further said: "The man of stature is naturally majestic; beneath his feet lies the primordial path. Letting go, he returns home at once—how could he have ever moved a single step? It is also said:
"Though the six sense-objects are illusory appearances, they are capable of rending the true nature asunder. How, then, can this be called the mind that transcends the world?"
Yet one does not follow after discursive thought. It is further said: "The traces of the response are entrusted to the human realm; the spirit is concentrated as it dwells in the ultimate state.

Having realized the mechanism of the iron ox, the furnace flames are as cold as ice. It is also said: "Facing the rain, the thousand peaks are still; gazing at the mountains, a hundred anxieties grow light.

Last night and this morning’s night, the white ox has been born in the open field. In the evening, I took up residence at Tianjie Temple, where I stilled the mind in meditative concentration and maintained the precepts.

He was so refined and disciplined that even veteran monks could not surpass him. At the age of sixty-two, knowing his time of passing had come, he sat upright in meditation while burning incense and passed away as if merely dozing (from *Ming Shi Ou Chao*, *Lengyan Meng Chao*, and *Jiangning Zhi*).

Chen Tinglu, whose given name was Zan, was a native of Changshu in Jiangnan. He passed the jinshi examination in the thirty-fifth year of the Jiajing era and served as a Palace Memorial Censor (Xingke Gishizhong).

He impeached and dismissed the remaining partisans of Yan Song and petitioned for the reinstatement of those who had been dismissed for offering remonstrances; however, he incurred the Emperor’s displeasure.
He was sentenced to sixty strokes of the cane and stripped of his official title. He remained at home, single-mindedly cultivating the pure karma of the Western Paradise.
When a guest passed by and rebuked him, saying, "Have you not heard the discourse of the Great Mirror (Huineng) on 'mind-only'? Why do you loathe the defiled and rejoice in the pure? He replied:
The Pure Land is Mind-only; this was proclaimed by Great Kāśyapa, yet it did not originate with him. "This mind creates the Buddha;
this mind is the Buddha"—the Buddha had indeed spoken these words long ago. It was likely because he feared that people would seek the Pure Land with an impure mind.
He did not mean to say that the land itself lacks purity; rather, he meant that what makes the Land of Bliss so delightful is not merely its jeweled ponds and pearls.
The chirping of birds in the pavilion and the wind in the trees are merely such things.

I am fortunate to roam with the assembly of sages, clothed in immeasurable light, passing through incalculable kalpas, realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and attaining the Unsurpassed Way to deliver boundless multitudes—this is truly joyful.
You, as a guest, take delight in meditation within this defiled land; I, as a host, take delight in meditation within the Pure Land. As for meditation, there is neither guest nor host.
"I delight in being neither defiled nor pure; you guests need not reproach me. In the early years of the Longqing era, he was reinstated as an official of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lika*).

Because he repeatedly spoke with straightforward integrity, he frequently came into conflict with the ministers of the day. During the Wanli era, he rose through the ranks to serve as Vice Minister (*Shilang*) of the Ministry of Justice (*Xingbu*).

In the seventh month of the sixteenth year, he lay ill; he recited the names of the Buddhas with ever-increasing devotion. According to custom, for high-ranking officials of the third rank or above in the capital during the summer...
The Emperor granted him ice for his use. Having placed the ice before his couch, the assembly saw a seven-storied pagoda emerge from within the ice;
its railings were interconnected and its latticed windows were exquisitely intricate. As time passed, the ice gradually melted, and the shadow of the pagoda gradually thinned.

Shortly thereafter, he passed away, and the shadow vanished. He was posthumously awarded the title of Right Grand Marshal (You Dushi) and the honorific title Zhuangjing (Ming Shi, Lebang Wenlei Xu, Tanhui).
Gu Qingfu, whose given name was Yuan and sobriquet Baochang Jushi, was a student (*zhusheng*) from the Tianren Academy during the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty.

In his youth, he was spirited and talented; he excelled at poetry and was skilled in calligraphy and painting. Upon reaching nearly forty years of age, he completely abandoned his former studies, renounced wine and meat, and constructed a small pavilion.
Therein he sat alone, diligently cultivating Chan meditation, attended only by a single young servant who offered him incense and flowers.
He used pure water, and his wife never even caught sight of his face. Every night at the fifth watch, he would rise and strike a large wooden fish-drum, chanting "Amitābha Buddha" in a loud voice.
Beside his house lived a butcher who, upon hearing the sound of the wooden drum, would invariably rise to slaughter pigs.
One day, the butcher rose late and scolded his wife in anger. His wife said, "Have you not heard that practitioner?"
He struck the wooden fish and recited the Buddha’s name, saying, "I myself do not know my own transgressions; why then do you reproach me? The butcher was startled;
he immediately broke his knife and ceased slaughtering. At that time, many among the butchers followed his example and changed their vocations.
He was on good terms with Master Yungu of Xixia, with whom he established a Western Paradise Society. One day, when Master Qing of Hanshan arrived at Xixia Temple, he saw from afar—
The Master was as leisurely and aloof as a solitary crane; when one approached him, his eyes did not blink, as if he had already cast off the world.

Later, he entered the hall door to pay homage at the Śarīra Stūpa. After gazing upon it for a long time, a five-colored light suddenly appeared from the top of the stūpa, shimmering like inlaid jewels.
Master Qing found this extraordinary and spoke of it to Yungu. Yungu said, "This is the Precious Banner (Ratnaketu), which is now manifesting in the West."
He contemplated the ear. After a short while, he manifested a slight illness and requested several eminent monks to sit opposite him and chant the Buddha’s name.

Shortly thereafter, a palace attendant ran to report, "The fragrance of lotuses is being smelled throughout the entire residence. The assembly was filled with wonder and joy, yet Qingfu remained serene and composed as if nothing were amiss.
He spoke softly to the monk, saying, "I sat within a lotus flower for more than half a month. I beheld the Dharma-body of Amitābha pervading the worlds of empty space;
all those worlds were golden in color. The Buddha gazed at me with a smile and took me by the hand, then covered me with his *kāṣāya*.
I am certain to go to the Western Land. His sons wept and entreated him, saying, "Father, you are indeed going; but what of us, your children?"
"What? Qingfu laughed and said, "Do you suppose I am either living or dead? Have you not observed the sun?
It rises in the east and sets in the west; does it truly set? Thereupon, he fixed a date, bathed, changed his robes, and passed away while sitting upright.
The fragrance of lotuses did not fade for three days (from the *Dream Journeys Collection* by Hanshan).
Zhu Yuanzheng was a scholar of Haiyan who had throughout his life been dedicated to the study of the Sage’s learning. He maintained a very strict discipline over himself.

When he was over sixty years old, he immersed himself deeply in the joy of Chan meditation. He lived in a dilapidated house behind his residence, closing himself off from the world and no longer attending to household affairs.
Every morning he would recite one scroll of the *Lotus Sūtra*, and once midday had passed, he would sit in quiet meditation. His disciple Chen Zeliang...
He visited him and said, "Sir, you are advanced in years; why not relax your prohibition on wine for a while? Wonjeong replied, "Do you think I need to nourish my blood and qi?
You do not know that I have already drawn a definitive line between life and death. He remained as solemn as Liang Song.
In the seventh month of that year, he said to his son, "I have nothing more to do here. When asked where he was going, he replied, "To the West."
He was about to depart. His son and grandson earnestly entreated him to stay, and he granted their request. On the first day of the twelfth month, he manifested a slight illness and ceased eating.

His family members were in a state of agitation as they prepared the funeral implements. Yuanzheng said, "Do not be anxious; this matter will occur eight days from now at midnight. When the appointed time arrived, he sat upright, intending to pass away.
He spoke again, saying, "In my life, I have never failed anyone by even the slightest fraction of a hair. Now, behind the house this winter, there is a craftsman..."
A man leveled a patch of ground for me at my rear gate, intending that on New Year’s Day of the coming year, I might leave the pass and walk abroad.
His kind intention remained unrequited; therefore, I took paper and composed a poem to thank him. He passed away silently while it was still cock-crow.
He had previously instructed his family that no women were to come near him when he was about to depart; they arrived only after two or three hours had passed. When they came...
"Do not weep. When daybreak arrived, his kinsmen came and all began to wail. Yuanzheng once again opened his eyes and shook his head, ordering the women to leave.
Only when they had all departed did he close his eyes (*Fahua chiyen jishi*).
Zhou Chufeng, whose given name was Tingzhang, was a native of Yunnan. He was born during the Zhengde and Jiajing reigns. By nature he was simple and honest;

in managing his household, he did not calculate whether he had wealth or not. Whenever he possessed anything, he would immediately distribute it to the poor. When people spoke with him, he would always smile; even if they mocked or insulted him, he would simply smile in return.
He had long been inclined toward the Buddha-dharma; upon rising each morning, he would invariably recite the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Amitābha* [Sūtras].

He read one fascicle each of the *Bhadrakarātrī-sūtra* and the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtras*, and said with a sense of full self-attainment: "I do not depart from daily life, nor do I involve myself in craving;
it is simply this. At the age of eighty-seven, on the day of Qingming, he went home to bid farewell to his ancestors.
He returned and said to his wife, "I am about to depart; Amitābha has come to welcome me, and both Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta have arrived together.
After a while, he added, "Avalokiteśvara told me that I may travel to the West after abstaining from meat for five days. Thereupon, he ate only one meal of gruel and one dish of vegetables each day.
When the appointed time arrived, he bathed and donned his cap, instructing his children and grandchildren to recite the names of the Seven Tathāgatas. Once the recitation of the sutra was completed—
He sat upright and passed away. On the following day, a fragrance emanated from his body, and his countenance appeared as if he were alive (*Record of the Miraculous Responses of the Vajra*).
Cai Huaiting, whose given name was Chengzhi, was a native of You County in Huguang. By nature he was solitary and aloof, indifferent to fame and profit.

At over twenty years of age, he observed a lifelong fast and devoted himself to the Buddha. He would recite the names of three thousand Buddhas, recording one name per day; this continued for three years before—
Upon graduation, he never forgot this throughout his life. He passed the jinshi examination in the eleventh year of the Wanli era and served successively as the Magistrate of Jiaxing.
While in office, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily. His chamber contained no superfluous items; there was only an incense burner, a censer, and a desk for the scriptures.
He restored the ancient Lengyan Temple and prohibited the common people from slaughtering livestock to sacrifice to deities. His proclamation stated: "Confucius said, 'Revere ghosts...'"
He revered the spirits and kept them at a distance; he never once claimed that ghosts and spirits did not exist. However, the manner in which spirits enjoy offerings differs from that of humans.

If humans, who delight in wine and meat, were to sacrifice wine and meat to the spirits, it would be like maggots feeding on excrement and offering excrement to people—how could they avoid incurring the resentment of those people?
This is because the nature of the spirits is pure and clear; when they hear of the wine [of humans]...
Flesh is filthy and loathsome; one has no leisure for it, so how could one deign to examine or taste it?

Therefore, those who perform suburban sacrifices use only plain wine, and those who receive the offerings are forbidden from alcohol and pungent foods—the intent is clear. As for hungry ghosts, they cannot even drink water, so how could they eat meat?
Those who wish to sacrifice to ghosts must use the *Vikṛti-bhakṣaṇa-mantra* (Mantra for Transforming Food), and this may not be done arbitrarily. For this reason...
I specifically inform you all: those who offer sacrifices to the deities should burn incense and prepare vegetarian offerings, and furthermore recite one scroll of the Diamond Sūtra.

The deities will naturally accept this with discernment. The Underworld Offices hold this sūtra in the highest regard. I have now petitioned the City God (Chenghuang) to remit the transgressions you previously committed.
Hereafter, you must not offend again. If you continue as before to slaughter livestock and defile the deities, it will not only be of no benefit, but...

Furthermore, that I have encountered this retribution and censure is a factual account; it is certainly not a falsehood. I once inquired about the Dharma with Master Yunqi Hong, whereupon I devoted myself exclusively to the cultivation of the *nien-fo* samādhi.
Subsequently, I served as the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Taichang Siqing*) and subsequently requested leave to retire.

Among my acquaintances, there was one who wished to recommend me for the post of Provincial Governor (*Xunfu*). When I asked him about this by letter, he replied with a laugh, "If you look at a provincial governor..."
He was born into a most noble family. "My Dharma directly transcends the three realms; even a Golden Wheel-turning King would not deign to value it, let alone a petty man.

When some advised him that he should educate his sons at the court of the Duke of Huai, he replied: "The matter of birth and death is of great importance. I am busy saving myself; how could I have time to worry about my descendants?
Whenever his sons praised the beauty of their palaces, he could not restrain them; he would simply cover his face with a fan and pass by. Late in life...
Each year, he constructed a thatched hut to establish a *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) assembly, leading the vegetable vendors to collectively dedicate their merits toward rebirth in the Pure Land.

He composed two verses to thank his guests; the first says: A guest longing to return to An-yang, A decaying Confucian by the Xiang River, I worry not for the affairs of tomorrow, But seek only the talisman of rebirth.
In this small room, I dwell according to conditions; With thin soup, I sustain myself as it comes. Within my breast, all worldly thoughts are severed...
"Regarding hatred and love, let them be as they will, even if called 'horse' or 'ox. The second verse says: Do not take idle words And trouble me, O Great One, again and again.
In recent years my nature has grown violent and evil; As soon as I open my mouth, I am muddled. My karma is heavy, so I vow to repent; People are close when healthy, but distant when ill."
As for Zhang San and Li Si, whether they were good or ill did not concern me. In the year of his impending death, he styled himself the "Man of the Way Who Will Not Last Long.
When he fell ill, he was carried to a Buddhist temple where he requested a monk to shave his head. Upon returning to his bedroom, he saw a silver platform appearing to welcome him;
he repeatedly invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and then passed away. His poems on the Pure Land and his writings on cause and effect have circulated in the world.
(*Mingwen Ouchao*, *Jingang Xinyilu*, *Cixin Baodian*). Yu Changru, whose given name was Chunchi, was a native of Qiantang.
From birth, he remained in a state of perpetual prostration and did not close his eyes. At the age of three, he chanted the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
A lotus flower and jeweled trees appeared within his room; he informed his grandmother of this, and his grandmother said, "This is the West..."
This was a manifestation of auspicious signs. Consequently, he was instructed to practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereupon he would frequently sit upright with his eyes cast downward.

His younger brother, Sengru, whose name was Chunzhen, had been close to him since childhood. While observing the mourning period for their mother, they practiced the *Tiantai* *Zhiguan* (Stilling and Contemplation) together.

As adults, they served as teachers for the children in their village; the boys practiced the "nose-contemplation" (*nigan*), which led them to offend their host, who showed them no concern. Having already passed the provincial examination (*xiangju*), he soon...
He taught his disciples at Mount Bishan. Together with his fellow practitioners, he recited the Liang Dynasty Imperial Repentance (Liang Huang Chan).

On the following day, a cloud-like light entered through the pillars, sweet dew moistened the walls, and the heavens rained down golden grains, dark millet, and liquid incense. Although it was mid-winter, ten thousand flowers bloomed in full bloom.

Changru, moved by these miraculous signs, became even more steadfast in his practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), eventually attaining the ability to foresee events. When Master Yunqi Hong heard of this, he rebuked him.
It was said: "Yusheng has fallen into the net of Māra. In the eleventh year of the Wanli era, he passed the jinshi examination and resided in the capital.

There, he would orally compose predictions regarding future events, such as fine or rainy weather, which invariably came true. Upon hearing of his father’s death, he wept so bitterly that he nearly died. He spoke to the monk Ruzhi, saying:
"If you and I cannot complete our service to our father, we shall fail in our duty as sons. What means is there to repay his kindness other than entering the mountains to cultivate the Way?
Returning home, he lived in a hut by the tomb for three years and received the precepts from Master Hong.

Every morning, after rising and paying homage at the tomb, he would go to Yunqi to inquire about the Dharma, whereupon he composed the *Forty-eight Questions on the Pure Land*, the contents of which are recorded in the *Yunqi Fahui*.
Living in the mountains, he daily offered meat broth and rice to the deer and rabbits. Whenever a tiger approached, he would simply shout at it and drive it away.

After his period of mourning ended, he rose to take office as a Director of the Bureau of Rites. Shortly thereafter, he requested leave to return home again and said to Sengru: "If I do not realize the Way, I will certainly never emerge from this life again."
"Could this be Lu He-fa? Or perhaps it is Wang Bo-an. He then took Seng-ru up Mount Tianmu and sat before the Dead Pass at the high peak.
He made an agreement with Seng-ru, saying, "Go ahead and climb the mountains and wade through the waters as you please; let me watch you for seven days until you attain realization.
Day and night he exhorted and urged him on without the slightest interval. When the twenty-first day arrived and he had not yet awakened, he became extremely weary and wished to go to rest.
While resting on his pillow, he suddenly saw Chan Master Gaofeng severing his left arm. He experienced a sudden awakening. Rushing to verify this with Master Hong of Yunqi, he said:
"One who awakens from sleep does not comb their hair or wash their face before returning to the quilt and pillow; they will surely fall back asleep.
One who awakens from delusion does not adorn themselves before returning to the defilements; they will surely fall back into delusion. A lotus born of fire easily withers. New...
"Bamboo stalks are easily broken; you must devise your own plan. Do not let a single moment’s distraction obstruct the path of your spiritual cultivation.

He therefore exhorted him to turn his merit toward the Pure Land to continue his prior causes. Changru then practiced this for the rest of his life. To those who did not believe in reciting the Buddha's name, he would say:
"To awaken oneself and to awaken others—when awakening is perfected, one is called a Buddha. Those who recite the Buddha's name are recollecting awakening."
Is it possible for every thought-moment not to be constantly awakened, while every thought-moment is constantly deluded? A person rests within the capital; a bird rests on a hillside.
Is it possible to rest in a place of non-good rather than resting in the ground of ultimate goodness? Someone asked, "How does one practice Buddha-recitation?

I replied, "It is simply to awaken right mindfulness and maintain its continuity without interruption. Among hundreds and thousands of skillful means, there is only this single word: *zhī* (to know/awaken).

Every thought-moment is infinite light; how could one not enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? When a student of the Way cultivates practice, they focus solely on seeking liberation from birth and death.

Yet every thought-moment is infinite life—what birth and death is there to be liberated from? Having finished his studies, he returned to official service and was appointed as a *Yuanwailang* (Extraordinary Councillor) in the Ministry of State Ceremonies (*Zhuguke Si*).
He was subsequently transferred to the Ministry of Merit (*Sikun*). Again, he requested to retire and lived with Monk Ruzi, strolling daily by the lake. At that time, Hong...
The Duke sat at Nanping to expound the *Jñānaprasthāna-sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng). He raised funds to redeem Wàngōngchí and established a society for the release of living beings (*fangshēng shè*).
Tens of thousands of monastics and laypeople gathered, and the sound of their chanting shook the rivers and valleys.

At that time, many men of pure integrity joined the assembly, with Zhǎngrú acting as their leader. Once, while traveling by boat with Sēngrú to the center of the lake, they passed the Three Pools. Sēngrú...
He sighed with regret and said, "This was an ancient pond for the release of living beings. How is it that it has been seized by fishermen? Consequently, Changru devised a plan to restore it;
he built an embankment and erected pavilions to establish a sanctuary for releasing life. Shortly thereafter, he entered Mount Nanping and did not emerge.
Monk Ruzi also remained in seclusion at Mount Lingjiu until his death (from the *Deyuan ji*, Appendix).

Huang Pingqian, whose given name was Hui, was a native of Nanchong, Sichuan. He passed the jinshi examination in the seventeenth year of the Wanli era and served as a compiler (biandu) alongside Tao Zhouwang;
both studied the supramundane Dharma. In his middle years, his wife died, and he did not remarry.

One night, he dreamed of ascending a jeweled pagoda, where his fellow graduate Jiao Ruohou presented him with a scroll of text. Upon examining it, he found it to be the *Yunqi Jiesha* (Yunqi’s Precepts on Abstaining from Killing).
This is the text. Having awakened to this, he observed the precept against killing. Whenever he received his salary, he would immediately purchase living beings to release them.

He carved the writings of Yunqi and distributed them throughout his village. Later, he submitted a letter to Yunqi, calling himself a disciple and expressing his sincere devotion to the practice of Pure Land.
He inscribed on his seat of honor: "If the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. If the three karmas are impure, the land will be filled with filth and evil; by what means could one go there?"
"Life arises; yet it is not a state of constant, unceasing awareness. To sever suffering as if with a single stroke of a blade—can the three karmas then be purified?
Upon hearing this, Yunqi praised it, saying: 'Truly so. Purify it again and again until, through the ultimate limit of purity, the light penetrates and one realizes one's own nature.'"

Amitābha was attained without seeking. Pingqian had previously received the five precepts; at this time, he further requested from Yunqi to receive the Bodhisattva precepts through remote transmission.
Once, he saw a spider; as he recited the Buddha’s name for it, the spider stood still for a long while and passed away.
He erected a small stupa and composed a record of his deeds. His friend Fan Ziqiao requested that he write a scroll on the precept against killing;

they traveled together to Mount Wudang, where a follower from their party rummaged through his bag and discarded the scroll into the Dragon Pool. Ziqiao searched for it and encountered a divine tortoise leading the way, whereby he recovered it;
yet the scroll remained unsullied by water. Shortly thereafter, he resigned from his post as Assistant Director of the Imperial Library to return home, wandering among the mountains and waters.

In his leisure time, he engaged in spiritual exchanges with monastics. Some wished to recommend him for official appointment, but a jealous official submitted a memorial stating that one who "forms societies to discuss Chan and takes as companions those outside the secular world" should not again defile the imperial court.
Consequently, he remained at home until old age (*Mingwen Ouchao*, *Yunqi Fahui*).
Zhuang Fuzhen, style name Guanghuan, was a native of Tongxiang in Zhejiang. In his youth he was a Confucian scholar; later, he studied medicine.
When he was over forty years old, he grew somewhat weary of worldly affairs and consequently devoted himself to the arts of longevity. After some time, he fell ill and sighed deeply, saying:
"Can I alone not be a man of leisure within the realm of heaven and earth? He then constructed a small garden, stacking stones and planting flowers and trees, where he would sigh and sing among them.
One day, observing the blooming and falling of the flowers, he realized the impermanence of the body.

He immediately demolished the garden, closed his door, and sat in meditation, taking up various sutras such as the *Vajracchedikā* to recite them. Once, while traveling to Hangzhou, he encountered an old man with whom he conversed.

He was studying Buddhism. The old man asked, "In your study of Buddhism, whom do you take as your teacher? He replied, "I have not yet. The old man said, "Have you not read Liu Zhitou’s *Book on Ingesting Qi*?
There is a Chan Master named Lianchi at Yunqi; he is nearby here. Why not go there to take him as your teacher?"
He replied, "Yes," and proceeded on foot to Yunqi. He visited Lianchi, who bestowed upon him the method of Buddha-recitation.

He subsequently received the five precepts and returned home, where he daily recited the name of Amitābha Buddha fifty thousand times. Before half a year had passed, his mind became profoundly tranquil.
At the age of eighty, he went to Yunqi once more to receive the Bodhisattva precepts and retired to live out his final years at home. He was often troubled by illness...
The people of my hometown were ignorant of the True Dharma and largely followed heterodox teachings.

Having read various sutras and treatises on the Pure Land, I have extracted their essential passages and titled this work *The Collection of Provisions for the Pure Land* (*Jingtu ziliang ji*) to guide the faithful. My fellow villagers subsequently turned toward conversion through it. (Preface to the *Collection of Provisions for the Pure Land*)
Bao Xingquan, whose given name was Zongzhao, was a native of Shanyin in Shaoxing. His family had been followers of Buddhism for generations.

Once Bao Xingquan reached adulthood, he renounced meat and alcohol and was able to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* from memory, completing one full cycle each day. His father once ordered him to sell paper in Jiaxing;
when the father became angry at his financial losses, he punished him by making him kneel. After a long while, Bao Xingquan rose, having already silently finished reciting the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

He once traveled with masters such as Zibai and Sanmu. In his later years, he turned his heart toward Yunqi, where he devoted himself earnestly to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism while also exerting great effort in the study of various texts, including the *Fangshan Heshang Heji*, the *Zongjing Lu* of Yongming, and other works. His faith and understanding were profound and penetrating.
He styled himself the Layman Heavenly Drum (Tiāngǔ Jūshì). He composed a book titled *The Heavenly Music Resounds in the Void* (*Tiānyuè Míngkōng*), in which his own preface states:

"The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'If there are sentient beings who, in a single thought-moment, believe and enter the Dharma-realm of Vairocana, even if they fall into the Avīci Hell due to evil karma, when the light of Vairocana touches their bodies, their lives shall end at that very moment and they will be reborn in Tuṣita. Thus he was transformed into—"
The sons of the gods experienced immeasurable pleasure. While they were thus enjoying themselves, a celestial drum suddenly resounded from the sky, proclaiming to the sons of the gods:
"This pleasure is empty and false; it will soon perish and vanish. Be careful not to be greedily attached to it; you should instead contemplate impermanence.
Upon hearing this, the devas immediately realized the non-arising of phenomena and attained the stage of fruition. This was because the light of Vairocana blazes forth constantly and without ceasing.
There is no distinction between them; yet, it is not necessarily the case that all sentient beings in the hells emerge.

Those who do emerge are simply those from the past who shared a karmic affinity with Vairocana and, in a single thought-moment, entered the Dharma-realm through faith. Thus, one knows that this light abides neither in Vairocana nor in oneself;
it is neither "I" nor "another," being utterly without a fixed location. Therefore, by responding to their thoughts, they are liberated from suffering. Having already departed...

Though dwelling in hell, one may still be addicted to celestial pleasures. When those pleasures have long since become impermanent and the signs of decay appear before one, one then hears the celestial drum sounding with such intensity that one immediately transcends the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Yet this celestial drum has no point of origin; there is only sound, utterly devoid of form or substance.

Although it lacks form or substance, it constantly resounds from within emptiness itself. For this reason, it is called the Dharma of the Seal of Knowledge Independent of Support (*anāśrita-jñāna-mudrā-dharma*).
Chapter: The Seal of Non-Dependent Awareness. How wondrous it is! In my region of Yue, there is a mountain named Goose Beak (Ebi), where the ancient Master Baoshang Qiansui once resided.
Those who ascend its peak often hear the sound of celestial music, clear and resonant, which everyone attributes to the Heavenly Emperor performing a concert;
thus, it is called the Village of Celestial Music (Tianle Xiang). Alas, celestial music is none other than the celestial drum (tenggu); the celestial drum is none other than non-reliance.

Based on the Dharma-gate of the Wisdom-Seal, it is the light of the Vairocana Dharmadhātu. Having entered this Dharma-gate of the Non-reliant Wisdom-Seal, celestial drums thunder and celestial music resonates;
day and night, it is heard throughout all realms without ceasing. I, moreover, strike them, desiring to awaken the ignorant and deluded.
Although they manifest through form and speech, their origin and departure are无从 (without source). For this reason, I have provisionally named them "Celestial Drums" and reside [within them].
This gentleman named this collection "The Heavenly Music Resounding in the Void.

As he approached the end of his life, he instructed his son to prepare a vegetarian feast and invited his dharma friends Wang Jichang, Dai Shengzhi, Xu Chunmen, and several monastics to attend. When they arrived, they chanted the name of the Buddha of the Western Paradise in unison.
