At sunset, he suddenly joined his palms in reverence and said to the assembly, "I bid you all a final farewell," whereupon he sat in the full lotus posture.
He passed away while seated. His writings were extensive and complete, yet none have been transmitted.
His *Preface to the "Celestial Music Resounding in the Void"* has been carved and included within the Canon of Jingshan Monastery.

Zhi Gui said: "The Sūtras state that although one knows the lands of the Buddhas and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates the Pure Land and teaches and transforms sentient beings. Nanquan also said, 'Ordinary mind is the Way.

The wise person who grasps the intent of Nanquan’s words proceeds toward it in every thought-moment without proceeding, and contemplates emptiness in every thought-moment without forming a conceptual understanding of emptiness. If...
As for the various lay practitioners (*kǔshì*), they may well be considered close to this ideal.
From the "Biographies of Lay Practitioners," Part 43:
The Biography of Li Zhuowu.
Li Zhuowu, whose given name was Zhi, was a native of Jinjiang County in Quanzhou. During the Jiajing era, he passed the provincial examination and served as a local educator.
At the beginning of the Wanli era, he rose through the ranks to become a Judicial Assistant in the Nanjing Ministry of Justice. He was subsequently dispatched as the Prefect of Ya’an.

Zhuowu possessed a singular and austere character that was prone to offending others. His learning did not adhere to conventional boundaries, moving freely between Confucianism and Buddhism, taking the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as his foundation.
Upon returning, the various teachers of the time all singled out Mr. Wang Longxi for recommendation. Mr. Luo Jinxi had formerly studied the Way under him and once engaged in a correspondence with Mr.

Geng Tiantai and Mr. Deng Shiyang to debate difficult points. Their exchange spanned over ten thousand words, stripping away the pretenses and falsehoods of contemporary Confucian scholars to reveal the true heart-mind;
it was as if the skin were peeled back to expose the bone, providing a model for self-cultivation in Ya’an.
He was pure and austere. In governing, he addressed the essential principles of affairs; he often delighted in associating with monastics.

While presiding over the monastery, he settled matters so that all business was efficiently accomplished. At that time, the high officials were severe and harsh, and the officials and common people were mostly unsettled.

Zhuowu said: "In these frontier regions where various ethnic groups dwell, it is difficult to apply the law exhaustively. It is enough to let each day pass as it may, sharing peace together with the soldiers and the people."
Those who serve here bring their families from ten thousand *li* away; yet, upon the slightest transgression, they depart in distress. One must especially consider this.

If one possesses even a single virtue, they are considered worthy; how can one allow them to be held fully accountable? After three years, he requested leave on account of illness, but it was not granted.
He subsequently entered Mount Jizu to read the Tripitaka and did not emerge. Censor Liu Wei submitted a memorial ordering him—
He retired from official service and subsequently lived as a guest in Huang’an. Soon after, he went to Longtan Lake in Macheng, where he shaved his head and discarded his cap and robes.
He converted his residence into a Chan monastery. In his daily life, he would discuss the matters of renunciation with his attendants, saying:
"There are three types of people in this world who should leave the household life. The first are those like Zhuang Zhou and Mei Fu, who regard life as a shackle and the physical form as..."
Wisdom is a disgrace to me; wisdom is a poison to me. It is as clear as day that this body and this world are like excrescences and tumors. Nevertheless, there is one thing I cannot avoid:
the necessity of abandoning office to live in seclusion. This is the first [reason]. Such people are like Yan Guang, Ruan Ji, Chen Tuan, and Shao Yong.
Yet, if I cannot compare myself to Fu Yue meeting Emperor Gaozong, Tai Gong meeting King Wen, or Guan Zhong meeting Duke Huan—[then my purpose remains unfulfilled].
When Lord Kongming met with the Prime Minister (Liu Bei), it was one instance where he would rather remain hidden than emerge. Another such case is that of Tao Yuanming.
He both loved wealth and honor and suffered from poverty. Because he suffered from poverty, he felt ashamed to beg for food and said, "My words are clumsy when knocking at doors.
Yet because he loved wealth and honor, he sought the post of Magistrate of Pengze; however, there was [no...].
Since he was unwilling to "bend his waist" [submit to authority], why did he depart after only eighty days? This is yet another instance of it.
An attendant stepped forward and asked, "Among these three cases, where does the Master stand? Zhuowu said, "How noble were the insights of Zhuang Zhou and Mei Fu!
I am not like them. I shall wait for a master who understands me before I emerge; such a person must surely possess world-transcending merit."
"Indeed, I too am not such a person. Could it be Master Tao? Master Tao’s pure wind has pervaded a thousand ages;
what person am I that I would dare claim to approach even his shadow? Nevertheless, his single thought was true: he did not wish to be bound by the constraints of the world."

Thus, we happen to be of one mind. Zhuowu delighted in receiving people; regardless of whether they were monastics or laypeople, he would open his heart to those who came seeking instruction, responding to them with such vigor that it stirred the very halls of the imperial court.
Occasionally, women would come to hear the Dharma. Some remarked that women’s vision was limited and that they were unfit to study the Way.
Zhuowu replied, "People have genders—male and female—but does their vision likewise possess gender? Furthermore, as for those..."

"Those who come for the sake of the Dharma are not like ordinary men. Subsequently, the scholar-officials among the *máhuáng* (hemp-wearing) crowd all raised a great clamor, denouncing him as a practitioner of heterodox ways who was deluding the masses, and sought to expel him.
Zhuowu laughed and said, "If I am truly a practitioner of heterodox ways, then you may place the official cap upon me.
Thereupon, he resumed his former attire. The Censor Ma Jinglun once went to inquire about the meaning of the *Yījīng* (Book of Changes). Great... [text fragment ends]
He served him with the rites due to a teacher. Upon entering Mount Huangbo, he was subsequently escorted to the Northern Guest House.
While in Tongzhou, he was again impeached by an official of the Censorate and cast into the Imperial Prison. When his sentence was finalized, he was compelled to return to his native place.
Zhuowu said, "I am seventy-six years old; I shall simply die. Why return? He seized a knife and committed suicide. Jinglun prepared the funeral rites according to protocol and buried him.
At the North Gate of Tongzhou (from the *Mingwen Ouchao* and *Wenling Waiji*).
Zhiguizi said: "When I first examined the writings of Layman Zhuowu on antiquity, I was startled by the traces of his words.
His conduct and actions were censured by the world, and I considered that the Layman had truly brought this upon himself. Subsequently, I read the Layman’s..."
The scholars discussed this book on learning and were moved by it. Alas! One such as this Layman may truly be called one who knows the fundamental.
Since the Layman has left the household life, he did not receive the precepts; shortly thereafter, he returned to wearing the cap and robes once more.
Was this a jest? Or was he acting out of some deeper provocation? As for that, I am not sufficient to know.

Wang Dashen said: "Zhuowu glares with eyes wide open; Yunchu lowers his brows. To depict one who glares with eyes wide open using a person who lowers his brows—his gaze suddenly becomes like lightning beneath a cliff.
Is this not what the 'Knower of Return' (Zhiguizi) meant by 'lofty and self-rejoicing'?"
Luotaisan said: "The sorrowful person of antiquity had a distinct inner disposition. I and Master Zhuowu also say the same.
Regarding this middle section: there is neither past nor present; amidst this vast and desolate melancholy, it is precisely suited for moments of leisure.
It strikes where it hurts; it touches where the itch is so unbearable that one cannot endure it. I borrow these cold words to provide a resolution.
Those who read this must not mistake them for literal truth. They blunt Zhuowu; they blunt the realization of the Way.
Today, as I read this, I see the points in which Master Zhuowu is worthy of respect and the points in which he is lovable. Today, as I read this...
As in reading Qu Yi’s "Heavenly Questions," reading the "Tianxia" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, reading Mei Shu’s "Seven Stimuli," and reading the biographies of the forty-four masters—
Guan, Yang, Tao, Jiao, Tang, and Ju— in the *Jushi Zhuan*.

Guan Deng, whose courtesy name was Zhidao, was a native of Taicang. Among scholars, he was known as Master Dongming. While serving as a *zhusheng* (commoner student), he was devoted to both study and practice.
At the beginning of the Longqing era, Governor Cai Gongjian established the Zhongwu Academy and appointed Deng as its teacher.
He gathered students to lecture on learning. He once said: "The world must first have the resolve to withdraw from society without being known and yet feel no regret, before it can carry the Way;
it must first have the strength to refuse to do one act of unrighteousness or kill one innocent person even to gain the empire, before it can establish its character.
Those who heard this were struck with awe. In the fifth year, he passed the jinshi examination and was appointed to office.

He held the post of *zhishi* (chief clerk) in the Nanjing Ministry of War (*Bingbu*). Upon the death of his father, he returned home to observe mourning. After completing his term of mourning, he was appointed as a *zhishi* in the Ministry of Justice (*Xingbu*).
At the beginning of the Wanli era, when Zhang Juzheng was in power and monopolized both authority and fortune for six years, [Wang] Deng submitted a memorial on nine matters.

The Great Design was to rectify the imperial administration, communicate the sentiments of the common people, and reform corrupt governance; it sought to strip Yang Tingyun of his power and return it to the Son of Heaven.

Yang Tingyun was displeased and soon appointed him as an Extraordinary Secretary (Yuanwailang) to serve as Assistant Commissioner of the Guangdong Surveillance Commission, assigned to the Southern Shao Circuit.
At that time, there were many bandits in Guangdong; Deng [Zhen] enrolled them into the military ranks, enforced strict joint liability for offenses, and stationed troops at strategic points.

The region under his jurisdiction became peaceful and settled. Meanwhile, the Minister of Works, Xi, harbored ill will toward Ju; he impeached him, resulting in Ju’s demotion to the position of Superintendent of the Salt Office.

The following year, during the external audit of officials, Ju retired from office due to old age and illness. When Ju Zheng was defeated, court officials submitted joint memorials to recommend him, leading to his appointment as Assistant Commissioner of Hubei.
He requested leave to return home on account of his mother’s advanced age. Initially, when Deng entered the capital via the selection and recommendation system, he stayed at Mount Xishan.
At Biyun Temple, while reading the "World-Ruling Sublime Adornment" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I suddenly awakened to the meaning of the *I Ching*'s "The Supreme Ultimate employs the Nine.
Looking back upon my own body and mind, I saw them as entirely identical to the Great Void.

I clearly perceived the wondrous functioning of the sages and worthies of all times—those who transcend the world and govern it—manifesting their vows and powers in accordance with the changing seasons. I concluded that while principles are mutually integrated, the teachings must necessarily...
Excessive. Sometimes they accord with one another in mutual inclusion; sometimes they oppose one another in mutual completion. Sometimes the real is concealed while the provisional is manifested;

sometimes the provisional is set aside to clarify the real. With various appearances and disappearances, and various tensions and relaxations, each possesses its own order, making it difficult to fathom.
This is for no other reason than that the virtue of the Dragon cannot be placed at the head [of the teaching]. Confucius held "neither yes nor no," and Zisi personally received [this transmission].
This is the lineage of our house; hence it is said that they are nurtured together and proceed in tandem. Like the flowing of rivers, they deepen and harmonize transformation.
Since the time of Mencius, there has been but one person, Master Zhou (Zhu Xi), who embodied the Great Ultimate and penetrated the three teachings.

Our Sagely Ancestor integrated the two [Buddhist and Daoist] traditions with Confucianism, organizing their respective systems: he governed Confucianism with Confucianism, Buddhism with Buddhism, and Daoism with Daoism. It was thus...
They complement one another without being confused; for the principles of the teachings must necessarily be round, while the substance of the teachings must necessarily be square.

Taking the roundness of Confucius to perfect the squareness of Song dynasty scholars, we ensure that Confucianism does not obstruct Buddhism and Buddhism does not obstruct Confucianism, ultimately reaching the state of non-obstruction in all things (*sarva-vastu-avighāta*). This opens the path for their simultaneous cultivation and concurrent practice.

If one wishes for the square to be truly square, one must take the "squareness" of Zhongni as being close to the "roundness" of the Confucianists, so that the Confucianists do not overstep into the sphere of the Śramaṇas, and the Śramaṇas do not overstep into the sphere of the Confucianists.
Extending this principle to its ultimate limit, even the Dharma does not overstep; thus, by means of a scale that maintains balance without harm or contradiction, all things are held in equilibrium.
Such were the general principles of his lifelong discourse on the study of learning. He once composed the *Congxian Weisu Yi* (Discourse on Following the Ancestors and Rectifying Customs).

In its "Protecting the Dharma" chapter, it says: "In the Buddhist gate, those who protect the teachings among the Confucians are called the 'Gold Wall and Moat of the Buddha-Dharma' (*buddhadharma-kimtaṅ*).

This describes how they protect the inner [teachings] from without, like a golden city and a moat that cannot be breached. Indeed, the Buddha-Dharma possesses two types of protection: the internal and the external. [This is] extracted from...
At the time of the Flower [Assembly], the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa were entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
At the time of his entry into parinirvāṇa, the compilation of the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures was entrusted to Ānanda.

Furthermore, after the kalpa of weapons has been exhausted and the cycle of decline and increase begins anew, the teachings of the Three Vehicles are raised and proclaimed; this was entrusted to the sixteen Arhats worthy of offerings. These three categories are collectively termed [the Transmission].
Regarding internal protection, there is what is called external protection by means of a golden moat, which is entrusted to kings and great ministers;

Regarding the discourse on the people and all things, there are those who intentionally cultivate their minds to draw them into a state of shared identity;

yet they cannot help but find that the sensations of pain and itching are ultimately different from their own. It is like looking at a person through a blurred mirror: though one may forcibly press the person's face against it, [the reflection remains indistinct].
Yet his beard and eyebrows could never be clearly distinguished. When the ancients were amidst their furrows and fields, they held no charge over the entire world;

yet when they thought of a single person, it was as if they themselves were pushing that person down a ditch. This was because their awakened nature was clear and penetrating, and the pain and itching of all sentient beings was as intimately connected as a single breath.
Thus, they could not restrain the churning of their burning entrails. Although ordinary people and sentient beings—though [the text here is incomplete]—are...
To seek intimacy and yet end up estranged; the Sage and sentient beings do not seek conditions, yet they are naturally not estranged—this is the distinction between awakening and non-awakening.

Being thus situated, he had no choice but to take the world upon himself as his own responsibility. Therefore, he is called Yi Yin.

This is the responsibility of the sage. Yi Yin’s responsibility likely arose from within his own self-awakening. Yi Yin’s responsibility for the world did not consist merely in rescuing the people from their mud and fire, or delivering them from water and flames.
If one takes this as the standard of responsibility, then the heroes, generals, and ministers of later ages were all likewise so;

If there were anyone who did not receive the grace of Yao and Shun, it would be as if he had pushed that person into a ditch.

Furthermore, those who suffer harm are likewise unable to realize their own true nature; they harbor thoughts of acceptance, thoughts of equality, and thoughts of compassionate pity.
Consequently, the deceiver continues to deceive, the oppressor continues to oppress, and the butcher continues to butcher.

It encompasses heaven and earth and brings all things to completion through its subtle workings. It is that by which the Sages participate in and assist the process of transformation and nourishment. How could this be merely a matter of physical form?

This is what is reached [by the sages]. Only the sages are able to exhaustively penetrate the spirit (*shen*); yet the common and the ignorant have certainly never been absent from it—they simply do not know that it is identical to the Dao.
Therefore it is said: "The common people use it daily but do not know it. Because they do not know it, they are uniformly enslaved by form.

People worry that they will limit themselves by considering lofty and remote matters to be beyond their reach; therefore it is said, "It is advantageous for it to be used in going out and coming in;

This divinity, when traced back, has no beginning; when pushed forward, it has no end. How could it be merely the physical life?
Thus, at the very moment of birth, does the form perish along with it? The form has its end, but the spirit is inexhaustible. Therefore, it is said: "Examine the origin and return to the end;

The spirit is born; when the form perishes, the spirit perishes. If we rely on the words of Zhin, then that which "persists when grasped" persists because the form is present, and that which "perishes when abandoned" perishes because the form is gone.

Now, as I recall the past, it is like being in Wu and knowing about Yue; how could such a form be capable of this? Your argument, Zhen, is profoundly lacking in reflection.
Your words cause people to value the physical form while neglecting the spirit, leading them all together into ruin and drowning. You claim that the form is identical to the spirit.
Thus, one abandons the form and denies the self. When the form is abandoned and the self is denied, then whatever the ordinary form desires becomes what the "self" desires;

yet this is constrained by ritual and righteousness. This is compulsion; this is external molding. To claim that the spirit does not perish while asserting it perishes is to say that Yao and Jie are equally extinguished, and Yan Hui and Zhi were equally born.
If they are equally born, then those who are licentious find their own comfort; if they are equally extinguished, then [the distinction between] the good... [is lost].
Those who practice such cultivation labor in vain. Thus, one must show them the blessings that follow from virtue and warn them of the hundred calamities that result from transgression;
yet they regard this as obscure and difficult to verify. If one proclaims benevolence and righteousness, they think that benevolence and righteousness disturb the human heart.

If one proclaims the inherent goodness of human nature, they think it is inherently evil; if one proclaims the mixture of good and evil, how could they possibly believe it? How long can such views persist? How many could truly be made to believe?

Thus, they were distraught over gain and loss, entangled in fetters; their greed and malice accumulated until they could no longer be concealed, their transgressions became so great that they could not be resolved.
Sunk in the dark alleys of delusion, they were unable to emerge on their own; they drifted once more through the currents of saṃsāra, suffering without end.

That which has flowed into Zhendan is but a single drop from the ocean of ink; this constitutes the present Great Canon. As for its discourse on retribution, it traces back through the three periods of time;
as for its discourse on nature, it exhausts the mystery of wondrous enlightenment. To know the retribution of the three periods is to realize that the inequality between Yao and Jie is not ultimate;
to know the mystery of the enlightened nature is to have no doubt regarding the inherent goodness of nature. Thus, those of lower capacity may attain [this realization].

Their discourse must necessarily inspire awe regarding the retribution of the three periods of time. Thus, evil is rectified without waiting for punishment, and goodness is practiced without waiting for exhortation.
Those of the highest caliber who grasp this teaching will wondrously accord with the truth of the inherent goodness of nature;

abiding in benevolence and following righteousness will be as natural as hearing with the ears or seeing with the eyes—how could anything disturb their minds? Therefore, the teachings of the sages and worthies, having attained the Tathāgata, [are fully realized].
How profoundly expressed! Alas, that Zhen did not investigate this; he claimed that when the spirit perishes, the form perishes, and thus gave rise to [the notion of] the Buddha.
Only the teaching of the Tathāgata can exhaustively fathom the vastness and subtlety of this spirit.

To speak of its greatness: heaven and earth are but a single bubble in the inexhaustible great ocean; the cycles of eons and ages are but a single instant in the inexhaustible flow of time. To speak of...

Its subtlety is such that it is without sound and without smell; this is the Truth of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-satya*). To concentrate on the One and hold fast to the Mean is the Perfection of Conduct (*śīla-pāramitā*).
A single word unfolds into immeasurable meanings; even if one were to examine them from antiquity to the present, one could never reach their end.

The right and wrong of Confucianism and Buddhism, the secrets of Huang-Lao, and the eloquent disputations of the hundred schools—all may be summarized in a single word, yet this remains more than sufficient.
By means of it, one assists Yao and becomes like Yao; one assists Shun and becomes like Shun. By means of it, a father is compassionate and a son is filial.
By means of it, those who protect the Dharma protect all sentient beings; by means of it, Śakra leaves behind craving; and by means of it, Brahmā...

By means of this, the devas attain transcendent wisdom; by means of this, those of the Two Vehicles dedicate themselves toward the True Vehicle; and by means of this, Bodhisattvas realize and enter Wondrous Enlightenment.
From the four classes of noble beings to the six realms of ordinary beings, there is none who is not reached. Thus, its words must reach as far as the ink of the oceans.

Its wondrous virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, cannot surpass the ultimate fathoming of the spirit. Therefore, its essential point must return to the One Vehicle. It transcends the mundane world...
There are no worldly dharmas that have not been exhausted without remainder. Therefore, among those who have risen in the world, there are none who do not hold them in high esteem.

Our Grand Ancestor, the Great Emperor Taizong, pursued this prosperity to its ultimate extent. Having already carved the Great Canon at the Eastern Capital (Liu-du), the Great Emperor Taizong further carved the Great Canon in the Imperial Capital.

The successive sagacious emperors who inherited the lineage have maintained this tradition down to the present day without decline. This extends even to the renowned ministers of successive dynasties.

Among the veteran scholars, some were of such lofty conduct as to stand alone in their generation, while others possessed literary prowess that would dominate for a hundred ages. These were the elite—talents like dragon-sprouts and phoenix chicks—and the virtuous, fragrant as orchids and pure as snow.

Those who took refuge in the flow of the Dharma and nourished themselves upon the divine raft of truth are so numerous that it would be difficult to finish enumerating them even if one changed attendants every time a name was called.
Alas! The four elements are but a temporary confluence; a hundred years are but a morning and an evening. What was experienced in the past, what remains now?

That which remains—how can it be relied upon? Ultimate love ends in separation; great undertakings end in abandonment. Before the spirit has reached its ultimate destination, one drifts in vast obscurity; where can one find refuge?
To travel a hundred *li* and fail to find a place of rest leads to restless wandering; how much more so when traversing the vast eons!
The seven realms of rebirth are crowded and chaotic, and the place of refuge is not fixed; one becomes habituated to the gains and losses of a mere hundred years.
Yet they treat the wandering through ten thousand kalpas with such lightness; can this not be called "Great Compassion"?

Thus, one who saves me for a single moment does not equal one who saves me for an entire lifetime; and enabling me to find peace for a single lifetime is not as good as enabling me to find peace throughout vast eons.
To seek salvation for oneself throughout vast eons is none other than the teaching of the Tathāgata.
How so? For now, I dare not yet discuss the stages of attaining the fruits or ascending the grounds.

Yet, if one can wade through the ocean of awakening and provide even a slight irrigation of its residual moisture, then one will accord with every sense faculty and every sensory object, such that there is nothing throughout the Dharma-realm that is not universally pervaded. Thereupon, the fetters and coverings cannot entangle them;
the yin and yang cannot constrain them. They soar with ease and gather with spontaneity; they exhaust kalpas of vast antiquity within a single kṣaṇa, uprooting the nine [realms].

It is akin to a half-verse; nothing surpasses this. Various eminent monks and great disciples have fully extolled these meritorious deeds. I, however, am particularly concerned that those in the world who fabricate the Buddha’s teachings might...

[He] used [my skin] as brushes to transcribe this sutra scroll; the accumulation was like Mount Sumeru. Now, in this land of China, *zhēnlí* (glutinous rice starch) is as pure as jade;
there is no need to use my skin for the purposes of this Dharma-treasury. To make my skin usable, I do not dare refuse being flayed.
As for Yu, he has brushes made from the hides of wild beasts; there is no need to split my bones. To make my bones usable, I do not refuse being split.

I dare not decline. Although I am currently living in poverty, I shall strive to provide the necessary offerings. Whether serving in office or returning to farming, I will prepare these according to my circumstances and means.

Zhu Zhao-long, whose courtesy name was Guo-zuo, was a native of Xiushui. In the eleventh year of the Wanli era, he ranked first among the successful candidates in the jinshi examinations.

During the Tianqi era, he served as a Grand Secretary (Daxueshi) of the Wuying Hall. In office, he was forthright and maintained a sense of great integrity; his conduct in advancing or withdrawing from service was always guided by ritual propriety.

This was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He then said to his son, "Throughout my life, I have not distinguished between prosperity and decline;

Furthermore, from time to time, he would call upon his elderly neighbors to explain the general meaning of the sūtra. In the fourth year of the Tianqi era, knowing that his end was near, he prepared wine for himself.

This was Kong Sheng. He was skilled in the calculations of the *huangji* (the Imperial Ultimate). Having calculated Lian’s destiny, he exhorted him to study Confucian texts, saying, "Next year you shall be enrolled as a *zhusheng* (common student).

"Various things from the past are like dying yesterday; various things from the future are like being born today.

one must reflect deeply on this and exert oneself. Yan later also passed the jinshi examination and served as the Magistrate of Gaoyao (from the *Wujiang Zhi*, *Feng Kaizhi Ji*, *Danguan Ji*, and the appended posthumous writings of Master Micao).

Biography of Yuan Zhonglang (Yuan Boshu).
Yuan Boshu, whose given name was Zongdao and style name Xiangguang Jushi, was a native of Gong’an in Hubei. His younger brother was Zhonglang.
The first was named Hongdao, styled Shitou Jushi (Stonehead Layman). The second was named Zhongdao, styled Shangsheng Jushi (Upper Birth Layman).
These three were born of the same mother, Lady Gong. She recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily.

One day, a large spider descended from a beam, circled the scripture several times, and suddenly crouched down and remained still before it. The mother said, "Have you come to listen to the sutra? and she continued her recitation.
When they reached the sixth verse, the spider moved slightly as if performing a prostration; when they unrolled the scroll to look at it, it had already transformed and departed.

They therefore enshrined it in a niche for burial and erected a small stupa there. All three men were famous for their literary talent in their youth, and in their maturity, they all took a deep interest in the Chan school.

During the Wanli era, they both successively passed the jinshi examinations. Boxiu rose to the rank of Right Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat, while Zhonglang served as the Magistrate of Wujiang.
He was swift and decisive in adjudicating cases; when the public halls were quiet, he would often delight in excursions through mountains and waters.

Later, serving as a Chief Clerk in the Ministry of Rites, he retired on account of illness and built a garden south of the city. There he planted ten thousand willow trees, naming it "Willow Waves" (Liulang), and associated with various Chan practitioners.
He dwelt within this community. Initially, he studied Chan under Li Zhuowu; his faith and understanding were penetrating and sharp, and his eloquence was unimpeded.

For millions of kalpas, this shall never be lost. It is like a bhikṣu who, because of his wisdom, possesses radiance from his body, yet because of his false speech, maggots flow from his mouth.

Even if these individuals do not find small satisfaction in their practice, but constantly cultivate according to the teachings, they would ultimately never say of themselves, "I have realized that the mind itself is Buddha.

How could they then be compared to those of middling or inferior capacity who recite the Buddha's name seeking rebirth in the Pure Land? While thoroughly understanding that birth is fundamentally non-birth, it does not preclude one from vigorously seeking [rebirth].

Only then shall you occupy a lotus throne of the highest grade and sit within a jeweled pavilion in mid-air.

At dawn, partake of the fragrant food of Saṃghāṭa; at dusk, roam through the realm of the Full Moon. Looking back upon those of the womb-birth class who stumble along the jeweled ground, [you will see them]—no [longer].
Though they hear the Dharma teachings, they do not perceive the Dharmakāya. Elephants and horses do not associate in herds; chickens and phoenixes are not of the same kind.

How much less so for those who dwell within the jar of the minor fruits of humans and devas—mosquitoes and gadflies! Yet, with empty bellies and haughty hearts, they cling to emptiness and destroy existence.

Therefore, know that this path is perilous and difficult, not easily traversed. To succeed is to become a Buddha; to fail is to become a Māra.

Householder, the path is straight and can serve to circulate this Dharma. However, since you are a householder, you differ from the śramaṇa disciples of the Śākya;

How much less so for subtler deeds? Within the cycle of birth and death, how could one ever hope to escape freely? Therefore, know that the single gateway of Buddha-recitation is of the utmost urgency for laypeople.

If worldly pursuits such as serving in office or managing a household are said to be no obstacle, how much less so are morning and evening prostrations and recitations? Furthermore, let us take the exhortation of reciting the Buddha’s name as a point of departure.
It is essential that this may serve as a reminder for the mind of Zen practice (*chán*). By borrowing the thorough penetration of the Zen gate, one can solidify faith in the Pure Land.
These two aspects supporting one another is most stable and substantial. To lack such faith is truly equivalent to being among the lowest of the ignorant.
Layman Shítóu had aimed early on at Zen practice; his faculties were sharp and keen, and within ten years he attained a profound realization. His capacity—

thus, superficial understanding could not overcome actual reality. I realized that without practicing after awakening, one will inevitably fall into demonic realms.

Consequently, I first curtailed my biased view of emptiness and entered the ocean of Samantabhadra. Furthermore, reflecting on the definitive essentials of the practice gate, I found none better than the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
However, as he provisionally led those of middling and inferior capacities, their doubts had not yet been entirely dispelled.

The mind is like a thousand waves rising in competition and ten thousand streams flowing crosswise; yet when one investigates where they converge and return, they all stem from a single source.

Xiangguang’s consciousness is inferior and his faculties weak;
