Indeed, awakening to principle cannot produce precepts; such is the madness of wisdom that lacks concentration, leading one back into the five turbidities. While you are still strong and healthy, you must truly awaken and truly practice, combining both [precepts and wisdom].
Uphold pure vows and diligently apply skillful means out of compassion for all beings; before long, we shall meet again. Once you have entered another path, it will be terrifying and fearsome.
If you are unable to maintain the precepts, there exists the "Six Fasting Days Method" of Nāgārjuna which may be followed;
therein, the precept against killing is most urgent. I send these words to my fellow students: never, even for a day, should you brandish the carving knife or greedily crave savory flavors.
These are those capable of being born in this land. Although one may preach the Dharma like clouds or rain, what benefit does it bring to the matter at hand?

You and I were brothers during the Kalpa of the Empty King; this was true even throughout the six realms of existence. Fortunately, I have attained this auspicious ground, yet I feared you might fall into ruin.
Thus, through skillful means and spiritual power, I have brought you here. Since the pure and the defiled are separated, you shall not remain long.
[The text] remains. At that time, Boxiu had already passed away. [Xiaoxiu] therefore asked about his place of rebirth, to which Zhonglang replied, "His place of rebirth is also excellent;
you shall know it for yourself later. Suddenly, he ascended into the air and vanished. Xiaoxiu stepped out onto the bank of the pond and suddenly felt as if he were falling into the water;
he leaped up and awoke. This was on the full moon of the tenth month in the forty-second year of the Wanli era. Xiaoxiu himself recorded this account. Initially...
Boxiu had a son named Deng. At the age of thirteen, he suffered from abdominal distension (pi) and was nearing death. He said to Zhonglang, "I am dying. Uncle, how can you save me?
Zhonglang replied, "If you simply recite the Buddha's name, you will attain rebirth in the Buddha-land. This world of five turbidities is not worth lingering over.
Deng then pressed his palms together and invoked the name of Amitābha Buddha; all his kinsmen joined him in unison.
He assisted her. After a short while, Seng Deng smiled and said, "I see a lotus flower, its color slightly reddish.
Shortly thereafter, she said, "The flower is gradually growing larger; its color is so brilliant it has no equal. Again she said, "The Buddha has arrived;
his marks and signs and radiance fill the entire room. After a moment, her breathing became labored. Bo Xiu said, "You need only recite the single word 'Buddha'. Deng then recited "Buddha."
After uttering a few words, he joined his palms and passed away (*Ming Shi*, *Ming Wen Ou Chao*, *Xi Fang He Lun Xu*, *Bai Su Zhai Ji*, *Ke Xue Zhai Wai Ji*, *Huai Yuan*, *Jin Gang Xin Yi Lu*).
Zhiguizi said: During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, the Great Master Lianchi propagated the Dharma-gate of Pure Land at Yunqi.

He strictly maintained the recitation of scriptures and upheld the precepts with rigor; those who followed him were numerous and refined, all being gentlemen of sincere practice and substantial virtue.
At the same time, the Elder Zhuowu also guided later generations through the Chan school, yet he delighted in learning from his own mind and lacked [discipline in] conduct.
The traces of these errors have flowed down in an endless stream; how could the Elder (Yuan Hongdao) not bear the blame?
When I read the early writings of the Yuan brothers, they mostly dabbled in intellectual understanding and hovered ambiguously around literary appearances; I privately regarded this as a malady.

Later, however, I encountered the *Western Regions Synthesis Treatise* (*Xifang helun*) by Zhonglang (Yuan Zongdao). I read it three times without weariness, and I was moved by the repentance expressed in the preface written by Baixiu (Yuan Cezhi).
How profoundly they cleared away the brambles and thorns to enter upon the level path! It is evident that the Yuan brothers were exceptionally adept at remedying their errors.
Students who observe this may take it as a mirror for themselves.
Wang Dashen said: "The Master said, 'I have not yet seen one who, upon seeing their own faults, can engage in internal self-reproach.
The Yuan brothers seem to come close to this. How vast and sincere are their hearts of awakening and compassion!"
Dashi also wrote to Yunchu, saying: "I have received your recommendation to read the *Xi-fang he-lun* (Comprehensive Treatise on the Western Paradise).
I shall look for it to read; if I cannot find it, I shall borrow it. As for Yuan's Zen, I do not dare hastily judge it as mere lip service.
He received the Dharma from Longhu, and there was no lack of evidence that 'mad spirits' had entered his innermost being. As for Yuan himself—"
He turned instead toward the light and pure demons, falling into a state of ease and pleasure where he acted as a mere vessel for worldly affairs.
Day after day he drifted in smooth, slippery places, giving rise to intellectual knowledge and views, never encountering a time when there was a silver mountain or iron wall to block him.
Later, realizing there was nothing to be gained, he returned his heart to the Pure Land; this is truly extraordinary. However, one must not, on this account alone—
In the Zen school, people falsely create distinctions of high and low regarding the Pure Land. You must know that as for the matters of the Zen school:
what Śākyamuni Buddha taught is this very thing; what Amitābha Buddha taught is this very thing;
and what Maitreya taught is also this very thing. There is no duality and no differentiation. If it is thus, then everyone living here is more than sufficient.

[The questioner said: "I understand. Why then is it necessary to be reborn in the Western Paradise? Why is it necessary to be reborn in Tuṣita? [Yuanwu] said: "This is the wheel of vows. [The questioner asked:
"Furthermore, why is the Western Paradise praised twice as much as Tuṣita? [Yuanwu] said: "When one is born as a human, there are those who wish to be born in the heavens;

yet there are also those in the heavens who wish to be born in the Western Paradise. Thus, the desires of both humans and devas are purified. When the desires of humans and devas are purified, it is precisely right [to seek the West]."
To resolve this matter: throughout the entire ten-direction Dharma-realm, there is no aspiration-wheel greater than the vow to be reborn in the Western Land.
Those who ride upon this wheel of aspiration must by no means give rise to intellectual interpretations based on the literal words.
To give rise to such interpretations is to activate a calculating mind; this calculating mind is the very root of the six realms of saṃsāra.
These are not the causes for rebirth in the Pure Land. Those who wish to be born in Tuṣita should enter through the poems of Pūgabhadra;
those who wish to be born in the Western Paradise should enter through the poems of Fenggan. These are the true causes.
Pūgabhadra was an emanation of Maitreya; Fenggan was an emanation of Amitābha.
Biographies of Eminent Lay Buddhists, Volume 47:

The Biographies of Zeng Duafu, Zhao Fanfu, and Liu Yushou Zeng Duafu, whose given name was Daqi, was a native of Taihe in Jiangxi. He possessed profound faith in the Buddha-dharma and was a scholar of extensive learning and eloquent debate.

He was a man of extraordinary brilliance. He authored a work titled *Tongyi* (Supplement to the Compendium), which drew from both Buddhist and Confucian scriptures to expound upon the causal conditions of sin and merit, as well as the principles of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
It resolved the delusions of the ignorant and common folk; its chapter on "Protecting Life" was particularly profound and earnest. Its text states: A guest asked:
The scriptures say that when humans eat sheep, the sheep will eat humans, life after life and age after age, devouring one another in turn. Why is this so?
For this reason, one remains in the cycle of birth and death for hundreds and thousands of kalpas. If one applies this logic to other things, it is no different.
Thus, as people navigate the world, every touch of their hands becomes a transgression; this is indeed something to be feared. Is this truly so? Tong replied:
"The words of the Sages are as they are; the purport of the scriptures is not false. The discourse on saṃsāra and the talk of karmic retribution appear to accord with the facts."
Upon investigating this principle, it is necessarily so. Of all human powers, none is greater than the mind. Drawn by the power of the mind, the physical form cannot resist it.
Thus, when the mind is sorrowful, the countenance wrinkles; when the mind is joyful, the countenance relaxes.

If even a transient emotion can thus enslave the appearance, how much more so must the full power of the mind govern the body? Mencius said: "The difference between humans and beasts is but slight. The common people abandon it."

The gentleman preserves this [human essence]. When it is nearly lost, one becomes of the same substance as birds and beasts. To be of the same substance as birds and beasts means that form follows the spirit in its departure;
if the force is violent, the transition occurs before life ends; if the force is slow, the transition occurs after death. The difference lies only in the speed of the process.
Ultimately, their principles are equal. The transformation after death—such as the horse depicted by the painter or the python conjured by Jin Shang—is one thing;
the transformation before birth—such as Feng Shao becoming a tiger or Mingzhen becoming a snake—is another. Mingzhen’s transformation follows the same principle as that of the painter:
in one case, for the sake of art, he projects his spirit onto the steed Lu'er; in the other, for the sake of discourse, he entrusts his contemplation to the serpent.
In the case of the *shūrān* (centipede), when the spirit departs, the body follows; when the thought is formed, the self is transformed into a snake or a horse.

Yet, while some undergo transformation quickly and others receive it slowly, this distinction arises from the difference between violence and mildness. Feng Shao’s transformation was identical to that of Jin Shang:

in one case, because of his ferocity, his disposition became like that of a tiger (*yú tú*); in the other, because of his malice, his principle became equal to that of a venomous python. When dispositions are identical, so too are the forms.

The principle is uniform, and thus the phenomena are equal; the python and the tiger resemble one another. Yet, while one may undergo transformation quickly and the other slowly, this is merely a difference in intensity and pace.
Based on this, the doctrine of saṃsāra is beyond doubt. Since saṃsāra is certain, [the cycle of birth and death is established].
Then even my own selfhood will not escape [destruction]. Why is this? For wholesome states are difficult to ascend, while evil paths are easy to traverse.

At this very moment, greed, anger, poison, victory-seeking, hatred, jealousy, attachment, arrogance, delusion, conceit, fame-seeking, profit-seeking, killing, and lust—these minds manifest in every encounter and flow forth.
The commentary states that this is never-ending. Who is not marked by the appearance of a serpent or a python? All are causes for becoming a horse or a tiger.

Thus, these four limbs and nine apertures are but a temporary human body; beloved children and beautiful wives are but momentary kin. Once a single breath does not return, who among humans or things can distinguish them?
Even so, some remain complacent at the cauldron of Duke Yi, finding pleasure at the gate of Zhu Hai, exhausting the wealth of the four seas.

At banquets, tens of thousands of coins are squandered on food and drink; one may pride oneself on riding in a procession like those in the Qin palace or boasting of abundance like that in the state of Jin.
Yet I fear the sorrow of a broken heart will soon reach us; would it not be tragic, as Zhou Yong said, for "humanity to be no different from material things"?
Now, humans and other creatures are not distinct, yet there are three ways by which humans do not kill one another. The first is: [The provided text ends here.]

First, they do not dare; second, they cannot bear it; third, it is due to long-standing habituation. Among the people with horizontal eyes and among the houses of wandering knights-errant, there are none who do not wish to thrust their spearheads against those who differ from them or plunge blades into the chests of their enemies.
Yet, they fold their hands and fail to act, harboring their malice without being able to manifest it.
It is simply because the *Zhushu* (Bamboo Annals) is to be revered and the inscriptions on the tripods are to be heeded; this is what is meant by "daring not.

Although the Lord of Destiny holds exclusive power over life and death and the masters of execution possess the authority to inflict violence—such that their influence could allow them to act with cruelty and their strength could satisfy their hearts for vengeance—yet they hesitate and do not proceed with the imprisonment of a single man, nor do they remain at ease with the death of a single person.
This is simply because all those with round skulls and square feet share the same physical form, which stirs their compassion. Few...
To see a wife or an orphan staggering and stumbling is truly pitiable; this is what is called "incapacity for cruelty.

When one is both fearful of wrongdoing and incapable of cruelty, then the act of killing becomes exceedingly rare in the world. One may spend a lifetime without seeing the blood of the Wei River, or pass a year without hearing of the slaughter at Henan.
When a household makes it its custom and a generation brews it into a social wind, even medicinal [remedies]...
Sung’s followers brazenly provoked the impatient sovereign, while Ji Xu’s faction mistakenly offended the fierce empress;

yet they still held their staves without lowering them and gripped their swords without advancing, their wills cowed by the prospect of execution and their hands trembling at the brink of death—this is what is called the accumulation of habit.
When these three matters are maintained together, the people of this vast realm find a place to entrust their lives within them. As for other things, it is not so:
the occupation of the butcher does not escape prohibition until one reaches old age, and those who subsist on fresh meat do not avoid retribution even in the era of Yao and Shun.
The intent to kill blazes toward another body, while affectionate concern lies dormant toward one’s own form. This is due to the conditions of sound.

Karma is thus distinct from the physical body; therefore, though it may appear cruel or gracious, those who hear of it do not pity the flesh. Though one must repay debts, these are not shared by others;
thus, while there is neither stench nor rawness, those who eat find it most delicious. When that life is suddenly requited, the past cause is difficult to perceive;
when my enmity is just beginning to form, who knows of the future fruit? When both cause and effect vanish, the block and the blade [of slaughter] remain.
They practice mutual giving; yet they see and hear of killing without ceasing from their ears and eyes. They kill on their own and incite others to kill without interval throughout the seasons.

While the compassion of straining water for insects and protecting grasses is peerless among the clergy, and the goodness of [the sage] Gao Chai’s fortunate spiritual resonance is matchless among the laity, recent Confucians have taken fragments of our Way—such as the discourse on moderation in expenditure and rectitude—and have used them to permeate and influence [the people].

It drenches his ears and saturates his heart; thus, though a thousand species enter his chopsticks, he never shows a flicker of emotion, and though a hundred varieties fill his kitchen, he hardly gives them a thought.

While the ten thousand directions indulge in violence and the four classes of creatures have no means of appeal, the strong seize men to struggle for their own momentary lives, while the weak swallow their voices to fill the bellies of the myriad people. They do not depend on man...
Those that eat [meat] hide in the mountains and forests; they would rather suffer the bite of a great beast than face the twelvefold calamities that can be avoided by fleeing.
Those who must rely on humans for food are kept in pens and cages, awaiting the needs of the untimely moment, with not even a one-in-ten-thousand chance of escape.
Alas! A person of the Tang dynasty said: "What kindness is there in their living? What fault is there in their being killed? How can it be that such a decree has arrived?
This is the ultimate limit. Yet, as previously stated, how does the retribution of the netherworld differ from secular law?
While the latter may be somewhat lax, the former exceeds it ten thousandfold in cruelty. How could one willingly endure such suffering merely for the sake of speech?

Even if one were to say otherwise, one should still treasure compassion and cease killing, restrain craving and preserve benevolence; observing that those with different forms share the same nature within them, and contemplating that those who are distinct possess a common essence.

Beyond the physical body, once one has practiced this contemplation for a long time, the power of compassion will arise spontaneously. When one no longer even forms the thought of one's own son’s flesh, how could there be any distinction between self and others?
As for those driven by habitual tendencies, these must be especially refuted and broken down. In the customs of the base and wicked, daughters are not raised;
among the Qiang and Hu peoples, the same is true for sons. Such things are caused by accumulated habit, such that even the distinction between one's own flesh and bone disappears.

Thus, if one practices the mind of non-killing, even toward other beings there may be no killing; how much more so toward one's own child? Yet if one practices a mind of killing, even toward one's own child there may be killing;
what need is there to mention other beings? This habitual mind is the very root of karmic action. If you wish to eliminate killing, [you must first eliminate this habit].

First, one must illuminate one's habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Once the illuminating mind arises, accumulated habits will naturally be eliminated. As for the errors of the Confucians of recent times, they conceal their own minds while seeking what is "good";
yet it is easy to understand that Mencius spoke of "benefiting the people" and "loving all things," meaning only that there are degrees of intensity in their love.
If one were to kill or slaughter while still claiming it is an act of love, then one would be no different from the *rākṣasa* described in the Buddhist scriptures.
What is so different about the conduct of women? A rākṣasī woman who eats humans says, "I think of you; I eat you.

Is it the same as a husband who eats his wife saying he "thinks of her," or one who eats food saying he "loves it"? Or is it different? The principle of the Mean (Zhongzheng) takes the central axis as its guiding thread.
To seek it by following individual instances is to stray far from it; how much more so when one claims that "slight killing" constitutes the Mean—on what scripture is this based?

[The Master] Wen heard this and could do nothing but smile with amusement. When Zilu played the *se*, a murderous intent resounded upon the strings; Confucius rebuked him, and his disciples consequently ceased their veneration.
Since the beginning of time, has there ever been a sage whose murderous intent was not yet exhausted? Yet perverse doctrines have arisen crosswise, shackling our Great China.
The Great Hero (the Buddha) once said that in the age of the Final Dharma, the paths of demons will flourish; for the sake of the demons—
By the power [of these teachings], people are made unaware [of their own delusions]. Even the heterodox doctrines of today are easily understood;

yet, though the earth spans ten thousand *li* and time has passed through a thousand years, those who are intelligent and discerning have all followed the crowd, failing to awaken to the words of our Buddha. This proves that he did not deceive us.
Formerly, the Master Tao (Tao Hongjing) cultivated the quest for immortality for many years, yet the phoenixes and cranes remained nowhere to be seen, leaving his heart deeply skeptical.
On another day, his domestic attendant, who had previously ascended [to heaven], came to inform him, saying: "The Supreme Deity has inscribed your name upon the *Bencao* (Pharmacopoeia).
Because you used leeches as medicine, you have taken many lives; therefore, despite the fulfillment of your other practices, this shall serve as your retribution.

The Recluse then attained awakening and changed to using other medicinal prescriptions. Modern Confucian commentators of the classics have unfortunately lacked such divine-human admonitions, thereby causing the world...
Their doctrines are settled; all things are consigned to their fate. Crying out to Heaven, they are not heard; entering the earth, there is no opening.
In this world, few are the mentors like Mengsun; who can stir the grief of the solitary beast? Lacking a sovereign like Jie, who can resolve the resentment of the three sacrificial victims?
The mother sees her child die, and the child sees its mother perish. Some are whipped upon their hides before descending [to death]; some end their lives only after shedding milk. Or...
Facing imminent peril, they protect their pregnancy; some even risk death to follow after their young. To see them is to have one’s eyes filled with distress; to speak of it is to wound the heart.

Furthermore, following the prince’s hunting expeditions or the general’s pursuit of game, ten thousand carcasses are laid upon the sacrificial tables, and hundreds of species are torn from their herds.
A solitary hen coos at night, as if embracing the grief of the Yellow Crane; a lone pheasant cries out at dawn, as if transcribing the lament of Shangling.
Chirping and clamoring, solitary and forlorn—truly we know that the seven emotions are not confined to humans alone;
even the wriggling creatures share them in this way. If one reflects upon this, then the ten thousand things...
The habitual mind of a kalpa can be reduced to ashes in a single thought. Once the habitual mind is extinguished, both resentment and audacity vanish.
The three miserable realms are simultaneously broadened; things become like humans. Furthermore, taking the Mahāyāna as one’s heart, one treats others with urgency as if they were oneself.

One person tells a hundred, a hundred tell a thousand, and so on, spreading the word until it reaches the incalculable. Thus, the teaching of great compassion becomes clear to the world, after which [the barriers] are cast aside.

Though they fall into the void, they do not perish; though they descend into the abyss, they do not become rigid. Although their ways may seem as distant as the world beyond and their ascent to the nests of the mundane seems remote, those among beings who have escaped calamity are indeed many.
Alas! Since there is a fruit that must inevitably be requited for that, and a cause that must inevitably be produced by this, my words, though bitter, might yet turn your thoughts.
As for the doctrines of the nearby Confucians, let us not even discuss how they differ from those of Kong [Qiu].

Meng [the benevolent] is the reality of Confucius and Mengzi; yet our Buddha is thus, while Confucius and Mengzi are so—that is, one is the Jing River and the other the Wei River, clearly distinguished from one another.
When Yao and Wu lived in the same age, people surely turned to Yao; when Confucius and the Buddha were born together, how could one not turn to the Buddha?
This is why he reigns as king over the three realms, encompassing the great chiliocosm as the father of fathers and the mother of mothers for all beings.
Furthermore, in the past, Mozi advocated universal love (*jian'ai*), and some people criticized him. Mozi said: "Suppose there is a man of universal virtue here;
this man of universal virtue regards the parents of others as his own parents, and regards the wives and children of others as his own wives and children.
A partisan of partiality (*bie*) acts in the opposite way. Now I ask you: if you were traveling far away and had to entrust your wife and children to someone, whom would you entrust them to?"
"Is it universal, or do you rely on partiality? The man replied, "I rely on universality.
Mozi laughed and said, "You are currently relying on universality for your wife and children, yet you speak against universality; why is this?
Those who call killing 'just' and those who call refraining from killing 'excessive' are merely fortunate enough to be human beings. Were they to possess horns..."
They dwell there, clothed only in their fur and feathers. Their lives hang by a thread beneath the hooks and snares; their spirits wander within the range of Hou Yi’s bow.

Before them are spread the nets of Fu Xi, and behind them they are pursued by the arrows of Confucius. Although Tang the Successful was benevolent, he still tied his nets together; although Mencius was truly compassionate, [he could not save them].
Never having heard his voice before, at this moment the Great Awakened One, moved by compassion, suddenly appeared.

Upon seeing him, that man must have felt a mingling of sorrow and joy, turning to him for refuge with trembling devotion, like a frightened dove seeking rest beneath the sheltering shadow to still its agitation.

A dying sheep, clutching a blade and praying for a guest—how could it have the leisure to take up the remaining arguments of former scholars to compare the relative merits of Confucius and the Buddha? (Tongyi)
Zhao Fangu, whose courtesy name was Huanguang, was a native of Taicang. His family was wealthy, and in his youth he was ostentatious and self-satisfied.

In middle age, however, he humbled himself to devote himself to study. He resided at Hanshan, where he built a cottage beside his parents’ tomb; he diverted springs and carved out rocks to construct a secluded dwelling.
In his daily life, he had always honored the Buddha and abstained from eating meat; even when guests arrived, he would provide only fruits and vegetables.
Even toward those of great wealth and status, he would insist that they eat them, saying, "One must not fail to let them know this flavor. Later, he fell ill, and some said he ought to eat meat.
"It is not so; the illness is both swift and severe. He replied, "If the illness were slight, would it be necessary to break the precepts?

Even if it should become more severe, it is merely approaching the path of return. Once one breaks the precepts, one departs forever burdened by karma; can regret then be pursued? Afterward, the illness also subsided.

There was a guest who had been stung by a millipede. He killed it, saying, "I repay resentment with straightforwardness. Fanfu said, "That is not so. It would be straightforward only if he did not kill it.
Since the millipede is insentient, there is truly nothing for which it can be resentful or angry; yet he kills it—can this be called straightforwardness?
Once, while traveling with a guest, they encountered two men driving six pigs toward a slaughterhouse. Fanfu recited the name of Amitābha for them.

The Buddha said, "One guest praised it as good. The ordinary person said, "In my recitation of the Buddha’s name, the merit of delivering six pigs is slight, whereas the merit of delivering two people is great.

Why is this? These pigs are now heading to the slaughterhouse; they will suffer the pain of a single blade and, once that debt is repaid, with every step thereafter they will proceed toward a land of bliss.
Yet for that pig-slaughterer, he drives the pigs one step forward while carving them with a blade; step by step, his mind is fixed on the act."
One takes steps toward creating the karma for hell; entering the realm of suffering, one remains complacent and fails to perceive the alarm or fear.
Is this not pitiable? Furthermore, I once exhorted an elderly man to abstain from meat. The old man said, "I am advanced in years and cannot do without the sustenance of meat.
I replied, "If even an old man cherishes his life, how can you find peace in your heart when the flesh of those who are not yet old is first subjected to the knife and the block?"
While not yet dead, he guarded against death; how could his heart find peace as he greedily swallowed and chewed the flesh of those who had suffered such a cruel end?

He composed a work titled "The Chapter on Protecting Life" (*Hushengpin*), widely exhorting the people of the world to cease eating meat. His words were profoundly poignant. During the Tianqi era, he passed away at Hanshan.
His wife, Lady Lu, styled Qingzi, lived in seclusion together with this ordinary man; she was capable of composing poetry and prose (Suzhou Prefecture Gazetteer, Section on Protecting Life).
Liu Yushou, styled Xuan, was a native of Changzhou. He was a *zhusheng* (junior scholar) and a friend of Yao Mengchang.

Having turned his heart toward the Great Dharma, they both maintained the *Buddhamātṛcundīdhāraṇī*. When he was about to go to the provincial examination, he established an altar and recited the mantra for seven days.

Upon entering the examination hall, bees swarmed around the tip of his brush as his thoughts gushed forth like a spring; he subsequently achieved distinction and passed the jinshi examination in the thirty-fifth year of the Wanli era.
He served as a Professor at Luling. Later, while responding to an invitation to serve as a provincial examiner for Yunnan, he stayed overnight at Xiasi Station.
There, he dreamed of a magnificent man, dark and tall with a prominent beak, who bowed to him and sat down, saying: "I..."

There was also General Cao Han of the Song dynasty. In the past, when the imperial army conquered Jiangzhou, he was filled with indignation that its defenders would not surrender and slaughtered the entire population.
Consequently, he received retribution by being reborn as a pig, paying back for those killed one head at a time; this has continued until now, and his suffering remains inexhaustible.
"In former days, I was fortunate to receive your compassionate care and was granted a second life. Yesterday, moreover, I repaid a debt owed by a person from a nearby district.
I never expected to encounter you here today. Having said this, he wept. He continued, "When I lived at home with Lady Yu, I had a slave who went to the countryside to collect rents.
He returned with a pig. At night, he dreamed of someone begging for its life; he kept the animal until it died. This is precisely what happened. Having finished speaking, he spoke again.

He said, "I was a minor official during the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty. I listened to a Dharma Master recite the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* and personally provided him with offerings.
Consequently, for life after life, I attained office and held high rank; yet when my retribution was exhausted, I fell into this great evil.
What more can be said? From now on, I beg you, sir: whenever you encounter people like us, whether they are to be bound and imprisoned or slaughtered..."
I shall sever [this connection]. By reciting the Cundī-dhāraṇī and the names of the Buddhas of the Western Quarter, may I be granted a temporary respite from this suffering.
Should I, through the power of these merits, escape this retribution of suffering and be reborn among humans, I vow never again to commit evil deeds so as not to betray you.
Yu Shou said, "This has been my long-held aspiration. The man bowed in thanks and departed. Previously, Yu Shou had once organized a *fangsheng* (releasing living beings) assembly;
thereafter, wherever he went, he invariably saved a pig. Later, while serving as the Magistrate of Wuhu, he kept two pigs in the official stables.
When his daughter was about to be married off, she dreamed that she accompanied her parents to perform Buddhist rites. Beneath the Buddha altar, she saw two people crouching there.

He asked, "Who are you? They replied, "We are two pigs from the government office. Because we had once heard the Mahāyāna sūtras in a previous life, we were granted the opportunity to see the light of day again;
thus, we have come to express our gratitude. The girl was startled and attained a sudden realization, whereupon she vowed never to kill living beings.

She requested her father to continue holding assemblies for the release of captive animals. Liu Youshou composed a preface for the occasion to promote the practice. During the Tianqi era, Liu Youshou held official office.

Yùshòu served as the Vice Commissioner for Education in Guizhou. When Ānbāngyàn rebelled and Guiyang was besieged, Yùshòu, along with the former Provincial Governor Lǐ Qián and the Surveillance Commissioner Shǐ Wǎng'ān, divided the city walls to defend them.
For nearly a year, their provisions were exhausted and the local population had died out almost entirely. Nevertheless, Yùshòu held his post with increasing vigor.
When the rebels attempted to scale the ramparts, they suddenly retreated twice on their own; those who fell from the ladders died without number.
[The siege] was calculated [to end]; when reinforcements arrived, it was finally lifted. His merits were recorded and he was promoted to the rank of Vice-Governor of Ningxia.
He retired from official service and returned home, passing away as a *dhūta* (ascetic). From Yushou onward, the practice of reciting the *Cundī-dhāraṇī* was propagated within the local community.
Among the scholars who followed thereafter were Yang Zicheng and his two sons, Weidou and Gonggan; Li Zimou; Xu Jiuyi; Liu Gongdan; and Yao Wen.

In the beginning, the worthies all established a Guanyin (Cundī) society. They selected the site of the former ruins of the Peach Blossom Grove and the Peach Blossom Hermitage to clear a vihāra for the cultivation of pure karma.
Zi Cheng, styled Dayin, was a gentleman of earnest practice who passed away as a student.
Weidou, styled Tingshu, sat for the provincial examination in Yingtian. Jiuyi, styled Qian, served as Assistant Director of the Imperial Library. Gongdan, styled Shu, by... [text ends]
The Jinshi was appointed to Nanchang County, but before he could take up his post, he encountered the fall of the Ming dynasty; all three men subsequently perished for their country.

Gongdan, whose name was Tingzhen, was also a student of the classics who possessed a pure and transcendent character; he died prematurely in his middle years, much to the regret of the scholarly community.
Wenchu, whose name was Zongdian, was the eldest son of Meng; as a student, he was recommended to the Imperial Academy. Zimu, whose name was Mo, held office... [text ends]...
The Censor [Yao Zongdian] retired from public life following the dynastic change.

Together with Wenchu, he founded the Shangshan Society, where he extensively gathered both monastics and laypeople to cultivate the pure practices of the Western Paradise until his old age (*Hanshan Mengyou Ji*; *Ming Shi*; "Stele for Zhunti Monastery" by Yao Zongdian; *Guangren Pin*).
Zhiguizi said: "When I read the book of Mencius, I felt a sense of earnest concern. He exhorted the sovereign of his time to extend his heart of non-cruelty so as to save life and cease killing.
Yet the sovereign ultimately refused to employ these teachings, leading to the ultimate tragedy of the Warring States period—the horrors of mass executions and slaughter.

The people were treated like dogs, pigs, chickens, and ducks. How lamentable! Subsequently, I read the Buddhist scriptures, investigating the source of cause and effect and examining the cycle of rebirth."

This is the root of my transformation. Repeatedly reflecting and contemplating deeply, I have severed my doubts and given rise to faith. Fortunately, we now enjoy the peace of a great era, and the people are happy and healthy;
yet, among the multitudes of beasts, birds, fish, and shell-dwellers, not a single day has passed without them suffering the bitterness of warring states.

Having recently read the writings of Zeng Du-fu, I was moved to deep sorrow in my heart. Consequently, I have compiled the accounts of the two masters Zhao and Liu and composed this biography for them. As the Sūtras say:
The Bodhisattva acted as a great king and, possessing mastery over the Dharma, universally practiced its teachings.
He issued commands throughout the cities, towns, and villages within Jambudvīpa to prohibit all acts of slaughter and to ensure that all beings constantly abide in the three types of pure precepts.

He likewise caused sentient beings to abide in this manner. How magnificent is this wind of benevolence and compassion! Since the advent of written records, there has never been anyone capable of [achieving such a thing].

This is one who has personally experienced its full intensity. Disorder and order revolve in cycles; grievances and retributions follow one another in turn. Calamity arises from what one has done oneself; karma does not come from without.
As the shrouds of affliction grow ever heavier, merit and wisdom become ever more diminished. Even were a Bodhisattva to manifest in person, there would be nothing that could be done about it.
May the gentlemen of later generations examine the past and discern the future; with a single thought of faith, may they forever sever the karma of killing.

May they give rise to a pure mind and form bonds of joy, compassionately protecting all sentient beings—whether of their own kind or another, whether animate or inanimate—and thereby bring about great benefit.
The merit of this act is inconceivable. May the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, dragons, and devas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges bear witness that these words are true and not false.
Luotaisan said: "The Buddha-mind and the divine eye may be subtle and profound, yet they still possess the affinity of a needle and a magnet. I pray—"
Life after life, from age to age, may I follow and never leave the man who knows the way home.
When you serve as Minister of Works, I shall be the Minister of Agriculture; when you compose verses on protecting living beings, I shall become a vajra-pestle.
Should we encounter demons or heretics who slander us, I shall fly up and strike down their teeth so that they cannot speak.
Biographies of Eminent Laymen, Volume 48:
Wang Dingzhu, Zhu Zhuanghuang, Wenhuang, Qianwen, Wuwang, Chenluo, Chengzhuan, Wang Mengsu.
Wang Mengsu’s name was originally Gong. He was a native of Kunshan in Jiangnan. In the twenty-second year of the Wanli era, he passed the provincial examination.

He paid his respects to Master Hong of Yunqi and declared himself a disciple. Subsequently, he served as the magistrate of Gaoyuan. While in office, he daily worshipped the Great Being of Universal Gate (Avalokiteśvara) and recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

During severe droughts, his prayers made while standing in the open air were immediately answered with rain. Whenever a famine struck, he would exert all his efforts to petition for relief on behalf of the people.

On occasions when there were cases of wrongful imprisonment that had already been finalized by legal verdict, he would invariably burn incense and appeal to Heaven, vowing to bring about their exoneration.
Xuě. Shàngguān also showed understanding and followed his lead. Xuě was subsequently appointed as a Vice Governor of Jǐnán.

Employing military tactics, he disciplined the officials and soldiers to pursue the powerful, the arrogant, and the bandits who plundered on horseback. He impaled their bones upon poles in the streets and displayed their corpses within tiger dens.
Far and near, all were brought to submission. One night, he instructed his subordinates to pack their belongings, submitted his resignation, and departed, passing through Wúmén.
He did not return home, but traveled between Jingshan, Tianmu, and Shiyu. He traveled up the Yangtze River into Sichuan, visited Mount Emei, Mount Kuanglu, and Mount Boshan before returning.
There, he took Chan masters Hanshan Deqing and Wengu as his teachers and friends, as well as the layman Zhu Baimin.
He read the Tripitaka and practiced the Samādhi of Buddha-recitation. In the seventh year of the Tiantqi era, he moved to Shifeng in Haiyan.
At the Buddhist temple, the eunuch Wei Zhongxian was at that time exerting his power and plotting a usurpation. Meng Su said to his disciples, "This place borders the sea to the north;
if one arrives at dawn, one shall worship here at dawn; if one arrives at dusk, one shall worship here at dusk.

Subsequently, he contracted a disease of the spleen and said with a smile, "It is well; let there be no burial in the belly of a fish. At midnight, he sat in the lotus position and passed away. (From *Mingwen Ouchao*)
(Yunqi Fahui). Ding Jianhong, whose courtesy name was Mingdeng, was a native of Jiangpu. During the Wanli era, he received the Three Refuges from Yunqi and styled himself Lianlü (Lotus Companion).
In the forty-fourth year [of the Wanli reign], he passed the jinshi examination and served as a District Magistrate of Quanzhou before being promoted to the post of Prefectural Governor of Quzhou.

Wherever he went, he exhorted people to the Buddha-dharma. According to the Dharma, those who were subject to corporal punishment were permitted to redeem their sentences by offering rice to support the prison inmates.
During the summer months, he repaired the prison cells and provided the prisoners with *harsinghar* (Andropogon aciculatus) decoctions, chrysanthemum fans, and, in the winter, pepper and ginger.
He selected physicians to attend to the sick and gave each person a string of prayer beads, instructing them to recite the Buddha’s name. —Master Yunqi Hong.
He once remarked that his neighbor, an elderly man who regularly recited the Buddha’s name, passed away after requesting his friend Yi-qing (One Request) at the moment of death.
Consequently, he painted a portrait of Yi-qing and hung it in his hall of offerings to encourage himself. During the Chongzhen era, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from Da-hui.

In the winter of the second year of the Shunzhi era, his illness became critical; on the first day of the eleventh month, he prepared a formal petition to the Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, and burned [incense] daily.
On the tenth day, she consumed her gruel as usual. At that time, her face was radiant with a brilliant glow.
She exhorted all her relatives and friends to cultivate the practice of the Pure Land. Then, turning her body toward the pillow, she passed away (*Jingtu chenzhong*).

Zhu Baimin, whose given name was Lu, was a student at the local school in Wujiang. From his youth, he possessed brilliant talent; tall and standing like a jade pillar, his demeanor was serene and remote.
His family was poor, so he taught students to support his parents. He would always keep several dozen coins by his bedside, calling them "money for buying laughter.
After his parents died, he abandoned his status as a student to study the arts of longevity. He traveled far until he reached the Western Peak (Mount Hua), where he ascended to Heaven.
Jing (the Well). Huang Tan wore a Daoist robe and would lift his beard while letting out long, resonant sighs; those who saw him took him for an immortal.
Later, he went to visit Master Yunqi Hong to seek the essential points of the Dharma. After Master Hong passed away, Bai Min paid homage at the stupa and composed this verse:

"When I first visited the Master, I asked whether Chan meditation and the recitation of the Buddha's name could be integrated and practiced together. The Master answered spontaneously: 'If it is so...'"
These two things are used with such seamless integration—how joyful is this single phrase! It causes one’s heart and spirit to rejoice.

I raise it up for people from time to time, and it is proclaimed everywhere throughout all quarters. Those who practice the Buddha-remembrance are inexhaustible; the pointing finger is likewise inexhaustible. The assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa has not yet dispersed;
the tongue of the Lotus Pond remains long and alive. This short verse serves as an offering; may it be like a seamless stupa, joined together with the King.
Mengsu traveled to Mount Jing with [his companion] and established a studio there to reside in.

While reading the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he met Master Hanshan Deqing, and the two men together took him as their teacher. Master Deqing named Mengsu’s studio "Great Power" (*Dàlì*), while Mengsu named his own "Great Gold" (*Dàjīn*).
He named his pavilion "Prajñā" (Wisdom) and inscribed this eulogy upon it: "Alas for this pavilion! Its radiance penetrates through and beyond;
within and without are perfectly clear, entirely free from bondage and attachment. At the gates of the six sense faculties, all is perfectly interfused, vast and open.

Both the mundane and supramundane worlds are cast away at once. The flavor of this pavilion is tranquil and desolate; the master of this pavilion dwells in the joy of body and mind, transcending all worldly passions."
Dust. Like a great fire upon a tiny spark. He asked about this Dharma-gate, which is named "The Unspeakable. At the beginning of the Chongzhen era, he arrived at the capital.
When our troops drew near the city walls, some urged him to return home immediately. He sighed with resolve and said, "Am I not a subject of the King? How could I dare to flee?
He resided quietly at Longhua Temple, where he annotated the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Once the troops had retreated, he traveled south; wherever he went, he painted bamboo.

He sold his goods to support himself and would not accept a single coin from others unjustly. In his later years, he resided at the foot of Lotus Peak in Suzhou, where he practiced the *nien-fo* samādhi together with mountain monks.
He styled himself the Layman Xikong. At the age of eighty, he composed a verse for departing this world, bathed, changed his clothes, and passed away.
At that time, Lou Zirou (whose given name was Jian), a student from Jiaxing, also studied under Yunqi.

He received the precepts and observed the long fast (the eight-precept observance). He was skilled in calligraphy, particularly favoring the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* and the *Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching*, saying, "These are the *Analects* of the Buddha-dharma.
His surviving calligraphic works were widely transmitted and treasured throughout the world. (From the *Mingwen Ouchao*, *Yunqi Fahui*, *Wujiang Zhi*, and *Hanshan Mengyou Ji*).
Zhuang Pingshu, whose name was Yan, was a native of Huating. From his youth, he shared an exceptionally deep bond of affection with his elder brother.

When his brother fell ill while traveling as a guest in Qianzhong, Pingshu traveled on foot to meet him. On the way, their boat capsized, but they were miraculously saved; yet his brother ultimately died of the illness.

Pingshu escorted his brother’s remains back home, whereupon the local people held him in high esteem for this act. In his later years, he attained profound insight into the Buddha-dharma, and whenever he encountered anyone...

She constantly exhorted others with the Buddha-dharma. Whatever remained of her clothing and footwear she would always give away to others. She had one son and one son-in-law, whom she regarded with equanimity.
From time to time she composed poetry and short lyrics (*ci*), all of which were refined, remote, and full of resonance.

She often chanted a *man-ting-fang* (Manjushri’s Fragrance) ditty that went: "Sixty-odd years have passed in a mere moment; When the spring dream awakens, it is already over. The yellow millet is steaming..."
Flowers and phantoms—what excellent scenery there is! With a cold eye, one lightly pierces through the illusion; quickly turning over, one snaps the silken tether.

Let children and grandchildren perform their plays as they will; what need is there to see them to the end? A handful of thatch upon the green mountains—a livelihood for the remainder of life, to be arranged otherwise.
Simply follow conditions to pass the time: wash the bowl, burn incense, and first send the mind back to the ultimate.
He delighted in carefree wandering. How lamentable that even beneath the cool shade of jeweled trees, one must turn back to behold the vast and boundless ocean of karma.
He passed away in the fourth year of the Tianqi era at the garden of his friend Hu Zhihao.
Wang Ruosheng of Kunshan recorded his verses, considering him the foremost among the practitioners of the Way he had observed over several years. (Wang Ruosheng, He...)
[From the *Zhují*].
Huang Yuanfu, styled Chenghui, was a native of Qiantang, Zhejiang. By nature he was upright and did not conform to worldly ways.

He could not manage the affairs of farming or production, yet he served his paternal grandmother and mother with complete filial piety. He delighted in giving alms; whenever a neighbor lacked clothing in the cold, he would take off his own garments to give them.
He clothed him. To those who had no food, he gave whatever money was in his own bag.
When his wife’s brother heard that his son had become so exceptionally austere, he led him to Master Hong at Yunqi, where he met him with the etiquette of a disciple. Master Hong named him Jingming.
Thereafter, he contracted a disease that caused him to vomit blood. For three years it persisted without remission and grew increasingly severe. Ziyu instructed him to recite the Buddha’s name.

Yuanfu was so tormented by his pain that he could not concentrate. Ziyu said in a stern voice, "When your visual consciousness falls to the ground, where will that which currently experiences this pain ultimately reside?
Yuanfu was struck with alarm and asked, "What shall I do? Ziyu replied, "Nothing is better than..."
When they were reciting the Buddha's name, Yuánfú asked, "Are you teaching me to recite the Amitābha of self-nature, or the Amitābha of Sukhāvatī?
Zǐyǔ replied, "Do you suppose there are two? Yuánfú suddenly attained realization and invited the Dharma Master Huìwén to come.

He set up an image of the Buddha and explained the causes and conditions of the Pure Land to him. Yuánfú joyfully requested the Dharma Master to shave his head and confer upon him the śrāmaṇera precepts.
He secluded himself from his family and chanted the name of the Buddha while silently reciting the Lotus Sūtra for seven days. All the family members smelled the fragrance of the lotus.
Suddenly, [Yuánfú] smiled and spoke this verse: "Not a single thing is brought here; not a single thing is taken away. High...
"A single autumn moon atop the mountain peak—this is the original, true meaning.

Thereupon, he instructed his family to prepare a vegetarian feast to offer to the Buddha and invite monks to chant the Buddha’s name and recite the *Vow Text of Yunqi*. When the text reached the passage, "Amitābha Buddha emits light to welcome and guide us;
He lowers His hand to lead us," he rose from his seat with joy, gazed intently at the Buddha image, and passed away (from the *Hanshan Mengyou Ji*).
I have heard that you bear the Dharma name Dasheng and are a fellow villager of Yuanfu. From your youth, you were prone to illness;

with the resolve to transcend birth and death, you went to Yunqi to receive the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-Recitation method. After Master Hongguang passed away, Master Hanshan Qing came to offer his condolences.
Ziyu performed a prostration and said, "I wish to shave my head and become your disciple. Master Qing said, "The Buddha-nature cannot be constrained by the four great elements;
how could mere hair and skin pose an obstacle? Furthermore, you have parents living; this is not yet permissible. Ziyu then desisted. Shortly thereafter, he fell ill.
Ziyu said, "I shall go straight to the Western Land; this illness will not harm me. When [the time came],...
His illness was severe; his spirit and consciousness were clouded and confused, and he could not support himself. He was greatly terrified and urgently ordered his family to invite a monk.
After chanting the Buddha’s name for more than a day, his confusion remained as before. Suddenly, with a start, he said: "The root and trunk of birth and death cannot be uprooted by another.
He immediately rose, washed himself, and put on his robes. Facing the Buddha, he burned incense and offered his arm in fervent, sorrowful repentance.
He sat through the entire night without the slightest weariness. Upon returning to his seat, his spirit and mind were settled and tranquil, and the Pure Land appeared before him.
He then shaved his head, donned the *kāṣāya*, and passed away apart from the assembly. Hearing of this, Master Hanshan Qing sighed and said: "How brave!
To hear of such a birth can truly be called a heroic and magnificent feat" (*Hanshan Mengyou Ji*).

Huang Ziyu, whose courtesy name was Yisheng, was a native of Taicang. He had long been devoted to the teachings of Yunqi and, together with his wife, Lady Wang, diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice.
In the Chongzhen era, he was recommended for office and appointed as the Magistrate of Xindu in Sichuan.

He would often provide meals for monks in the magistrate’s hall, personally serving them with chopsticks and distributing alms, followed by prostrations. When Zhang Xianzhong’s rebel forces invaded Sichuan and passed through Xindu...
Du Ziyu led the people to fortify Xindu. A thousand monks, moved by Ziyu’s virtue, led one another up the city walls to beat drums and chant the names of the Buddha.
In the middle of the night, the sound shook the heavens. The rebels soon withdrew. For his merit in defending the city, he was promoted to the post of Governor of Jizhou.
When the Ming dynasty fell, he resigned his office and returned to Yinxi. The pavilion where he lived was called the Lianrei Pavilion; he styled himself "Lian" (Lotus).
The Layman Rui organized a vegetarian feast to honor the Buddha, daily reciting the Buddha’s name tens of thousands of times.

Later, having been bedridden with illness for over a month, he personally prepared his final instructions and had images of Amitābha hung on all four walls. He invited Master Xian of Huishan to bestow upon him the Bodhisattva precepts. Addressing Master Xian, he said:
"My spirit and faculties have become even stronger, and my vows have become even firmer; I am confident that my rebirth in the Western Paradise is certain. At dawn the following morning...
Master Xian was about to depart; he had fixed the eighth day as the date for his departure, and it turned out exactly so.
He was sixty-four years old (*Xianguo suilu*, *Mingwen oucao*).
Qian Bo-yun, whose given name was Bing, was also a native of Taicang. He was a man of pure and virtuous character who, having been selected as a tribute scholar, was appointed as a local educator.

At the age of over seventy, he was transferred to serve as the magistrate of Fuyang County. One day, while interrogating a major thief, the thief falsely claimed he had been falsely accused and begged for leniency.
Bo-yun said, "You have killed many people; by law, you deserve the death penalty. The thief sprang up, seized a inkstone from the desk, and hurled it [at him].
Boyun collapsed in pain to the ground. The officials rushed forward, seized the thief, and beat him. Boyun suddenly rose and sat up;

with one hand he rubbed his chest and with the other he stopped the officials, saying, "Do not strike me, do not strike me! My pain has ceased. Those who heard this spread the story and laughed at it.
Later, after leaving office and returning home, he devoted himself to spiritual practice, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day. At the time of his death, he composed a self-...

After reciting the funeral liturgy and verses, he recently ordered his attendants to fetch "cooling water" for him to drink. When asked where the cooling water was, they replied, "It is the water from the pond for releasing living beings.
Once the water arrived, he drank it and, joining his palms, said, "By the power of the Buddha, I shall go directly to the Pure Land.
He then sat peacefully and passed away (*Xianguo suilu*).
Wu Zhanlou’s name has been lost, though he was also a native of Taicang. He cultivated the practices of the Pure Land from an early age;

later, having entrusted his household affairs to his two sons, he set his mind solely on proceeding toward the West. Each day he recited the Buddha’s name ten thousand times, while simultaneously practicing the visualization of the Western Paradise, never mixing in other activities.
For twelve years, he practiced as if it were but a single day. Within his room, auspicious signs appeared repeatedly, and white lotus flowers welled up before his bed.
It was as large as a mortar. Children all saw it. At over seventy years of age, he passed away while sitting peacefully.
His descendants have continued their family tradition by serving the Buddha (from the *Xianguo suilu*).
Wang Xianmin, whose original name was Chun, was a native of Yangzhou. He was bold and unrestrained by nature and skilled in archery.

He traveled to Chang’an with his paternal uncle, bringing along singing girls and spending his days intoxicated in the market pavilions. One day, he suddenly burst into the military training grounds just as a grand review was underway.

Xianmin drew his bow and loosed arrows that pierced the targets one after another; he then drew two swords and danced, moving with a suddenness like a crashing thunderclap. The general descended from the steps and seized him.
He wished to raise his hand to crown him [as the victor], but [the other] laughed and declined, saying, "My family has been of the Confucian scholar class; I was merely jesting with you.

Upon returning home, his parents betrothed him to a wife, but he declined on the grounds of physical frailty. He arranged for his two younger brothers to take wives, and subsequently withdrew from society to travel extensively through the mountains and waters of Wu and Yue.
There he attended upon Chan Master Yiyu, received the Upāsaka precepts, and while dwelling in the mountains, recited the Lotus Sūtra daily.
After this, he returned to Ciyun Hermitage in Yangzhou, where he devoted himself to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. He named his dwelling "Abode of Precious Blooms" (Baoruqi).
Knowing that the time had come, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away while monks chanted the Buddha’s name around him (from *Mingwen oucao*).
Chen Yongzhuo, whose courtesy name was Zhishan, was a native of Changshu. As a child, whenever he heard his grandmother reciting the names of the Buddhas, his crying would immediately cease.

Later, when he entered the village school and read the *Analects*, reaching the passage, "If one hears the Way in the morning, it is fitting to die in the evening," he went home and asked his mother, "When a person dies, where do they go?
His mother could not answer him. He told his father about this, who asked, "What is your own view on this? Yongzhuo replied, "I wish..."
"Knowing the nature of birth and death, will he not surely hear the Way? His father said, "This child will certainly enter the Dharma of Non-arising in the future.
When he grew up, he heard of the reputation of Yunqi and admired it; he devoted himself earnestly to the practice of Pure Land. There was a Master Ji who had inherited the Dharma of Yunqi.
Subsequently, he settled in a thatched hut by the Tengtī River. Using his own modest means, Yongzhuo initiated a fundraising campaign to construct a Chan temple.

The local gentry of the county established a society for the release of living beings (*fangsheng she*) and requested that Yongzhuo preside over it; he regularly supplemented their expenses with his private funds. The number of creatures released was beyond measure.
One day, Master Ji dreamed that Yongzhuo, dressed in black robes and tied with a yellow sash, smiled as he bid him farewell. Startled, he rushed out to see.
When he saw that his methods were ineffective, he began reciting the Buddha’s name. He passed away reclining on his right side (according to the *Changshu Zhi*).
Luo Jianming, whose courtesy name was Leihai, was a native of Huiyang. During the Chongzhen era, he passed the provincial examination and served as the District Schoolmaster of Teng County.

He was appointed as a Secretariat Drafter (Zhongshu Sheren). He studied the teachings of Huashou and devoted his mind to the purification of his karma. Initially, he served his parents with filial piety;

when his father fell ill, he was moved by a supernatural being who bestowed medicine upon him, and the father recovered. When his mother fell ill, he invoked the deities, requesting that his own lifespan be shortened to benefit her;

she recovered the following morning. After the fall of the Ming dynasty, he lived as a private citizen, closing his door to the world. He took up the classic texts to teach others, seeking only to guide people toward goodness.
Mr. Luo was humble, retiring, harmonious, and respectful; he never uttered a word that exceeded propriety, nor did he ever have anything that could not be told to others.
Regardless of whether people were noble or lowly, worthy or unworthy, there were none who did not praise Mr. Luo as a man of great character.
A villager named Tao Ruoyao died and then revived, saying that in the underworld he was being supervised in the construction of a "Good Bridge," which was for the sake of Luo Minglei.

Jian also had a grove that was particularly tall; he once went into it until midday before returning and said, "I have just witnessed the thundering of a raven and the construction of a locust tree pavilion.
His wife, Lady Deng, was also devoted to the recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha. One day, she lit a one-foot-long incense stick in the burner;
when the flame was spent, the ash remained unbroken. The fire then traveled backward up the stick to its tip, where the ash vanished and it turned crimson—a manifestation of her spiritual excellence.
Thus [ends] the "Mingwen Ouchao" (Extracts of Illustrious Writings).
Cheng Jiqing, whose secular name was Wenji and Dharma name was Tonghui, was a native of Xin’an. He moved to Huzhou to spend his final years there.
He once studied at Mount Tianmu and visited the stupa of Chan Master Gaofeng; overcome with emotion, he wept uncontrollably and cut flesh from his own arm as an offering. Thereupon—
He vowed to investigate the Way with single-minded resolve and paid homage to Chan Master Xueqiao. After a long period of intense pressure and rigorous inquiry, he gradually gained some insight.
Later, he visited Chan Master Wuyi of Boshan, who held him in high esteem; upon his departure, the Master walked five li to see him off.

Ji Qing often reflected that in this degenerate age, those in the Chan school who do not penetrate the principles of the teachings are like the blind without a guide, falling into the dark pit and unable to emerge.
Feeling deep pity for himself, he established a lecture society at Lianju (Lotus Dwelling) with a term of six years.

He invited ten Dharma masters to ascend the seat in succession to expound various Mahāyāna sūtras. Furthermore, he extended an invitation to the Dharma master Ziping to his chamber in Gucheng, where they again expounded the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
During the intervals between sessions, Jiqing withdrew to reflect deeply, gradually attaining a mastery of the essential principles of the Ci'en school.

In his daily life, he frequently read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*, weeping as his voice rose with emotion. He styled himself the "Gentleman of the Ten Vows" (*Shiyuan Jushi*).
Whenever there were assemblies in the village for releasing captive animals, delivering ghosts, performing repentance rituals, or chanting scriptures, Ji Qing invariably served as their leader.
His friend Qian Yuan-chong lost his son. Ji Qing gave him the Great Xing Temple for this purpose, at a cost of three hundred thousand *jin* of gold.
When Yuan-chong passed away, Ji Qing also lost his own son; he then shut his door and declined visitors, devoting himself exclusively to the visualization of a sixteen-foot Buddha image.
At first, it was obscure, but gradually it began to appear faintly, though its color was very dark. While he was concentrating his thoughts, suddenly it became empty.
Within this, there was a verbal instruction that said: "If you wish to see the golden body, you must first form the mental image of the Buddha's body as being red.

If you practice visualization according to this instruction, you will indeed see the Buddha's body with its radiance penetrating in all four directions, such that all the household articles within the room become golden."
His wife was Lady Lu, whose Dharma name was Zhifu. She was benevolent and fond of giving, observed the long fast, and daily recited the names of the Buddhas twenty or thirty thousand times.
At the age of thirty-nine, she fell ill and invited the Venerable Master Gu to confer the five precepts upon her. The Master then expounded for her the essential teachings of the Pure Land.
Thereupon, she set her mind solely on returning to the West. Later, Qing also recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for her until they reached the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter.

"O being, you shall be assailed by ghostly copper dogs; you shall be pierced by swords and blades; you shall be oppressed by fire yourself.

Considering what these two men have related, the principle of retribution for good and evil is inherently natural; there is nothing in it to be wondered at. [Poem]
It says: "I look upon your dreamy confusion; my heart is filled with sorrow. And it further says: "Why do you not stand in awe? Do you not stand in awe of Heaven? Alas!

One part of luminosity gains one part of the power of reciting the Buddha's name; one part of fragrance and purity gains one part of the power of reciting the Buddha's name.
When the entire interior of the body becomes luminous and the entire interior of the body becomes fragrant and pure, this..."
This is precisely the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Yet nowadays, people desire it to be long or short;
they muddle their inner being until it is pitch black and foul-smelling within. If one’s entire being becomes so black and stinking, this is hell;
even a Buddha cannot save such a person.

Biographies of Cai, Liu, San, and Huang.
Cai Weili, whose courtesy name was Maode, was a native of Kunshan in Suzhou. His grandmother, Lady Shen, had cultivated the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. One day...
He took leave of all his relatives and neighbors and passed away without illness; even as he drew his last breath, the sound of his recitation of the Buddha’s name did not cease.

His father was Yunzhong, a man of charity and kindness who possessed noble integrity and observed the Buddhist precepts. His mother was Lady Xu, who maintained a lifelong vegetarian fast for sixty years.

At over seventy years of age, he suddenly became able to read characters and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily. Wei Li had been fond of the writings of Wang Shizhen (Prince Yangming) since his youth.
In the forty-seventh year of the Wanli era, he passed the jinshi examination and was appointed as a District Magistrate of Hangzhou. He was subsequently promoted to Director of the Bureau of Rites.
At the beginning of the Chongzhen era, he served as Director of the Ministry of Rites and was then dispatched as Vice Commissioner for Education in Jiangxi, where he elucidated [the teachings].

The School of Innate Awareness (Liangzhi) is particularly rigorous in distinguishing between the good and the beneficial, establishing it as the code of conduct for the Gate of Sages to bind and exhort its students.
He was appointed as Right Vice-Governor of Zhejiang, assigned to oversee the regions of Jiaxing and Huzhou, but resigned his office due to the mourning for his mother.

While living at home, he traveled to Dengwei Mountain, where he attained realization upon meeting Master Cang of Sanfeng. He composed a verse on "Three Blows of the Staff," which says: "It turns out that the Buddha-dharma has nothing much to it."
"Son, three blows and three punches are already quite a lot. If you were to awaken right now, I would give you but one slap.

You have erred by going to Gaoyuan to study with that old woman. He once established a secret society with the worthies Jin Zhengxi, Huang Yuangong, Qian Qizhong, and Xiao Shiwei to investigate the Great Matter.
Whenever he spoke, he said that many practitioners fear the dark, vast expanse after death; he did not.
People know that the vast, dark earth before them is more painful, and they speak entirely of the great magnitude of birth and death;

yet they do not realize that the moment-to-moment cycle of birth and death right before their eyes is even more urgent. At this critical juncture, there is a single blow upon a heavy barrier—how can one apply oneself to it? Those who heard this were struck with awe.
Upon the completion of his mourning period, he was appointed as the Military Commissioner for Jingxing, and subsequently served in Ningyuan and Jinan. In the fourteenth year of the Chongzhen era...

He was appointed as the Provincial Governor of Shanxi. Wei Li served his official duties with integrity and frugality; he possessed the ability to discern the talents of others and fully utilized their strengths.
Being well-versed in military affairs, he repeatedly quelled violent bandits. When discussing governance before the Emperor, he held that the Great Learning (*Daxue*) must come first, stating:

"Since scholars have failed to clarify the study of the mind, they have clung to single doctrines and considered themselves correct, thereby frequently falling into partiality and factionalism, unaware of the Great Mean and Ultimate Rectitude."
This is the way through which disorder arises. When he was about to depart for Shanxi, the Emperor asked how he would govern the suppression of bandits.
He replied, "The rise of banditry stems entirely from the destitution of the people. In my capacity as a pacifier, I shall ensure that the impoverished have food to eat.

However, to love the people, one must first examine the officials; to examine the officials, nothing is more important than examining oneself. I wish to rectify myself and lead those under my charge."
To ensure that the people do not turn to theft, yet for me as a minister there is no visible merit;
I do not wish to harm the common people in order to achieve fame for myself alone. While serving in office, he wrote a letter to his nephew Fang Xian, exhorting him to study the Way, saying:
"My nephew has undergone great calamities and experienced every kind of suffering. Amidst this, you must find a way to turn over a new leaf and breathe freely. Thus he set forth.
Every step is a true site of enlightenment; every movement is the precious sword that slays demons.
Now, as your field of vision gradually opens and your inner mind gradually expands, you will find within all sufferings a place to settle yourself and establish your life.
Yet, if you hold fast to a lapis lazuli flask and sit fixedly within a nest of ease, unable to move, this too is a realm of suffering. My nephew, at the moment when fatigue has just subsided—
When walking leisurely across the courtyard, or when just beginning to wake upon my pillow at the fifth watch, I suddenly awaken with a start. This state must be clearly known by oneself;

it is not something that can be explained to others. It was only after I reached the age of thirty that I gained a rough understanding of faith and aspiration, yet I have not yet undergone the great forging of the furnace.
Thus, I have been unable to enter or exit directly within the field of birth and death. Nevertheless, I rely upon these various sufferings...

The objective realm is my place of practice; indeed, I dare not let even a single step pass by in negligence. Within this region, there is no one else to support the cause alone, leaving me to shoulder it with my own strength.

Furthermore, fame and achievement have long been cast aside, and matters of life and death are likewise clear to me. My only fear is that I might err in the affairs of the borderlands and thus fail upward toward the sagely wisdom of the Emperor—how could such a thing be?

Nevertheless, I swear by my own death that I shall... [my] self... (Note: The original text appears to be a fragmentary draft or a note containing personal reflections on duty, spiritual practice, and loyalty. The final clause "則吾" suggests an intended continuation regarding a vow or commitment.)
This was his final act. In the sixteenth year, when rebel bandits overran Shaanxi, Wei Li alone led three thousand soldiers to resist them at the river.

While he was in command, the Surveillance Commissioner Wang Zongyou impeached Wei Li for being improper to return to Taiyuan. Consequently, Wei Li was relieved of his post and ordered to undergo investigation.

Bao Cheng defended the city, killing a great many enemies. When the city fell, he faced north, performed two prostrations, and handed his final memorial to a messenger.

He then went to Sanli Temple and hanged himself. During the reign of the Prince of Fu, he was posthumously honored with the title Zhongxiang (from *Mingwen Ocao*, *Sanfeng Dengshi*, and *Zhongxiang Yigao*).
Liu Changqian, whose courtesy name was Daozhen and also known as Jibin, was a native of Qiongzhou in Sichuan. In his youth, he was well-versed in the classical arts and passed the local examinations.
One day, while passing by a shrine to Mount Yue, he encountered the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* and experienced a profound awakening. Thereupon, he placed his faith in the Chan school.

Subsequently, having encountered successive sorrows and calamities, he resolved his mind solely upon Chan meditation. Taking the two records of Dahui and Zhongfeng as his guide, he constantly exerted himself with self-urgency.
Whenever he reached the point where the path of words was cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceased, it was as if silver mountains and iron walls stood before his eyes;
yet he never relaxed his effort. This continued for eighteen years. In the fourth year of the Chongzhen era, after failing the examinations, he traveled south. Upon arriving at...
In Nanjing, he met a monk who had come from An-yin Temple in Hangzhou and obtained the *Recorded Sayings* of Master Sanfeng Zang.

Upon reading it, he sighed in admiration, saying, "How is it that in this degenerate age I have encountered such a Dharma-treasure? He then hurried to Wu Gate to pay his respects to Master Dingmu Che.
He questioned Master Shicheng. Both masters were disciples of Sanfeng; they had investigated the koan of the bamboo stick until their state of doubt was fully aroused.
Although more than seventy days passed, neither attained realization. Later, he went to Sanfeng, who was observing the summer retreat at Mount Dengwu.
His confusion and distress increased all the more. One day, Master Dashi Zheng arrived from Mount Yu, and he went to seek his guidance.
Suddenly, upon hearing these words, his mind was cleared and he realized enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "The Elder Miaoxi stirs up waves where there is no wind;
How lamentable, Sanfeng—adding salt to the sauce! Leaping out of Yunmen’s 'clinging and avoiding' barrier, A bright moon hangs in the azure heavens at night.
Sanfeng then invited him into the room and asked: "You cannot say you have attained it, nor can you say you have not. Changqian clapped his hands in approval.
[The Master] gave a blow. Sanfeng said, "Speak quickly! Changqian shouted loudly, "Before the Yellow Crane Tower is Parrot Isle. Sanfeng said, "Not yet.
Changqian seized the bamboo staff with his hand, cast it to the ground, prostrated himself, and departed.
The next day, Sanfeng raised the phrase: "There is no intent within the sentence; the intent lies within the sentence. Changqian was at a loss. Sanfeng said, "Do you not understand?"

After some time, he happened to cite the words of an ancient worthy and suddenly awakened to the underlying meaning within them.

Only then did he clearly understand such phrases as "the cypress tree," "the chariot wheel crushing the drill," and "the daughter-in-law riding the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it. Sanfeng said, "I am glad that you, Layman, have understood one phrase.

He entered the samādhi of no-mind; naturally entering both the Buddha-realm and the Mara-realm, he attained mastery over birth and death. Changqian was filled with clarity and inspiration.
Later, at Baiyang, he again studied the dialogues of Deshan’s bowl-carrying and Linji’s fundamental essentials, through which he deeply realized their underlying meaning.

His firm citadel was like an iron mountain; though the blade and saw were before him, he had no spirit of fear.

It was solely because he had passed through the barrier of birth and death that, facing death, he again composed a verse, saying: "Face-to-face, beyond all deliberation, The Vajra King is revealed alone. If you ask where he dwells at ease,"
"The Mountain of Swords is the site of enlightenment. Subsequently, the Great Commander provided a pass for the funeral procession of Master Yuan’s coffin to return to the New City Gate.
The officials buried him beside Zhongxiao Bridge. Originally, Master Yuan’s mother, Lady Li, was wise, benevolent, and a devoted believer in the Buddha-dharma.

At the summit, the Buddha’s light illuminated his body. He said to Master Yuan, “The time for my departure to the West has arrived.
Not long after, he manifested a slight illness and passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name.

Huang Jiazi, whose given name was Yuti, was a native of Jiangyin in Changzhou. During the Chongzhen era, he was selected as a *zhusheng* (a scholar recommended for advanced study) to enroll in the Imperial Academy (*Taixue*).
