The official returned home and proposed that they both retire together to live in seclusion, forming a "White Society" as a plan for their final years.
Jiezi did not agree, saying, "If one does not undertake affairs of state, how can one repay the nation? If one does not sacrifice one's life, how can one become a true man?
When his teacher descended to Jiangdong, the local magistrate Chen Mingyu and others raised an army to defend the city. Jiezi and his disciple Xu Qu gathered the masses to carry out [the defense].

Tang Ying responded to him. When the city fell, he escaped; however, the matter was soon exposed and he was captured. Those in authority wished to mitigate his crime by treating it as that of a common thief.
Jiezi (Zhao Jie) would not consent, saying, "Yutiqi—how could he be a thief? As he was about to be executed, his disciple informed him of the appointed time.
He composed a verse of final parting, then took his formal robes to dress himself for burial, sat in the lotus position, and passed away. Zixi was also imprisoned.
In prison, Zhou, the wife of Xi, was due to be confiscated by the state. She hanged herself but did not die; she abstained from grain for several days on two occasions but did not die;
she threw herself into water but did not die; she swallowed gold twice but did not die; she cut her own throat but did not die. Finally, she hanged herself and died.
Xi’s elder sister, the nun Hanhui, said that Zhou had once stayed in the nunnery, where at night deep in the hour, she was walking in meditation beneath a crystal lamp.
Her gaze was noble and resolute, utterly devoid of any feminine affectation; she was truly a vessel of the Dharma.

After Xi had been imprisoned, Zhou recited the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī every day until her death, yet her spirit remained undisturbed. The Daoist Dan-gui remarked: "Wen Tianxiang swallowed mercury and did not die;
he starved himself to death and did not die; he finally died at the Chai Market—these were three deaths. Yet Zhou has now undergone eight deaths."
"Ah, how heroic! (From the *Ming Shi*, *Yu Xue Ji*, *Ming Wen Ou Chao*.
Huang Yunsheng, whose given name was Chunyao, was a native of Jiading, Suzhou. His father had no son until middle age; he recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* daily.

One night, he dreamed that the Great Being (Guanyin) appeared, holding a child in his arms, and said to him: 'Because I observed your diligent and arduous recitation of the sūtra, I have now found [this child] for you.'"
I shall grant you one fine scholar. Once born, he will possess the aggregates (skandhas) from birth; in his youth, he will serve as a student.

Wearing coarse robes and eating simple food, he will investigate the lost classics and exhort himself with integrity and principle. He will compose the *Zijian lu* (Record of Self-Examination), wherein he must record every action performed during the day and whether his thoughts were pure or impure.
A fellow student from the same county, Tang Changquan, possessed noble conduct and was able to invoke spirits through spirit-writing (jī).
The divine immortal Shenlü was moved and took possession of him. His speech traversed the realms of both immortals and Buddhas. Upon hearing this, Yunsheng felt faith and joy;
together with his younger brother Yuanyao and friends such as Chen Chu, Hou Yuanyan, Yuanjie, and Xia Yunjiao—some ten people in all—they went together to inquire about the Dharma.
As for Bodhisattva Huiyun Di, he was born during the reign of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty at the age of twenty, and having renounced [the world]...
He entered Jinguishan and studied the Way under a master. Through diligent and fierce investigation, he ultimately realized the fruit of the Way. At that time, he descended together with Lü Zhenren.
When someone asked about the distinctions within the Chan school, the Bodhisattva showed him, saying: "The Great Way is a single gate; it does not retain provisional consciousness.
Fundamentally, there is neither teaching nor sect; how could there be differentiation? Our Buddha appeared in the world out of compassion for sentient beings who cling to their minds."
It is not destroyed; it merely cuts its own root. Thus, provisional words used to stop a child’s crying are fundamentally not true, and their absence is likewise not real.
When both meanings are eliminated through refutation, the One becomes the target. The true source of the Buddha-dharma transcends both *Tao* and *De*.

Fools seek dreams, tracing tracks and imitating footprints; therefore, these are swept away below. As various provisional means emerge, they collectively sever the habitual mind and lead one back to...
Do not practice. Not practicing is excellent; practicing is a thief. Though both emerge from the same faculty of seeing and hearing, the sage and the madman differ.
One’s original nature is heavenly and good; all things must have their standard. To imitate the ancients and model oneself after the present is to lose one's own spirit.

If you do not urgently seek the mind, on what day will you deliver yourself? The flourishing teaching of our school is nothing other than the reforming of habits. When the true command is renewed daily, self-illumination is unified. Hold fast to this.
It is like that. How is it that when ordinary beings imitate the work of the Creator (*huagong*), ten thousand things do not equal one?

Yet when the Creator imitates things, they gather together without deliberation. Why is this so? It is because supreme sincerity is singular. When it is singular, Heaven is complete; though hidden and subtle, it cannot be fathomed.

If one seeks this excellent remedy, nothing compares to the elimination of consciousness (*vijñāna*). When consciousness is empty, the nature (*prakṛti*) manifests; when consciousness persists, the nature is obstructed. This is like a person in the dark: the space is naturally [there].
To slander the Sun is like seeking the stars; to go and feel for stones is to fail to see their true nature and instead merely discern their traces.
The numinous light of the ocean of nature becomes the six thieves; when the One Mind does not function, heaven and earth are all in error.

I do not open a school, nor do I establish a teaching; Śākyamuni and Bodhidharma are but the tracks of donkeys and horses. I have this One Mind, which the ten thousand ages have failed to recognize—not that it cannot be known, but...
It can be known, yet it has no form that can be grasped. The sound of a spring at the bottom of a ravine and the bright sun in the azure sky can be seen and heard;
who can see or grasp them? They possess color and sound, yet they have no fixed image or substance. The numinous light pervades everywhere, and this single principle never errs.

You who seek the mind must not, by all means, become mired in traces. The true exposition of the Buddha does not reside in written characters; let each thing return to the mind. Otherwise, it is the teaching of Māra.
This is also possible. If one is divided in mind, even what the Buddha taught is lost. To shatter these Buddhas and Māras, let every thought be free from delusion.
After ten years, the disciples compiled the successive instructions into a single book titled *Zhèngjiào Lù* (Record of Orthodox Teachings).

Shu said: "Not so. Though I desire to remain without words, there still remains the record of the *Lunyu* (Analects); though I have never spoken a single character, the texts of the Great Canon now circulate. Therefore, the ancients..."

How much more so when the True Spirit is near, sparing one the toil of carrying a satchel; when the sacred teachings are present, one possesses the joy of striking the bell.

One who is as ignorant as a fool can gain silent understanding, and one who knows two things can likewise receive the current of the tradition. As for the sun hanging like a candle, how could those with eyes not see it clearly? At this time—
When rain falls upon the withered, how could those who pray for a bountiful year fail to receive its grace? If the human heart does not die, then this Way ought to be made clear.
If one has not yet drawn from the true source, yet instead ridicules heterodox teachings, it is because they hear the Way and laugh—a common failing of base scholars.
Such people possess the view of one sitting in a well; I, however, regard them as my fellow beings. Yunsheng approved of these words and followed them.
After Yunsheng heard the Dharma, he investigated the matter of the Ultimate in silence and redoubled his self-discipline. From time to time, he would expound the Buddha-dharma to his colleagues.

His friend Zhang Zihao had recently taken the precept against killing and said to Yunsheng, "Would it be acceptable for you to temporarily manifest the form of an elderly layman (*upāsaka*) and preach the Dharma?
Yunsheng joyfully composed a poem in the style of Su Shi’s "Qi-ting Poems" to show him.

He then reread the *Record of Pointing at the Moon* (*Zhizhuyulu*), and his understanding became clear and resolved. After another month, all the prisoners were spared from an epidemic and released from prison. Both...

The people were involved in this matter. Like a farmer, [Yanru] was eventually able to see his mother for several days. When the Emperor heard that the two men had been released from prison, he grew angry and sent them back to their cells.
Shortly thereafter, Yanru was convicted of a crime and granted a death sentence; although many officials of the Censorate sought to save Yushan, the Emperor would not listen.
The Ministry of Punishment nevertheless proposed that he be sentenced to redemption for his term of exile, but this was again refused. This was the sixteenth year of the Chongzhen era.

The following year, he was dispatched to garrison duty at Hangzhou. He arrived at his post in the third month, at which time the rebel bandits subsequently fell upon and captured the capital in that same month.
Yan’er once asked Yushan about the Dharma in a letter, saying: "Lately, I have been investigating and contemplating within the state where both mind and environment are empty."

One may roughly understand the direction [of practice]. However, one merely attains the Confucian "stopping at what is known" (*zhizhi*); as for stillness, concentration, and settled reflection, one fails to reach the point where it is impossible to scratch oneself without feeling the itch or pain.
Consequently, various masters vehemently disparage the excellence of stillness, comparing it to saying, "If the sun and moon were not still, how could they be bright?
An ancient worthy said: "It is just like a wooden man seeing flowers and birds. Once one reaches the state of the wooden man...
"Is this not the state of quiescent excellence? Why then does Yushan reply, 'I have received your instruction that you roughly understand the direction toward emptiness'?
What is this 'emptiness' that can accommodate a person's treading and a person's turning? If there is something toward which one can tread and turn, can it still be called 'emptiness'?

It is simply because you have never exerted yourself in investigating the *huatou* (critical phrase); thus, while the dust of worldly toil has temporarily ceased, you occasionally perceive [something] as existing."
Emptiness may be grasped; stillness may be sought; tranquility may be enjoyed. It is like obtaining a single pool of clear, still water;
one only fears that someone might disturb it, causing silt and impurities to rise again. Thus, Gaozi’s “immovability of mind” already contains error.
To find a place of realization through the words of the ancients merely confuses and deludes people. Therefore it is said: "If you do not succeed in words, do not seek it in the mind. Not...
One knows that as soon as there is even a slight failure to grasp the mind, it is already not still, not concentrated, and not at peace;

thus, there arises the affliction of failing to contemplate when one ought to contemplate, and succeeding in contemplating when one ought not to. Furthermore, how can one forcefully assume mastery by claiming, "I have already attained stillness and victory"?
This is like the sun, the moon, or a wooden man—they have never known what "stillness and victory" are, and therefore they do not engage with them.
Yet they shine forth; flowers and birds are not startled. As soon as one realizes there is "stillness and excellence" (*jing-sheng*), one has already ceased to be still and excellent.
The wooden man has traveled ten thousand miles from the sun and moon. For stillness and movement are opposites, and extinction and birth are opposites.
When first turning toward the Way, one perceives that past restlessness is loathsome; naturally, one considers stillness and extinction to be the superior realm for us. If one possesses clear eyes—
To the ordinary person, gold filings and tile shards appear no different from one another. You must know that there is yet a matter beyond this.
What is this matter beyond? To call it by name is to encounter it; not to call it by name is to turn one's back on it. Ultimately, what should it be called?

Turning one’s body within the vajra-circle, closing off the throat and exhaling the breath, eating in the morning and lodging in the evening like a bird flying through the sky—regarding the questions in your letter:
when this old monk approaches death, I know in advance that the time has come; this is because it arises from within the *huatou*.
This is attained from within the excellence of stillness; you must simply question this monk to find it, for it is not something that can be known by the ignorant.

What is prized in the study of the Way is the thorough understanding of birth and death; therefore, one should disregard danger and ruin, and take a step forward toward that place where there is no handle to grasp.
If you merely seek what is smooth and easy to cling to, you will settle upon the notion that there is a realm of clear emptiness existing as an object.
It lies neither within the mind nor between the eyes; this is considered being close to the Way.

Even if one were to sit within the Buddha’s belly for ten thousand kalpas, it would still be but stagnant water—clear when left undisturbed, but turbid when stirred. Wang of Tang was a *gongke geshi* (Imperial Secretariat Drafter) who rose from Fish Mountain in Min;
he served successively as a Grand Secretary (*dongge daxueshi*) before requesting retirement due to illness and resided in Ting.
In the province, when the city fell, he became a monk, changing his name to Jeongji (正志) and taking the sobriquet Beoam (蘗菴).
He received the Dharma from Master Gyeonggi (繼起) of Inyeon-sa. He lived in seclusion at Chwiryeon-sa on Lotus Peak and spent his later years at Yusan.

Furthermore, Yu Nong also went to guard the frontier in Xuanzhou at the same time as Uisan; later, he shaved his head at Huangshan and resided in Suzhou until his death. At that time, there was also...

Zhang Dayuan, whose courtesy name was Youyu, was a native of Jiangyin. He passed the jinshi examination in the second year of the Tianqi era and served in various offices until his appointment as Minister of Revenue (Hubu Shangshu).
When Nanjing fell, he fled to Mount Wukang and took refuge with Chan masters Jiqi and Shoji, where he engaged in intensive investigation day and night.
His innate wisdom suddenly blossomed. Subsequently, when Jiqi became the abbot of Lingyan Monastery, Dayuan followed him there and devoted himself to spiritual cultivation with total sincerity.
Upon receiving this instruction, his doubts were completely resolved like ice melting away. At the age of seventy, he extensively expounded the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
At eighty, he composed a layered commentary on the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety). He resided at Lingyan for twenty-five years, during which time his disciples urged him to return home.

In the ninth month of the forty-fifth year of the Kangxi era, they went to welcome him; as he was departing, he bid them farewell. Upon arriving, he joined his palms and said, "The time for my disciple has come; I shall depart tomorrow morning."
The next day, he spoke again, saying: "Now, let both the Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas be cast aside together.
I only wish that you will not be parted from me in every lifetime. Having finished speaking, he passed away (*Ming Shi*, *Yushan Shengao*, *Bianan Bielu*).
Zhiguizi said: Huang Zongxi remarked that among the scholar-officials of the late Ming dynasty who studied the Way, many entered the Chan school;
such were Mr. Jin, as well as Cai Mude, Ma Shiqi, and Qian Qizhong. Yet all of them were renowned throughout the world for their loyalty and righteousness.
The Chan school takes "neither good nor evil" as its fundamental tenet; for men such as these, [to follow it] would be to stain their hearts with blood.

It has not yet been transformed; this is what the Confucians call "sincerity that cannot be concealed. In the Gate of the Patriarchs (the Buddhist tradition), this is not called "knowing one's nature.
How stubborn An Xi is! Do the Confucians and Buddhists have two different natures? Mencius said: "When those in the world speak of human nature, they simply rely on its 'constants.
These constants take 'beneficial spontaneity' as their foundation. To be sincere and spontaneous is loyalty and righteousness, such as that of Yu.
When one acts according to the Way, how could blood and heart have any part in it? Dàhuì also said that the bodhicitta is precisely the mind of loyalty and righteousness.

I have read the writings of the two masters Jīn and Xióng; their innate sincerity was so powerfully aroused within the bonds of sovereign and subject, and teacher and friend, that it was like water becoming cold or fire becoming hot. Truly, they were heroic among great men and preeminent figures within the Dharma gate.

Ah! However, the world’s assessments of Yushan (Mount Fish) differ considerably. I have examined his deeds in detail and recorded them here in this chapter, awaiting those who discuss history to consult them.
Wang Dashen said: "In my youth, before I had heard the Way, I was most devoted to men of loyalty and righteousness, regarding loyalty as..."

A man of righteousness is himself a sage and a worthy; he is himself a living Buddha and a living Bodhisattva. Beyond this, what other sages or worthies could there be? What other Buddhas or Bodhisattvas could there be?

Later, through repeated investigation and examination, I finally came to understand that among those who possess loyalty and righteousness, it is truly rare to find one who can bring matters to a successful conclusion.
As for the study of the sages and worthies: when it is time to live, one lives; when it is time to die, one dies.
Death follows the natural order of Heaven; this very fact is loyalty and righteousness, and this very fact is the Way.
There is no Way other than loyalty and righteousness. Yet, within loyalty and righteousness, not even the slightest admixture of anything else is permissible.
As soon as one mixes even a small amount [of worldly concerns] in, it is no longer in accord with the Way of Heaven; thus, regarding the Dao, there is still something left unfulfilled.
What constitutes loyalty and righteousness in the study of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? It is said: "It is original emptiness. What is meant by "original emptiness"?
It is said that loyalty and righteousness are correct; their very substance is simply one reality.
This itself is loyalty and righteousness; this itself is the Way. Furthermore, there is no other Way apart from loyalty and righteousness.
However, even the slightest defilement cannot be applied to loyalty and righteousness; were it defiled by even the slightest bit, it would no longer be reality.
Regarding the Way, there is still that which remains unexhausted. As for myself, though I have heard the teachings of the Way and have advanced toward them, I lack the necessary courage;

this is simply because my heart of loyalty and righteousness is faint. That this heart of loyalty and righteousness is faint is merely because it has been muddied by thoughts of seeking fame and beauty.
I vow to face these directly and cut off the paths of Daoism and Buddhism, leaving not even a single character or word of them behind.
Cut off the "feet" below—meaning both name and form—and do not leave behind a single character or syllable.
Solely uphold the two characters "Loyalty and Righteousness" as a vajra-treasure mallet. Whether a Buddha comes or a Mara comes, strike them once!
What room is there for Linji or Deshan? What room is there for Dahui or Gaofeng?
Biographies of Lay Practitioners, Volume 53:
The Biographies of Wen Yuefeng (Cui Yingkui), Jiang Huchun, and Li Sheng.
Wen Yuefeng’s name has been lost, and his place of residence is also unknown; he lived in seclusion at Fushan in Yihuang County, Jiangxi.
Sunfeng did not marry nor did he shave his beard or hair. He wore a simple headcloth and rustic clothes, living in a state of serene detachment.

In his daily life, he delighted in "escaping into Chan" (Buddhist meditation). In his leisure time, he was diligent in planting and cultivation. Whenever his provisions for food and clothing were slightly in surplus, he would immediately share them with others.
One day, while walking through the garden, he encountered a thief who suddenly fled. Later, while passing by another place, he saw a laborer working with great exertion.
Ku asked him, "Do you have no family? He replied that he did not. Ku then took him back with him. When Ku tested him with various tasks, the man always accomplished them.
Yuefeng was pleased and entrusted all his affairs to him. Fusun listened to this. Later, the hired laborer became somewhat arrogant and overbearing; he even attempted to seize control of Fusun.
Yuefeng perceived this and apologized with kind words, saying, "Fusun has his own duties; I have no business with him. He then took a measure of rice, a sickle, a hoe, and a tile.
He took a set of cauldrons for each and departed. About five *li* from the peak, he crossed a steep and rugged pass and dwelt in a cave, shielding himself with hanging pine needles.
He went out to cultivate his garden as before. There were many tigers in the mountains; Yuelong (Moon Peak) kept pigs as livestock, perhaps as a means of defense.
[When someone] smiled and said, "Is this body truly yours? while he was tending his garden, a tiger approached and glared at him.
Yuefeng bowed and said, "Do you wish for this? I shall feed you now. He immediately untied his robes and approached the tiger. The tiger lay prostrate and did not move.
Yuefeng spoke again, saying, "Do you think of me as being without a companion? Nod your head three times for me; I will be your friend."
The tiger nodded its head three times. From then on, Yuefeng always accompanied the tiger whenever he went out or came in.
When he slept, he would spread straw mats upon the ground and lie upon them. Occasionally, when someone looked inside, a python was found coiled there; yet it caused him no harm.

He passed away at the beginning of the Chongzhen era, at over eighty years of age. He had once composed a book on the study of human nature that was quite comprehensive, but after his death, the work did not survive.

(*Xueta bian*). Cui Yingkui was a native of Yongping, Beijing. In his youth, he practiced medicine; whenever anyone requested his services for an illness, he would treat them exhaustively regardless of the payment.
In his later years, he studied the Buddha-dharma and traveled up and down Mount Pan for eighteen years, where he attended upon various elder masters.

[The Master] Xing. In the autumn of the twenty-seventh year of the Kangxi era, he manifested a slight illness. He informed all those with whom he regularly associated, setting a date for his final parting.
When the time arrived, the assembly gathered; they sat in a circle and conversed and laughed as they did on ordinary days.

After a long while, he said: "All things are impermanent; a hundred years are finite. Follow my instructions, and you will certainly not be led astray. He requested a brush and wrote a verse, then passed away. His...
The verse says: Coming and going, stark naked, not a single thread or hair hangs upon them. Originally there is not a single thing;
moving freely in all directions, they wander at ease. (Panshan Zhi)
Jiang Huchen, whose given name was Chao, was a native of Jintan. He passed the jinshi examination in the fourth year of the Shunzhi era and served as a Court Editor (xiu-zhuan) at the Hanlin Academy.
He was renowned for his literary talent and was by nature broad-minded and generous, often repaying enmity with virtue. He later served as the Commissioner of Education for the Tianjin region.
He maintained a life of purity and prudence. He frequently raised loans to relieve impoverished scholars and submitted a memorial requesting the restoration of classical studies.

He petitioned the authorities throughout the empire to prohibit the penalization of students. The scholarly community praised him for this. When Hu Chen was young, he repeatedly dreamed that he was a bhikṣu.
At the age of fifteen, two men of the Way sat at his gate and said, "Hu Chen has a teacher on Mount Emei; be careful not to forget him."
"Due to past causes, we shall meet again in the future. He habitually abstained from pungent meats and delighted in friendships with those outside the conventional world.
While residing in the capital, he attended upon Master Dabo. One day, while entering the imperial court, he heard the sound of the ceremonial proclamation and attained a sudden realization.

He went to present his understanding to Dabo, who interrogated him repeatedly before finally granting his approval. When his term as a provincial education commissioner ended, he informed Dabo of his intention to return home.
Passing through Baiquan, he paid his respects to Sun Zhongyuan. After conversing for several days, he departed for Mount Kuanglu, traveled to Lukuanmen, and proceeded directly to Mount Emei.
He resided at Fuhu Temple for some time, during which the local authorities requested that he compile the *Emei Gazetteer*. Consequently, he traveled once to Chengdu.
Shortly thereafter, he fell ill. He left a letter of parting for those in authority, bathed, sat upright, and passed away while reciting a poem.
On the following day, a man named Hu encountered him on a mountain peak; he called out repeatedly, "Master Jiang! but received no response.
Upon entering the temple, he learned that Hu Chen had already died, whereupon he was greatly astonished (*Panshan Zhi*; *Shi Yushan Ji*).
Li was a man from Jiangxi; his name is unknown. He traveled between the Yangtze and Han rivers for thirty years, always appearing to be about fifty years old.
He carried a single ladle with him and wandered through the marketplaces, begging for beef and pork fat, which he ate. Any leftovers he stored inside tattered clothes;
even during the height of summer, their color and flavor did not change. Whenever he encountered paper or a brush, he would write, never exhausting his supply.
He was easy to understand. Sometimes he would intersperse one or two characters from talismanic scripts; when people spoke to him, he did not answer.

There was a provincial vice-president who found this man extraordinary and invited him to his official residence. After staying for several days, the man took his leave. The vice-president gave him a garment of ramie cloth and patterned leather shoes, and the man adorned his head with flowers.
He strolled leisurely through the marketplace, where the children vied with one another to seize them; he would simply hold his head fast and refuse to give them up. Thus it was.
His hemp garments were worn to tatters, yet he remained composed amidst the wind and snow. During the Kangxi era, Mao Jike of Suian traveled to Hanchang and encountered the Master at an inn.
The Master wrote several poems on the handles of fans for him; all were worthy of being read. Jike recorded and circulated them. The poems say:
"The clouds have their deep mountains, the cranes have their forests; Without leaving their proper places, they realize Zen."
Mind. Last night the moon shone upon the long corridor; a single phrase of Amitābha is a sound beyond kalpas. It is also said:
When light and darkness are both cast aside, the True Eye opens; a single branch emerges, and there is a Tathāgata. When ordinary beings reach this point, they all become sages;
clapping hands as we meet, we turn back with a smile. It is also said: Wander at will through a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks; layer upon layer, they are inexhaustible and yet layered again.

How weighty! How about reclining in high repose within one’s native mountains? Before one are secluded bamboos, behind one are pines. It is also said: "The colors of the mountains and the clarity of the stream illuminate the Patriarch’s intent;
the birds’ cries and flowers’ laughter awaken the karmic conditions. Sometimes I sit alone upon the terrace; at midnight, there are no clouds, and the moon fills the sky.
It is also said: "To speak of 'the Way' or 'no Way' is all idle talk; to call this 'purity' or 'meditation' is entirely a forced construct."
[This is] merely a name. One has darkened their original nature and gnaws on dry bones; submerged in the sea of suffering, they do not know spring. It is also said:
"The Way-practice is solitary and lofty, transforming those with whom there is affinity; subduing dragons and taming tigers, one remains naturally at ease.

Now, having joyfully attained true samādhi, the moon sets and the wind turns by the green trees. It is also said: "Zhaozhou’s cassock weighs seven pounds; the place of loss is clear, and the place of attainment..."

"Truly! Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all covered over. Who is the one who severs [delusions] when the opportunity arises? He further said: "A thousand cliffs are damp with rain, the pines grow old;
a single flavor of autumn sounds, the chrysanthemums turn fresh. Do not say there are no *jiǎzǐ* years in the mountains; each bead of the prayer rosary marks the passing seasons.
At that time, there was also one named Sheng from Dongting, who begged for alms among the mountains of Dongting. His appearance was as follows:

The madman would sleep at night beneath the eaves of the temple. When the monks drove him away, he would return again. He once inscribed a poem on the wall, saying: "I do not believe the universe is vast;
I transcend it, peerless among all in the world. I swallow the waters of the Three Gorges with my mouth; I tread upon the clouds of the myriad regions with my feet.
He also said: "All that has form is merely false; what is truly real is the formless. Having realized the ground of non-arising, the plum—"
Flowers filled the four neighboring directions. Furthermore, his poem on New Year’s Eve reads: "Lamps and fires blaze in celebration of this night;
Deep in the night, children do not call for one another. Upon my worn meditation cushion at the third watch, Who cares that tomorrow is the dawn of a new year?
Wang Wan of Changzhou recorded and transmitted this. As for the two students, their final whereabouts were unknown thereafter (*Anxutang Ji*; *Chibei Outan*).
Zhiguizi said: "Observing the conduct and practice of the various gentlemen such as Wen and Li, they resemble those of old described as 'profound and reclusive.
Tasting their words, they are perhaps the equals of Hanshan and Shide. Their inclination is far removed from that of Master Jiang. Are they not officials?"
"O Bhikṣu, how could I possibly fathom this?
[This concludes] the Biographies of Lay Practitioners, Volume 54:
The Biographies of Yan Zhongguo, Song Wensen, and Bi Zilan."
Yan Zhongduo’s Dharma name was Dacan; he styled himself the "Dueli Dao Ren" (The Carriage-Treadling Wayfarer). A native of Jiaxing, he received the Dharma transmission from Master Feiyin of Tiantong.
His own account states: "The Wayfarer constantly delights in sailing with the wind and roaming freely according to conditions.
Once, while traveling to Shuangjing, I encountered the Great Master Wengu, who bestowed upon me the 'one stroke' that points directly upward. I investigated it with great diligence."
For three years, he made no progress whatsoever. While reading the "Curtain" kōan from the *Fayan Wujie Lu*, his body, mind, and the entire world suddenly fell away completely;
the pivotal lock of the patriarchs was overturned to its very depths.
He subsequently visited Master Wengu, Master Hanshan, and Monk Tianyin, all of whom granted him their approval. He then went to see the Elder Miyun, who raised his staff.
He immediately assumed a posture of falling over. The old man planted his staff and rose to sit upright. The old man laid his staff across [his shoulder], withdrew his body, and ran off.
The old man pursued him, turned around, and said to him: "Alas, old monk! You have come again to wash a clod of earth in the mud.
Thereupon, the old man desisted. He lived in seclusion for twenty-eight years. The Venerable Master Feiyin Rong was the primary successor of this old man.
At a Dharma assembly, a monk went to ask him, saying, "The ancients said, 'Advance further from the top of a hundred-foot pole.
I do not ask about the hundred-foot pole itself; what is the place of advancement? Yunrong immediately struck him, saying, "Turn yourself around right here.
The monk said, "This is still just the hundred-foot pole; it is not yet advancement. Yunrong struck him again, saying, "You fellow who does not know when to advance or retreat!"
The practitioner said, "A wildcat originally has short legs. Yunrong said, "This beast! The practitioner made the gesture of a tiger-leap.
Yunrong said, "Do not feign such things. The practitioner made the gesture of seizing a monk and roared as he went out.
Yunrong immediately ascended the hall and said, "Today, everyone, do not scatter sand. Try to listen as this mountain monk describes it with a single finger. In Jiahe, there is an old..."
Little mouse! You have stolen a grain of millet from the heavens. You are accustomed to flaunting your claws and fangs in all directions, stirring up a fragrant breeze that sweeps everywhere.
Only this mountain monk is not lenient; with a white staff he strikes you out straight through the sky. But as for the turning-around phrase—how would you say it?
The practitioner covers his ears and exits behind the hall. [The Master] hands over the *ruyi* (willow-sprout) staff and says: "I entrust it to you."
You are expressing your faith. The practitioner raised his hand and received him, saying, "The person who has 'passed away' (mòshǒu) can receive [me].
Zhìróng said, "I have received you. The practitioner spread out both hands. Zhìróng said, "It is being passed on. Zhìróng then bowed and departed. He once painted his own portrait.
Fèiyǐn composed a eulogy for it, which says: "The straw hat does not shield the eyes; the hoe does not touch the ground. How could this compare to—"
A man of the mountains: his mind is utterly free of entanglements. His skirt is tied low at the waist; his arms hang bare and cold. He wishes to go, yet does not go; before him there is no gate.
He has bored a single hole through the void, permitting all people upon this great earth to defecate and urinate therein.
This is the very thing that crushes one’s ordinary enjoyments. Ha ha! A great laugh—seizing up the hoe, he must let it go.
[Feiyin] took off his straw sandals. "Why don't you take them off and sell them? "Du du du! Bright moon and clear wind—attaining mastery!
Zhongke bowed in thanks. Feiyin paid no heed and gave him a kick. Feiyin said, "He looks like a mad dog. Zhongke said, "I have already bitten him once!
His friend Zhou Zhimiao was critically ill. Zhongke went to visit him, and as they spoke of it...
Regarding household affairs, Zhongkuo said, "The point at which you gained mastery in your lifelong study of the Way lies precisely here:
one must not allow distracting thoughts. Zhimiao immediately raised his fist and asked, "What is this? Zhongkuo replied, "That too is just idle talk.
Zhimiao nodded and said, "I wish to be as close as flesh and bone to you, my brother, in every lifetime within the Way. Zhongkuo said, "Go straight ahead."
Knowing the subtle signs, he passed away while sitting upon his chair (the karmic conditions for his passing).
Wen Sen of the Song dynasty was named Shelong; he was a native of Changzhou. His father, Xuecheng, dreamed that Mañjuśrī was holding a child and handing him over to him, and thus [Wen] was born.
Consequently, he was initially named Wen. At the age of four, when he listened to his father recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he was immediately able to recite four lines.
Verse: Having long served as a restorative for all living beings, he reached over fifty years of age. Encountering many domestic misfortunes, he became oppressed by illness.

By chance, upon encountering the passage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding "liberation without attachment or bondage," he attained a profound realization. He subsequently observed a perpetual fast and renounced desire, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily.

After more than a month, his illness subsided. On the evening of the Mid-Autumn Festival, he noticed that the light from a lantern at the corner of the hall was not penetrating through. Unconsciously—
Filled with emotion, he sat in silence. After investigating for a long time, suddenly his sweat broke out over his entire body and his chest became vast and clear.
He composed a verse, saying: "Host and guest, host and guest—no host and no guest. Pointing it out clearly only muddles the ford. By chance the wind strikes the lamp’s flame;
Suddenly one meets the original master of the house. He spoke again: "Today I finally know that I have lost myself. Ordinary sentiment and sainthood..."
All at once, they were withered away. When friends asked me, "What is it? there was not a single word of "this" or "that.

Shortly thereafter, I heard that the Zen style of Master Tianli Zhen was flourishing greatly, and I wished to go there to seek his guidance and resolve my doubts. It happened that the Master was passing through Suyang at Dayun Hermitage, so Wen Sen went to visit him.
Upon seeing him, [Wen Sen] immediately said, "The fragrance of camphor-mint has been renowned throughout the world. The Master replied:
"Do you want a dried piece of excrement? he asked, and as Wen Sen questioned him, "What is a dried piece of excrement? the Master replied, "Spring breeze on all eight sides.
Wen Sen asked, "Why have you come here? The Master said, "I seek neither Buddha nor Dharma; I wish to find a definitive resolution.

The Master spoke with a stern voice, saying, "Ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes will not bring resolution! At these words, Wen Sen attained realization. The Master [said]: [Note: The final sentence "The Master" appears to be a fragment or a concluding marker for the narrative.]
He subsequently went to Nanjian in Hangzhou. Wenshen went there again to pay his respects. The Master asked, "Where did you previously obtain this news?
Wenshen replied, "Previously, while studying the chapter on Mengzi eating coarse grain and wearing grass, I once gave it a thorough turning over.
The Master asked, "How so? Wenshen said, "Pang Gong said: 'But if one is personally without mind toward the myriad things, what...'"
"Obstructing the myriad things, it constantly surrounds them. Before he had finished speaking, the Master struck the armrest and said, "What a pity that one Pang Gong has been split into two pieces!
Wenshen suddenly attained realization at that moment. The following year, he went again to Nanjian to visit the Master.
While he was in the hall, someone asked about the appearance prior to birth. Wenshen replied, "The Spiral Topknot Peak. Shortly thereafter, he entered for an audience with the Master.
The Master said, "What a fine Spiral Top Peak! I only fear that it is not yet willing to nod its head.
He then cited the story of the Sixth Patriarch regarding the Bodhi tree and asked, "How would you say it, Reverend? The Master replied, "Overturn the Bodhi tree; smash the bright mirror stand;
let skulls be ground to dust, so that everywhere is free from dust and grime. Wenshen said, "This too does not go beyond reaching this point."

The Master shook out his robes and rose. Patting Wenshen on the shoulder, he said, "Now you must take the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, Shenxiu, myself, and you, layman, and tie us all together into a single bundle. Cast us into the Qiantang River!

At that moment, Wenshen suddenly awakened to the essential meaning behind Linji’s three blows of the staff. He then composed a verse on the spot, saying: "The face before birth is beyond all seeking."

The high Śaṅkhacakrā Peak knows how to nod its head; with a single phrase, one suddenly transcends the three blows of the staff. Ordinary sentiments and saintly understandings flow eastward away. He resided there for three years.
When the Master passed through Suzhou, he moored his boat at Panmen and called for Wen Sen, saying to him:

Zhou Anshi, styled Mengyan and also known as Sirin, was a student of the classics from Kunshan. He was extensively versed in the scriptures and the Tripitaka, and possessed profound [understanding].
Believing in cause and effect, he constantly reflected: "Sentient beings are deluded and commit immeasurable sins; the two karmas of lust and killing truly account for the greater half.

Thereupon, exhausting his sincere heart and deeply contemplating the meaning of the scriptures, he pierced the subtle and penetrated the obscure, uprooting the mountains and smashing the dens [of evil]. Sharp blades were brandished toward the swine. At that time, the swine, knowing they could not escape, let out great cries of lamentation, but no rescue arrived.

Such are the evil causes and such are the evil fruits. When tracing their origins, they are all brought about by our own mouths and bellies.

The Biography of the Layman Zhiguizi (The Transmission of the Layman Zhiguizi).
As for Zhiguizi (The One Who Knows His Return), his name and surname were not passed down. Throughout his life, he was aloof and self-satisfied; no one recognized him.

He once traveled with Kongkongzi (The Empty-Empty One), who marveled at him. Zhiguizi had been a Confucian since birth; both his father and elder brother held office in the court through their literary talents.
Before he had even reached the age of twenty, Zhiguizi had already attained the imperial examinations by means of Confucian discourse. Furthermore—
He devoted himself day and night without rest to studying the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the ancient classics as well as secular literature.

He often admired the upright and outspoken men of antiquity, such as Jia Yi of Luoyang, and desired to examine the causes of success and failure, present treatises on governance and security, and establish a brilliant reputation for his achievements in the world. After a long time, he reflected upon himself and said: "This is not my [true path]."
This was his endeavor. Thereupon, he focused his mind in quiet contemplation, turned inward to cultivate virtue, and did not practice anything that was contrary to propriety.

After a long time, he again examined himself and said, "I have not yet clarified my mind; what shall I do? He went to ask the Master Kongkong, but the Master Kongkong remained silent and spoke no word.
Someone informed him of the methods of cultivation from the Daoist school. He practiced them for three years without success. Subsequently, he read...
His mind was opened by the Buddhist scriptures, and he concluded that the ultimate destination of the Way lay therein.

Having heard that in the West there is the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, who emits great radiance to welcome and lead sentient beings of the five turbidities to be reborn in the Pure Land, his heart was filled with longing for this.

"Green grass before the courtyard, A pleasant breeze beneath the trees; I delight in this Great Peace, Neither winter nor summer. Shortly thereafter, he finally renounced the eating of meat.

He severed his carnal desires and composed a verse, saying: "My body is your body; your flesh is my flesh. You were born as a man of great virtue; I shall raise you together. He further composed a verse:
"From delusion arises craving, leading to ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births. To suddenly hew it apart with a blow—then heaven and earth are pure and tranquil.
Not long after, he vanished, leaving behind a final verse: "Coming, there is no place from which one comes; departing, there is no place to which one goes. Ultimate Bliss."

"It is not far; it is right here when one is mindful. Kongkongzi said, "Some say that Zhin gui zi goes back and forth among the cities and occasionally encounters people there, yet I have sought him and never seen him."

He invited me to close my retreat at the Changzhou Hall on the street of Yanshou Temple. There, with one copy of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Yuanjue jing) and one scroll of the *Zhuangzi*, we would sometimes sit in meditation in profound silence, and sometimes discuss emptiness with frank eloquence.
Upon leaving the retreat, I traveled to the provincial government to visit my elder brother in Wenshang County.

I have long been poor and lowly, yet I have polished my integrity; when I received this letter, I marveled at it, deeming it extraordinary, like hearing the cry of a phoenix at sunrise.
The birds warble harmoniously in the high catalpa trees. At that time, my heart felt at every moment as if it possessed one who had found his home.

At that time, I desired to thoroughly investigate the origins and foundations of Confucianism, Buddhism, and the teachings of Huang-Lao. I longed for a companion, wishing to exert myself yet unable to do so.

He fanned kindness toward others with a compassionate and pure countenance, though his physical appearance was emaciated. He shunned power and influence, and was wary of the weak and the stubborn. Thus he accumulated his reflections without ceasing; his resolve was vast and expansive, like the King of Garuḍas parting the ocean waters to swallow the dragons.

A single bottle of incense, a single burner, a single meditation cushion, and a single alms bowl; chanting the Buddha’s name tens of thousands of times, or reading one or two scrolls of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—is this not joyful?
Is this not joyful? As the waters of the pond overflow and the days and months pass by, how can you fail to reflect upon this?
In the year Tongtan (41st year of Qianlong), under the cyclical designation Rouzhao, on an auspicious day in the first month, I composed this postscript to the *Biographies of Laymen*,
comparing the paths of Confucianism and Buddhism. Though their outward manifestations appear as diametrically opposed as the east and west, when one follows them back to their source, they are one.
Enough! You, Zhiguizi, have studied between Confucianism and Buddhism; from the beginning you never forced them to be the same, yet ultimately you saw no difference between them.
Is this not what is meant by "knowing the root"? Having already attained self-benefit, you now wish to benefit others.
From the past several thousand years down to the present, I have gathered the words of all those eminent men and great scholars who were in accord with this Way.

I have compiled these accounts according to historical methods into a single work titled *The Biographies of Lay Practitioners* (*Jushi Zhuan*). I have extracted the essentials of the events and traced the origins of the narratives;

it is truly a Dharma-gate comparable to those of Ban Gu and Sima Qian. Having lost my formal education at a young age, I was addicted to the five desires and followed the current of worldly life until I forgot my way back.

At the age of thirty, while traveling for official service in the capital, I happened to encounter the *Fahui* (Collection of Dharma) of Yunqi on the market. My heart was suddenly moved; I took it home and completed its study, only then gaining true faith and understanding.
After returning to my rural estate, I lived as a guest in Wumen, where I became well-acquainted with the reputation of Master Gui at the Xiaofeng Hermitage.

Having finished reading it, I rose and sighed, saying: "Among those who study as Confucians and Buddhists, few are lost and ignorant of the fundamental source."
Factions favor their own while attacking those who differ; like weeping at a forked path with no way home, they remain lost. The Master Zhiguang arose to save them.
The composition of this work was intended for students to eliminate views of difference and identity, to return to the fundamental source, and apply themselves there.
